## What the New Spider-Man and The Odyssey Have in Common

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/chelovek-pauk-i-odisseya/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-08-21 (21 August 2026)
Tags: blockbuster, notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/chelovek-pauk-i-odisseya/

What do [the new *Spider-Man*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/chelovek-pauk-novyy-den-2026/) and [*The Odyssey*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/odisseya-2026/) have in common?

It’s striking how these two summer blockbusters actually echo each other. In ***The Odyssey*** the hero has forgotten himself and, roughly speaking, where he was going. In ***Spider-Man*** it’s the other way round: everyone around the hero has forgotten him, and because of that he no longer knows where to turn. By and large, these are two dimensions of one and the same phenomenon; the only difference is whether the personal crisis we see on screen is expressed outwardly or inwardly.

And Tom Holland (not only he, as you can see from the meme, but that’s beside the point right now) has got to stand, through his characters, both on the outside of the protagonist’s suffering (Odysseus’s son Telemachus, who is trying to cope with the world somehow while his father remembers where he belongs) and on the inside (Peter Parker himself). The actor really did land two roles from the “choose your type of existential crisis” series — and both, happily, come across as convincing and rounded, as portrayals by a contemporary, for contemporaries.

So it turns out that the biggest blockbusters of 2026 centre on heroes who are not so much fighting evil as trying to redefine themselves, recover a sense of belonging and work out where to go next.
*The existential crisis has officially become a plot for mainstream cinema — apparently because it has stopped being something purely personal*.

---

## Minions & Monsters: Unexpectedly Cinephile Entertainment

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/minony-i-monstry-2026/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-08-19 (19 August 2026)
Work: “Minions & Monsters” is a 2026 film directed by Pierre Coffin.
Tags: animation
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/minony-i-monstry-2026/

[*Minions & Monsters*](https://youtu.be/V-O-uBaHk3c?si=_26y1Bj5o3K1WPww) has unexpectedly turned out to be very cinephile entertainment.

The first thing to know: the trailer for this feature about evil’s yellow henchmen sets you up for a completely different plot from the one you are actually going to see. Going by the trailer, I wasn’t expecting much, and what I got was a genuine multi-genre production drama about the Minions making a film.

I don’t see much point in writing about the plot: this is one of those cases where you just need to catch the Minions’ vibe, take a spin on this ride and spot all the film references to Charlie Chaplin, Buster Keaton and anything else you associate with 1920s Hollywood. And a bit of the Minions’ own backstory, from the dawn of time, is great fun to learn too: it’s the very enjoyable buddy-movie part of the whole film :)

All that’s left is to work out what the hares from *Restlessness* (the Russian animated film) are doing in a film about the Minions.

---

## Olivia Wilde’s The Invite: Go In Without Expectations, and Keep an Eye on the Costumes

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/priglashenie-2026/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-08-16 (16 August 2026); updated: 2026-08-17
Work: “The Invite” is a 2026 film directed by Olivia Wilde.
Tags: dramedy, costumes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/priglashenie-2026/

## 16 August 2026

The film [*The Invite*](https://youtu.be/OJ19I9q_hOQ?si=emKmsv1_YOeCZUYU) is best watched without any firmly formed expectations.

This dramedy, staged like a chamber play, has plenty of surprises in store. Joe and Angela, a long-married couple whose relationship has been knocked about by life, played by Seth Rogen and Olivia Wilde (who is also the film’s director), have long since stopped talking to each other in any way other than quarrelling. Joe, a music teacher, is unhappy with his job, his pupils and his everyday life, while Angela, a housewife, is looking for new acquaintances and suddenly invites round the neighbours, who frankly drive him up the wall because they are noisy at night 🔞

It sounds like the standard set-up for a comedy about a couple putting their relationship back together after one decisive encounter, but in fact *The Invite* is nothing of the kind. Practically a television play for four characters, it comes with a stunningly well-judged backdrop of classical music, and is full of shifts in emotional register and play with the visual side of things.

The film deserves separate credit for the pair of neighbours played by Penélope Cruz and Edward Norton. As a duo they have stunning chemistry, but each on their own has a simply magnetic energy too. I especially like how Cruz’s character, next to Norton, comes across as a kind of Tyler Durden: she instantly sees through the psychology of whoever she is talking to and manipulates them masterfully. One of the best female characters I’ve seen lately, and one of the coolest ensemble casts all round.

## 17 August 2026

By the way, pay special attention to how the characters of [*The Invite*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1723) are dressed.

The hosts, Joe and Angela, wear clothes in dull pastel shades (washed-out mint and faded denim), which each go with the flat’s interior but don’t harmonise with each other at all. And indeed, the two of them have long been a poor match, tormented by the boredom of their life.

We see a quite different combination with the guests: Pina and Hawk are dressed to go with each other. Both wear black tops, which underline their deep bond and at the same time their air of mystery (and they did, it has to be said, turn up on distinctly mysterious vibes).

The costume designer Arianne Phillips [said](https://www.wmagazine.com/fashion/the-invite-costumes-olivia-wilde-arianne-phillips-interview) that she deliberately made Joe’s and Angela’s costumes clash in shade — it is an important marker of their relationship. The black on the guest couple she explained as a symbol of togetherness and mutual chemistry. And the simple silhouettes were chosen to keep viewers from drawing premature conclusions about the characters.

---

## Daneliya’s Heads and Tails: If Brother Were a Rom-Com

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/orel-i-reshka-1995/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-08-13 (13 August 2026)
Work: “Heads and Tails” is a 1995 film directed by Georgiy Daneliya.
Tags: rewatch, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/orel-i-reshka-1995/

If *Brother* had been a rom-com with a happy ending, you would have got [*Heads and Tails*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/40866). It’s a great piece of luck that Georgiy Daneliya actually made it, in 1995.

The plot is simple enough: Oleg Chagin (Kirill Pirogov, who, incidentally, found fame in *Brother 2*) comes back to Moscow from a work stint in the far north to win his beloved back from the husband she has suddenly acquired. In Moscow, naturally, nobody is waiting for our hero — nothing but a fateful meeting with Zina Prishchepkina, an ordinary canteen worker played by a veeery young Polina Kutepova. What follows are adventures of the “just a normal Tuesday in Russia” kind: the hero accidentally saves the life of a woman he doesn’t know, meets a New Russian (an unrecognisable Leonid Yarmolnik), instantly becomes his friend, and then falls victim to Gypsies, capitalism and hasty conclusions.

The most precious thing in the film is the inimitable aura of an era — the turn of the millennium — that is amply represented on film, yet here it isn’t plastered with the usual clichés but shot as if through the eyes of a witness watching what becomes of an ordinary contemporary. The views of 1990s Moscow are mesmerising too: the Oktyabr cinema alone flashes past a dozen or so times, as if to remind us that in thirty years everything in the city has changed — and nothing.

But the main thing is Chagin as played by Kirill Pirogov: a real hidden treasure in the line of generation-defining heroes like Kostik in *The Pokrovsky Gate*, Bananan in *Assa*, Ivan in *Messenger Boy* and Danila in *Brother*. Chagin is lost, cynical and crafty in moderation, but not in the least cruel or underhand, and he hasn’t lost his humanity. He is, of course, a protagonist with a full set of negative qualities, but, as if on purpose, he switches them on only with the best of intentions.

---

## Obsession: The Year’s Most Talked-About Horror Turns Out to Be a Comedy Too

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/obsessiya-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-08-09 (9 August 2026)
Work: “Obsession” is a 2025 film directed by Curry Barker.
Tags: horror, comedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/obsessiya-2025/

I would never have thought that the most talked-about horror film of 2026 would also turn out to be an excellent comedy.

During the first half of [*Obsession*](https://youtu.be/0NK6s9o3hkE?si=AyntY76tkq4X4rT9) I laughed practically every five minutes. The awkwardness of Bear’s attempts at socialising is exaggerated to such a degree that it comes across as an out-and-out comic device.

But once the horror side of it gets going, the impression it leaves is, of course, indelible. Director Curry Barker creates terror with a minimal set of tools — what triggers you most is the characters’ unnatural, instantaneous swings of emotion. Inde Navarrette in particular does something blood-curdling with nothing but her facial expressions. Even when you notice, here and there, a dummy with some CGI in place of a human figure (the film has a modest budget), it is still outweighed by the shock you’ve already been through.

The concept itself — the body being taken away from the mind (as in *Get Out*) — leaves you frozen. And the theme, of course, is a burning one — both that love is blind and that you can’t make someone love you. An unequivocal recommendation to watch (though maybe not over dinner).

---

## Spider-Man: Brand New Day: A Chance to Feel Like a Superhero’s Equal

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/chelovek-pauk-novyy-den-2026/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-08-03 (3 August 2026)
Work: “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” is a 2026 film directed by Destin Daniel Cretton.
Tags: superheroes, blockbuster
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/chelovek-pauk-novyy-den-2026/

[*Spider-Man: Brand New Day*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1687) lets every viewer feel like a superhero’s equal.

Nothing could be easier, because in the new instalment Peter Parker is someone starting over from scratch, a little burnt out and, like any young adult, confused. It seems the friendly neighbourhood Spider-Man of 2026 could hardly have been any different: this kind of new sincerity in Tom Holland’s take on the character is disarming at the very least, and at most it reboots the franchise perfectly. A reminder: after the previous instalment, thanks to Doctor Strange’s spell, everyone in the world (even those closest to the hero) has forgotten Peter Parker.

Spider-Man’s adventures in a world where he loses not only his outer anchors but his inner ones too feel more than believable. Special effects of every kind are in place, of course, and top-notch, but Parker’s flights between the skyscrapers are convincing not only because of the cool CGI. Holland has made his Spider-Man not just a “neighbour” but a true contemporary, someone learning to find an anchor in himself and to offer one to others, even when it feels as if breaking point has come. But he gets on with his superheroing: turning enemies into friends and emptiness into connections, and all of it to a cool soundtrack.

Maybe, in 2026, that is the superpower that matters most.

---

## Monsters, Inc.: The Speech Quirks That Dubbing Hides

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/korporatsiya-monstrov-2001/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-07-28 (28 July 2026)
Work: “Monsters, Inc.” is a 2001 film directed by Pete Docter, David Silverman, Lee Unkrich.
Tags: animation, dubbing, rewatch
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/korporatsiya-monstrov-2001/

To repair my nerves after [this](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/den-razoblacheniya-2026/), I had to rewatch ~~Heated Rivalry~~ **Monsters, Inc.** in the original. [As usual](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/shrek-2001/), I kept track of the quirks of speech that the dub hides from us:

- The most meme-worthy pet names of Wazowski and his sweetheart, which recently went viral as a trend, are “Zmeyusik-lapusik” and “Kruglik-bublik” in Russian (roughly “snakey-sweetie” and “roundy-bagel”). In English they are, respectively, Schmoopsie-poo and Googley Bear (sometimes Googley-woogley). I think this is one of those cases where the dub came out on top :)

- Little Boo was voiced by the three-year-old daughter of one of the voice actors, so in the original this tiny heroine literally sounds like a real child.

- And the next two points are for the most seasoned viewers. Roz, the obnoxious administrator who terrorises Wazowski with bureaucratic nitpicking, talks exactly like the fixer Mike Ehrmantraut from *Better Call Saul*/*Breaking Bad* once she reveals her true role. His famous “That’s what happens next” matches the animated heroine’s right down to the intonation, and it’s astonishing.

- The main villain, the purple lizard Randall, gives off ferocious Rozanov-from-*Heated Rivalry* vibes in one scene (comically enough, in the locker room). If you’ve watched the series, there’s no way you’ll miss the matching intonation in the line “Aha, sure”, with its villainously blunt sneer. The character is wonderfully voiced by Steve Buscemi :)

## Disclosure Day: A Spielberg Thriller with a Fantastically Bad Script

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/den-razoblacheniya-2026/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-07-27 (27 July 2026)
Work: “Disclosure Day” is a 2026 film directed by Steven Spielberg.
Tags: science fiction, thriller
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/den-razoblacheniya-2026/

**Disclosure Day** turned my day off into Disappointment Day.

Steven Spielberg’s thriller, which has a fantastically bad script as well as Emily Blunt and Josh O’Connor, literally traumatised me.

The first half of the film, about two humans chosen by an alien intelligence and trying to make sense of their gift, raised no particular suspicions. A few genre conventions, portentous faces, thoughts of saving the planet, if not the entire universe: that’s par for the course. The bit of pandering that has Blunt’s character speak Russian with the appropriate accent is duly noted as well; I actually perked up ([I love that sort of thing](https://t.me/kino_voice/1213)).

But in the second half some kind of phantasmagorical absurdity set in: a spectacle devoid of logic, plausibility and common sense. Neither the kind-heartedness of the story nor sweet nostalgia can account for it. Specifically, the problems are these:

- It turns out that the characters started preparing for the arrival of the gifted Margaret (Blunt) before they even knew who would turn out to be the bearer of the alien abilities. They spend the whole film building a set that is an exact copy of her house and childhood bedroom, and then, with the most guileless air, are surprised to meet her.

- The collective antagonist that has been terrorising the gifted pair all film long eventually finds its zen, so that the finale can play out in “come what may” mode, while the chief villain sinks into heavy thoughts about the fate of humanity.

- In the finale the heroes put classified footage of the aliens on air, and the broadcast is instantly picked up by channels in every state, and then around the world (we do get shots of everyone in Russia glued to the screen). It is, after all, so true to life that in 2026 the world is still united by television. But don’t worry, the writers haven’t forgotten about neural networks: one of the producers of one of the broadcasts in one of the states declares with an air of importance that the material they have received is definitely not AI. You can literally see with the naked eye that the aliens in the footage are as real as they come.

- The leads, a delicate weather presenter and a skinny IT guy, manage to cling for quite some time to the bonnet of a mangled car that a train is dragging along the tracks at full speed, and then to leap onto a carriage as well, dodging an oncoming train. Not a single item of clothing torn, not a single wound, dislocation or bruise sustained: sheer dexterity and no trickery whatsoever. I understand that the film is science fiction, but any science fiction has to be grounded in some rules of its on-screen world, not give the writers a free hand for utter nonsense.

- The alien device can do whatever the script happens to need at that moment and plugs any plot hole. The gadget lets you get inside another person’s mind, take on anyone’s appearance and even generate electricity in case the TV studio suddenly loses power (of course: the world has to learn the truth about the aliens from television, after all).

At best, while I was watching *Disclosure Day* I found it hysterically funny. But the net result is that I have been fuming for three days now.

---

## Crowdfunding for the Short Film My edem khoronit dedushku

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/my-edem-khoronit-dedushku-kraudfanding/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-07-26 (26 July 2026)
Work: “My edem khoronit dedushku” is a work.
Tags: Russian cinema, short films, road movie, announcements
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/my-edem-khoronit-dedushku-kraudfanding/

I usually write here about films that have already been made, but this one is going to be an exception.

A team of young filmmakers is shooting a short, [*My edem khoronit dedushku*](https://t.me/markandrus) («Мы едем хоронить дедушку», “We Are Going to Bury Grandpa”), a road movie about two brothers played by Makar Khlebnikov and Illarion Marov (actors in whom I personally have enormous faith).

The description alone brings to mind a whole host of great films, from ***How Viktor “The Garlic” Took Alexey “The Stud” to the Nursing Home*** («Как Витька Чеснок вез Леху Штыря в дом инвалидов») to [*She’s So Cool*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/ona-takaya-klassnaya-serial/) and [*Rock It, Stone Fish!*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/tantsuy-seledka-solntse-moe/). In short, a whole scattering of motifs that are important and interesting to watch on film, because this is the reality we all share.

But for this film to happen, the team needs help raising the rest of the money. The guys have launched a crowdfunding campaign where you can [chip in](https://planeta.ru/campaigns/markandru) and get tickets to the premiere, a thank-you in the credits and plenty of other nice things in return. This is one of those cases where the future of a promising project is in our hands, yours and mine, as viewers, and it’s a chance we should take.

Any good film is a huge chain of lucky breaks and coincidences, and I very, very much want *My edem khoronit dedushku* to get lucky.

---

## The Odyssey: The Quintessence of Nolan’s Directorial Signature

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/odisseya-2026/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-07-26 (26 July 2026); updated: 2026-07-30
Work: “The Odyssey” is a 2026 film directed by Christopher Nolan.
Tags: blockbuster, adaptation
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/odisseya-2026/

## 26 July 2026

***The Odyssey* is my new favourite Christopher Nolan film.**

*Jumping ahead, I’ll headline this post with the thought that this seems to be the quintessence of Nolan’s directorial signature: all the Nolan themes (from the search for an unreachable home to the responsibility that comes with genius), the formal and structural devices, with their asynchronous storytelling and leaps in time, the appearances of the actors — all of it is here in peak form, the best possible. The only one now capable of surpassing the degree of perfection in each of these ingredients of success is, perhaps, Nolan himself in his next film.*

First and foremost, this is a practically perfect screen version of the familiar stories of ancient Greek folklore: the Cyclopes, the Trojan horse, the giant Laestrygonians, Circe, who turns sailors into pigs. Each of these stories is brought to the screen so painstakingly, and with such respect for its legendary status, that for that reason alone I’m ready to talk everyone into seeing this film. None of the stories involving these creatures is some hollow scare, there for the sake of an adrenaline spike in the audience or of slotting in a showy fairground attraction. They come across, as befits elements of Homer’s *Odyssey*, as monumental to the point of awe. I had never thought of a Cyclops looking like this, or of the turning into pigs happening like this, because I could never have imagined these things being so realistic, so inseparable from the elements of the world we know. I simply fell in love with the way Nolan has pulled this off and stitched it into the fabric of a spectacular blockbuster.

**\*️⃣** Incidentally, I should make clear that I took all the news about *The Odyssey*, during the shoot and in the run-up to the premiere, with a certain scepticism. Some of Nolan’s work (*Tenet*, for example) has stayed in my memory as a pretentious attempt to build a film on formal devices without any particularly meaningful content, and the fear that the same would happen with *The Odyssey* was great. But all my sceptical thoughts were dashed against the magnificence of what I saw.

Don’t be afraid of the three-hour running time (the pacing is perfect for letting that time fly by unnoticed), of miscasting (there isn’t any) or of the film’s twisted structure — the balance of all its parts makes it truly outstanding and a must-see.

## 30 July 2026

Another thing that makes [*The Odyssey*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1666) interesting is its gallery of characters and the key ideas they embody (and which are turning into memes beautifully).

 1️⃣Matt Damon’s Odysseus is not shown as a trickster or a schemer with a dash of comedy, as you might have expected looking back at the original text. More than that, he is all but reduced to a “little man” whose lot it is to live through historic times (now why would anyone be dwelling on that subject in 2026) — thanks in part to Damon’s screen type, since he has often been cast as “regular guys”. The result is a hero we can relate to completely: guided by the laws of his time (it happens to the best of us), he took the decision to build the Trojan horse, and only later realised that there is something higher than the mores of an age. And the years the hero spent wandering in search of home, or in oblivion altogether, can be read in different ways — from PTSD to a liminal purgatory in which Odysseus pays for his moral crime. Even the memes about *The Odyssey* come with stills from *Oppenheimer*, whose hero came to regret his own invention.

**2️⃣** This is the place to mention Zendaya’s Athena: she serves as the embodiment of that very timeless law — of humanism, if I can put it that way — which Odysseus disregarded. The shots of her silent judgement have turned into memes about one ice cream too many or hours spent scrolling your feed precisely because everyone knows what it is to disapprove of their own actions, on whatever scale. So nothing human is alien to the hero of the ancient Greek poem — and that is one of the secrets of the film’s success.

**3️⃣** The memes about Penelope, the bow and the suitors feasting on Ithaca take in, if only superficially, the second major plot strand of *The Odyssey*. To my mind the film gives it slightly less attention than it might have, but the priorities are still the right ones. While one person is trying to get back home, another has to watch that home literally cease to exist and fill up with people who shouldn’t be there. Both funny, as the memes suggest, and impossibly sad.

---

## Kidnapping: A Chameleon Thriller Worth Your Time, with an Outstanding Ensemble

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/pokhischenie-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-07-25 (25 July 2026)
Work: “Kidnapping” is a 2026 series directed by Kirill Pletnyov.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, thriller, mystery
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/pokhischenie-serial/

There’s been a [*Kidnapping*](https://youtu.be/yrEaOKm8w0Y?si=m8V-KrEa50xEURNR): a really worthwhile chameleon thriller from Okko (the Russian streaming service) that literally pulls you in as you watch.

Going by the first four episodes, it has almost everything: Timofey Tribuntsev as an investigator who calls everyone “kitten” (*kotik*, in the tone of this [meme](https://t.me/kino_voice/1642)), Marina Vasilyeva, who is excellent as an absurdly contradictory heroine, and even Rinal Mukhametov, whose character has drug issues and mommy issues at once. This whole gallery of types has assembled over the disappearance in the woods of a five-year-old boy, though it is unclear whether there ever was a boy at all. But the company is outstanding, so against a backdrop like that even a plain, ordinary investigation is rather interesting to follow.

I’ve [written](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/news/4013049/) about the series in more detail on Kinopoisk (Russia’s largest film database, media and streaming service): why *Kidnapping* resembles *True Detective*, *The Method* and other films, right up to Zvyagintsev’s* *Loveless*.

* Andrey Zvyagintsev (Звягинцев Андрей Петрович) has been designated a “foreign agent” by Russia’s Ministry of Justice (listed on 18 September 2026).

## Pluribus and Heated Rivalry: Their Parallel Release Is a Phenomenon in Itself

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/pluribus-heated-rivalry-paralleli/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-07-24 (24 July 2026)
Tags: series, analysis
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/pluribus-heated-rivalry-paralleli/

Naive parallels you never needed.

It seems that we as a society have not reflected enough on the fact that the parallel release of the series [*Pluribus*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/pluribus-serial/) and [*Heated Rivalry*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1205) is a phenomenon in itself.

**Pluribus** showed us a universe in which the protagonist, a writer, had created a series of staggeringly popular fantasy novels whose main characters were in a conventional relationship, and yet she herself considered her work mediocre and hypocritical, because she could not count on success for the unconventional romantic storyline she really wanted to write. To please the fandom, she had to go on writing about the kind of love that suited her readers.

In real life, while that series was coming out, the whole world was also watching **Heated Rivalry**, an adaptation of exactly that kind of novel, whose author chose not to bank on traditional mores and wrote as she felt. Need I add that both the series and the book ended up with a certain popularity (to put it mildly)?

*And what if Carol Sturka from Pluribus had been writing the novel she always wanted to, without looking over her shoulder at public taste? Would that have worked as a butterfly effect, turning things in the end onto the branch of reality where no armageddon happens?* Makes you think.

Either way, it’s a good thing the apocalypse happens in the universe where creativity is hemmed in by prejudice. And for our reality, it seems, all is not yet lost.

---

## Restlessness: The Heroes Find Themselves in Something Like a Quantum Purgatory

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/nepokoy-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-07-20 (20 July 2026); updated: 2026-08-07
Work: “Restlessness” is a 2025 film directed by Leonid Shmelkov.
Tags: animation, interview
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/nepokoy-2025/

## 20 July 2026

A great rarity: behind this stylish poster lies a film no less intricately put together, [*Restlessness*](https://youtu.be/3Qiu-KRJsMw?si=_BSi1e_hxAMYkxnI) (*Nepokoy*).

The plot of this adult animation is simple precisely because it dissolves fairly early on, giving way to a controlled chaos of events whose interpretation is left to the viewer.

Yasha and Bernard are driving, just the two of them, to an unnamed, far-off destination, and on the way they decide to spend the night at an ordinary, moderately shabby roadside hotel called the Rosa. And there everything turns out to be stranger than strange.

Without going into the details of what happens, it is probably fair to say that the heroes have ended up in something like a quantum purgatory. The hotel has a Madame — receptionist, cook, chambermaid and entertainer rolled into one: she makes breakfasts out of dishes from roughly every cuisine in the world and hosts concerts, film clubs and all manner of garden games. Only none of it gives the new guests any pleasure, because they can’t manage to leave the hotel — first physically, and then mentally too.

What the hotel will be for you, and what the plot’s many metaphorical turns will turn out to be, is a matter of associations, imagination, how much you have watched (you can see Lynchian absurdity if you like, or a Wes Anderson aesthetic if you prefer) and your appetite for reflection: *Restlessness* leaves all the room in the world for that. For myself, I summed up what I saw as an extended visualisation of the opposite of what Pushkin wrote about in the lines *“there is no happiness in the world, but there is peace and freedom”*. When you have everything you need for happiness but no way of making your own decision in its favour, restlessness sets in.

And you can experience the very particular *Restlessness* in cinemas (and only in cinemas: no streaming release has been announced) from 30 July.

## 7 August 2026

After [this interview](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/4013087/) I felt like rewatching [*Restlessness*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1648).

Director Leonid Shmelkov talks about the idea behind this animated feature in a way that has you literally discovering some things all over again. It was nice to find that I had read the meaning of the pink hares and the irritating runners, who flit across the screen more than once, exactly as intended.

---

## Cold: A Series So Immersive It Knocks You Off Your Feet

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kholod-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-07-16 (16 July 2026); updated: 2026-09-22
Work: “Cold” is a 2026 series directed by Aleksey Kazakov.
Tags: series, interview
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/kholod-serial/

## 16 July 2026

From today you can watch [*Cold*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1629) (*Kholod*), a bone-chilling series with Lyubov Aksyonova.

Watching the first episode, I literally lost track of time: from about the fifth minute I just sat with my head in my hands, trying not to start spelling out, aloud and in unprintable terms, the scale of the catastrophe in the plot. So many misfortunes befall Zhenya, Aksyonova’s character, that at times you genuinely just forget to breathe. It’s exactly the kind of series during which you’re never once tempted to check your phone.

And Zhenya herself is so resilient, hardy and patient that it’s hard to refuse her your sympathy, and the urge to root for her is the main motivation to watch to the end. Every scene shows very bluntly just what real hardships we’re talking about (emotional and physical), without sparing the viewer and without trying to, as it were, “hide” the story’s uncomfortable moments off screen. A series of rare sincerity about the powerlessness of the little person in the face of fate’s unjust blows.

## 6 August 2026

In a recent interview with Sobchak (the Russian TV journalist), Lyubov Aksyonova told a story that is hard to forget: her father spent 4 years in a penal colony and then proved his innocence in court. She was 19. Now she plays Zhenya in [*Cold*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1643), a drama from Ivi, START and Wink (Russian streaming services) about a woman unjustly convicted over a crash. Once you know that, you see the role in a completely different light.

Today my [interview](https://theblueprint.ru/culture/specials/cold-interview) with Lyubov Aksyonova, Linda Lapiņš and Alexandra Babaskina came out in The Blueprint. We talked about trauma — how it breaks you, makes you grow up and sometimes becomes a source of strength — and about how to stay human through all these ordeals.

Inside there is plenty the trailer won’t tell you: why Aksyonova, for the first time in her career, drew up a detailed map of her character, and why the early Zhenya went by the code name “Snegurochka” (the Snow Maiden); Lapiņš’s true story of a girl whose fate seemed sealed — and ended at Yale University; and why Sasha Babaskina is sure that children are sometimes stronger than adults.

The piece has come out insanely beautiful — not only in its ideas but visually too: special love to the photographer Maxim Tarakanov and the whole team.

As always, I’ve picked the quote that is key for me — it comes from Lyubov Aksyonova ⤵️

> *Cold* is a story about how, even out of the most terrible ordeal, a person always has the chance to come through to love and lean on it. Love can prove stronger than the desire to destroy. And only love can truly conquer death. And that, I suppose, is the most important thing for me.

Incidentally, after talking to the actresses you watch the next episodes differently: you start to notice how, from one period to the next, Zhenya changes the way she moves, the rhythm of her speech and even her breathing. I’ve checked this personally.

You can read the piece [at this link](https://theblueprint.ru/culture/specials/cold-interview).

## 15 September 2026

I deliberately let a good few episodes of [*Cold*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1643) pile up so I could watch them in one go, and it paid off.

The series, and Lyubov Aksyonova’s performance in particular, has a kind of immersive pull that knocks you off your feet. I lost touch with reality during the first two episodes, and I lost it again watching all the ones that followed back to back.

All thanks to what I would call “the aura of a thick novel”. This series is nothing like the usual alternation of events and their consequences for various characters. *Cold* feels like a vast tapestry woven from a multitude of threads in different shades. First, the “threads” never get lost, though it may be many years before they meet again. Second, there is anything you like among them except black and white. Third, while this “tapestry” is being woven you would do well to stock up on patience — just like the heroine, Zhenya. And the “embroidery” is so dense that you feel a physical urge to “reread” the series before it has even reached its finale. I really can’t wait for the last episode.

## 22 September 2026

Rounding off the conversation about [*Cold*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1772)

I took part [in a survey run by colleagues at Kinopoisk](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/4013398): we swapped views on the series finale. I’m satisfied, as my 9/10 rating makes clear, but what seems especially important to me is the room left for the viewer’s hope in the closing shots. What matters is not so much that Aksyonova’s character had some kind of choice and some kind of decision was made as the reminder that, after the most terrible scrapes, a person still has some power over themselves, even when the outside world can’t be controlled. Lyubov [talked to me about this in our interview](https://t.me/kino_voice/1698) — it’s great that this is exactly what you feel once you’ve finished watching.

I’d also recommend reading my colleagues’ opinions: each of us took a liking to (or, on the contrary, remembered for the wrong reasons) something different. And I invite you into the comments — I’m sure there’s plenty to discuss ⬇️

---

## The Holy Boy: A Town That Would Be Better Off Without Its Saint

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/dolina-ulybok-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-07-13 (13 July 2026)
Work: “The Holy Boy” is a 2025 film directed by Paolo Strippoli.
Tags: horror, drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/dolina-ulybok-2025/

Now in cinemas: [*The Holy Boy*](https://youtu.be/G7DFSS3WGH0?si=x8BHvR6czpg-vqMD) (*La valle dei sorrisi*, released in Russia as *Dolina ulybok*, “The Valley of Smiles”), an Italian horror drama about a strange little town where everyone is far too happy.

The story centres on Sergio, a PE teacher who has closed himself off after losing someone close (we are kept short of specifics about that loss for a very long time) and who comes to the small town of Remis to fill in for 3 months. At first glance he notices that everyone is in suspiciously high spirits, and then he learns outright that the town has a saint of its own, who heals those stricken with grief after the loss of loved ones. The miraculous powers belong to Matteo, a 15-year-old schoolboy, who gradually takes over as the protagonist.

*The Holy Boy* seems to be a case where, contrary to the proverb (the Russian saying has it that no village stands without a righteous man), the village would be better off without its righteous man. And the problem is not Matteo himself but how the locals treat him: their consumer attitude towards him is precisely what triggers the catastrophe. The script, incidentally, lets you focus on all sorts of things, from the difficulties of coming of age and the problems of parenthood to a condemnation of the current vogue for non-toxic communication, worked-through trauma and all the rest of it. At times, admittedly, so much is left unsaid that the gaps start to look like plot holes, but that comes down to how ready you personally are for a little abstraction.

By the way, before you go to a screening, bear in mind that a couple of moments will be missing: these days not every scene in the film meets the requirements for being shown on the big screen, but it is good that, on the whole, it has made it to us.

In Venice, at any rate, *The Holy Boy* picked up an award from the Federation of Italian Film Clubs. Which means there really is something in it to discuss after watching.

---

## Fuss: So Far More Derivative Than Original

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/sueta-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-07-07 (7 July 2026)
Work: “Fuss” is a 2026 series directed by Anton Rodin.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, crime, comedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/sueta-serial/

I’ve watched [*Fuss*](https://youtu.be/fR0a8jRoUiM?si=0Ze_zk9VxyyAcXM8) (*Sueta*), but I didn’t quite catch the spirit of the Pyatigorsk fussologists (slang for lads who love stirring things up).

The plot, about four guys who decide to rob a cash-in-transit crew but land themselves in extra trouble, is so far rather more derivative than original. Its charm of small-time southern crime loses out to shows like [*SWWW*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/yuzzz-serial/), and all the adventures of the hapless robbers seem to lack a hidden depth: the bunglers of [*Inkassatory*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/inkassatory-serial/) («Инкассаторы», “The Cash Collectors”), for one, were far more convincing as they plumbed the depths of stupidity.

For now the bright spot is the cast: every actor is a perfect fit for their type, and the part of a petrolhead robber suits Denis Vlasenko very nicely indeed. I hope a pleasant surprise is lying in wait for me in the episodes to come.

## Nam kranty: A Convincing Trio of Hapless Friends and a Gallant Gangster

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/nam-kranty-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-07-06 (6 July 2026); updated: 2026-07-31
Work: “Nam kranty” is a 2026 series directed by Alexandr Sobichevsky.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, dramedy, crime
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/nam-kranty-serial/

## 6 July 2026

*Popados* (“Busted”) has turned into ***Nam kranty*** («Нам кранты», “We’re Toast”) and moved closer to its premiere.

It’s a really cool series that I [wrote about back at last year’s Pilot](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/festival-pilot-2025/) (the Russian series festival in Ivanovo) — I’ve been waiting for it, and at last there’s news. Three ordinary friends accidentally land in a mess with criminals, and their lives start sprouting new problems. We’ll watch all their adventures unfold at a very brisk pace, with rowdy jokes and, of course, action scenes.

The cast includes Makar Khlebnikov, Timofey Tribuntsev, Elizaveta Ishchenko and other actors who are a pleasure to watch. The premiere on Kion (the Russian streaming service) is, by the look of it, just around the corner.

## 31 July 2026

All the episodes of [*Nam kranty*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1626) came out on Kion today — a moderately serious dramedy about why you shouldn’t flirt with the criminal world.

Going by the first episodes, it’s an absorbing watch, if not one hundred per cent new. But the devil is in the details — or rather, in the main characters. Makar Khlebnikov, Anton Shokalyuk and Sharifbek Zakirov make a very convincing trio of hapless friends whose types (the “hustler”, the “follower” and the “undecided one”) everyone will recognise.

The older characters are every bit as good. Over the course of the season, the pensive security guard played by Timofey Tribuntsev is obviously going to come into his own. And the insolent smirk of the criminal world is the job of the gallant gangster played by Andrey Prytkov. His temperament, by the standards of central Russia, is practically Mexican.

## Diary of a Wimpy Kid: A Funny, Fast-Paced Film for Viewers of All Ages

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/dnevnik-slabaka-2010/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-07-05 (5 July 2026)
Work: “Diary of a Wimpy Kid” is a 2010 film directed by Thor Freudenthal.
Tags: comedy, family, adaptation, American cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/dnevnik-slabaka-2010/

*Found the kids-singing-badly meme in its natural habitat*

That, by the way, was not the only thing that marked my viewing of ***Diary of a Wimpy Kid***. The film is rich in memes generally: for instance, it has the absolutely canonical wild older brother, who has been cut up into clips that went everywhere. They kept insistently popping up in my feed and in the end nudged me into watching. Alas, almost all the funny moments with him are in the second film, so I got caught out twice.

Still, it’s worth saying that I was very surprised to see these universes overlap. And even setting aside the thrill of meeting a meme in the wild, the first film is very funny and fast-paced for viewers of all ages (which is rather rare). At certain moments I even caught niche overlaps between one of the characters and Vovan from *Real Boys* («Реальные пацаны», the long-running Russian TV sitcom set in Perm) — please don’t be jealous, it’s purely a matter of how much you’ve watched.

As for the second *Diary of a Wimpy Kid*, I’ll definitely be watching it, and this time with certain expectations.

## Raz malchishka, dva malchishka: A Short Read That Makes Itself Felt

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/raz-malchishka-dva-malchishka-kniga/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-07-04 (4 July 2026)
Work: “Raz malchishka, dva malchishka” is a 2024 book by Asya Demishkevich.
Tags: books, horror
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/raz-malchishka-dva-malchishka-kniga/

It’s not very often that I like something from contemporary fiction in Russian, but recently, on a recommendation, I read Asya Demishkevich’s novel [*Raz malchishka, dva malchishka*](https://books.yandex.ru/books/iVnOelfS?utm_campaign=users_referral&amp;utm_medium=referral&amp;utm_source=direct_link) («Раз мальчишка, два мальчишка», “One Boy, Two Boys”) practically in one sitting, and now I’m going to recommend it to you.

I’m not sure how best to pin down its genre: it is a coming-of-age novel, folk horror and topical allegorical absurdism all in one. Thirteen-year-old Andrey gets sent off to the army by his wicked stepmother (the morphology of the folktale crops up a lot in this text, don’t be surprised), and everything there is somehow strange: the unit includes a couple of dead men, there are no barracks at all, and in their place iron bedsteads stand in a bare field under the open sky.

The further adventures of the “recruits” are more interesting to read than to learn from a summary, so here I’ll confine myself to general raptures. Demishkevich’s style is ultra-contemporary in the best sense of the word, and that doesn’t show in attempts to somehow mimic the plausible speech of a Russian teenager! I’m talking about the complete removal of the boundaries between the reader and what is happening — boundaries that are usually formed, so to speak, precisely by the author’s style. The words seem, all by themselves, both to tell the story and to comment on it for the reader (and there is plenty in that story to think about and to laugh at). And the ending, to my mind, for all its unexpectedness, is more than logical. A short read in page count, but one that makes itself very much felt.

---
