[*Radar*](https://youtu.be/DpkESLR3iD8?si=klU5YWzpzAWEBIh_) is a brisk watch: a science-fiction story about schoolchildren from a small town who come up against an unearthly evil.

Two episodes in, what I’m enjoying most is the music: Mumiy Troll, Mujuice, Kino (Russian rock bands and an electronic musician) and, no doubt, plenty more to come. The plot has a hook as well: Soviet schoolchildren alone with the supernatural (a touch of *Kitchenblock*, «Пищеблок»), surrounded by late-Soviet everyday life, and the school even has its own Afghan (a veteran of the Soviet war in Afghanistan; hello, *Peace! Friendship! Chewing Gum!*, the 1990s-set series). The adult cast is more than distinguished (from Polina Kutepova to Viktoria Isakova), and the young actors are very convincing at playing the decent and, at times, the rather nasty. I want to keep watching, because it is hard to predict how all this will play out.

## Hostage: From Business Shark to Hostage of Circumstance

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/zalozhnik-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-04-25 (25 April 2026); updated: 2026-05-17
Work: “Hostage” is a 2026 series directed by Sergey Popov, Rustam Mosafir.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, thriller, drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/zalozhnik-serial/

## 25 April 2026

Meanwhile, [*Hostage*](https://youtu.be/vj5D5WSQmXY?si=r6dzanmnjKc34nR-) with Maxim Matveev has begun.

Maxim Pozharsky (a convincing Matveev), a financial analyst without a conscience in every sense, has to swap his spotless office for dangerous Syria in a single day: his sister Nina is being held captive there. That is what the first two episodes show us, and it has to be said that however much of a hardened old hand the hero looks in his professional world, alone in the face of disaster he turns out to be defenceless.

This forced transformation from business shark into hostage of circumstance is, to my mind, the story’s main strength at the outset. Maxim Matveev is excellent at switching between personas (just think of [*Other People’s Money*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/chuzhie-dengi-serial/)), so the chaos in the outside world is compounded by the hero’s own breakdown.

The story promises to be compact (just six episodes) and still keep you on edge right up to the finale.

You will certainly be surprised by the particular skill Maxim Matveev picked up to make his character convincing on screen. And by Nikolas Muavad’s dream screen adaptation, especially after his role in *Hostage*.

## Project Hail Mary: Mainstream Cinema with Taste and Humanity

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/proekt-konets-sveta-2026/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-04-24 (24 April 2026)
Work: “Project Hail Mary” is a 2026 film directed by Phil Lord, Christopher Miller.
Tags: science fiction, adaptation
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/proekt-konets-sveta-2026/

I’ve got round to [*Project Hail Mary*](https://youtu.be/m08TxIsFTRI?si=1Sprxcx5D8tQfoOo) (released in Russia as *Proekt “Konets sveta”*, “Project Doomsday”), and it really is a cosmically cool film.

This story of a teacher who ends up on a space mission against his will has a lot going for it: stunning cinematography and CGI, a delightful Ryan Gosling (I don’t like all his roles, but this one is a bullseye), and a convincing script with no excess of melodrama and no lapses into humour that is too black. By the way, it is also a great adaptation of Andy Weir’s novel of the same name (the author previously wrote *The Martian*; space is his forte). In short, a practically perfect example of mainstream cinema, made with great technical skill, but with taste and humanity.

And that last quality I want to write about separately. It’s probably obvious that you are instantly tempted to compare the film with *Interstellar*: in scale, in its themes, in the places where the plots overlap. But *Interstellar*, in my view, is simply an anti-advert for the space sci-fi genre next to *Project*. The Gosling film doesn’t put up a wall of grandeur and ambition between the action and the audience, the kind you are meant to look at only from below and with reverence. The detail of *Project*, unlike that of *Interstellar*, doesn’t demand homework on picking apart what you’ve seen before you can understand and remember anything at all. And, surprisingly enough, that doesn’t make the script flat or predictable; on the contrary, it helps you get involved and enjoy the film all the more.

So go figure, as they say. And do watch *Project Hail Mary*, it’s worth it :)

---

## RBC Style’s Quality-of-Life Event: Kidults, Starry Skies and Light in Film

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/ivent-rbk-stil-kachestvo-zhizni/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-04-18 (18 April 2026)
Tags: notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/ivent-rbk-stil-kachestvo-zhizni/

Another thing I’ll remember this week for is an [event](https://t.me/rbcstyle/5999) held by colleagues at RBC Style (the lifestyle outlet of the Russian media group RBC), who set up a huge forum for discussing quality of life. It’s an aspect worth keeping in mind, because in the daily rush our own well-being is forever being put off till later.

There were sessions with talks by experts and influencers, and a cool investment pitch session for projects that are only just launching, with the aim of helping us live better in the future. At first glance it has little to do with film, but I took away a few cool facts that I’ll now be noticing when I watch things:

- The big swings that have appeared in many city squares in recent years are part of a playful urban environment, which is good for grown-ups. Its growth has been shaped by the emergence of a new type of city dweller, who might be called a “kidult” (kid + adult): someone who doesn’t give up their childlike, playful side but builds it into an adult life of work and responsibilities. We often see this type in films — they’re always brightly dressed, slightly goofy guys and girls who, as a rule, turn out to be the most sincere and decent characters (a recent example is Vanya from [*You Drive Me Crazy*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/svodish-s-uma-2025/)). So that’s who’s hogging all the swings at Mayakovskaya (the square by the Mayakovskaya metro station in Moscow) :)

- Because cities are lit up around the clock, our circadian rhythms are changing, and on top of that we hardly ever see the stars. From now on I’ll look at a starry sky appearing in a film just a little differently

- Indoor lighting (like the stars) affects our physical and emotional state. A fact from the Captain Obvious files, you might think, but we often don’t realise it in the moment, when we feel uncomfortable in one setting or another. Film has long made constant use of this device, playing with colour grading and with the light or shadow falling on the characters, and here art is closely intertwined with physical reality. It’s very sobering when a speaker opens their presentation by saying that light has been shaping our lives ever since ancient humans lit the first fire.

Thanks to the team for the invitation and for a quality day off.

---

## Pasha Tekhnik: Who Is Behind the Underground? A Doc That Doesn’t Romanticise Its Subject

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/pasha-tekhnik-za-kem-stoit-andegraund-2026/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-04-17 (17 April 2026)
Work: “Pasha Tekhnik: Who Is Behind the Underground?” is a 2026 film directed by Vladislav Kuznetsov.
Tags: documentary, music
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/pasha-tekhnik-za-kem-stoit-andegraund-2026/

Yesterday I went to a screening of [the documentary about Pasha Tekhnik](https://youtu.be/Nkr89DLuvM0?si=Ti2_wAgEFPEIlMYL) (the Russian underground rapper), which has a great subtitle: “Who Is Behind the Underground?”. The title announces straight away that the focus is on the man himself and on his relationship with a particular segment of culture — and that is exactly how the film is structured.

I’m not the most deeply immersed in Tekhnik’s work, so I went with a great deal of exploratory curiosity. And I have to say the film does look like the ideal guide for anyone who either wasn’t up on the finer points or simply wanted to remember once more how it all began.

With documentary biographies there is always the fear of running into romanticisation, excessive sentimentality or, God forbid, a tedious idealisation of the subject. I found none of that in the Tekhnik doc — it feels like the story of an ordinary man who slipped up somewhere, somehow got on the wrong side of the law, and in some respects turned out weaker than life requires. You want to trust his story, because this isn’t some performer who was headed for the stage from childhood and then performed flawlessly all his life, never once straying from the showbiz gloss. If there were good moments, they are shown as just that, and if there was something base, with no beauty or dignity in it, that ended up on screen too, because that is honest.

The music journalist Nikolai Redkin described the phenomenon of this artist with complete accuracy, and yet rather paradoxically, when he said that Tekhnik is “the Yuri Nikulin of the lowbrow internet of the 2010s” (Nikulin being the beloved Soviet clown and comic actor). For my part, I spent the whole screening thinking that Tekhnik’s life story somehow, unexpectedly, rhymes with Dostoevsky’s famous line: “*Man is a mystery. It must be unravelled, and if you spend your whole life unravelling it, do not say you have wasted your time*”. It seems we all had a bit of a try, and it was definitely not in vain.

---

## The Balance of the Universe in Flight: Pelevin for Me, Kubrick for My Neighbour

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/balans-vselennoy-v-polete/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-04-14 (14 April 2026)
Tags: notes, books
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/balans-vselennoy-v-polete/

**On the balance of the universe**

The day before yesterday I had the pleasure of making my first fully solo flight with a layover, but, inexperienced as I was, I hadn’t downloaded anything to watch in advance. I was counting on the airport wi-fi, but in 3 hours of layover it couldn’t manage to load even a single episode for me. So on the plane it was just me and the books I had once downloaded at random. I settled on Viktor Pelevin’s *Omon Ra* and, I must say, got through 80% of it during the flight, so I had an interesting time of it either way.

My neighbour across the aisle, unlike me, unsheathed his tablet a little later and settled down to watch *Full Metal Jacket*. Given the nature of the book I was reading and the film he was watching, our row 100% took on a certain aura :) What’s more, I’m quite prepared to believe that my fellow passenger may actually have dreamed of reading a book on the way but hadn’t managed to download it, so he had to make do with the Kubrick that happened to be lying around on his tablet.

In short, if next time I manage to carry out my in-flight film viewing as planned, I’ll suspect that somewhere in the cabin sits a passenger who is getting to grips, quite unplanned, with a work of literature.

## Radio Pepel, the Album by Dayte Tank (!): Music as a Time Machine

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/radio-pepel-dayte-tank/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-04-11 (11 April 2026)
Tags: music, notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/radio-pepel-dayte-tank/

Today’s slot is a “musical interlude”, in honour of the new album by Dayte Tank (!) (a Russian indie rock band)

[*Radio Pepel*](https://music.yandex.ru/album/41194184?ref_id=70CF5446-369F-412F-A613-E96C81BE71E9&amp;utm_medium=copy_link) («Радио Пепел», “Radio Ash”) is exactly the kind of music that feels like the soundtrack to a film called “life”. If you like to picture yourself as the main character, this recommendation is for you.

The title, by the way, is a nod to the album [*Radio Ogon*](https://music.yandex.ru/album/12348427?ref_id=D05E3D4A-B6A2-469E-9F95-803FEE7587EE&amp;utm_medium=copy_link) («Радио огонь», “Radio Fire”), which the band released 10 years ago. How fire managed to turn into ash between 2016 and 2026 needs no explaining, I think. But while the lyrics do let you know that time has passed, the same certainly can’t be said of the sound. The music here literally works like a time machine, taking you back to the era of the first album.

I’ll be waiting for songs from the new album to turn up on the soundtrack of some film — Dayte Tank (!) always make the shots more striking.

## Undertone: An Audio Horror Built Around a Paranormal Podcast

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/poluton-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-04-08 (8 April 2026)
Work: “Undertone” is a 2025 film directed by Ian Tuason.
Tags: horror, American cinema, announcements
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/poluton-2025/

It’s interesting how much demand there is for audio horror this year.

We’ve only just had [*Rabbit Trap*,](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/lovushka-dlya-krolika-2025/) and now [*Undertone*](https://undertonemovie.com/about) is getting ready to hit cinemas — there the plot actually revolves around a podcast. A paranormal horror podcast, naturally, which at some point gets out of control.

This kind of concept appeals to me more than standard jump scares, because in my scheme of things hearing the grisly stuff is slightly less frightening than seeing it. Perhaps that’s an occupational hazard of working with podcasts all the time. We’ll see whether I change my mind once I’ve watched it :)

## Where Sanding Dreams Was Filmed: My Piece on Shoyna for RBC Style

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/gde-snimali-kosmos-zasypaet-shoyna/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-04-07 (7 April 2026)
Work: “Sanding Dreams” is a work  Anton Mamykin.
Tags: Russian cinema, drama, interview
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/gde-snimali-kosmos-zasypaet-shoyna/

**Film and travel journalism have never been so close**

A very beautiful film, *Sanding Dreams* (*Kosmos zasypaet*), is in cinemas now. In it, Pasha (Mark Eydelshteyn), a student in St Petersburg, goes back to the place he comes from to help his mother and brother, and along the way realises something important about himself and the world. But what went on behind the scenes is interesting here too!

One of the film’s main draws is the place where it was shot: Shoyna, a village beyond the Arctic Circle. There you can see the northernmost desert in the world, and that means utterly Martian landscapes combined with the northern lights and the polar day.

To look beyond the edges of the frame, I [asked](https://style.rbc.ru/impressions/69cfd93d9a79476d3573c729) the filmmakers and local residents what makes Shoyna remarkable, and I think I know which trip is worth planning for the near future.

## How to Make a Killing: An Unpunished Crime, Left to the Viewer’s Conscience

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/naslednik-2026/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-04-05 (5 April 2026)
Work: “How to Make a Killing” is a 2026 film directed by John Patton Ford.
Tags: black comedy, thriller, world cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/naslednik-2026/

I’m not seeing many reviews of the film [*How to Make a Killing*](https://youtu.be/BxBof_p3_es?is=zPAz0kdRlwL3WHKm) with Glen Powell, and yet it is actually a very interesting one.

Becket (Powell), a scion of the noble Redfellow family who has been done out of his share since childhood, grows up and decides to take what is his. For the whole fortune to pass to him, he has to become the eldest of the heirs — in effect, the only one. The main question: how do you deal with the 7 members of the clan who stand between you and the fortune? And this is where the film’s main moral dilemma starts to take shape.

At first the film reminded me of *Scott Pilgrim vs. the World*: 7 evil exes there, 7 evil heirs here, and all of them have to be defeated. Then, once I no longer felt like laughing, it began to look more like [*No Other Choice*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/metod-isklyucheniya-2025/): once again we are faced with the question of what your own well-being costs in a world full of competitors.

But what makes *How to Make a Killing* so riveting is precisely its philosophical side. The question of whether a crime that goes unpunished can be acceptable lands squarely on each viewer’s conscience and lets everyone read the ending in their own way.

---

## Ruki Bressona’s Duality’25 Project: Taking Stock of the Film Year in Two Films

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/dualnost-25-ruki-bressona/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-04-01 (1 April 2026)
Tags: list, notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/dualnost-25-ruki-bressona/

I was delighted to take part in [*Duality’25*](https://t.me/handsoffbresson/30116), the signature project of the Telegram channel Ruki Bressona (“Bresson’s Hands”), which takes stock, as it were, of the film year just ended.

The idea is simple: each participant is asked to pick one film that best captures the essence of the past year, and one film that seems not to come from our timeline at all — so sharply does it contrast with the reality around us.

I chose [*No Other Choice*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/metod-isklyucheniya-2025/) as a reflection of the enforced hard-heartedness that falls to our lot, and [*Legends from the Past*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/legendy-nashikh-predkov-2025/), by contrast, as a bright dream from a time when everything was different. Many colleagues also picked *No Other Choice* as their first film, but [*One Battle After Another*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/bitva-za-bitvoy-2025/) crops up there even more often, which is perfectly understandable too. But the most valuable thing is that you come across completely unexpected associations, ones that broaden the way we see the recent past.

You can see it all together in the insanely stylish PDF album attached to the original [post](https://t.me/handsoffbresson/30116) **👇**

## The Black Countess: Of Freaks and Men Meets Son of a Rich

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/chernaya-grafinya-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-03-29 (29 March 2026); updated: 2026-05-04
Work: “The Black Countess” is a 2026 series directed by Ilya Kulikov, Ivan Korvin.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, supernatural
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/chernaya-grafinya-serial/

## 29 March 2026

After the screening of **The Black Countess** (*Chyornaya grafinya*) at Original+ (the Russian series showcase), I honestly hoped a couple of episodes would land at once on Okko (the Russian streaming service) on premiere day. The first episode, incredibly eventful though it is, breaks off at the most interesting moment. Here’s what I [wrote](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/festival-original-plus-2026/) about the plot:

> The present day. In a lavishly decorated country estate, rehearsals for a play are in full swing. The director, Timur (Yuri Chursin), never tires of reminding the actors that the client has paid a million dollars. The sole spectator (Kirill Käro) arrives, and nothing impresses him: not the artless delight of the actress playing the “niece”, not the drawing-room talk in the manner of 19th-century plays, not even the voyeur’s crack in the wall of the room he has been given, which lets him spy on the ladies at their ablutions. His eyes light up only once one of the actors dies for real. The gun turned out to be loaded with a live round, and the carefully rehearsed shot proved fatal. The oddities don’t end there: first the terrified company discovers that the satellite phone (the only means of communication in a deliberately created offline space) is broken, and then it learns that the mansion where the show is being staged is cursed. Legend has it that it once belonged to a countess who, driven mad by her husband’s death, tormented the peasants until they walled her up inside the building. Ever since, the story goes, nothing has dwelt there but death and disease.

But only one episode came out, and that, of course, is the best way to leave viewers impatient for the second. What interests me most is where the show will take its blend of the aesthetics of *Of Freaks and Men* (Alexei Balabanov’s 1998 film) and *Son of a Rich* (the 2019 hit comedy about a rich man re-educated in a staged 19th century). What we have looks like a colossal, hand-crafted performance for an audience of one — and yet also like a bad dream about captives bound together by a corrupt pact of mutual complicity.

## 15 April 2026

I’m still watching [*The Black Countess*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1378), and by the end of episode three you do, of course, start expecting some new mechanism to keep the suspense going.

We’ve already seen dead characters, and the theories of those who are left don’t look remotely credible. There’s a certain sense of going round in circles, which I hope the events of the next episode will break, because the story has a great deal of potential.

Incidentally, in the way it takes you backstage into actors’ lives, *The Black Countess* is faintly reminiscent of *The Actresses* — another show about the lot of actors, only with nothing mystical about it and firmly rooted in the present day. We can only guess which way *The Black Countess* will lean more.

The character posters are a hefty spoiler as to who will last longer than the rest in this meat grinder.

## 4 May 2026

The deeper into the woods we go, the less I understand what on earth is going on in [*The Black Countess*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1403).

The killing of characters is no longer the main engine of the plot; its place has been taken by a sifting of suspects. That in itself gives events a fresh angle for the closing episodes, but, added to all the other ingredients, it completely blurs the show’s genre. In other words, it pulls the rug out from under the viewer. In some ways that’s even a good thing, but there are caveats.

The Black Countess, the legend of whose fate has already been spelled out more than once in the course of the series, now has a storyline of her own. We now see her whole story — husband, children, peasants — played out on screen, in retrospect, as it were. And this repetition seems to put a noticeable brake on the storylines of the present-day characters (even though only a handful of them are left). It isn’t entirely clear what this on-screen duplicate of the legend is for, but I’ll be hoping very much that it pays off handsomely in the end.

## The Voices of Cats in the Museum 2 and the Real Cats of the Nika Foundation

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/koty-ermitazha-2-intervyu-fond-nika/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-03-28 (28 March 2026)
Work: “Cats in the Museum 2: Treasures of Egypt” is a work  Vasily Rovensky.
Tags: animation, Russian cinema, interview
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/koty-ermitazha-2-intervyu-fond-nika/

I’ve written about a [space dog](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kosmicheskaya-sobaka-lida-2026/) this week, so it’s high time for museum cats (and not only museum ones).

To mark the release of *Cats in the Museum 2* (*Koty Ermitazha 2*, “The Hermitage Cats 2”), the voice actors Darya Blokhina, Snezhana Samokhina and Roman Kurtsyn gave an [interview](https://kino.mail.ru/news/120538-intervyu-so-zvezdami-koty-ermitazha-2-romanom-kurcynym-i-darej-blohinoj/) about the ins and outs of working on the animated film, serving up a heap of interesting facts about how the characters’ vocal personalities were created.

And the interview comes with the sweetest photo shoot featuring real-life fluffballs, who are in the care of the Nika foundation (an animal welfare charity). The feline models were, wait for it: spotted Frosya, shy Lapatulya, sociable Krem, green-eyed Puma and playful Thomas. I don’t know about you, but just listing the names has warmed my heart already :)

The coolest thing about this initiative is that any of the kitties can be taken home, into a real family. A film is always nicer to watch with someone purring at your side.

## The Dog of Many Tomorrows: The Celebration of Cinema We’ve Been Missing

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kosmicheskaya-sobaka-lida-2026/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-03-26 (26 March 2026)
Work: “The Dog of Many Tomorrows” is a 2026 film directed by Evgeny Sangadzhiev.
Tags: Russian cinema, science fiction, family
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/kosmicheskaya-sobaka-lida-2026/

In Russian cinemas from today: [*The Dog of Many Tomorrows*](https://youtu.be/j1VeIolxYfU?si=IK6Kb0isEJE5DzLB) (*Kosmicheskaya sobaka Lida*, “Lida the Space Dog”), an absolute, unqualified celebration of cinema, the kind we’ve been [missing](https://t.me/kino_voice/s/120).

The plot is simple enough to retell — but this, as they say, is one you have to see. Igor is 13, and more than anything he misses his cosmonaut dad, yet for one more birthday all Dad does is send him Lida, a dog who has been to space and came within a whisker of being written off for experiments. At first the boy doesn’t take to the dog, but when he learns of his stepfather’s plan to send him to a cadet school, he runs away from home with his four-legged companion.

That’s when the space dog’s superpowers come to light, letting the kid literally peek into the future and pick his true self from the many versions in the multiverse. Every adult variation of Igor, from a portly beggar to a brazen get-rich-quick guru, is played by Evgeny Tkachuk — astonishing and inimitable, reborn on screen dozens of times in two hours. He’s got Brendan Fraser’s *The Whale* in there, and Doc from *Back to the Future*, and who knows who else — in a word, sheer greatness.

The mention of “multiverses” has surely brought something like *Everything Everywhere All at Once* to mind, and that is exactly the right association. Only in *The Dog of Many Tomorrows* the momentum of fantastical madness comes with the atmosphere of the 2000s, so dear to the heart, a soundtrack running from Delfin to Korol i Shut (Russian rock acts of the era) and, in essence, a story about getting in touch with your eternal inner child. Sangadzhiev has managed to combine a coming-of-age film, science fiction and a road movie, inventing some never-before-seen genre in the process. Everyone will make a discovery of their own, and for that the film is definitely worth seeing.

---

## Wuthering Heights: A Rose Wrapped in Plastic

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/grozovoy-pereval-2026/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-03-23 (23 March 2026)
Work: “Wuthering Heights” is a 2026 film directed by Emerald Fennell.
Tags: drama, adaptation
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/grozovoy-pereval-2026/

I’ve watched **Wuthering Heights**. I can understand a lot of things, but this I did not understand.

The film has come out somehow emotionally out of reach. For its entire running time it tries insistently to plunge us into the sensual abyss of Catherine and Heathcliff, promising, among other things, untold eroticism, but it doesn’t work — not even a little. Some invisible barrier gets in the way, built out of the impossibility of believing either in the characters’ feelings or in the drama around them. It’s as if someone had wrapped a rose in plastic and was holding it out to you, expecting to hear you admire its scent.

At first glance, it’s utterly impossible to fathom how a film with a cast like this, such carefully worked costumes, such inventive camerawork and, when all is said and done, such an outstanding literary source could come out so self-absorbed. But 2 days after I finished watching, I’d venture that the reason lies specifically in Emerald Fennell’s directorial gaze.

It’s no secret that the script takes in only one fragment of the novel, and even that has been reshaped to fit the filmmaker’s concept. And that’s where the answer lies: perhaps the story Fennell chose to tell simply turned out to be weak. We’ve all seen our fill of toxic, co-dependent relationships, and there’s no new lens on them here. The love scenes, seeing as the promo made a point of them, can’t be called revolutionary either. I literally let slip out loud, mid-viewing, that every other contemporary Russian series offers a more interesting reflection of this side of a relationship, and I’ll write it here too.

In a word, the new *Wuthering Heights* was short of a divine spark.

---

## Onegin. I Wasn’t Finished: The Classics Have Been Taught to Go Hard

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/onegin-ya-ne-dogovorila-teatr/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-03-21 (21 March 2026)
Work: “Onegin. Ya ne dogovorila” is a 2026 stage production directed by Natasha Shurganova.
Tags: theatre
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/onegin-ya-ne-dogovorila-teatr/

*Onegin. Ya ne dogovorila* («Онегин. Я не договорила», “Onegin. I Wasn’t Finished”) at the Moscow theatre [a39](https://t.me/a39theatre) is a total knockout.

Zoomer actors are absolutely the best thing that could have happened to theatre in the 21st century. And they seem to have done the best thing that could have happened to *Eugene Onegin* right now. The classic text has been through deconstruction and come back together again — relevant in a new way and clear to everyone.

The “bodily commentary” announced in the production’s subtitle was there too. The utterly mind-blowing techno that accompanies the unfolding of the characters and relationships of Zhenya, Tanya, Olya and Vova (yes, exactly like that: the diminutives of Eugene, Tatyana, Olga and Vladimir) sweeps away every last trace of scepticism. Because the classics have been taught to really go hard. Just think of the 2 women of mature years googling Sydney Sweeney with keen interest during one of the monologues.

I see all of a39’s premieres, and I usually leave pleased to one degree or another. But *Onegin* is an absolute revelation, even alongside the other cool things at this theatre. Every time, I’m impressed by how bold and innovative these guys are, and I recommend them to you with all my heart.

---

## Pride: A Romcom, a Road Movie and a Coming-of-Age Story in One Series

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/gordost-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-03-19 (19 March 2026); updated: 2026-04-20
Work: “Pride” is a 2026 series directed by Sergey Arutyunyan.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, rom-com, road movie
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/gordost-serial/

## 19 March 2026

Thanks to the festival I’ve finally got round to the charming series [*Pride*](https://youtu.be/U4iHVnrZS_s?si=CYT0QA8XxPTpTgj7) (*Gordost*)

It’s the story of a young woman called Alana (Alana Chochieva; that’s her in the video, ranking Ossetian pies), who dreams of making a career as a chef in Moscow, but her Ossetian family has other plans. They want to marry her off, as is only proper, to an Ossetian. So Alana talks her colleague Maxim, a bartender (Aleksey Onezhen), into coming to Ossetia with her as her fiancé — to get a flat refusal and put the whole marriage question to rest. It sounded like a plan, but no such luck.

As Aleksey Onezhen put it, “Everything came from the heart and from love”, and you can absolutely feel it in every frame. Somehow a romantic comedy, a road movie and its characters’ coming-of-age story all sit together in harmony here. And it’s an absolute breeze to watch, which always draws you in so pleasantly.

## 20 April 2026

I’ve finished the romantic, fairy-tale [*Pride* (I wrote about it from the Original+ festival, the Russian series showcase),](https://t.me/kino_voice/1358) and on the whole I’m pleased.

It’s a sweet, unpretentious series with very charismatic leads and an artifice inoffensive enough to pass for a virtue rather than a flaw. *Pride* has vivid visuals, humour that lands — cosy and plentiful — and the right message too: you can’t be happy without being honest with yourself.

Alana Chochieva and Aleksey Onezhen are the best of romantic duos: funny, convincing, and serious when they need to be. And the show’s posters are just too beautiful — I had to attach two at once.

## A Tour of the Gorky Film Studio at Original+: Facts from Film History

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/festival-original-plus-2026/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-03-18 (18 March 2026); updated: 2026-03-21
Tags: festivals, film history, Soviet cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/festival-original-plus-2026/

## 18 March 2026

Bright and early on the first day of the [festival](https://t.me/kino_voice/1347) I raced over for a tour of the Gorky Film Studio (a historic Moscow film studio), where the showcase is being held this year. I’m not joking: I wanted to get in so badly that I woke up at 5 a.m. without an alarm. And I really did add a few cool facts from film history to my store of knowledge. I’ll go by the numbers of the photos in the set, because almost every fact has an illustration:

- Photo 3: this reel holds just 10 minutes of a film. These days, of course, that’s mostly no longer how it works, but every time the sight is a great reminder that cinema is a physical thing. To screen a film like this in a cinema, more than 10 cans of film had to pass through the projectionist’s hands.

- Photo 4: and this is an editing table. Here they looked at every tiny frame of the film against a backlight, cut it (physically), edited it (that is, literally glued the right stretches of film together) and made all sorts of changes to the film-to-be.

- Photos 5 and 6: ingenuity truly worthy of a museum. The round bronze pieces of chain mail are nothing other than bits of tin cans (sprats, saury and similar goodies), bent into the right shape and turned label-side in. With no other fish in the sea as far as materials went (forgive the pun), the costume workshop resorted even to tricks like these; to make the point, one of the pieces has been turned to show the very side with the name of the tinned fish.

- Video and photo 7: a real piece of history, the camera on which Tatyana Lioznova shot *Seventeen Moments of Spring* (the cult 1973 Soviet spy series). The tour gave me a rounded picture of what everyday work with the camera looked like.

- Photo 8: to the right of the guide is a hand-held camera (just 5 kg, light as a feather by the standards of the equipment of the day) with the intriguing name Konvas. It was used to shoot the first footage of Earth from space, the 1980 Olympics and many other historic moments. And it was named after its creator, Konstantin Vasilyev, by joining the first syllables of his first name and surname.

- The most touching fact, though it comes without an illustration. The film *The Dawns Here Are Quiet* is dedicated to the field nurse Anna Chugunova, who rescued the director Stanislav Rostotsky from the battlefield. At the film’s premiere in 1972, Rostotsky personally talked Anna through the film, since by then, because of her age, she could no longer see well.

## 21 March 2026

[Olya](https://t.me/hightechlowlifee) and I have [written about the best](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/news/4012484/) of the Original+ festival (the Russian series showcase) in a piece for Kinopoisk (Russia’s largest film database, media and streaming service).

I’ve already told you about the charming [*Pride*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/gordost-serial/) («Гордость»), which was the one that won; we’ll be watching that to the end. In the piece, be sure to read about ***The Black Countess*** (*Chyornaya grafinya*), coming up from Okko (the Russian streaming service), ***Call Vitya!*** («Зовите Витю!») and ***Pochti nastoyashchy detektiv*** («Почти настоящий детектив», “An Almost Real Detective”), which are worth the wait.

---

## Tryoshka: A Story That Goes Far Deeper Than Domestic Friction

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/tryoshka-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-03-17 (17 March 2026)
Work: “Tryoshka” is a 2026 series directed by Nikolay Burlak.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, sitcom, 2000s
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/tryoshka-serial/

For the last couple of days I’ve had a television at my disposal. That made me want to give a chance to a purely made-for-TV series, ***Tryoshka*** («Трёшка», “The Three-Room Flat”), and I didn’t regret it :)

According to the series, the “housing question” has spoiled the people of Voronezh no less than Muscovites (a nod to Bulgakov’s *The Master and Margarita*), so a family of 9 gets along no better than neighbours in a communal flat. But only the simplest part of the humour is built on the domestic friction between the people sharing the flat.

Watch beyond episode 3 and the story turns out to go far deeper: there is the teenage heroine’s trauma of rejection at school, the brilliant love-hate relationship between the ex-spouses, the classic “fathers and sons”, and a hint of neurodivergence in one of the characters.

The chemistry between Nikolay Naumov and Yulia Aleksandrova is terrific, by the way, and you could watch it for the two of them alone. And the episodes run 25 minutes each, so they’re easy to binge-watch.

---

## Oscars 2026 Results: What Pleased Me and What Disappointed Me

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/itogi-oskara-2026/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-03-16 (16 March 2026)
Tags: industry, Hollywood, notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/itogi-oskara-2026/

[The results](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/news/4012451) of the Oscars both pleased and disappointed me.

On the one hand, a thoroughly deserved Best Actress award went to Jessie Buckley for Agnes in [*Hamnet*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/khamnet-2025/). And an absolutely (in my unpopular opinion) deserved snub for [*Marty Supreme*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/marti-velikolepnyy-2025/) — it’s good when the winner is a film made as art rather than assembled like a construction kit for winning awards.

On the other hand, the main awards went to [*One Battle After Another*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/bitva-za-bitvoy-2025/), which I never warmed to — Best Picture, Best Adapted Screenplay, Best Casting, Best Supporting Actor for Sean Penn, and plenty more besides. The way the individual statuettes were shared out among the crafts and individuals is probably fair, but I find it hard to accept it as the best film overall. I wrote back after my first viewing that for me the pieces somehow all come apart, and I know I’m not alone in that opinion. Luckily, the Academy’s decisions are always something of a compromise, so this year, too, we’re not all that surprised.

---

## On the Ice: A Figure-Skating Series Focused on Its Characters

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/na-ldu-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-03-11 (11 March 2026)
Work: “On the Ice” is a 2026 series directed by Maksim Kulagin.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, sport, drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/na-ldu-serial/

I’ve started the series [*On the Ice*](https://youtu.be/xrbg5wIwAZQ?si=a07EzRgjn_VV6Ykz) (*Na ldu*), and going by the first episode, it has everything in just the right measure.

An instant like for not turning a series about figure skating into a collection of clips of tricks. The focus is squarely on the characters’ personalities, while the ice-rink theme is deftly arranged in the background. The one thing is that introducing the heroine, Ksyusha, by way of skates strewn with shards loses a few points for being formulaic, but the series knows how to work with that too.

A couple of scenes offer a literally meta level of playing with clichés. First, Roman Vasilyev’s character, who pointedly (for the viewer’s benefit, obviously) introduces every girl on the ice to Ksyusha, promptly gets a rude question from her about what all this chatter is for. Second, Ksyusha herself, having ordered “a Bloody Mary, only without the juice” at a bar, is immediately called out by Artyom Bystrov’s easygoing character as a very “original” individual (and thank God, because that way of wording a bar order had my eyes rolling all by themselves). It’s definitely interesting to keep watching: there are plenty of characters, and each comes with some compelling trauma that you just can’t help wanting to watch.

## I Swear: The Most Inspiring Heroine in a Long While

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/ya-rugayus-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-03-08 (8 March 2026)
Work: “I Swear” is a 2025 film directed by Kirk Jones.
Tags: tragicomedy, biopic, European cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/ya-rugayus-2025/

And to continue the theme: I can’t shake the thought that the film ***I Swear*** seems to have created the most inspiring heroine in a long while!

This tragicomedy about a young man with Tourette’s syndrome, trying to live his life despite the whole world’s failure to understand him, would have been impossible without a huge ray of hope. And that ray is Dottie, played by Maxine Peake; I’m attaching one of her kindest scenes to this post.

This heroine is an incredible example of patience, kindness and care for someone who needs it. And, by the way, [a year on](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/mezhdu-nami-khimiya-serial/), I still never tire of comparing characters like this with Walter White from *Breaking Bad*. Dottie, whom the doctors have given six months before cancer kills her, finds the strength to take an incurably ill young man whom society has already written off and pull him through, save him, draw him into life, if you like. It is no spoiler (not least because the film is based on real events) to say that she succeeded. Zero criminal schemes in her attempts to leave a mark behind her for her family and the world — as they say, “makes you think”.

By the way, while you’re watching the video, please also take in Robert Aramayo’s finely wrought performance (he has already won a more than deserved BAFTA for it) and the incredible accents, which give everything that happens an almost documentary tone. The gratitude that fills your heart after watching a film like this is impossible to overstate.

## How “Love Yourself Tender” Was Made: A Piece for Kinopoisk

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kak-sozdavali-k-sebe-nezhno/

Published: 2026-03-05 (5 March 2026)
Work: “Love Yourself Tender” is a work  Ivan Kitaev.
Tags: Russian cinema, comedy, adaptation, notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/kak-sozdavali-k-sebe-nezhno/

While I’ve been musing on adaptations of books that are not exactly “self-help”, the screen version of [*Love Yourself Tender*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/news/4012423/) («К себе нежно», after Olga Primachenko’s self-help book) is arriving in cinemas — and I wrote about how it was made, at the invitation of my beloved colleagues at Kinopoisk (Russia’s largest film database, media and streaming service).

The most intriguing part, of course, is turning non-fiction into a scripted comedy: according to the filmmakers, it was fascinating to do and it did the *Love Yourself Tender* universe good. ## The Time of the Happy: The First Episodes Convince Me Life Is Pain in Any Era

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/vremya-schastlivykh-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-02-26 (26 February 2026); updated: 2026-03-06
Work: “The Time of the Happy” is a 2026 series directed by Ilya Silaev.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/vremya-schastlivykh-serial/

## 26 February 2026

I’m eyeing the upcoming series *The Time of the Happy* (*Vremya Schastlivykh*) with interest (and can’t help connecting its poster with that of the recent *Here* (released in Russia as «Тогда. Сейчас. Потом», “Then. Now. Later”)).

What will unfold before us is a drama about the life of one family — Marina and Ivan Schastlivykh (the surname means “the happy ones”). Before the viewer’s eyes the characters will live through three different eras — 1985, 1999 and 2012 — and be tested not only by time but also by the hardships of family life. All of this is already set out in the [teaser](https://youtu.be/nLbr8L7euQA), where you can also see the two generations of actors who will play the characters.

I think we’ve long been missing a show that would portray the end of the 20th century not from the gangster side but from the point of view of people who were simply trying to live at such a moment in history. *Peace! Friendship! Chewing Gum!* had some of that — it’ll be interesting to see how it plays out this time. We’ll be watching from 5 March.

## 6 March 2026

I never thought [*The Time of the Happy*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1307) would start out like a roller coaster called “33 Misfortunes” (the Russian title of *A Series of Unfortunate Events*). But what surprised me most was something else.

From the very first episode I felt the deepest contempt for the protagonist, Ivan, who is established straight away as an out-of-control cheat and a pathological liar. Despite that — apparently out of sheer contrariness — I watched all 3 of the episodes released so far in one go: it turned into a little hate-binge. I suppose I was hoping to see as soon as possible just how life would punish this character, but so far it feels as though the only ones being punished are the women and children around him.

On the whole, contrary to my expectations of some kind of life-affirming tone, watching it has so far only convinced me that life is pain in any era. It’s funny how the line that “now is a time of opportunity” recurs like a refrain from year to year (the series covers 1985, 1999 and 2012). You get the feeling that so far the only opportunity the characters are taking is the opportunity to lose or ruin something — but what is that if not a subtle hint at marginal realism? :)

Special respect is due to the casting decision for the young and the mature versions of Raisa. Sonya Arzhanykh and Viktoria Zabolotnaya are quite simply the Milly Alcock and Emma D’Arcy of Russian television — an undeniable, unmistakable likeness, and a great stroke of luck for the credibility of the character.

---

## Olga Kromer’s Kazhdy atom: A Hidden Gem, If Not for Its Strange Epilogue

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kazhdyy-atom-kniga/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-02-23 (23 February 2026)
Work: “Kazhdy atom” is a 2023 book by Olga Kromer.
Tags: books, historical novel
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/kazhdyy-atom-kniga/

A book break

Reading [two books](https://t.me/kino_voice/1284) in parallel was not enough for me, so I started a third — and that is the one I finished fastest.

I mean Olga Kromer’s novel [*Kazhdy atom*](https://books.yandex.ru/books/f5m79nAg) («Каждый атом», “Every Atom”): a story packaged as young adult about a 16-year-old Soviet boy in 1937 (I suspect you can roughly guess the hero’s adventures from there). In a broader sense the book turns into a minutely described process of an idealised worldview being replaced by a realistic one. Despite the coming-of-age frame, it is written very vividly, is interesting whatever your age, and is even (something I always particularly value) cinematic, which is why it really does pull you in. The little things of domestic life, of the characters’ everyday existence, of the city and its transport are described in detail.

Pavel Filonov, for instance, flits by in a cameo: the painter who went down in the history of art as the theorist of analytical art, so all is in order there as far as historical accuracy goes. It would be interesting if he were played by, say, Yura Borisov.

I’d even call the novel a hidden gem, if not for one “but”. An epilogue that completely cancels out the characters’ entire journey. To my mind, what the author chose to end the book with turns all its fresh virtues into an incredible truism. This is perhaps that rare case where I would sooner have had an open ending (and I can’t stand open endings) than what is offered as the conclusion of the story. So I highly recommend this book, but advise you to be ready for a strange epilogue.

---

## A Private Life: A Mystery That Is Hard to Take Entirely Seriously

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/chastnaya-zhizn-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-02-21 (21 February 2026); updated: 2026-03-03
Work: “A Private Life” is a 2025 film directed by Rebecca Zlotowski.
Tags: mystery, comedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/chastnaya-zhizn-2025/

## 21 February 2026

I’ve caught the lively trailer for ***A Private Life***, with Jodie Foster, in cinemas more than once, and now my colleagues at [@provzglyad](https://t.me/provzglyad) have shared the details of its release.

This tongue-in-cheek mystery is about a psychiatrist (that would be Jodie Foster) who can’t come to terms with the death of one of her patients and takes on the investigation herself. Given the genre, the whole affair will come with moderately dark jokes and unexpected twists. The trailer even finds room for a romantic storyline of sorts — well, you can’t do without a few bright spots in a set-up this grim, after all :)

Look out for it in cinemas from 19 March.

## 3 March 2026

The tongue-in-cheek mystery [*A Private Life*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1297) will be hard to watch if you take everything in it entirely seriously. Elena Malysheva (the Russian TV doctor and presenter) demonstrated as much by her own example at the film’s premiere — I’m attaching her mini-analysis (watch it only if you’re not afraid of spoilers).

The role of a slightly obsessive psychotherapist with no empathy whatsoever for her own life suits Jodie Foster very well. She isn’t easy to follow, and it’s harder still to feel for her, or even just not to be infuriated by her, but all of that speaks for how three-dimensional the character is. In the mystery’s fictional world she is surrounded by people who are every bit as many-sided. My favourite is the ex-husband, who is such a green flag on every count that he still stands a decent chance of shedding that unpleasant “ex” prefix from his status!

Genre-wise, in fact, I’d also file the film under absurdist comedy: many of the heroine’s decisions point that way, as does the brisk pace at which one gives way to the next. The most interesting thing about the film is talking it over afterwards, and that is always valuable. The hero of the discussion at the premiere, by the way, I officially declare to be Egor Moskvitin (the film critic) — a level of unflappability to aspire to. Thanks to him and to my colleagues at [@provzglyad](https://t.me/provzglyad) for the evening.

## Poster for the 4th Short Film Competition Dedicated to Agniya Barto

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/konkurs-korotkometrazhnogo-kino-barto/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-02-19 (19 February 2026)
Tags: short films, theatre, notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/konkurs-korotkometrazhnogo-kino-barto/

The [4th Short Film Competition](https://t.me/sedmoeiskysstvo/883) has a really cool poster. It’s one of those cases where the textures of film and theatre merge very beautifully: an ordinary child’s ball, just as it would look as a prop on stage, takes on new meanings — and suddenly it looks like the sun slipping behind the smooth surface of the water.

And this year the competition is dedicated to Agniya Barto (the Soviet children’s poet). In Konstantin Khabensky’s words, “she spoke to children as equals, and to adults with the utmost precision”. I believe that is exactly the superpower of the stage and screen arts — so I recommend that everyone concerned take note of the competition :)

## Rabbit Trap: A Film Where Form Gets the Better of Content

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/lovushka-dlya-krolika-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-02-16 (16 February 2026)
Work: “Rabbit Trap” is a 2025 film directed by Bryn Chainey.
Tags: horror, thriller, world cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/lovushka-dlya-krolika-2025/

And from 19 February [@provzglyad](https://t.me/provzglyad) (a Russian distributor) is releasing [*Rabbit Trap*](https://youtu.be/E-JI2acJ26I?si=R51s2-6odT7aeP0I) in cinemas — an enigmatic folk audio thriller that leaves plenty of room for free interpretation.

This is exactly the kind of film where form gets the better of content, which is at once its chief strength and its weakness. It’s set in the 1970s. A couple — sound designers, as we’d call them now — are deep in a remote forest, chasing inspiration to write music. And all goes fairly well until a mysterious child turns up on their doorstep, a child who knows the local evil spirits like the back of their hand.

The associations that spring to mind straight away are the recent [*Die My Love*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/umri-moya-lyubov-2025/) (as a psychological slow-burner) and the by now slightly more classic *A Quiet Place* (for its emphasis on sound as a catalyst of horror). The film’s technical merits (sound and visuals) largely outweigh its screenplay, so in places it can look like video art. For some viewers that may get in the way. But if you’re ready to bring all your senses to bear while watching, *Rabbit Trap* won’t let you down.

---

## Hamnet: A Film That Plunges You into Speechless, Total Surrender to All-Powerful Art

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/khamnet-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-02-12 (12 February 2026)
Work: “Hamnet” is a 2025 film directed by Chloé Zhao.
Tags: drama, adaptation
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/khamnet-2025/

[*Hamnet*](https://youtu.be/xYcgQMxQwmk?si=2Mc0purezlb4R6tJ) is a film that plunges you into speechless, total surrender to all-powerful art.

Chloé Zhao’s film is uneven, its pacing faltering in places, yet it leads in a very straight line to one key scene. I would even say, to a visual image of catharsis, one that in this case we can not only feel but actually see.

What is also unique is how easily the film lets us peek “behind the scenes” of creation — and here Akhmatova’s famous line about poems growing “from what rubbish” takes on, before the audience’s eyes, the grandeur and doom of ancient tragedy. But that is not all there is to find in the film: you also get a small love story (with *Romeo and Juliet* vibes to it), a family comedy (the brightest scenes in the film) and a slightly mystical storyline about the witchy nature of Jessie Buckley’s character.

In a way, incidentally, both Agnes and Paul Mescal’s William are healers. Agnes follows nature’s recipes to heal the body; William is a sorcerer of word, stage and image. A perfect match between the characters as a couple, and a perfect match between the elements of the film.

---

## Caught Stealing: A Crime Farce Best Watched Without Expectations

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/poyman-s-polichnym-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-02-10 (10 February 2026)
Work: “Caught Stealing” is a 2025 film directed by Darren Aronofsky.
Tags: American cinema, crime, black comedy, thriller
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/poyman-s-polichnym-2025/

[*Caught Stealing*](https://t.me/kino_voice/773) is one of those films best watched without seeing the trailer.

I knew it would be something about crime, that there’d be a [cat](https://t.me/kino_voice/773) in there somewhere (he really does turn out to be a partner in crime!), plus a couple of well-known Russian actors — and nothing more. And that upgraded my viewing experience by several levels. Following the twists and turns in the fortunes of the main character, played by Austin Butler, without the faintest idea how much more he still has to get through is the best viewing experience there is. Of course, the adrenaline-charged storytelling here is undeniable, but what lets it show itself at its best is precisely having no expectations at all before you watch :)

Incidentally, it’s impossible not to appreciate the way the film weaves the funny together with the grotesque (which feels especially true to life on the day Telegram is being blocked in Russia). Darren Aronofsky has made a genuine crime farce, one that combines sheer fantasy with the full awareness that even stranger things are possible. All that’s left is to admire it: cinema, unlike life, lends dramatic twists a great deal of style.

## Spring Blossoms: A March Anthology That Wins You Over with Its Artless Sincerity

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/tyulpany-2026/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-02-06 (6 February 2026); updated: 2026-03-12
Work: “Spring Blossoms” is a 2026 film directed by Anna Kuznetsova, Yulia Lysova, Yuliya Uzkikh, Vladislav Ikonnikov, Yury Korobeynikov.
Tags: Russian cinema, anthology, comedy, melodrama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/tyulpany-2026/

## 6 February 2026

The next film I’m looking forward to in cinemas is **[*Spring Blossoms*](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ptLhAqYHM30)** (*Tyulpany*, “Tulips”) from the studio [@redpepperfilm](https://t.me/redpepperfilm) (they won me over, of course, not least with the purple poster!) :)

The film will be made up of 5 different segments with a blossoming March mood. The directors include Yulia Lysova ([*Morozko*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/morozko-serial/)) and Anna Kuznetsova ([*Intermission*,](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kanikuly-2023/) [*Breathe*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/dyshi-serial/)), whom we have long known and loved for their distinctive style. Look at who is in the cast and that is a sheer delight too: Alexandra Babaskina, Gosha Kutsenko, Yaroslav Mogilnikov, Vyacheslav Chepurchenko and many other actors it is always a joy to see on screen. A spring mood won’t create itself, so I plan to go to the cinema to get one.

## 12 March 2026

Not exactly on the holiday date (8 March, International Women’s Day), but I did make it to [*Spring Blossoms*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1274) — and now I want a spin-off of one of the segments!

This March variation on *Yolki* («Ёлки», the Russian New Year anthology comedy franchise), made up of several segments about love and spring, wins you over with its artless sincerity. Across the four storylines we get the stories of:

- Gosha Kutsenko’s hapless but hard-trying character
- a single-minded journalist played by Yulia Topolnitskaya
- Slava Kopeikin’s amorous zoomer
- (my favourite) Alexandra Babaskina’s and Yaroslav Mogilnikov’s characters, who change each other the way spring does
- a devoted reader of detective novels in the guise of Elena Yakovleva

Everyone, I’m sure, will find a story to their own taste. In places the segments are funny, in places unusually guileless, in places deliberately absurd. But all of them manage to catch the spirit of light, festive cinema that is comfortable to watch and a pleasure to discuss.

The spin-off I want is, naturally, about Babaskina’s and Mogilnikov’s characters :) They are just so sweet, and the situation is one that could perfectly well happen in real life: chance and a bit of spring luck.

---

## Get Back On Your Feet: A Dramedy of Undeniable Realism and Sincerity

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/vstat-na-nogi-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-02-05 (5 February 2026); updated: 2026-03-22
Work: “Get Back On Your Feet” is a 2026 series directed by Pavel Timofeev.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, dramedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/vstat-na-nogi-serial/

## 5 February 2026

I’d been really looking forward to the series [*Get Back On Your Feet*](https://youtu.be/8APSRYcGHE0?si=UByTqt_HIG6u4rlz) (*Vstat na nogi*) — and every second of the wait was worth it.

The story of a man who returns to his home town after 20 years in prison and gets to know his daughter, who is in a wheelchair, all over again may sound from the description like some kind of social-issue gloomfest. But in this case it is nothing of the sort. *Get Back On Your Feet* is an excellent dramedy, and one whose realism, conviction and sincerity towards the viewer cannot be denied. It has a vivid atmosphere, perfectly chosen music and dialogue whose lines sound alive. And above all, the chance to recognise a little piece of yourself in every one of the characters.

Gosha Kutsenko (Stary, just out of prison) and Mila Ershova (the strong-spirited Olya) turn in stunning performances. Thanks to their tense interplay on screen, just 2 episodes in you understand what a gigantic echo the deeds of the long-gone 90s and 00s still have in our time. On the one hand, there are the awkward jokes about almond milk (“what, do they milk the almonds?”); on the other, the maimed family photo albums and entire lives. And this approach is no less important and serious a reckoning with that era than the numerous series set directly in the “wild 90s”.

I’d also like to single out the way the character posters are done. It’s as if someone (fate/the universe/God, take your pick) is looking down on each character from above, weighing up how they will use the chance that has come their way. For some it’s a chance at freedom, for others at love, and for some at nothing less than a new life. It’s nice when a series’ overarching idea is reflected so painstakingly in the details of its promo.

## 27 February 2026

[*Get Back On Your Feet*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1268) is past its halfway mark, and episode 5 cements the series’ reputation as the most finely crafted content since the start of 2026.

It’s amazing how a story about an ex-convict, light-fingered taxi drivers and a not especially empathetic coffee-shop owner can turn into a circle of mutual help and mutual forgiveness, where people start to understand one another and rescue cats. It’s incredible what a blend of light and sorrow is packed into the modest little plot strand about Sanka the barista, who rescues Olya when she gets stuck in the mud in her wheelchair. After this episode, living becomes a little less frightening, which means none of it is in vain.

And of course, the whole way through I’d been racking my brains over where the cats were, if we’d been promised a “Kotofeynya” (a cat café)?! Thank you, two cats shown at once, quota met :)

## 20 March 2026

In between festival series I found time to take in the finale of [*Get Back On Your Feet*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1326).

It fits the concept of “simple and tasteful” perfectly. And it does so with such talent that you want to appoint simplicity, in place of Chekhov’s brevity, the sister of talent.

The way the final problem with the meanie played by Alexandrova is resolved turns out to be so humane and artless that it’s actually surprising. How little it sometimes takes for a happy ending and catharsis. Which makes the imperfect resolution of the conflicts around Olya and Roma’s relationship look all the more realistic. There is no point waiting for every problem to be solved once and for all, otherwise you may never start living.

## 22 March 2026

And to go with the finale of [*Get Back On Your Feet*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1365) I wrote [an important piece](https://theblueprint.ru/culture/specials/okko-on-your-feet) for The Blueprint (a Russian fashion and culture outlet) on the rules of simple humanity.

The piece brings together comments from Anton Sankevich (Sanechek, the barista from the cat café), Zlata Varlamova (a consultant on the series *Get Back On Your Feet*) and Yulia Saponova (head of the Inclusion in Cinema project). Do read them — to my mind, these simple truths hold the very thing the whole world is so short of right now.

And the quote that, for me, is the key one in the text belongs to Anton — but I’d be glad if it became a thought we all share:

> I love love

---

## 14 Films for Valentine’s Day: A Blind Date

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/14-filmov-svidanie-vslepuyu/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-02-03 (3 February 2026)
Tags: list, melodrama, rom-com
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/14-filmov-svidanie-vslepuyu/

**14 Films for Valentine’s Day**

Valentine’s Day gets plenty of attention in the media, but your mood doesn’t always match the adverts about romance. Some people spend the day as a couple and some on their own, but a great film is sure to brighten it up — and you can pick one from this list.

>  Below I’ve gathered 14 films, but without their titles: each is described only by the mood it leaves you in afterwards — a blind date of sorts. Click on the effect you like the sound of and you’ll land on the film’s page on Kinopoisk (Russia’s largest film database, media and streaming service), so you can decide for sure whether it’s the one for you. You could pick one every single day until 14 February

## Rag Union: A Half-Forgotten but Heart-Warming Film

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/tryapichnyy-soyuz-2015/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-01-31 (31 January 2026)
Work: “Rag Union” is a 2015 film directed by Mikhail Mestetskiy.
Tags: Russian cinema, comedy, flashback
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/tryapichnyy-soyuz-2015/

I’m taking up the \#KinoFlashback baton from Olya Belik’s [KinoKotik](https://t.me/kinokotik/11859) (thank you) to tell you about a slightly forgotten but heart-warming film.

I thought long and hard and in the end settled on Mikhail Mestetskiy’s [*Rag Union*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/742198/) (*Tryapichny soyuz*). It’s a film from 2014, not all that old, but to my mind nowhere near enough people have seen it :)

Here we get a young Ivan Yankovsky, Alexander Pal and Pavel Chinaryov as we’re quite unused to seeing them. They play three charismatic rebels who make up a cell of actionist artists. By chance they meet Vanya (Vasily Butkevich), an ordinary lad who is so thrilled with his new friends that he’s eager to join in all their schemes (anything beats advertising gravestones).

Judging by what happens in the film, the life of an actionist turns out to be pretty full — and not always of art. So there’s room here for absurdist comedy, wonderful black humour, a rom-com (once female company appears) and the pithy motto “*Push one thing and another falls*”, which you just want to carry off into your own life afterwards (which is, in fact, what I did).

In short, you’re guaranteed the atmosphere of a summer adventure you’ll spend the rest of your life doubting ever really happened.

I’m passing the nostalgic baton on to the channels [Sedmoe Iskusstvo](https://t.me/s/sedmoeiskysstvo) and [Bloknotik o kino](https://t.me/s/kinobloknotik) — I’m sure your film flashbacks will be impressive.

## The Viral Potential of Sport in Cinema and the Cannibalisation of Attention

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/virusnyy-potentsial-sporta-v-kino/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-01-27 (27 January 2026)
Tags: series, sport, industry
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/virusnyy-potentsial-sporta-v-kino/

On the viral potential of sport in cinema and the cannibalisation of attention

I can’t help setting [*Heated Rivalry*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1243) alongside [*Marty Supreme*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/marti-velikolepnyy-2025/) when it comes to the viral potential of showing sport on screen. Both centre on athletes who travel to international competitions, which makes for plenty of spectacular scenes of the sporting contests themselves. Both works have made waves of a sort: the hockey story has created a fully fledged new fandom, while the tale of a ping-pong player is already building Oscar expectations for Timothée Chalamet.

And yet with *Heated Rivalry* we are seeing hockey mania everywhere: rising ticket sales for hockey games (Bloomberg [reports](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-01-21/heated-rivalry-tv-series-draws-casual-fans-to-nhl-hockey-games?utm_source=chatgpt.com) a rise of more than 20%), rising sign-ups for hockey classes and other knock-on effects you can see in online trends. With *Marty Supreme*, though, there is practically no such effect — even though ping-pong was aestheticised there for all it was worth (just think of the film’s orange promo in honour of the hero’s branded balls). There is, of course, a rise in ticket sales for ping-pong matches — also of more than 20%, the Guardian [says](https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/jan/24/ping-pong-american-revival-marty-supreme-table-tennis) — but going by gut feeling you would never know it.

Of course, the two belong to fundamentally different genres, to say nothing of the fact that one is a series and the other a film. But something tells me that if *Marty* hadn’t come out at the very peak of the whole world finishing *Heated Rivalry*, our feeds would be filled with the aesthetics of table tennis rather than hockey :)

---

## Marty Supreme: A Comic Hymn to Faking It Until You Make It

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/marti-velikolepnyy-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-01-25 (25 January 2026)
Work: “Marty Supreme” is a 2025 film directed by Josh Safdie.
Tags: drama, sport
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/marti-velikolepnyy-2025/

[*Marty Supreme*](https://youtu.be/67nRr6DubE0?si=ZIqRfpmQusE3a7SR), it seems to me, is not one of those films that set out to please the audience. Paradoxical as that may sound, given its adrenaline-fuelled pace, its snowballing events and its panoramic historical backdrop.

First and foremost, this film is a rather comic hymn to the fake-it-until-you-make-it approach — that is, pretend until you get there. Its living embodiment is Marty Mauser himself, played by Timothée Chalamet. Not, to put it plainly, a hero who inspires much sympathy, both because of his brazen nature and because of certain things the plot leaves unsaid (the reasons for his fierce hatred of his mother never did become clear to me). And much as one would like to believe in the inevitable success of said approach, the most satisfying thing here is the ending the hero arrives at. Does he win? Yes, but not at all in the way he was counting on.

As for the performance by Chalamet, whom everyone is tipping for an Oscar for the role of Marty — in my humble opinion, it isn’t so outstanding a piece of acting as to be in the running for the statuette. It’s an impressive but not a staggering role, if you set aside the 6 years the actor spent learning table tennis and the deliberate worsening of his eyesight so that the prescription glasses would look convincing on screen. The problem is that all this escapes the notice of a viewer who may know nothing whatsoever about how actors prepare for their roles. And what actually happens in the film doesn’t work on you at so fundamental a level.

Still, that doesn’t make the story any less carefully worked out or any less likely to provoke discussion after the credits, which is the main thing.

---

## A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms: The Sweetest Corner of the Game of Thrones Universe

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/rytsar-semi-korolevstv-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-01-21 (21 January 2026); updated: 2026-02-24
Work: “A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms” is a 2026 series directed by Owen Harris, Sarah Adina Smith.
Tags: series, fantasy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/rytsar-semi-korolevstv-serial/

## 21 January 2026

The sweetest corner of the *Game of Thrones* universe has been found!

Such are my impressions after the first episode of [*A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms*](https://youtu.be/IvGDPA9SbFE?si=l_FFQL-NFU_MSrSh). In a single episode the story manages both to charm and to mark out where it stands apart from the main franchise in genre and tone — everything here is somehow lighter and more naive, yet more accessible. Convincing and without unnecessary drama, as they say.

Dunk, a hedge knight (meaning he doesn’t serve one lord but hires himself out to various ones — a sort of medieval freelancer), sets out from scratch in the world of knights after the death of the old man he served as squire. At the very first inn he meets his future squire, Egg — a very stubborn but loyal boy. From that moment on, things swerve into a charming buddy movie that holds your attention through its two opposite extremes. All of this, incidentally, takes place 100 years before Daenerys’s fight for the throne, so Targaryens will turn up somewhere along the way too.

Dunk (Peter Claffey) is one of the most guileless heroes I’ve seen in a modern series. His character does a great job of making you believe in what is happening and, at the same time, of deflating the pomp — and that is a real find for Martin’s universe, where until now practically everything has played out in deadly earnest. Here, though, it’s the irony that wins you over most of all — it turns out to have a place even in the brutal Middle Ages :)

## 29 January 2026

And [*A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1235) keeps on delighting.

The second episode actually comes across as a great family dramedy in fantasy trappings (well, if you forget the first scene). A really lovely, complementary bond has taken shape between Duncan and Egg, in which the child is sometimes wiser than the adult, and the adult more guileless than the child. It all makes for a great viewing experience — made for grown-ups, it would seem, yet with a warmth and humour we often get only in children’s content.

But even though there is none of the stifling haughtiness of the other parts of the *Game of Thrones* universe here, the pace is still pretty slow. 2 of the season’s 6 episodes have gone by, and our hero still hasn’t begun competing in the tournament. They’re taking their time saddling up, but after [*House of the Dragon*](https://t.me/kino_voice/170) we’re used to that.

## 3 February 2026

The ending of the third episode of [*A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1235) is greatness in its purest form!

A single scene pays off both the slow pace of the first episodes and the seeming toothlessness of it all. What’s more, the twist revealing Egg’s origins lands perfectly at the midpoint of the season: there are 3 episodes still to come, which is just the right amount of time to explore the character in his new capacity.

The showrunners deserve separate praise for the slow build within this particular episode — an out-and-out buddy movie slid smoothly and hypnotically into palace intrigue. And here, as they say, watch closely: in the final minute of the episode every glance, every shift of tone and every gesture counts. I rewatched that scene about 4 times and am now, of course, impatient for what comes next (and I’m also sorely tempted to run a couple of chapters ahead of the series in the book)

## 7 February 2026

Thanks to the Super Bowl, HBO decided to put out the new episode of [*A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1264) a couple of days early (so that the game wouldn’t go and snatch the viewers’ attention) :)

As for the episode itself, it is simply a raw nerve with a running time of 35 minutes. The hero’s nightmare (in both the literal and the figurative sense), in which utterly insoluble problems arise one after another, snowball-fashion (true to life, on the whole).

But as you watch, of course, you admire the staging of this ever-tightening plot 1000%. Peter Claffey gets to show his acting range in style — we have seen him embarrassed, cheerful, upset, and now the palette has gained the shade of a genuinely stung knight, one who no longer resembles the awkward peasant of the earlier episodes. Before us stands not a boy but a man, as the saying goes. And watching him is a great stroke of luck for a viewer.

## 18 February 2026

In the fine tradition of HBO shows, one of the episodes of [*A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1276) was bound to lead us away from the main plot and introduce us to the hero’s past or to entirely new characters.

That episode turned out to be the fifth, which combined Duncan’s life story with a wonderful battle scene. The device that allowed these events to run in parallel is in some ways already familiar — remember how, in *Game of Thrones*, Tyrion fell at the Battle of the Blackwater and missed the whole thing. Only there it looked more like a way of saving the budget, whereas in *A Knight* it comes across as a clever way of handling the episode’s modest running time and the viewer’s attention.

All the same, never before have I wished so much for a season finale to run a couple of hours :)

## 24 February 2026

The finale of [*A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1295) leaves you with a feeling of complete harmony about what you have watched.

The six episodes of the first season are a wonderful example of how to combine a buddy movie, gripping action, drama in measured doses and finely calibrated humour. It leaves the viewer (however deep into the lore of the *Game of Thrones* universe they may be) practically no chance of getting bored or, God forbid, of going away dissatisfied. An exemplary miniseries that will clearly take its place among the best of 2026.

It’s especially heartening that the series has already been renewed for a second season, which will come out in 2027. So we add it to our watchlists and finish reading Martin’s source text :)
