## Heated Rivalry and Collaborations: How Brands Jumped on the Series

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/heated-rivalry-kollaboratsii-brendov/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-01-20 (20 January 2026)
Work: “Heated Rivalry” is a work  Jacob Tierney.
Tags: series, pop culture, notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/heated-rivalry-kollaboratsii-brendov/

Speaking of collaborations, by the way: the series [*Heated Rivalry*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1213) has shown beautifully how global brands can jump on buzzy shows and react in the moment, on social media and beyond.

IKEA Canada, for example, played on the catchphrase “I’m coming to the cottage” (to be read strictly in a strong Russian accent) by recreating the cottage’s interior with its own furniture. And the ginger ale one of the characters adored went one further and set off for the cottage itself.

After that, the least I want is to see a signature [squid salad](https://t.me/kino_voice/715) inspired by [*Outsource*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/autsors-serial/) on a delivery app somewhere :)

## The Cheshire Cat: Three Facts About the Character’s Origins

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/cheshirskiy-kot-proiskhozhdenie/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-01-19 (19 January 2026)
Work: “Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland” is a work  Lewis Carroll.
Tags: books, notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/cheshirskiy-kot-proiskhozhdenie/

In the course of the [giveaway](https://t.me/kino_voice/1214) of a Cheshire Cat figurine, I got curious about his origins myself and found out a couple of interesting facts:

- In Nabokov’s translation of *Alice in Wonderland* (which is called *Anya v Strane chudes*, “Anya in Wonderland”) the character is named, of all things, Maslenichny kot (“the Shrovetide Cat”)

- The illustrator John Tenniel, who did the pictures for the 1890 edition of Carroll’s text (the first picture is, as it happens, a detail from it), had already drawn a nameless grinning cat for a political cartoon before that. Such is the prosaic side of the character

- The Cat’s geographical tie to the county of Cheshire is explained by local cheesemaking! It all comes down to the shape of the cheeses made in the area: they were sometimes moulded with the imprint of a cat’s head, which may have cemented the link between cats and the county in folklore.

---

## Anora and Heated Rivalry: Russian Characters Best Heard in the Original

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/anora-i-zharkoe-sopernichestvo-bez-dublyazha/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-01-15 (15 January 2026)
Tags: dubbing, world cinema, pop culture
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/anora-i-zharkoe-sopernichestvo-bez-dublyazha/

On the subject of watching without dubbing

For the last 2 years I’ve been delighted by the sheer weight of the works that Russian-speaking viewers can — simply 100% — watch without dubbing, because the whole point of them is the Russian characters :) Incidentally, the Russian characters’ names there seem hand-picked to be unpronounceable (that’s my impression) for English speakers — Igor and Ilya, come on.

Yes, I mean [*Anora*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/anora-2024/) and [*Heated Rivalry*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1213). And in both cases the interesting part is not the characters’ Russian but their English — with the charming accent of home, a pronunciation all its own and a recognisable intonation. Sometimes with inimitable bursts of Russian swearing thrown in, of course. It’s nice when your native language becomes part of pop culture!

## Shrek in the Original: Every Character Has Their Own Accent

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/shrek-2001/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-01-15 (15 January 2026)
Work: “Shrek” is a 2001 film directed by Andrew Adamson, Vicky Jenson.
Tags: animation, rewatch, dubbing
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/shrek-2001/

After this [revelation](https://t.me/kino_voice/1182), *Shrek* got rewatched in the original over the holidays, and it turns out every character in it has their own accent! I noticed it from how differently they pronounce the word “donkey”, and after that there was no stopping my linguistic investigation.

First of all, of course, Shrek himself: surprising as it is for us, he has a Scottish accent. Mike Myers, the original voice actor, wanted it to give him a working-class association. Originally the character, like Myers himself, had a Canadian accent, but at the last moment all the lines were re-recorded. Incidentally, in the original Shrek sounds nothing like he does in the dub we are used to. He is less distinctive and less matey than in Russian — to my taste, the character even pales a little because of it.

Next, Donkey. In the original his accent comes from Eddie Murphy: colloquial American, the so-called African-American Vernacular English. In the Russian dub, again, that colloquial quality doesn’t seem to come across; if anything, Donkey just seems like a party-loving dude :)

Fiona gets the happy medium, which makes sense. As a representative of two worlds at once, she speaks with a Californian accent. It is associated with switched-on young people, sometimes from a subculture, which in the case of Fiona and her transformations is almost true :)

Our beloved son of Snow White and a Dwarf, Lord Farquaad, speaks pure British English. Here, admittedly, it does him no credit: the accent was chosen only to underline the character’s arrogance and misplaced pride.

A bonus: the first *Shrek* has a scene where they meet Robin Hood in the forest. This noble outlaw speaks with a pronounced French accent — even though he belongs squarely to British folklore. I’m waiting for your theories, because no sane explanation has been found.

---

## Reservation: A Dystopia That Really Draws You In

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/rezervatsiya-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-01-14 (14 January 2026); updated: 2026-01-28
Work: “Reservation” is a 2026 series directed by Aleksey Andrianov.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, science fiction, thriller
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/rezervatsiya-serial/

## 14 January 2026

I’m watching the trailer for ***Reservation*** (*Rezervatsiya*), and for now, of course, I don’t know where to look first.

The adaptation of Stanislav Gimadeev’s novel *Printsip chyotnosti* («Принцип чётности», “The Parity Principle”) arrives on Kion (the Russian streaming service) from 1 February. The cast includes Filipp Yankovsky, Polina Gukhman, Yuri Nasonov and other interesting actors.

The sci-fi plot spins around a hero who wants to rescue his family from an anomalous zone, cut off from the outside world by an invisible barrier after a mysterious incident. And here, of course, themes of moral choice, the loss of home and the post-apocalypse all get mixed together, while the series itself is billed as a detective thriller. I hope they manage to combine it all harmoniously, because I’d very much like to watch characters played by actors like these.

## 28 January 2026

[*Reservation*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1216), Kion’s dystopian thriller, had a big premiere yesterday at the Khudozhestvenny (a historic Moscow cinema), and I came away from it with a completely new attitude to the genre.

I’ve always been wary of science fiction with a dash of social commentary. In this genre it’s quite hard to sketch out the set-up in a way that wins your trust rather than making you sceptical about the overly earnest behaviour of characters whose world we haven’t yet had a chance to get into properly. Here, by contrast, everything is put together so harmoniously, each part complementing the others, that the story really does draw you in. And the details are very carefully worked out, too.

In the story, Sergei (Denis Shvedov), given the chance to return home, discovers that his home town has turned into the closed zone of an unknown anomaly. His wife and daughter want nothing to do with him, and the rules of the reservation are more reminiscent of a prison camp. In the middle of all this he is trying to work out what is going on, survive, win some support and hold on to his humanity.

➡️ So for us, the viewers, the world of the reservation opens up first and foremost through the secondary characters, who represent the different sides of that world. I’ve grown especially fond of the local “IT guy” (making allowances for the level of technology left in a zone with no internet or mobile signal), played by Yuri Nasonov. He somehow manages to combine the character’s shadiness with what seems to be a noble core. And Nikita Pavlenko’s character looks promising too: his villainous charisma makes it clear straight away that you’d better not relax.

It premieres on 1 February; I’ll keep watching with interest.

---

## Total Recall After the Holidays: A Synopsis for Going Back to Work

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/vspomnit-vsyo-posle-kanikul/

I’ve slightly tweaked the synopsis from the film’s [page](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/2443/) on KP (Kinopoisk, Russia’s largest film database, media and streaming service) to make it more [relevant to you and me:](https://t.me/kino_voice/1211)

> Life for Doug Quaid, an ordinary working guy, is dull and monotonous. So, to get at least some fun out of it, he decides to take 12 days off work. During that time impulses are sent into his brain from an endless stream of tangerines, mayonnaise salads and New Year films — now he is a different man, living a different, interesting life. All would be well, but after the session Doug has to go back to work. Now it is utterly impossible to tell who he really is — an ordinary working stiff or a chill guy who has mastered every form of rest and doing nothing, as well as the recipes for 6 varieties of Olivier salad (the Russian New Year salad). His colleagues fear him, people want him dead over deadlines, management has declared open season on him; even his beloved wife is trying to wring his neck, because the December pay ran out back last year. Now, to survive, he needs total recall.

P.S.: The still shows what I didn’t forget to take to work today in place of my head.

## Gone with the Wind: The Bottomless Grief of a Lost World

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/unesyonnye-vetrom-1939/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-01-06 (6 January 2026)
Work: “Gone with the Wind” is a 1939 film directed by Victor Fleming.
Tags: American cinema, adaptation, historical, film history
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/unesyonnye-vetrom-1939/

When, if not over a long weekend, are you supposed to watch epic historical adaptations?

That is how I made the acquaintance of ***Gone with the Wind***. I expected roughly nothing of the film and hadn’t read the book beforehand, so I simply put my trust in it. And I was right to.

Not only is the film fantastic for 1939, it is extremely impressive by the standards of screen adaptations too. But the main thing is that neither the particular stretch of history nor the text of the source novel sets any limit on the bottomless grief you can feel through the screen: grief for a lost world, for a life gone by that will never come back. An astonishingly ageless story.

In that respect the atmosphere is, of course, [reminiscent](https://t.me/kino_voice/1198) of *Burnt by the Sun*: the same vibe of one particular world collapsing hopelessly before our eyes. The same fateful irreversibility paired with a paradoxical will to live in spite of everything. It’s great that this motif comes in different incarnations: everyone can find a film of their own.

## Buratino: A Children’s Blockbuster with a Charming Italian Accent

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/buratino-2026/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-01-03 (3 January 2026); updated: 2026-04-02
Work: “The Golden Key: A New Pinocchio Story” is a 2026 film directed by Igor Voloshin.
Tags: Russian cinema, fairy tales, family
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/buratino-2026/

## 3 January 2026

What’s good about [*Buratino*](https://youtu.be/wbNkmDCZS94?si=CNZw3QUpPerYPRTs) (the Russian Pinocchio; international title *The Golden Key: A New Pinocchio Story*) is its individual strokes of inspiration.

First, this children’s blockbuster comes with a charming Italian accent: all the lettering, the signs and some of the musical numbers are in that melodious language, and an impassioned “Basta!” keeps slipping into the characters’ speech (and no, this is not an attempt to summon Vasily Vakulenko, the rapper known as Basta). Karabas Barabas’s actors, for instance, aren’t performing any old thing but Italian commedia dell’arte! It made me want to rewatch the Italian-style New Year special of *Evening Urgant* (the Russian late-night show).

Second, the performances are, without exception, very good. And although none of the “human” characters gets much screen time as such, every appearance by the characters, from Papa Carlo and Harlequin to Alice the Fox and Duremar, is vivid and distinctive. To my mind that is quite a rarity, especially in the fairy-tale genre.

Third, the film is focused on one central theme: finding yourself in a world where you are different. Director Igor Voloshin’s fairy tale says it loud and clear from the screen: be you a log or a cockroach, the main thing is not to listen to the ill-wishers and to go your own way, guided by sincere motives and the support of your friends. As messages go, it is therapeutic at the very least, for adults and children alike :)

## 2 April 2026

For the online release of [*Buratino*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1194) I’ve gathered all the interesting facts about the characters’ costumes into a single [piece](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/4012524/) for Kinopoisk (Russia’s largest film database, media and streaming service).

If you didn’t see this fairy tale with an Italian accent in the cinema, watching it online is the ideal way to take in every detail at once. I, for one, completely failed to notice in the cinema which animals are embroidered on Harlequin’s costume, or what jewellery Malvina wears. I was delighted to find out while writing the article, and I want to share it with you.

---

## The Incredible Adventures of Shurik: The Navazhdenie Salon as a Nod to Gaidai

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/neveroyatnye-priklyucheniya-shurika-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-01-02 (2 January 2026)
Work: “The Incredible Adventures of Shurik” is a 2025 film directed by Roman Kim, Misha Semichev.
Tags: Russian cinema, New Year, musical, Soviet cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/neveroyatnye-priklyucheniya-shurika-2025/

This isn’t the first time I’ve found some less-than-obvious treats in the New Year film medleys from TNT, the Russian TV channel (as happened last year, see [here](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/novogodnie-parodiynye-shou-kapsula-vremeni/)).

In [*The Incredible Adventures of Shurik*](https://youtu.be/Vgmx9YBJ0rw?si=d6Rv49NnIm0RHD_s), for example, there’s a moment when the main characters, engrossed in the lecture notes, walk into a nail salon and both pick a mustard-coloured polish (still 3), a nod to the scene with the sausage and the mustard in the original, Gaidai’s *Operation Y and Shurik’s Other Adventures* (still 4). The interesting thing here is that the salon is called Navazhdenie, “Obsession” (still 1) — just like Gaidai’s segment about a slacker student before an exam (still 2)! The name is even written in a similar typeface, so it quotes the famous title card visually as well :)

## No Other Choice: Everything We Love About Korean Cinema

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/metod-isklyucheniya-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-12-30 (30 December 2025)
Work: “No Other Choice” is a 2025 film directed by Park Chan-wook.
Tags: Korean cinema, black comedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/metod-isklyucheniya-2025/

Of everything that went unwatched in the pre-New Year rush, [*No Other Choice*](https://youtu.be/MRgxBgJyu6k?si=o0BgzHHDwwDlXcNe) (released in Russia as *Metod isklyucheniya*, “Process of Elimination”) definitely deserves your attention.

It’s a black comedy from Park Chan-wook in which everything we love about Korean cinema works at 100%. A manager laid off by his company because of automation, after decades on the job, does everything in his power to win back his work and the full life he had with his family in a home of their own (it could very well happen to any of us in the near future).

Since this is a Korean film we’re dealing with, there’s ultra-violence, and a critique of capitalism and its social inequality, and a moral dilemma left for the audience to ponder. The protagonist, who is his own antagonist, is played by Lee Byung-hun, and he hypnotically steals your attention for the full 2 hours, making you make every choice along with him. And the ending — unexpected for this kind of hero, and impossible to describe as either a happy ending or a tragedy — makes the film unforgettable in the best sense.

You can still find screenings in cinemas, and in early January the film will arrive on streaming. It’s one of those cases where a film makes a big impression all the way from its poster (I couldn’t choose, they’re both that beautiful) down to its inner details.

---

## Unboxing the Book Based on the Film Legends from the Past

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/raspakovka-knigi-legendy-nashikh-predkov/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-12-26 (26 December 2025)
Work: “Legends from the Past” is a work  Ivan Sosnin.
Tags: Russian cinema, books, notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/raspakovka-knigi-legendy-nashikh-predkov/

The unboxings continue

I’m terribly grateful to my friends at [@redpepperfilm](https://t.me/redpepperfilm), who sent me a parcel with the most wintry mood and my [dream book!](https://t.me/kino_voice/697).

Having opened the box, I rewatched [*Legends from the Past*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/legendy-nashikh-predkov-2025/) that very evening, quite unplanned, simply to recharge on its atmosphere and light (it works beautifully as a New Year film too, by the way, so take a closer look). The book is a fantastic gift for anyone who loves this film: it brings together the mythology of the characters and the behind-the-scenes story of how the film was made, and the two complement each other perfectly. It is also simply very beautiful, with a textured cover and the bindings of its two halves, ribbons with ornamental patterns and detailed illustrations on every page. It is a pleasure not just to read but simply to hold in your hands, like a precious old tome.

Also waiting in the parcel were fragrant spruce sprigs and real forest cones — a hello from the forest spirit Nyulesmurt — along with the sweetest personalised card (guys, you’re besties too!) and a set of drip coffee built on the concept “cup = short film”. It includes my beloved [*Thirty Seconds*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/tridtsat-sekund-2024/) as well as other shorts by Ivan Sosnin, which will now keep me company over the New Year holidays. And the book, by the way, came wrapped up Siberian-warm, in a fur case with a Nyulesmurt aesthetic :) I show it all in the video: details like these are what make the magic of cinema and a real celebration.

## Luc Besson’s Dracula: The Last Romantic, and a Fly in the Ointment at the End

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/drakula-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-12-24 (24 December 2025)
Work: “Dracula” is a 2025 film directed by Luc Besson.
Tags: adaptation, melodrama, gothic
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/drakula-2025/

I’d been meaning to see Luc Besson’s [*Dracula*](https://youtu.be/9ZV0TaSpiG8?si=fyI48zRgiX8L_AGS) for ages, and on balance I’m more pleased than not, but there’s a catch :)

In terms of suspense, atmosphere and the way it adapts the long-established Dracula story, the film works really well. Caleb Landry Jones is simply beyond praise: I believed his every look, every gesture, every shade of his smile, and I’m already planning to watch him in *Dogman* as well. I’m very taken with the idea of an eternal search for the one and only love, and with that proverbial romantic “I love you, I can’t live without you”, which in any other setting might ring false, but not here. And the way the plot arrives at the classic tale of Dracula and another man’s bride comes as a very pleasant surprise — it really freshens up the story as a whole.

But there is a fly in the ointment too. I followed Dracula with great faith in the character — as a rebel, the last romantic, even a punk of his day. You could even say I was rooting for him the way you root for your team. And the ending, in the form it takes in the film, will most likely disappoint a viewer who comes to it in my frame of mind. And it isn’t even a matter of taste here: it’s a problem of logic and motivation, with a hero who had seemed fairly stable and single-minded but who, towards the end, gives in to some impulse the script hasn’t really worked through. I wouldn’t say it cancels out the whole impression, but philosophical questions about the film’s overall idea do arise.

---

## Betsy Isakova: Meet the Author of the Channel

A lot of new readers have turned up here over the past year. I’m very glad to see you all, and I’d like to take the occasion to introduce myself once more.

## Volchok: A Buddy Road-Movie Adventure in the Trappings of the Late Russian Empire

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/volchok-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-12-19 (19 December 2025)
Work: “Volchok” is a 2025 film directed by Konstantin Smirnov.
Tags: Russian cinema, adventure, historical
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/volchok-2025/

I’m seeing criminally few good reviews of [*Volchok*](https://youtu.be/nTPxko3_V8M?si=nY_Hr5hxNPhPjxFq) — and yet what we have here, mind you, is a buddy road-movie adventure with Evgeny Tkachuk, in the trappings of the late Russian Empire.

The premise sounds simple: after his father’s death, an orphaned heir to a fortune sets off to seek protection from a family friend in Nizhny Novgorod and hires the bare-knuckle fighter Volchok to help him. But don’t be too quick to file the film under typical specimens of the genre. The plot here gathers nuances, the convolutions of self-serving family ties and criminal twists at a surprising rate. In the second half, just when you’re ready to catch your breath, the action dashes off on one new loop after another, as if stopping had never been part of the plan. The same goes for the ending — at least several storylines spill out of it, enough for a sequel.

Besides the wonderful Evgeny Tkachuk as good that packs a punch, the cast also includes Daniil Vorobyov as a slippery relative and Sergei Makovetsky — at the very peak of his double-edged charisma. Young Mark-Malik Murashkin handles his part beautifully too — it’s surprising that I had somehow missed all his previous work. The film is also a great success as a piece of craftsmanship — it is sturdily put together, just like Tkachuk’s Volchok himself. The period atmosphere, the costumes, the sets — huge, on the scale of a town — and the camera flying over it all simply don’t let you switch off from what’s happening for even a minute. You want to pore over everything and admire it, as if you were travelling along with the characters.

All in all, it has turned out a very finely tuned and handsome genre piece — how could I not recommend it :)

---

## Polden (Noon): Another Strugatsky Adaptation on the Way

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/polden-serial-treyler/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-12-15 (15 December 2025); updated: 2026-09-18
Tags: series, Strugatsky, announcements
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/polden-serial-treyler/

## 15 December 2025

Monday begins with the series [*Polden*](https://youtu.be/C3Ti4M9c_JE?si=fFF3M7cI92M9Yo1D) (“Noon”)

Exclusive stills have rolled in from [KION](https://t.me/kionru/11642) (a Russian streaming service), taken on the set of this science-fiction story based on the Strugatsky brothers’ novella *Beetle in the Anthill*. The plot promises interplanetary missions, other civilisations and, as so often with the Strugatskys, elements of utopia. And visually it looks like a photo shoot for some fashion brand — all the more so when [Yuri Kolokolnikov](https://t.me/yurikolokolnikovofficial) is in the shot!

Today, by the way, is a milestone birthday for the actor: he turns 45. I can’t help wishing him even more great projects, harmony and beauty — on a fantastic scale.

## 18 September 2026

This week brought the poster and the [trailer for the series *Polden*](https://youtu.be/kvrv87KDAto?si=98Noo2jXjwFN_sxC) («Полдень», “Noon”), another Strugatsky adaptation that we’ll see this autumn.

It reminded me of what Maxim Matveev told me in an [interview](https://daily.afisha.ru/cinema/31863-maksim-matveev-i-nikolas-muavad-o-semkah-zalozhnika-i-ekranizaciyah-mechty/) about his character, Lev Abalkin:

> …I liked Lev Abalkin enormously, because he carries the tragedy of a man left behind, abandoned, turned by chance into someone everyone takes for a monster \<...> He’s interesting for his outward traits too, to my mind — the long hair, the black eyes. That’s cool! He’s come out as a tragically intriguing character, I think.

That description of the character’s inner world is intriguing enough, so I’m looking forward to the premiere on 1 October.

---

## Zootopia 2: The Same Charm as the First Film

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/zveropolis-2-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-12-13 (13 December 2025)
Work: “Zootopia 2” is a 2025 film directed by Jared Bush, Byron Howard.
Tags: animation, family, American cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/zveropolis-2-2025/

It’s been a long time since I saw as many people at a cinema screening (not a festival one) as at the second [*Zootopia*](https://youtu.be/BjkIOU5PhyQ?si=88JVa-fgJtTZ3GXr).

If you look past the picture, cropped for some reason (what, as if we’d never seen subtitles?), the cartoon works practically the same charm as the first film. I could have done with a little more screen time for Nick the fox (yes, he’s my favourite). What did seem too long, on the other hand, was the spelling-out of the psychological subtext in how the partners feel about each other — surely that’s not what we all came to a 6+ film for? :)

In any case, it was nice to see familiar characters in a story about finding a home. And I put all the misunderstandings down to the fact that I watched the first film, after all, 10 years ago, back when the grass was greener too.

## A Blind New Year Selection: 22 Films by Mood

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/novogodnyaya-podborka-vslepuyu-22-filma/

Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/novogodnyaya-podborka-vslepuyu-22-filma/

**22 films for different New Year moods ⤵️**

December has well and truly taken over, the shops are crammed to bursting with New Year bits and bobs, and the festive mood still hasn’t shown up? Never mind: I have a selection of very different films that will help you catch exactly the shade of jingle bells you need most :)

>  Below I’ve gathered 22 films, not by title but by a description of the mood each one leaves you in after watching — a blind date of sorts. Tap the effect you fancy and you land on the film’s trailer or its page on Kinopoisk (Russia’s largest film database, media and streaming service), so you can decide for sure whether it’s the one for you. You could pick one every single day until the end of December.

- [See for yourself that everything happens at the right time](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/821/)

- [Work out which present is truly the most longed-for](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/664/)

- [Get up to mischief and wreck strict plans](https://vkvideo.ru/video-40191159_456266543)

- [Give in to warm nostalgia](https://vkvideo.ru/video5705388_167736432)

- [Save your New Year from the villains](https://vkvideo.ru/video-108943641_456239414)

- [Feel the Epiphany frosts through the screen](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/45694/)

- [Lose yourself in the romance of pre-New Year coincidences](https://vkvideo.ru/video-23482289_456240814)

- [Remember the true spirit of Christmas](https://vkvideo.ru/video-161516291_456239342)

- [Share in miracles made by hand](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/79450/)

- [Laugh at someone else’s workplace commotion](https://vkvideo.ru/video-12332522_167616867)

- [Remember a song that will be stuck in your head until the holidays are over](https://vkvideo.ru/video-61357277_456241887)

## Do Whatever: More Inventive and Original in Form Than Many a Feature Film

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/ty-mozhesh-tak-ne-delat-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-11-30 (30 November 2025)
Work: “Do Whatever” is a 2025 film directed by Farid Aziz.
Tags: Russian cinema, short films, drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/ty-mozhesh-tak-ne-delat-2025/

You don’t often get to see short films on the big screen, but in the case of [*Do Whatever*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/10249471/) (*Ty mozhesh tak ne delat*, “You Don’t Have to Do That”) it’s an interesting experience.

Bear in mind that the film is as metaphorical as they come, so don’t expect clear answers to the questions it raises. The plot, about opposite types of people who destroy each other literally and figuratively, is pretty far removed from reality — and that leaves room enough for differing readings for it to strike a chord with different viewers.

But what makes the film especially notable is its style. This is one of those short films that turn out to be, in many ways, more inventive and original in form than many a feature. There’s the 4:3 framing (it underlines the contrast in what the characters are striving for), and the Nordic chill on screen, and a play with shot sizes that is dense with meaning — in a word, it’s simply very beautiful. And that, you could say, even makes up for a few lapses in meaning.

---

## Hipsters: An Unreal Riot of Colour and Music on the Big Screen

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/stilyagi-2008/
Author: Betsy Isakova

Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/stilyagi-2008/

## 29 November 2025

On overcast December days, when you crave colour so badly, the re-release of *Hipsters* (*Stilyagi*) comes to the rescue!

The director’s cut will be on the big screen from 11 December, and even before that you can catch one of the [special screenings](https://taplink.cc/stilyagi_). In the year of its premiere, too, the film took a huge box office right around New Year, so the folks at [K24](https://t.me/k24films/910) (a Russian film distributor) have a more than solid plan :)

I already can’t wait to brighten up one of these cold evenings with the vivid musical by Valery Todorovsky, whose [*The Thaw*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/ottepel-serial/) I rate very highly. So, as you’ll understand, I couldn’t not share the news.

## 11 December 2025

By the way, [*Hipsters*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1124) is in cinemas from today

Having seen it on the big screen, I’m sure this is one of those films that really are worth watching in the cinema. It is the only way to get the full effect of the unreal riot of colour, music, complex long takes with a flying camera and the film’s other cinematographic flourishes. Although I didn’t include it in [my list of New Year viewing,](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/novogodnyaya-podborka-vslepuyu-22-filma/) you definitely walk out of the auditorium in an uplifted, elated mood that would suit any holiday.

The story doesn’t end once the screening is over: I personally rewatched the film on streaming the very next day, and as for how much I’ve talked about it, that is simply beyond counting. So that is my warm recommendation for the remaining December weekends and evenings.

## Five Russian Films Streaming in November: From You Drive Me Crazy to Postmarks

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/rossiyskie-filmy-noyabrya-onlayn/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-11-27 (27 November 2025)
Tags: list, Russian cinema, streaming
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/rossiyskie-filmy-noyabrya-onlayn/

I don’t usually do round-ups like this, but so many great films worth your attention landed on streaming services in November that I wanted to write them all down, so that nobody misses anything. Here they are, from left to right:

- [*You Drive Me Crazy*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/svodish-s-uma-2025/) (*Svodish s uma*): if I were addressing this film in friendly conversation, I’d say “You Delight Me”. A wholehearted recommendation for any evening, romantic or not so romantic — and it is on pretty much [every streaming service.](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/6103378/)

- [*Lermontov*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/lermontov-2025/): a source of rapture at the opening of Mayak (the Russian film festival in Gelendzhik) and the best motivation to reread Mikhail Yuryevich’s biography with fresh eyes. Available on [Kinopoisk](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/6456151/) and [Okko](https://okko.tv/movie/lermontov-646095801?) (Russian streaming services)

- [*Dad Croaked on Saturday*](https://t.me/kino_voice/469) («Папа умер в субботу»): a story about the family traumas that make us who we are, told without half-tones or smoothing over, but with a smile and a readiness to forgive. Available on [Kinopoisk,](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/5134586/) [Okko](https://okko.tv/movie/papa-umer-v-subbotu?) and [Wink](https://wink.ru/movies/papa-umer-v-subbotu-year-2024?)

- [*Seems Like Love*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/pokhodu-lyubov-2025/) (*Pokhodu lyubov*): a film that has pulled off the feat of combining the present day with *Walking the Streets of Moscow* (Georgiy Daneliya’s 1964 classic) and creating something unique. Coming to Kion, Okko, Wink and Ivi (all Russian streaming services) from 30 November

- [*Postmarks*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/5431555/) («Филателия»): a film I haven’t seen myself yet, which makes its online release all the more welcome. Colleagues write that this drama about the tender relationship between a sailor and a lonely post-office worker is definitely worth watching for its originality and its delicate work with detail. Available on [Kinopoisk](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/5431555/) and [Okko](https://okko.tv/movie/filatelija)

## Yudol: A Pensioner’s Side-Splitting Attempts to Join Satan

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/yudol-kniga/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-11-25 (25 November 2025)
Work: “Yudol” is a 2025 book by Mikhail Elizarov.
Tags: books, black comedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/yudol-kniga/

A book break

I’ve got hooked on Mikhail Elizarov’s new novel (remember the series *The Librarian*? it was based on a novel of his) with the catchy title ***Yudol*** («Юдоль», “The Vale of Tears”). At the centre of the story is a pensioner, Andrey Timofeevich Sapogov, who in the course of his (frankly, unremarkable) life has acquired nothing except the idea of joining Satan.

It’s his side-splittingly funny and at times frighteningly serious attempts that we get to watch. The black humour is just the thing, and the link to the present day is easy to read too. Naturally, everything described is cinematic in the extreme and lets you picture it all in detail right as you read, the way we like to. I’ll keep reading and, of course, wait for the screen adaptation!

By the way, a reminder to everyone who loves reading books on paper: the [giveaway](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/rozygrysh-istoriya-otechestvennogo-kino/) of a wonderful collection about Russian cinema is in full swing — don’t miss it.

---

## One Battle After Another: A Film That Doesn’t Speak to Me at All

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/bitva-za-bitvoy-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-11-24 (24 November 2025)
Work: “One Battle After Another” is a 2025 film directed by Paul Thomas Anderson.
Tags: world cinema, drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/bitva-za-bitvoy-2025/

[*One Battle After Another*](https://youtu.be/kQUPdVxZNPk?si=RZpYgM9QRvwrSQsm) is a film that doesn’t speak to me at all. Even so, all its ambitions for the upcoming Oscars are obvious, as is its overall message.

For the most part I don’t understand the characters or what motivates them, but I understand even less a world in which the heroine seizes military bases yet goes completely unpunished for a long time, then calmly becomes a mother and, after sinking into postnatal depression, returns to her revolutionary cause. What the police and related agencies are busy doing in the film’s universe remains a mystery, one that turns a perfectly realistic film into some kind of science fiction. Naturally, I feel for the young woman, but that doesn’t make the questions go away.

As for the elements in the running for awards: there is, of course, superb acting from absolutely every member of the cast, a distinctive soundtrack and cinematography. For me, the film’s main trouble is how disconnected all its strengths are from one another; because of that, it seems to fall apart into pieces that don’t inspire confidence.

Its central idea, that violence cannot be stopped by violent means, is, frankly, as old as the hills. But the final scene with Sean Penn’s character gives it a topical reading: it is done perhaps more elegantly and more clearly than anything else in the film, and that’s already a good thing.

---

## Kinopoisk’s “Hi, My Name Is…” Bowling Party: Third Place for Team Random

It turned out to be a great event, with bowling, networking and a warm, cosy atmosphere. ## Sentimental Value: A Film About the Healing Powers of Art

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/sentimentalnaya-tsennost-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-11-20 (20 November 2025); updated: 2026-01-11
Work: “Sentimental Value” is a 2025 film directed by Joachim Trier.
Tags: drama, festival films
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/sentimentalnaya-tsennost-2025/

## 20 November 2025

Speaking of atmosphere, by the way.

I have yet to see Joachim Trier’s [*Sentimental Value*](https://youtu.be/c1ykfCes1so?si=1jvm3omzBDwJtWYQ), but I’m looking forward to it, because I want to watch it with maximum attention to detail and, if possible, on the big screen. It’s the Cannes Grand Prix winner, after all!

As it happens, you can see this melancholy dramedy about family, memory and the reconciling power of art, with Elle Fanning and Stellan Skarsgård, this coming Sunday at [Garage Screen](https://garagemca.org/ru/event/film-screening-sentimental-value) (the cinema of Moscow’s Garage Museum of Contemporary Art). It’s a great space: watching films there, or listening to lectures, say, is a real pleasure. My wish is to slip away there despite my mountain of things to do, and I’d advise you to do the same.

## 11 January 2026

[*Sentimental Value*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1104) chimed nicely with the melancholy of the tail end of the New Year holidays.

However many themes the film raises, for me it is first and foremost about the healing powers of art. And the film’s paradox is that it’s easy to connect with every character — no matter how empathetic (or not so empathetic) a person you are.

When the elder daughter, Nora, who has resented her father since childhood for leaving the family and has ended up a depressive, finds something that saves her in stepping on stage and reading the script, you understand her. When the younger daughter, Agnes, has the strength to understand both her sister and her father, you share her impulse 100%. When Gustav himself, a feckless father and a slightly less feckless director, is torn between a fatherhood already lost for good and a life in art that is not yet beyond hope, it’s hard to condemn him. This range of empathies lets you look at yourself as if in a many-faceted mirror: in some facets you look better, in others worse, but the reflection is always honest. And the ending, I think, is a rare case of the notion of “hope” making it onto the screen in full, and for that alone it’s worth getting to.

The film is hurt, ever so slightly, by its deliberate touches of melodrama. Such as Gustav’s brief spell in hospital, or Agnes’s fleeting unwillingness to approve of her son taking part in the film. I’m not inclined to excuse manipulative devices, even though they are, of course, there. But for the subtleties listed above, and for the sequence with a whole family’s history told as if from the point of view of the house, I’m grateful to the film in the end.

---

## Fallout, Season 2: Like Scrolling Through a Feed of Horizontal Reels

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/fallout-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-11-13 (13 November 2025); updated: 2026-02-04
Work: “Fallout” is a 2024 series directed by Frederick E. O. Toye, Jonathan Nolan, Clare Kilner.
Tags: series, world cinema, post-apocalypse, video game adaptation
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/fallout-serial/

## 13 November 2025

We’re expecting the second season of *Fallout* on 17 December, and in the meantime we have the [trailer](https://youtu.be/oWtt280YodE?si=YbdZ5cwFV79jSJuE) to watch.

As I recall, the first season left me with more questions than answers, but that is exactly what we want the next one for. Judging by the first footage, it has even more body horror, principles and moral choices.

## 4 February 2026

As for the second season of [*Fallout*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1082), though — I came down with a *mild* case of not following what was going on.

On the one hand, it’s great that not a single storyline has been dropped: as a rule I’m a big believer in continuing to follow every character myself. At times even characters from the first season whom pretty much everyone had forgotten all about turn up here. But in *Fallout*’s case this makes for such a crowd that having to spread your attention as a viewer so thin becomes uncomfortable.

On the other hand, it may come down to how the episodes are directed. After all, constantly switching between the characters’ practically unconnected storylines was a deliberate choice of method. It’s like scrolling through a feed of horizontal reels, only all within a single show’s universe. Whether this bet on the modern viewer’s particular kind of attention has paid off is hard to judge, but I’ll allow that this way of serving up content is simply not my cup of tea.

Most likely, I won’t be putting on the third season. By the end of the second I had the firm sense that what was flickering across the screen was a narrative an AI had generated for itself: with no room for reflection, no attempt to give the switching between storylines any logic or rhythm. I understand all about the value of attention in today’s world of endless algorithmic feeds, but from a series I would like a more balanced season structure.

---

## Die My Love: A Film That Will Appeal to Deeply Empathetic Viewers

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/umri-moya-lyubov-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-11-11 (11 November 2025); updated: 2025-11-14
Work: “Die My Love” is a 2025 film directed by Lynne Ramsay.
Tags: world cinema, drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/umri-moya-lyubov-2025/

## 11 November 2025

I couldn’t tear myself away from the trailer for *Die My Love* with Robert Pattinson and Jennifer Lawrence.

The story centres on newlyweds who move to the middle of nowhere to devote themselves to their feelings, but instead run into the deepest of crises in their relationship. Judging by the trailer, it has been made with far more depth than you would imagine from the synopsis. Not for nothing does the film have such a promising team:

> The film was made by director Lynne Ramsay, producer Martin Scorsese, cinematographer Seamus McGarvey (a two-time Oscar nominee), and the team behind the films
*The Substance*
>  and
*La La Land*
> .

Personally, what draws me is the contrast between the bright, pastoral colour grade and whatever monstrous events the pair will have to go through. I’ll be waiting for it in cinemas — from 27 November, courtesy of [@provzglyad](https://t.me/provzglyad).

## 14 November 2025

[*Die My Love*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1077) is a film that will appeal to deeply empathetic viewers. And to less empathetic ones too — happily, it has Robert Pattinson’s character, who will be bewildered right alongside them.

The plot, to recap, follows a young couple who move from New York to the middle of nowhere to love and create there (he wants to make an album, she wants to write a book). Instead, the lovers stray into the thickets of a psychic split, brought on both by the changes a baby brings to their life and by their own unfulfilled potential. The catalyst for this madness of the mind is Grace, played by Jennifer Lawrence, who is unsurpassed as a young woman with postnatal depression — and more besides.

There is no need to recount the specific plot turns, because the film exists more on the level of sensations, visual images and blurred feelings. Lynne Ramsay’s direction conveys this, balancing perfectly on the line between the real and the unreal in the artistic world she has created. As a viewer I focused on the heroine, and understood her, as they say, from A to Z. Being unable to put into words what is going on inside you, while knowing that outside forces are carrying you further every second from the self your loved ones are used to — that is exactly what watching Grace over the course of the film lets you understand without words. The stills I’ve chosen for this post are about the same thing: on the outside Grace seems to be part of some celebration of life held for no reason at all, while on the inside she is a scrap of confetti forgotten on the floor, confetti that once glittered in the party lights.

I was especially won over by the scene in which the bathroom gets trashed: it is at once like a claustrophobic horror film, a black comedy and an audiovisual thrill ride that you even feel a little like joining in. So the big screen is recommended — from 27 November, courtesy of [@provzglyad](https://t.me/provzglyad).

---

## Pluribus: The End of the World as a Chance to Amount to Something in Your Own Eyes

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/pluribus-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-11-09 (9 November 2025); updated: 2025-12-27
Work: “Pluribus” is a 2025 series directed by Gordon Smith, Vince Gilligan.
Tags: series, science fiction, drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/pluribus-serial/

## 9 November 2025

I’ve watched the first episodes of [*Pluribus*](https://youtu.be/a6lzvWby9UE?si=KUNaXOPF7IBpFwfh), the sci-fi drama from Vince Gilligan (*Breaking Bad*, *Better Call Saul*) about a virus that merges the minds of all the surviving humans into a single whole. All, that is, except the writer Carol — the heroine, played by Rhea Seehorn — and a dozen or so other earthlings from various countries.

It’s a vivid story that stirs up complicated emotions and questions about what you would do in the heroine’s place. That is exactly why the flawless way it’s all shot takes a back seat, its finely calibrated technique never overshadowing the moral dilemma.

Two episodes in, I’m still mulling it over. The analogies come thick and fast, from Covid and utopian hopes for ChatGPT to video-game NPCs and the trend for non-toxic communication. That is exactly what makes the story multi-layered and ambiguous — above all thanks to its unpredictability, which is quite rare and, of course, makes you want to keep watching. What I find especially interesting is how the heroine’s desire to✨save the world✨ (in the tradition of American cinema) actually serves as compensation for her hang-ups over being unable to write a book that meets her own high standards. The end of the world becomes a chance to amount to at least something in her own eyes — and for that, of course, you might well rise up against the whole world.

It’s curious how Vince Gilligan, known above all for the story of a man who falls ill and starts a new life, has arrived at the story of a woman around whom the whole world has fallen ill — and who has no plans whatsoever to start a new life :)

## 15 November 2025

Episode 3 of [*Pluribus*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1070)

This is the first episode not written by Vince Gilligan, and I was prepared for the earlier pace to be gone. But not to this extent :) Then again, let’s remember that *Breaking Bad* and *Better Call Saul* were also pretty slow to build momentum on their way to greatness.

The series, like the members of the unified mind in its story, seems to have switched into a mode of saving energy and reallocating resources for some future, as yet not entirely clear, purposes.

Nor, by the way, is it obvious where the story might go from here. Everything seems to have stalled, and Carol isn’t asking any of the questions that we viewers would dearly love to have answered.

On the other hand, I’ve started to enjoy the slightly absurd comedy we’re being served. Showing the hundreds of people it takes to run a supermarket where the “self-sufficient and independent” heroine will buy everything for herself is funny and, what’s more, very sobering for everyone on this side of the screen about how everyday life actually works.

## 22 November 2025

Episode 4 of [*Pluribus*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1085) flies by in an instant (and reminds you just how nice it is to binge Vince Gilligan’s shows).

It looks as though the first 3 episodes have taken the measure of the cruelty the new collective world is prepared to resort to. Now it’s Carol’s turn, and she doesn’t seem inclined to make allowances — neither for herself nor for the members of the new race. The unpredictability of her decisions, and of the surrounding world’s reactions to them, is still up to scratch, and that’s a pleasure to watch. Especially given the very easy-to-spot humour at the expense of AI chatbots, famous for their neutral, meaningless answers :)

I hope the second half of the season will give us a better idea of the goals of the heroine and of the “uninfected” like her. But it’s already clear that there’s no getting by without a second and even a third season.

## 28 November 2025

Episode 5 of [*Pluribus*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1109) can, on the whole, almost be squeezed into a quote from *A Clockwork Orange*: *“to have a glass of milk and do a bit of the old ultraviolence”* (only, naturally, with a “not” in it).

It does the story a great deal of good to step beyond the aftermath of an apocalypse that has already happened and move into uncharted territory. The second half of the season is just the time to do it. In particular, Carol’s investigation into the love of milk among the members of the collective mind looks set to spill over (pun not intended) into one of the season’s main plot twists, one that will set future events in motion.

Incidentally, I don’t know whether it’s by design or simply arises as things go along, but the heroine’s attempts to lead the ranks of the scattered “survivors” are played quite comically (and she herself, for one, is aware of it). There’s no point waiting for a turning point at which the series steps into comedy for good or, on the contrary, drops all irony about the absurdity going on. As *Better Call Saul* and *Breaking Bad* taught us, Vince Gilligan is superb at combining all of this (I, at any rate, laughed without holding back at the bit with the drone that couldn’t carry off a bag of rubbish).

## 16 December 2025

Episode 7 of [*Pluribus*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1138) (the most uneventful one, at first glance) could have been labelled “sleeping-pill” content.

Were it not for a couple of genuinely tense moments that show which of the characters is ready for what in this new world! If I ever have to explain what the term “slow burner” means, this is probably the episode I’ll point to. Vince Gilligan is brilliant at this — we remember it from the first season of *Better Call Saul*, which was slow from start to finish.

Here, too, nothing happens, and yet in the background there are shifts on the scale of tectonic plates as far as plot and character development go. Through Carol and Manousos, stagnation and backsliding are set against movement and self-overcoming. The difference in their motives becomes obvious at once: who really cared about saving the world, and who cared about being needed by someone in this new world. And from here on, clearly, the most interesting thing will be to see what endings characters with starting points like these arrive at.

## 23 December 2025

So what’s going on with [*Pluribus*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1155)?

It’s unexpected (though understandable from the point of view of the show’s makers) that the meeting between Manousos and Carol is being put off for so long. Were it not for a couple of striking tendencies in these characters’ behaviour, episode 8 could even be called filler, given how utterly self-contained the two characters’ storylines are.

But what clearly awaits us is an impressive end to the season, with a meeting that ought to justify having to wait for the continuation. In the second season, the clash between ways of adapting to the new life will probably go on and be even fiercer than Carol’s rebellion at the very start. It’s impressive how long the show’s writers have managed to keep the new world order ambiguous — yet another successful example of grey morality, with arguments both for the infected and against them.

## 27 December 2025

The finale of [*Pluribus*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1165) is as imposing as an atomic bomb.

It’s one of those episodes that made all the season’s slow and uneventful ones worth watching. In a modest 50 minutes the finale turns everything upside down twice, and for sheer density of moral about-faces it is simply unsurpassed.

Once again it turns out that man is an alien to man, even when the world is ending. And where the line runs that wipes out cultural contrasts, we find out only in the final shots.

Episode 9 of *Pluribus* has the second-highest IMDb rating of the season — 8.5 (against 9 for the pilot) — and that’s not a bad sign. I’ll be waiting for season two with moderate impatience :)

---

## Tunnel: A Plot That Twists and Turns Like the Road Inside a Real Tunnel

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/tonnel-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-11-07 (7 November 2025); updated: 2025-12-01
Work: “Tunnel” is a 2025 series directed by Fluza Farkhshatova.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, thriller, crime
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/tonnel-serial/

## 7 November 2025

More details are emerging about [*Tunnel*](https://t.me/kino_voice/858).

We now know not only that Elizaveta Boyarskaya’s character will be rescuing her husband, played by Sergei Gilev, somewhere on the border with Finland, but also that we’ll hear Finnish in the series! Hardly first in the queue of languages everyone dreams of learning, but that will make it all the more interesting to listen to. Here is how Boyarskaya learnt it:

> I can’t say I had a lot of scenes in Finnish, but there were some. Looking back, it feels as if I spent forever learning them, because Finnish is a very difficult language. I know German and English well, but Finnish isn’t like anything else; it belongs to the Finno-Ugric group of languages, which is very different from all the other groups. So I might as well have been learning Chinese. But it mattered to me to do it well, so I really did cram the scenes in Finnish and practise with a coach. Those were the most nerve-racking and most difficult moments of the shoot

My inner linguist is intrigued.

## 1 December 2025

Meanwhile, [*Tunnel*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1060) has premiered on Kion (a Russian streaming service)

Going by the first episodes, I’d say you could watch it simply for Sergei Gilev as a funny dad. But seriously, the thriller’s plot twists and turns exactly like the road inside a real tunnel, and behind the solution to one problem the roots of the next are already lurking.

Despite the somewhat TV-style exposition and character introductions, it’s worth sticking with it until the action gets going. From there the cast of characters is richer (Alexander Averin alone, who gives off young Viktor Sukhorukov vibes, is worth it), the motives are more varied, and there are more chances to hear Finnish :)

A rare vibe to catch while watching is the atmosphere of [*Peculiarities of the National Fishing*,](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/osobennosti-natsionalnoy-okhoty-1995/) where the characters ended up in Finland by accident and didn’t immediately work out what was what (luckily, there wasn’t a whiff of thriller about their story).

## The Magic District, Season 2: The Fairy Tale Grown-Ups Have Been Missing

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/volshebnyy-uchastok-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-11-06 (6 November 2025); updated: 2025-12-28
Work: “The Magic District” is a 2023 series directed by Stepan Gordeev.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, comedy, fantasy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/volshebnyy-uchastok-serial/

## 6 November 2025

One of the best feelings a viewer can have is starting the second season of a series the moment you’ve finished the first.

That’s exactly what I did with [*The Magic District*](https://okko.tv/serial/volshebnyjj-uchastok) (*Volshebny uchastok*), having got to know its universe right on the eve of the sequel’s premiere on Okko (the Russian streaming service). It was the best decision: from the very first shot you don’t want to climb out of the story for a minute, and the season finale didn’t let you relax at all. How nice it turned out to be not to have to wait 2 years for the continuation.

Then again, it would have been worth it either way. The second season doesn’t just inherit all the strengths of the first; it multiplies them with interest. Lyokha Popov used to be simply funny in that Perm way — now he’s immortal as well, with all the gags that follow from it. The Gnome used to be simply a foul-mouthed gnome (hard to believe, but he is one hundred per cent my totem character) — now he’s not a gnome at all and not even foul-mouthed (and his vocabulary is cooler still — I’ll be expanding my lexicon). We used to have the familiar Moscow; now we have a St Petersburg that is international in a fairy-tale way (with jokes about mushrooms and salt, of which you can never have too many (jokes, that is)).

There’s plenty to admire beyond the plot and the performances, too. It’s all here: the characters’ fairy-tale looks, worked out in stunning detail by Anna Bashtovaya, Stepan Gordeev’s rhythmic direction, seriously cool music and the enchanting atmosphere of that very fairy tale grown-ups have been missing. Falling in love with this show is the best range of emotions you can experience at the end of 2025.

P.S.: As it happens, I also had the rare experience of watching *The Magic District* and *Realnye patsany* (“Real Lads”, the long-running Perm sitcom) in parallel, but I’ll write about that separately some time.

## 13 November 2025

I’m still happily watching season 2 of [*The Magic District*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1050), and I’ve brought you a find!

I’ve just had occasion, for work, to listen to some fresh, superb episodes of the podcast [Cinema is punk](https://cinemaispunk.mave.digital/) from the production company Mesto Sily (“Place of Power”) — and it’s the best companion to the series. Take note of 2 episodes:

- Stepan Gordeev (the series’ director) and Ilya Sobolev [discuss](https://cinemaispunk.mave.digital/ep-8) the role of the Gnome in *The Magic District*. They reveal who else auditioned for the part of the Foul-Mouth, how much a single shot with the character cost and which scene was filmed first of all (that one you really won’t guess, because the moment came out gorgeous in the end). They also talk about a set of shot glasses with the character’s portrait that have an audio function: swearing at whoever is drinking. Now I want one.

- Anna Bashtovaya, the costume designer on both seasons of *The Magic District*, [tells](https://cinemaispunk.mave.digital/ep-9) Stepan how she originally wanted to dress Baba Yaga, how old the fabric in Merlin’s robe is, why the Gnome is dressed in rags and what fly agarics have to do with it. Her channel, by the way, also has lots of [fascinating stuff](https://t.me/kinocostume/32003) about the series. The coolest fact in the episode: real costumes from Alexei Balabanov’s films will appear on screen in the second season. How can you not look forward to the final episode?!

## 8 December 2025

Meanwhile, in [*The Magic District*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1050), everything is as fairy-tale as ever

I came back to the series after a couple of weeks and was very glad to see no fewer than two great female characters in episode 5: the Mermaid, played by Valentina Mazunina (with the unmistakable intonation of Valya from *Realnye patsany*), and a cameo by Anna Semenovich (in the story, the singer has been taken captive by the no-good owner of a wish-granting pike). It reminded me once again that part of the series’ charm lies in exactly these little treats — charismatic bit-part characters :)

I keep waiting to see how the story will get itself to New Year — the last episode of the season is scheduled for 25 December, after all, and the New Year mood won’t create itself! I trust the writers have seen to it — look, the pike, which is traditionally caught through a hole in the ice, has been pulled out of the water in the middle of summer, so maybe some more winter folklore will come our way too.

P.S.: The wisdom tooth dispensing that very wisdom in the voice of Losyash (the moose from the animated series *Kikoriki*) is the pinnacle. I spent the whole episode waiting for it to say “my fairy-tale friend!”

## 28 December 2025

However far removed [*The Magic District*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1139) may be from New Year themes, the series still managed to create a naively festive atmosphere for its season finale. The keys to its success are these:

- Of course, it couldn’t do without wall-to-wall New Year promo. Which, as you can see from the poster, suits the series.

- Perhaps Ilya Sobolev’s “Happy New Year” [greeting](https://t.me/mc2_prod/1884) at the premiere meant the story’s new year — 1996, announced in the finale — rather than the literal holiday, as one might have thought. Well, that final change of era is more of a “Happy Old New Year”! (And yes, the 90s don’t annoy me)

- We love and cherish New Year films precisely for their naive, life-affirming happy endings. That’s just what we get here — a perfectly acceptable one, to my mind, if an abrupt one, given how the action speeds up towards the denouement. Let’s hope the wait for the next season won’t drag on either :)

## Peculiarities of the National Hunt: Digital Detox and Anti-Stress

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/osobennosti-natsionalnoy-okhoty-1995/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-11-03 (3 November 2025)
Work: “Peculiarities of the National Hunt” is a 1995 film directed by Aleksandr Rogozhkin.
Tags: rewatch, Russian cinema, comedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/osobennosti-natsionalnoy-okhoty-1995/

Well, here’s to the classics!

In October I was also exploring the universe of Aleksandr Rogozhkin’s films: the three parts of *Peculiarities of the National Hunt* (in one of the films, of the National Fishing). I had caught bits of these films on television long ago, but only now did I get round to watching them properly, from start to finish. And it was worth it: that was one of the best weekends of the month! If I were asked to name films synonymous with the words “digital detox” and “anti-stress”, these are the ones I would pick.

These jokes about the timeless face of the Russian soul, put on screen with the utmost seriousness, manage, surprisingly enough, to combine utterly carnivalesque humour with a deeply existential philosophy. It is out of this very paradox that an undeniable sense of being part of what is happening on screen is born: both in the fun you share with the characters and in a common attitude to the absurdity of life. It is for this inimitable feeling that you want to rewatch the films and think them over again, sinking once more into a world without ranks or cares that flares up and dies away in flashes somewhere on hunting trips in the forest (and, well, out of self-interest too: to memorise for future use all the general’s pithy toasts, each beginning with the fundamental “Well…”).

## Every 88: The Quiet, Assured Gravitas of What Unfolds

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kazhdyy-88-2015/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-11-01 (1 November 2025)
Work: “Every 88” is a 2015 film directed by Darya Lebedeva.
Tags: Russian cinema, short films, parable
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/kazhdyy-88-2015/

Still riding a wave of admiration for [*You Drive Me Crazy*,](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/svodish-s-uma-2025/) I also watched one of director Darya Lebedeva’s short films, called *Every 88* («Каждый 88»).

It is a pithy story about a young Soviet soldier who is killed in battle and finds himself in a mysterious place where a French athlete, a lady-in-waiting to an Austrian princess and many other figures from different times and nations have gathered too. They are all standing in a lengthy queue, waiting for their lot in the next life (which, of course, is handed out according to their karma in the one just lived). The artifice of this world is entirely convincing, comic in places and even melodramatic in a good way. But the main thing you recognise in the director’s style is the quiet, assured gravitas of what unfolds, the point of which lies not in how fantastical the action is but in what it truly means once translated into the language of reality. It’s great that a skill like this can be built into films, with the result getting better every time.

---

## You Drive Me Crazy: The Feeling of Thrilling Love, Bottled on Film

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/svodish-s-uma-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-10-29 (29 October 2025)
Work: “You Drive Me Crazy” is a 2025 film directed by Darya Lebedeva.
Tags: Russian cinema, rom-com, science fiction
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/svodish-s-uma-2025/

If you had no cinema plans for the coming evenings, urgently plan a trip to [*You Drive Me Crazy*](https://youtu.be/39T_q4gt7HE?si=g9iPXzTNF-iuOeUm) (*Svodish s uma*). It’s definitely worth catching while you can.

I saw the film last night, and it’s a real find for any viewer. Director [Darya Lebedeva](https://t.me/lebedevadao) has pulled off a terrific feature debut that combines a convincing plot, fantastic performances from Mila Ershova and Yuri Nasonov, romance and humour in harmonious proportions, and a love of cinema you can feel through the screen. I have so much to rave about that I’ll lay it out point by point (the film’s **8.5 rating** on Kinopoisk will bear me out).

- Not since *Palm Springs*, perhaps, has a fantastical element suited a romantic comedy so well. The story of a guy and a girl who live in the same flat in different versions of the universe, but see each other in the mirror and fall in love, fits the logic of the world of *You Drive Me Crazy* so well that it raises no questions whatsoever. It is every bit as convincing as the premise of *Piter FM* (the 2006 St Petersburg rom-com), about two strangers who talk only on the phone and can never quite manage to meet. The setting, by the way, is that same fateful St Petersburg, and it is very beautiful here. So even if you’re on the side of realism, go ahead and watch it without fear.

- After the film I spent the whole evening and this morning discussing the details of what I’d seen and how to decode them. It’s been a long time since I got so deep into picking a film apart afterwards, which is why you absolutely must take your favourite people to talk to along to the screening. Everything matters here: the protagonist Vanya’s quirky glasses, Alisa’s fringe, the jokes about *Twilight* and cocktail recipes, the changed locks on the doors and the stickers stuck on the mirrors. The film is rather like an absorbing quest that you’re invited to complete alongside extremely likeable characters, who, by the way, become better people in the process, infecting the viewer with the same urge.

- From the moment you leave the cinema your soul demands an immediate rewatch, and that’s fairly rare. *You Drive Me Crazy* is something you want to stretch out, prolong, repeat and never let go of. To convey the feeling, let me draw a parallel with Ray Bradbury’s *Dandelion Wine*. He had “summer caught and stoppered”, and here, caught and stoppered on film, is the feeling of thrilling love and of two people who are a little lost but deserve happiness sincerely growing close. How good that the film will most likely come out on the platform Start (the Russian streaming service), which is listed in the credits, so this story will always be within reach.

---

## Nazad v proshloe: An Audio Series About Time Travel

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/audioserial-nazad-v-proshloe/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-10-28 (28 October 2025)
Tags: podcasts, notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/audioserial-nazad-v-proshloe/

A podcast off-topic

As part of my job, I had a hand in making and releasing a seriously cool audio series for lovers of history and time travel. It’s called [*Nazad v proshloe*](https://zvuk.com/podcast/42757431) («Назад в прошлое», “Back to the Past”) — with a film reference, naturally, because how could it be otherwise?

I listen to every episode before it goes out and (despite years of listening to podcasts for work) I’m amazed all over again at just how well audio formats can do cinematic storytelling. You are literally listening to a film, or an episode of a series, filling in the picture in your own head, and the feeling is indescribable. The podcast has professional actors and immersive sound design, and the plot surprises you every time and lets you travel in your mind to one era or another. In short, when my eyes get tired of watching films, I’ll be listening to them in this podcast. The first episode is already out, and the second arrives tomorrow — the perfect time to give it a try.

That ultra-rare thing, a podcast recommendation on a film channel — at your service.
