## Cashier: Four Heroines at Opposite Poles of Control over Their Lives

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/obnalschik-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-10-27 (27 October 2025); updated: 2026-01-07
Work: “Cashier” is a 2025 series directed by Boris Akopov.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, crime
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/obnalschik-serial/

## 27 October 2025

Now here is some news that makes me happy: from 13 November, Wink (a Russian streaming service) will be showing the series *Cashier* (*Obnalshchik*, “The Cash-Out Man”), a twisty story from Boris Akopov.

The series is set in 2013 and centres on the relationship between a father, Mikhail, and his son, Lyosha. After a string of setbacks, the two of them start cashing out money for dangerous people. The threat of a prison sentence, murders, betrayals: this is their new everyday life.

The cast includes Alexander Yatsenko, Elena Nikolaeva and Fyodor Kudryashov, and it was shot in the Russian Far East, which means that besides the crime plot we are also in for landscapes like nowhere else (I love that region dearly myself, and I can vouch for its beauty). The lead, Mikhail, played by Yatsenko, looks to be my favourite type, the “bad good man”; here is what the actor himself says:

> Mikhail, like me, isn’t exactly on first-name terms with pedagogy and parenting. Still, he tries to find common ground with his son, to reach an understanding. You know how it goes: you do one wrong thing, and because of it your whole life starts heading the wrong way. And then it’s very hard to rewind, to admit you were wrong, to apologise and start changing something… Our series is about exactly that: how a person makes a mistake and tries to steer his way out of it. Mikhail isn’t a very good man or father, but his love for his son and his wife keeps him from turning into a criminal for good

Adding it to my watchlist, and waiting.

## 10 November 2025

[*Cashier*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1036) treats us to character posters and a [trailer](https://youtu.be/D02WcdPwhzA) (with a certain [*Daring*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/likhie-serial/) vibe)

What’s new is the premiere date, which has moved to 15 November. We’ll be seeing the story of a father and son who pull off complicated financial schemes for none-too-pleasant clients as early as the end of this week.

By the way, on the poster for Igor Mirkurbanov’s character, who goes by the Fish King, the lamp in the foreground is exactly like the one I have at home. Clearly, the series must be watched by its light and no other.

## 19 November 2025

So far [*Cashier*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1071) (*Obnalshchik*, “The Cash-Out Man”) looks to me like the sum of *Daring* (*Likhie*: crime in the Far East and Elena Nikolaeva as the mother of the family) and *Na avtomate* (“On Autopilot”, Boris Akopov’s previous series, where young people also got drawn into criminal adventures). But that doesn’t hurt the series one bit!

Among other things, it’s now clear why the poster makes such a point of the hand of Alexander Yatsenko’s character (those who have already seen the first episode will know what I mean). On the whole, the plot unfolds fairly quietly, yet it hooks you and, of course, wins you over. The criminal world here is heavily disguised as ordinary life, which makes sense: this is, after all, not the 1990s but the 2010s, even if hardly the calmest of times. I’m also curious to see where the theme of young people who have got their hands on easy money will lead: the brothers in *Na avtomate* were teetering on the brink of just that kind of moral choice too.

## 10 December 2025

[*Cashier*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1094) has very skilfully picked up speed by the end of episode 5.

What strikes me most is how the 4 main heroines stand at opposite poles when it comes to control over their own lives and the lives of those around them. Two of them, Olga (Elena Nikolaeva) and Alyona (Sofya Lopunova), are not in charge of their own lives at all. Their existence is a shadow of the plans that Alexander Yatsenko’s and Fyodor Kudryashov’s characters are trying to carry out, and total ignorance of what is actually going on.

The crime bosses Mama (Olga Tumaykina) and Katya (Elena Nesterova), meanwhile, are their inverse. The whole town is in their power, and any lie, if one is ever told, is brutally punished. Quite unlike the situation of the women the two leads love, who are having the wool pulled over their eyes in the most blatant way.

You could even see a growth trajectory in this: perhaps Vostochny’s current crime queens were once in the same position themselves, and it was from precisely that point that they grew to the scale we are shown.

In Boris Akopov’s stories something is always buried deeper than it first appears, so I have great faith in the women’s storylines.

## 7 January 2026

I’ve finished [*Cashier*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1143) and, of course, I’m impressed not so much by the finale as by the development of one particular heroine: Olga, played by Elena Nikolaeva.

Mid-season I wrote that she has no control over her life at all. Towards the end came a 180-degree turn: her weakness became her strength, a silky weapon with a gentle tone of voice. While her husband and son — Alexander Yatsenko’s and Fyodor Kudryashov’s characters, as convincing as ever — acted as outside circumstances and other people’s orders dictated, she simply took matters into her own hands.

Just think: she drove her guard (whose job was to kill the heroine a couple of hours later) to take himself out! I’m thrilled: Boris Akopov has come up with a heroine who showed up every gangster in the Far East with a single scene. She may not be much of a psychologist, but as a moral annihilator she delivered in full :)

---

## Zhora Kryzhovnikov on Gaidai’s Comedies: Highlights of His Director’s Breakdown

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kryzhovnikov-razbor-gaydaya/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-10-15 (15 October 2025)
Tags: Soviet cinema, analysis, comedy, film history
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/kryzhovnikov-razbor-gaydaya/

Zhora Kryzhovnikov has released a [new director’s breakdown](https://youtu.be/busSf9off_k?si=sLc8EfNnMnlzn6aL) — this time of the work of Leonid Gaidai!

As [last time,](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kryzhovnikov-razbor-sluzhebnyy-roman/) I’ve put together a recap post with the main and most interesting points (and added, in brackets, bits of my own musings, on topic and off)

- The most American of Soviet directors, Gaidai was in many ways geared towards stunts, attractions and entertainment more than towards exploration. Analysing a single film is not enough to examine his style, so the breakdown covers Gaidai’s work as a whole.

- The situation comedy Gaidai worked in rests on holding the viewer (*uderzhanie*). That hold runs on two other Russian “U”s: recognition (*uznavanie*) and surprise (*udivlenie*). But whereas for Ryazanov it was the believability of what was happening that mattered (hence, too, the inserts of semi-documentary street footage), Gaidai’s priorities are entirely different. Most of the gags that play on surprise are utterly fantastical — take Gorbunkov’s trip to a capitalist country in *The Diamond Arm*, for one. It bears no relation to reality, but it holds you thanks to the directing and the pacing.

- The pleasure of the attractions is by definition greater than the need to ask questions about what is going on. Paradoxically, the fantastical gags in Gaidai’s films tell us about the characters and win our trust. That is the phenomenon of this director, and to this day it has not been repeated.

- The concept of comedy as taught at school took shape in Stalin’s time. The details are in a book Kryzhovnikov recommends, *State Laughter: Stalinism, Populism, and Origins of Soviet Culture* («Госсмех. Сталинизм и комическое») (*onto my reading list it goes*). A Soviet person could laugh only the laughter of the victor — at swindlers and petty, conniving officials. A Soviet comedy always has a positive hero. Hence the stock view of comedy as something with an educational function. That was the reality Gaidai landed in at the start of his career.

- Gaidai is a unique director who, while outwardly still belonging to Soviet comedy, made pure entertainment.

- Gaidai’s first films, *Zhenikh s togo sveta* («Жених с того света», “The Groom from the Other World”) and *Thrice Resurrected* («Трижды воскресший»), were very hard ordeals for the director, ones he disliked recalling to the end of his life (*and we have practically never heard of them*).

- Gaidai adored silent film. Kryzhovnikov, too, holds that a film should make sense even with the sound off (*an evening’s entertainment: I’ll rewatch* Bitterly! *(«Горько!», Kryzhovnikov’s 2013 wedding comedy) with that idea in mind*).

- Gaidai worked with a stopwatch: he timed the gap from one laugh moment to the next — which is exactly why, 60 years on, we still watch his films with interest.

- The director was drawn to the short film: the format grabs attention faster. His features often consist of several separate stories, and long films made him uneasy because the audience might tire.

- Gaidai’s concept of situation comedy is safe entertainment. There is no real pain in his films; nobody dies and nobody leaves anybody. The basic principle is “beautiful women + funny men”. Every element of Gaidai’s comic style is unique and grounded in his favourite films (the nods to Buster Keaton, for example). Perhaps one day Russian cinema will produce someone to carry on Gaidai’s work.

---

## My Mom’s Penguins, Season 2: The Bet on Novelty Pays Off

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/pingviny-moey-mamy-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-10-14 (14 October 2025); updated: 2025-11-26
Work: “My Mom’s Penguins” is a 2021 series directed by Natalya Meshchaninova, Nadezhda Stepanova.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, dramedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/pingviny-moey-mamy-serial/

## 14 October 2025

*My Mom’s Penguins* (*Pingviny moey mamy*) is coming back.

Kion (a Russian streaming service) promises to release the second season of the series this very autumn, so there isn’t long left to wait.

Gosha, Makar Khlebnikov’s character, has grown up: he does stand-up, argues with his girlfriend (Elizaveta Ishchenko) and earns the rent for his flat. His parents are wrapped up in moving to a new house and are expecting their 6th child. And keeping an eye on his growing brothers and sisters falls, of course, to Gosha.

I can’t wait to see how Liza Ishchenko fits into the team, all the more so since she is a fan of the show herself:

> I loved watching the first season of *My Mom’s Penguins* and I’m a big fan of it. What drew me to the second season was the chance to try a new side of myself, with a new story and with a magical team that was making a very interesting project with love. My character, Vika, is a scorching combo of two elements, fire and water, so I dived in and soaked her up completely on set. I was changing before people’s eyes, and those close to me on set were amazed at what a volcanic temperament I could show. I had wanted to work with Makar for a long time, because we’ve known each other for ages — and, sure enough, the stars aligned!

## 26 November 2025

Are you watching the new season of [*My Mom’s Penguins*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1042)? I’ve started, and for now I’m getting used to the many changes.

If the bet was on novelty, it has paid off. Now Gosha’s step-brothers and step-sister have fully independent storylines of their own, and set them in motion, which widens the frame compared with the first season. Clearly the range of themes will grow too: at any rate, we won’t be worrying only about the biological son. The change of location does the show good as well, by the way: almost everyone in the second season sets off on a journey of one kind or another (as always, not only geographically but also towards their true self).

Gosha’s stand-up is shown at the very start of episode 1, and thank you for that: it’s nice to be back in that “room”. The whole season is already out; I hope they carry on in the same spirit.

## Comeback: The Air of the 2000s Wafts Through the Screen with Unfeigned Youth

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kambek-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-10-11 (11 October 2025); updated: 2025-11-16
Work: “Comeback” is a 2025 series directed by Dinar Garipov.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, 2000s
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/kambek-serial/

## 11 October 2025

I’ve finally got round to [*Comeback*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/series/6605654/) (*Kambek*), an ultra-atmospheric series with Alexander Petrov as a homeless man who has lost his memory.

It’s set in the 2000s, and the air of that era literally wafts through the screen with a kind of unfeigned youthfulness. That atmosphere is heightened by the teenage leads — strong, brave, wise in their own way. And it is all set to tracks by Mujuice, who always gets right to the depths of your soul. And the plot, of course, brings out something unhackneyed, episode after episode, about friendship and about kindness to your neighbour and to yourself. Simple and tasteful.

Watching it gave me feelings I had long forgotten, not felt since [*Peace! Friendship! Chewing Gum!*](https://t.me/kino_voice/13) (the 1990s-set series), so I’m with this series to the end.

## 18 October 2025

Still ~~watching~~ adoring [*Comeback*](https://t.me/kino_voice/997)

The fourth episode is a perfect example of an episode’s vertical plot complementing the story’s overall horizontal structure so organically that it’s hard even to tell them apart. My thanks to the show’s makers and to [@russian_c0de](https://t.me/russian_c0de) for work this thorough, of course.

The series is at its halfway point and picking up speed very skilfully. The [record](https://t.me/kinopoisk_Industry/5558) viewing figures say as much, eloquently. That kind of demand, it seems to me, can be explained by interest in the chosen era. All of us, to one degree or another (younger viewers especially), come from the 2000s — from that culture, that starting point for how we see the world and ourselves. And revisiting your relative youth always draws you in.

## 20 October 2025

A separate pleasure is the aesthetic of the school that the kids in [*Comeback*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1013) go to

For me these are the landscapes of home. What matters most is that it is an *ordinary* school (even if that only came about because of the period — in 2004 all schools were like that). I went to exactly this kind of school, and my eye delights in the familiar set-up of the classrooms, with those peeling wooden chairs (which were forever snagging your tights — the girls will know what I mean), the scuffed lino, the wooden shelving, the wide windowsills and the haphazard plants on them. The canteen was a little bigger than the one in the still from the series, but with the same serving line of metal pots with red lettering. In my last years there, admittedly, the chalkboards were replaced with whiteboards and then, in part, with electronic ones, but everything around them stayed just as it was :)

You hardly ever see schools like that on screen these days, and certainly not in stories about the present — everywhere there has to be a swimming pool, a canteen with a hotel-style buffet and ultra-trendy refurbishments. Schools like that really do exist, but old-style schools exist and operate alongside them (I visited mine last year — the authenticity is all still there). And it is a real pleasure to recognise on screen a little piece of my own youth, which, it turns out, can even serve as a film set.

## 23 October 2025

Time for wild theories

After the powerful, practically journalistic investigation that Yura from [*Comeback*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1013) carried out in the latest episode, I can’t stop thinking that, in his show’s universe, he could have grown up to be Yury Dud*\* (the journalist and YouTube interviewer).

**✅** Born in the late 1980s
**✅** Adores football
**✅** The name and the physical resemblance speak for themselves
**✅** Most likely, Yura is a humanities type (we’ve seen him copying maths off Ptakha)

How do I unsee this?

\* Yury Dud* has been designated a “foreign agent” in Russia

## 31 October 2025

Episode six of [*Comeback*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1013) very neatly takes many of the storylines off the table — precisely to put the emphasis on a new variable, Alexey Chadov’s mysterious character. He is obviously going to be one of the main players in the two final episodes, and that calls for a little extra room, both artistically and in running time.

A separate joy is the quotation of a scene from the film *Brother* (Balabanov’s 1997 cult classic). If you remember, at one point Danila tries to stand up for Sveta, the tram driver, against her husband, who beats her. Having put the man out of action, Danila asks her to leave with him, but she stays with her husband, who is suffering from a bullet in the leg and will obviously go on beating her. The same thing is repeated almost shot for shot in *Comeback* and, you might say, has now reached the level of an archetypal plot.

By the way, I’m watching the series very closely so that I can log every episode in a Kinopoisk [piece](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/4011978/) — if you find yourself mulling over the details, drop by.

## 16 November 2025

And the crowning touch to the finale of [*Comeback*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1043) is the [news](https://t.me/kinopoisk_soon/20435) of a second season.

In the last episode the density of events went off the scale, but, happily, none of the storylines suffered for it. That said, I preferred the first half of the story, where, for one thing, the kids still seemed to have everything ahead of them (😭), and for another, there was enough time to take in each event. But the last episodes have a drive of their own too, combined with the sense of an era slipping away — an era of great adventure and the carefree early 2000s.

What will I be looking for in season 2? Updated versions of the kids (in particular, developments in Dasha’s love life, with her assorted candidates and with Petya, who vanished as suddenly as he appeared). A late-00s look that, in the show’s tradition, isn’t glossy, naturally. And Kompot’s life getting back to normal: showing the hardships of a homeless man’s life is half the job; it is far harder to portray honestly the difficulties of his fitting back into society and overcoming the stigma that trails behind him from his former status.

It’s great that the show has deservedly been renewed, and I’m genuinely looking forward to the new season.

* Yury Dud (Дудь Юрий Александрович) has been designated a “foreign agent” by Russia’s Ministry of Justice (listed on 15 April 2022).

---

## Lighthouse: A Multilayered Reflection on the Nature of Guilt, Grief and Family Trauma

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/mayak-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-10-09 (9 October 2025)
Work: “Lighthouse” is a 2025 series directed by Ilya Malakhova.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/mayak-serial/

Okko (the Russian streaming service) and the production company Sreda have stunned everyone yet again.

The closing series, *Lighthouse* (*Mayak*), is
a pick of jeweller’s precision, made to end the festival on the highest note, in full flight.

The series is graced by Mikhail Turbin’s superb script, by piercing performances from Evgeny Kuntsevich, Sergei Gilev and Yulia Snigir, and by Natalya Makarova’s camerawork — alive, mobile, in sync with the characters’ lives on screen. Ilya Malakhova’s direction pulls it all together. Thanks to this, the story of Egor, a high-school student who looks after his younger brother with cerebral palsy in place of parents who have fled into their work, becomes not just a bleak tale of human misfortune but a multilayered reflection on the nature of guilt, grief, family trauma and living through loss.

The show’s real discovery is Evgeny Kuntsevich. In the space of 2 episodes this actor has played almost everything — tender love for a younger brother, sincerity in standing up for himself, eyes shining with first love, carefreeness, responsibility, the emptiness of loss, anger, despair and hopelessness. I’m sure the coming episodes will bring yet more uncharted facets of emotion.

Okko’s general producer, Gavr Gordeev, says the platform’s philosophy is built on an empathetic attitude towards the viewer. With empathy in return, I’ll be waiting for *Lighthouse* to premiere in 2026.

---

## The Good Life: An Imagistic Attempt at Adapting The Blue Cup

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/khoroshaya-zhizn-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-10-08 (8 October 2025)
Work: “The Good Life” is a 2025 film directed by Tatyana Rakhmanova.
Tags: Russian cinema, adaptation, festival films, drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/khoroshaya-zhizn-2025/

*The Good Life* (*Khoroshaya zhizn*) is a film I had been looking forward to because of Serafima Goshchanskaya, and she is wonderful in it (though she gets frustratingly little screen time)

The plot, based on the short story *Golubaya chashka* («Голубая чашка», “The Blue Cup”) by Arkady Gaidar (the classic Soviet children’s writer), doesn’t solve all the riddles of the original text (once again, [different bits of culture intertwining](https://t.me/kino_voice/973)). For me this story is a very powerful childhood impression, powerful because I never fully understood it, and I expected the film to unlock some of the plot’s secrets. That doesn’t seem to have happened, though I would call the film a very cool imagistic attempt at adapting this text (and a reminder to reread it).

## Above Eternal Rest: A Difficult Film You Want to Go On Thinking About

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/nad-vechnym-pokoem-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-10-08 (8 October 2025)
Work: “Above Eternal Rest” is a 2025 film directed by Svetlana Proskurina.
Tags: Russian cinema, festivals, drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/nad-vechnym-pokoem-2025/

The final film of the competition programme, Svetlana Proskurina’s *Above Eternal Rest* (*Nad vechnym pokoem*), is very much a mirror image of [*My Son*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/moy-syn-2025/), which we watched first. This premiere has every right to be called a contemporary *Cargo 200* (Alexei Balabanov’s film) crossed with *Crime and Punishment*. Only where evil used to be done shamelessly, out in the open room, now it is hidden under the floorboards, and people are driven mad by their complicity, by ending up in a “random hell”, as the director put it — and that is something different.

The story of a mother and son bound by one terrible secret will not let you look away from the ordinariness of killing in the name of salvation — not even “crime”; that word sounds too formal here. Yet it is hard to condemn Rita, the heroine played by Masha Leonova: she is not a villain, not a murderer and not a bad person. She is a victim too. And grasping that this is how things truly stand in the story is what weighs on the viewer most of all.

A difficult film, one you want to go on thinking about and talking through. Masha Leonova is a wonderful actress whom I would love to see in subtle roles like this more often. She gives us a heroine who keeps you in doubt to the very end: has she gone mad, been brutalised by indifference, or coldly calculated what she did? I think it may be the best female performance of the festival.

---

## Yura Was Here: A Film About Wonderful People, Inner Beauty and Loving Your Neighbour

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/zdes-byl-yura-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-10-08 (8 October 2025); updated: 2026-02-05
Work: “Yura Was Here” is a 2025 film directed by Sergey Malkin.
Tags: Russian cinema, festivals, music
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/zdes-byl-yura-2025/

## 8 October 2025

*Yura Was Here* (*Zdes byl Yura*) is an unimaginably beautiful film about wonderful people, inner beauty and love for your neighbour — the kind of love that saves, above all, the one who loves. Don’t imagine this is some kind of sentimental syrup: on the contrary, the film is punk, dynamic and out of the ordinary.

The heroes, a group of musicians, suddenly have Yura (Konstantin Khabensky) dropped in their laps: the uncle of one of the guys, who because of a birth injury cannot speak or, for that matter, live on his own. On top of their troubles with a neighbour in their communal flat and their attempts to break through to the big stage, they now have to care for a relative whom, at first, nobody seems to need. In time, he becomes the most important person for everyone in the story.

The film’s world is filled with music, colour and details that bring everything to life. I spotted, for instance, the cool café Chifanka in Moscow’s Kitay-Gorod :)

I have to confess my love for the songs of the band Kick Chill as performed by Kuzma Kotrelev; the filmmakers promise to release a separate soundtrack. This, to my mind, is the hit of the festival, as the song “Alle, Marina” from *Year of Birth* once was. The references are in good shape here too, by the way: as the candles on the cake are lit, for example, someone says “Everyone out of the Gloom”, the line Khabensky’s character in *Night Watch* is famous for.

I’ll be going to see it a second time as soon as it is in cinemas: from 5 February, courtesy of [@bosforpictures](https://t.me/bosforpictures) and [@volgafilms](https://t.me/volgafilms).

## 18 December 2025

**Found: the best way to kick off your 2026 in film**

One film that did not make the best-of-2025 lists (simply because it is not out yet) is the wonderful [*Yura Was Here*](https://t.me/kino_voice/967): utterly astonishing in every respect, from the plot and dialogue to the directing, camerawork and editing, and one that won the hearts of everyone at Mayak 2025 (the Russian film festival in Gelendzhik).

Luckily, the team at the Bosfor studio is already preparing for the release: it opens on 5 February, and tickets for the first public premiere on 25 January can be bought [right now](https://t.me/bosforpictures/609). Don’t miss it: it is a wonderful way to start your film year on a high note :)

When we come to draw up the best-of lists of Russian films for 2026, *Yura* will be among the first names on them — you have my word.

## 5 February 2026

And as of today, [*Yura Was Here*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1128) is in cinemas: a film I have been raving about ever since Mayak, the Russian film festival in Gelendzhik (which was back in October, mind you)

I [wrote](https://t.me/kino_voice/967) about the film right after seeing it, and today I have put together a short list of reasons to see it on the big screen:

- Kuzma Kotrelev singing (if you know [what](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/mezhdu-nami-khimiya-serial/) I mean) and gorgeous music all round
- An impressive performance by Konstantin Khabensky. You seriously won’t recognise him.
- Lively dialogue peppered with contemporary memes (mostly improvised!)
- The kindest humour, without a single cloying note
- Wonderful details you want to study up close, from the interiors of the communal flat to the side streets of Kitay-Gorod
- Plenty of reasons to smile gratefully at this film afterwards (and perhaps wipe away a tear)

I am sure that after seeing it, everyone will be able to draw up their own list of reasons to recommend this film to others.

---

## Tied Up: A Cinematic Celebration of Animation, Sincerity and Kindness

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/na-vybros-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-10-07 (7 October 2025)
Work: “Tied Up” is a 2025 film directed by Konstantin Bronzit.
Tags: animation, Russian cinema, festivals
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/na-vybros-2025/

Konstantin Bronzit’s *Tied Up* (*Na vybros*, “For the Dump”) is a true cinematic celebration of animation, sincerity and kindness. In the spirit of Pixar, but with a home-grown soul.

The story of things thrown out on the dump which, just like people, want to be needed and useful is so moving precisely because that thought is close to everyone’s heart. They try desperately to make it to paradise — a rubbish-dump paradise, but a paradise all the same — and how could you not understand them?

The film gives you the feeling of a real dramedy, bringing on laughter and tears at once. The humour is built on paradox, so it never fails. Just take the joke from the rat that feeds on books, about Pasternak being a bit bland. At times it even feels like a dystopia in the vein of Pelevin, but only in the good ways.

Konstantin Bronzit, who worked on the film for 5 years, modestly laughs it off — it’s only a kids’ cartoon, he says :) But the message about eco-friendly handling — not just of rubbish but, first and foremost, of living people — is unmistakable.

In cinemas from 20 November — an unequivocal *recommandation*.

---

## Nouvelle Vague: A True Love Letter to Cinema

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/novaya-volna-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-10-07 (7 October 2025)
Work: “Nouvelle Vague” is a 2025 film directed by Richard Linklater.
Tags: world cinema, European cinema, film history
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/novaya-volna-2025/

Richard Linklater’s [*Nouvelle Vague*](https://t.me/kino_voice/899) is a very structured, rhythmic account of how Jean-Luc Godard’s *Breathless* — yes, that one — was made.

Every character is introduced, the context is set, so just watch and enjoy — the film eases you so lightly into the everyday world of French filmmakers that the humour of their discussions lands quickly and delights. It’s a real journey into the French New Wave for anyone who decides to watch the film.

The casting is a delight all of its own. Each of the actors is as convincing as the real person they play and comes across as practically documentary. But the one who won me over most was Aubry Dullin, who plays Jean-Paul Belmondo.

In short, the result is a true love letter to cinema — and you can share the feeling on the big screen from 6 November.

---

## Transparent Lands: A Film That Demands Extra Attention, If Not a Second Viewing

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/prozrachnye-zemli-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-10-07 (7 October 2025)
Work: “Transparent Lands” is a 2025 film directed by Dmitry Davydov.
Tags: Russian cinema, festivals, drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/prozrachnye-zemli-2025/

*Transparent Lands* (*Prozrachnye zemli*) is a film that demands extra attention from the viewer, if not a second viewing.

The story of three old men living alone in a traditional village (outstanding work by the production designers), as if outside time, unfolds almost without words. They while away the time with tea, the banya (steam bath) with cupping jars, and hunting, until they fish out of the pond a man frozen to the point of turning to glass. In the hut he thaws out, comes back to life and even starts baking bread, presenting it to the old men as a true miracle (and prompting a wonderful scene of celebration in the snowy night). Only, once he disappears, life for the villagers changes.

Contrary to its title, you could hardly call the film transparent. It opens up a discussion of the fear of death, the preservation of memory and the philosophy of life. Director Dmitry Davydov gradually leads us into the world of a dying village, showing its passage into a space of transparent memories, where the whole village whirls in the eternal round dance of the ancestors, which no longer belongs to our world, just like the life reflected in the film.

---

## Scenes of Friendly Ties: A Mood Piece Woven from Fragments of Friendship

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kartiny-druzheskikh-svyazey-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-10-06 (6 October 2025)
Work: “Scenes of Friendly Ties” is a 2025 film directed by Sonya Rayzman.
Tags: Russian cinema, festivals, dramedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/kartiny-druzheskikh-svyazey-2025/

*Scenes of Friendly Ties* (*Kartiny druzheskikh svyazey*) is a mood piece woven from fragments of the friendship and downtime of a group of film-industry pals. I’d call it “fan service for insiders” — with in-jokes about the woes of film people, the type Lev Zulkarnaev gets cast as, and the peculiarities of drama schools :)

The storyline about one of the friends (Alexander Pal) going away serves more as a backdrop than as the engine of the plot, and the pals’ professional conflicts turn out to be more interesting. In that respect the film does sometimes break up into episodic sketches — not that this is much of a problem, because each of them is like a small dramedy, complete in itself regardless of the main storyline.

The only thing that raises questions is the scene with the cat. The thing is, the film opens with him being put to sleep (emotionally crushing for Maria Karpova’s character and for every viewer), although no illness of any kind is mentioned. Later we see a flashback of the cat being found back when the characters were at drama school — and that was not so many years ago, so the picture becomes more paradoxical still. Clearly, the cat’s death is a metaphor for the end of the characters’ relationship, but an awfully cruel one.

---

## Fire Boy: Uneven, but Alive and Reaching for the Light

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/ognennyy-malchik-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-10-06 (6 October 2025)
Work: “Fire Boy” is a 2025 film directed by Nadezhda Mikhalkova.
Tags: Russian cinema, festivals, drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/ognennyy-malchik-2025/

Nadya Mikhalkova’s *Fire Boy* (*Ognenny malchik*) is an uneven film, but one that is alive and reaching for the light.

The story of what a young man goes through after a person accidentally burns to death before his eyes (the “fire boy” of the title) holds your attention on several fronts at once. There is the lack of contact with his mum (comically echoed by the lack of mobile signal for most of the film), the danger of everyday indifference, and a search for himself with a touch of the mystical. On that score Denis Kosikov conveys every facet of his character’s state with paradoxical precision. I can say the same of Bogdan Goloshchuk, a dazzling actor whose character turns up briefly at the very start to set the tone for the whole film straight away.

I find the themes of *Fire Boy* have a lot in common with *Acid* by Alexander Gorchilin, who set out a similar cluster of problems — indifference and the subsequent attempt to forgive yourself — in the pithy line “if you want to jump, jump”. And that is why the film, despite its rough patches towards the end, did on balance hit home with me.

---

## Skladki: An Uplifting Body Horror About the Beauty of the Human Body

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/skladki-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-10-06 (6 October 2025)
Work: “Skladki” is a 2025 film directed by Katerina Skakun.
Tags: Russian cinema, short films, festival films
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/skladki-2025/

The short film competition is over — there’s one film I’m extremely fond of, so that’s the one I’ll write about here. As for the rest, read about them in the piece that will be up here in a couple of days :)

*Skladki* («Складки», “Folds”) is an uplifting body horror, as its director, Katerina Skakun, herself put it. And it really is a very charming story about the beauty of the human body, of life and of love, which can be literally all-consuming (and all-saving too). Whether to take fright at it or to nestle up to this life-giving feeling is for each of us to decide.

In the story, an enthusiastic tour guide and a female chiropractor fall in love, but their relationship doesn’t unfold as smoothly as it might. But the main thing is how it all happens, and that is what the film is worth watching for. Recommended for lovers of magical realism, of Suzdal (the old Russian town) and of that love-at-first-sight atmosphere.

---

## Fireworks in the Afternoon: The Kind of Film You Go to Festivals For

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/feyerverki-dnem-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-10-05 (5 October 2025)
Work: “Fireworks in the Afternoon” is a 2025 film directed by Nina Volova.
Tags: Russian cinema, festivals, dramedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/feyerverki-dnem-2025/

*Fireworks in the Afternoon* (*Feyerverki dnyom*) is exactly the kind of film that makes going to festivals worthwhile. Alive, sparkling and elusively beautiful, like those very fireworks, set off in the afternoon.

This airy, realistic story about three sisters trying to save the family nest from being sold is an extremely successful feature debut from Nina Volova. A drama poised between non-stop laughter and bitter tears, it has also managed to soak up the mood of Chekhov’s writing, both *Three Sisters* and *The Cherry Orchard*.

At the same time the film steps with one foot into the territory of talk about the mysterious Russian soul: the outsider’s gaze is supplied by Wang Bing’s character, a Chinese businessman who is very calculating at first. It is largely his gaze that creates the comic sensation of studying yourself in a mirror, though it is a good-natured kind of studying, and one open to the new.

The team got about 10 minutes of applause; I caught a couple of moments on camera. So far it is the best film I’ve seen in the programme, and I’ll be really looking forward to its release so I can show it to everyone.

---

## Lermontov: A Journey Through Time to What Time Does Not Change

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/lermontov-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-10-05 (5 October 2025); updated: 2025-10-16
Work: “Lermontov. Doomsday” is a 2025 film directed by Bakur Bakuradze.
Tags: Russian cinema, biopic, festivals
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/lermontov-2025/

## 5 October 2025

And really, [*Lermontov*](https://t.me/kino_voice/941) is an astonishing journey through time to what time does not change.

From its first shots the film wraps you in the texture of the period and the place, literally letting you touch a way of living and thinking. We slow down along with the static camera, which is in no hurry to follow the characters’ movements and instead records the overall picture almost impassively. Like fate, so often woven out of fatal mistakes.

Nothing about the poet’s last day before the duel gives away that the moment is anything special. On the contrary, the day seems to interest everyone except the protagonist. And Ilya Ozolin is excellent at conveying an ironic indifference to himself and the world, laughing things off in a few caustic words against a pastoral country backdrop.

This film could be called a kind of polar opposite of *The Poet* (the Pushkin musical biopic). All they have in common is that both turn to the lives of poetic geniuses. Otherwise *Lermontov* is quieter, more modest, more realistic and more everyday, especially when it comes to the terrible moment of a senseless death. But death is not where the reflection ends, and Bakuradze places his full stop far more gracefully. Perhaps that is exactly why the film is screening out of competition: it is hard to sit in judgement on the eternal truth that violence is senseless.

Catch it in cinemas, released by [@volgafilms](https://t.me/volgafilms) and [@k24films](https://t.me/k24films), from 16 October.

## 16 October 2025

Bakur Bakuradze’s wonderful [*Lermontov*](https://t.me/volgafilms/6926) is in cinemas from today. Following up my [enthusiastic recommendation from Mayak](https://t.me/kino_voice/942) (the film festival in Gelendzhik), I also want to highlight one significant detail for everyone who has yet to see the film.

I mean the epilogue scene. It is the director’s very inventively constructed version of an alternative universe in which everything might have turned out differently. Watch out for the film’s last scene, where Lermontov, in his usual manner, sets up a practical joke on the husband of a lady who has been playing billiards with him. It is all arranged in such a way that (given a husband of a certain temper) there would have been every right to challenge the poet to a duel. But that doesn’t happen. In this case what prevails is the trust between husband and wife, a sense of one’s own dignity, the humanist principle that life has value. In short, everything that saves not just poets but people in general.

---

## My Son: A Film Rich in Symbols You Have to Decipher

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/moy-syn-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-10-05 (5 October 2025)
Work: “My Son” is a 2025 film directed by Vyacheslav Klevtsov.
Tags: Russian cinema, drama, festivals
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/moy-syn-2025/

Opening the programme (which is largely devoted to family ties) is the film *My Son* (*Moy syn*). It is director Vyacheslav Klevtsov’s feature debut. It stars Yulia Snigir, Leon Kemstach and Pavel Tabakov (who presented the film together with the crew).

The film, styled with a minimalist coldness, is rich in symbols, and you should go in ready to decipher them. Here we have a successful lawyer who has tangled herself up in lies to the whole world and to herself: at first she lies even to her psychologist. Her son is someone else’s son. Her home is a perpetual dusty building site. Her appearance is a mask that she managed to take off too late. Yulia Snigir is extremely convincing in this angular vacuum, yet without winning a drop of sympathy from the audience. Only on losing her son does her character realise that she has lost herself. What convinces her of it is being rejected, on top of everything, by an admirer who is blind to her sins. And bribery and bought verdicts make an excellent backdrop.

As one of the film’s key young characters puts it: “Our generation weeps for the sins of yours.” The fathers-and-children conflict is settled here in something like a draw. According to the filmmakers, “the main character finds strength in being able to feel emotions”. What the younger generation finds its strength in is for the audience to decide.

---

## The “General’s Ticker” Meme: How a Mikhalkov Scene Became an Internet Phenomenon

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/mem-generalskie-kotly/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-09-28 (28 September 2025)
Work: “Burnt by the Sun 2: Citadel” is a work  Nikita Mikhalkov.
Tags: Russian cinema, pop culture, notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/mem-generalskie-kotly/

I can’t just walk past the “general’s ticker” meme («генеральские котлы», literally “the general’s cauldrons”, criminal slang for a wristwatch).

You have probably come across the scene from *Burnt by the Sun 2: Citadel* somewhere in vertical videos over the past month. Paradoxically, the meme took off because the incredible bombast of the source scene met the absurdity and post-irony of today’s memes. The “wild general’s ticker”, so to speak, has become “the general’s ticker now”.

A scene this rich in meme material, with a bandit whose look recalls Grigory Leps (the Russian pop singer), a Wolverine glove on Nikita Mikhalkov’s hand and lines that sound like ready-made quotes, was bound to become an internet phenomenon sooner or later.

On this overcast autumn evening I’m attaching my favourite version: nothing superfluous, just the “general’s ticker” and the music from the series *The Kitchen* (the hit Russian sitcom).

By the way, drop a **🐳** if you’re interested in breakdowns of film memes, and post your favourite film memes in the comments.

## Ruslan and Lyudmila: Interviews with the Team for Kinopoisk

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/ruslan-i-lyudmila-intervyu-s-komandoy/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-09-25 (25 September 2025)
Work: “Ruslan and Lyudmila” is a work  Egor Chichkanov.
Tags: Russian cinema, interview, adaptation, fairy tales
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/ruslan-i-lyudmila-intervyu-s-komandoy/

You’d think it was too early to be looking forward to a 2027 premiere, but I already am.

It’s all because of the charming team behind *Ruslan and Lyudmila* («Руслан и Людмила. Волшебное путешествие»), who [told me about the shoot](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/news/4011823/)[,](https://t.me/FBChu/48186) and so vividly that I’m already dreaming of seeing it all. These really were some of the most fun and heartfelt interviews I’ve ever done.

Here, for example, is how the director Egor Chichkanov talks about the knight Farlaf, a minor character in Pushkin:

> ...We took Roma Evdokimov and made sure that every appearance he makes on screen gets a laugh. I gave Roma a task: to play it as if his character were starring in a film called *Farlaf and Lyudmila* and there were no Ruslan at all. In every scene he really did have us dying of laughter.

A stroke of genius as an acting brief, if you ask me! :) As for who the screenwriter Denis Danilov pictured in the role of Ruslan, I won’t even drop a hint: let it stay a bonus for those who read the [piece](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/news/4011823/).

## Nanny Oksana: Faithful to the Style of 2000s Series

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/nyanya-oksana-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-09-23 (23 September 2025)
Work: “Nanny Oksana” is a 2025 series directed by Evgeniya Abdel-Fattah.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, sitcom, 2000s
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/nyanya-oksana-serial/

Some things never change: in series about nannies in rich families, the funniest jokes are invariably delivered by the butler.

I’m talking about [*Nanny Oksana*](https://youtu.be/ji9PJSF7Ys0?si=p-FVD2OhCDGTw0Bq) (*Nyanya Oksana*), which had its premiere yesterday at the Khudozhestvenny (a historic Moscow cinema). The show wins you over with its faithfulness to the style of 2000s series (even more so than the new *Moscow Does Not Believe in Tears*). There are the transitions between scenes done in the style of the opening titles, the children’s cartoonish personalities, and the implausibly miraculous way the nanny lands a job with a rich man’s family. This kind of naivety can be considered the plot’s calling card, and you’ll find it without fail in every frame.

What keeps it all fresh is the abundance of jokes about the trademarks of the Russian TV channel Pyatnitsa (“Aren’t you that chef who drives every contestant on the show to hysterics? I adore you!”), a sprinkling of modern clichés like “harassment”, and a cunning streak in the head of the family that wasn’t there in the source. The one thing is that this show’s Zhanna Arkadyevna (the nanny’s rival in *My Fair Nanny*, the 2000s Russian version of *The Nanny*) is lagging behind in bitchiness for now, but that may be a matter of time, and it will all come after the premiere on 29 September.

---

## One Call Bar: A Chamber Piece About Fixating on Missed Chances

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/bar-odin-zvonok-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-09-22 (22 September 2025); updated: 2025-10-24
Work: “One Call Bar” is a 2025 series directed by Sergey Filatov.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, supernatural
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/bar-odin-zvonok-serial/

## 22 September 2025

All the episodes of [*One Call Bar*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/dva-seriala-s-daniloy-kozlovskim/) (*Bar “Odin zvonok”*) are out on 1 October!

After the news that the show was coming back, we didn’t have to wait long for a premiere date, and that’s great. What makes it even more interesting is how the crew see the show. Here is what director Sergey Filatov says:

> This is a story about regret. We often regret what we have done and, perhaps even more often, what we haven’t. Some things cannot be undone — that is the whole horror and beauty of life: it is fleeting. It’s important to remind yourself of that now and then.

It’s good that the series is coming out after all, and we won’t have to feel any regret over it.

## 24 October 2025

By the way, [*One Call Bar*](https://t.me/kino_voice/909) goes down very well in a single sitting!

The show’s high concept (a mysterious bar where an ironically burnt-out bartender is always happy to offer you a call to the afterlife in exchange for a round of Russian roulette) is, of course, stronger than what ended up on screen. But the series is still enjoyable to watch. It is a tightly constructed chamber piece, a meditation on fixating on missed chances and devaluing your own life. The closest comparison, I think, is a collection of short stories with this paranormal premise running through them as a single connecting thread, while the characters change from one story to the next.

The ending deserves a special mention: it completely cancels out all the black humour that Danila Kozlovsky’s character leans on so heavily, and closes the story on a genuinely bright note. It is also entirely convincing and wraps up the most mysterious storyline, which is something of a rarity. In short, the series is a sure way to spend an autumn evening in style.

---

## The Paper: A Well-Made, Gentle Comedy in Tune with the Times

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/gazeta-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-09-15 (15 September 2025)
Work: “The Paper” is a 2025 series directed by Greg Daniels.
Tags: series, comedy, sitcom, American cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/gazeta-serial/

While my colleagues toil away at Novy sezon (“New Season”, a Russian series festival), I’m amusing myself with [*The Paper*](https://t.me/kino_voice/839) — yes, that spin-off of *The Office*, only this time it’s not just about paper but about an honest-to-goodness newspaper.

Of course, you shouldn’t expect this series to have you laughing without pause for breath, the way *The Office* used to! But that’s no drawback at all — just a small problem with our expectations, which are tied to its predecessor.

*The Paper* has a great set-up, vivid characters and cringe that has been tidied up just enough — half of it specific to the media world, half of it the universal office kind. It’s a very well-made, gentle comedy in tune with the times — in other words, a pleasant companion for any free evening. Here’s a little checklist of what to expect (it doubles as a list of reasons to watch *The Paper*):

- Toilet-paper jokes
- An Italian villainess
- Oscar from the original *Office*
- Great opening credits showing people doing anything with a newspaper except reading it
- The show’s own Jim and Pam — and we need nothing more

## DOKer Festival 2025: What to Catch Before It Closes

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/festival-doker-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-09-13 (13 September 2025)
Tags: festivals, documentary, Moscow
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/festival-doker-2025/

Moscow’s [DOKer International Film Festival,](https://www.midff.ru/schedule) which brings together the best docs from all over the world, comes to a close on 14 September.

Personally, I’m looking forward to the closing for the premiere of [*Flamingos: Life After the Meteorite*](https://www.midff.ru/product-page/flamingos). It’s a touching film about how Caribbean flamingos start families. The shoot took more than 9 years, and it was worth it — just look at the footage of these colourful cuties, you can’t take your eyes off them. It’s showing at the Oktyabr cinema, [tickets here,](https://karofilm.ru/film/14910?date=2025-09-14) so the big-screen effect is guaranteed :)

Screenings at DOKer come with discussions with the filmmakers, psychologists and film critics, which is always cool. And new this year is DOKer Art, a programme about art created together with the Béton Centre for Visual Culture, where you can see both personal portraits of renowned artists and studies of entire cultural eras.

What else you can still catch at DOKer:

- 13 September, 19.00. [*Protokol Tukdama*](https://www.midff.ru/product-page/tukdam) («Протокол Тукдама», “The Tukdam Protocol”). On the dialogue between Buddhism and modern science.
- 14 September, 14.00. [*Norsoyan*](https://www.midff.ru/product-page/norsoyan) («Норсоян»). A confession about dreams, creative freedom and the price of high fashion.

The full schedule and details are [here](https://www.midff.ru/schedule).

**Tell me, which documentaries do you love and would happily recommend?**

## Mayak Festival 2025: Jury, Programme, Winners and Impressions

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/festival-mayak-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova

Tags: festivals, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/festival-mayak-2025/

## 11 September 2025

The morning starts with festival news — Mayak (the Russian film festival in Gelendzhik) has announced its [jury](https://mayakfestival.ru/jury/)!

The feature competition will be judged by:

• Bakur Bakuradze, jury chair, director, producer, screenwriter (and director of the festival’s opening film, [*Lermontov*](https://t.me/kino_voice/760))
• Eduard Gimpel, cinematographer
• Evgenia Gromova, actress
• Natalya Kudryashova, director, actress, screenwriter
• Sergey Melkumov, producer

And the short films are in the hands of:

• Sergey Kornikhin, producer
• Anna Kuznetsova, director, screenwriter (and director of [*Intermission*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kanikuly-2023/), which won at Mayak 2023)
• Ekaterina Smolina, cinematographer

All that’s left is the small matter of finding out the programme.

## 23 September 2025

The Mayak festival now has a [programme](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/news/4011863/).

I have particularly high hopes for ***Yura Was Here***, with Khabensky and Kotrelev, and for the animated film ***Tied Up***, from Konstantin Bronzit.

And, ironic as it may sound, I’m also looking forward to ***The Good Life*** — by the look of it, it puts an unexpected spin on Gaidar’s story *Golubaya chashka* («Голубая чашка», “The Blue Cup”), and the lead is the [theatre](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/vishnevyy-son-teatr/) star Serafima Goshchanskaya.

## 9 October 2025

The Mayak 2025 results:

- Grand Prix — *Yura Was Here*
- Best Director — Sonya Rayzman, *Scenes of Friendly Ties*
- Best Debut — *Fireworks in the Afternoon*
- Best Actor — Konstantin Khabensky (*Yura Was Here*)
- Best Actress — Maria Karpova (*Scenes of Friendly Ties*)
- Best Screenplay — Ekaterina Tirdatova (*Above Eternal Rest*)
- Best Cinematography — Oleg Lukichev (*Above Eternal Rest*)
- Best Short Film — *Igra v pryatki* («Игра в прятки», “Hide and Seek”)

## 9 October 2025

I [guessed](https://t.me/kino_voice/984) 4 of the categories right! Not bad — and the element of surprise was still there.

## 10 October 2025

Last but not least.

Mayak 2025 was the festival’s third edition but my first, and I’m very happy to have become part of it — it’s a big, long celebration of film that has surprises of its own in store for every viewer.

The video shows the Mayak team, who spend the whole year preparing for the festival: that many people won’t fit on a stage or into a lens (but I tried). I’m grateful to every one of these professionals for the fact that the festival happens, that the films make it to us and that audiences and filmmakers get to talk to each other.

The festival’s programme director, Stas Tyrkin, really does have an astonishing gift for assembling works of cinema into extraordinary combinations. This year we kept catching parallels between the films: in the relationships between mothers and sons, in attitudes to cats, in close-ups of ears of wheat symbolising the hero’s inner world and, of course, in the title of the closing series, *Lighthouse* (in Russian *Mayak*, like the festival), which will serve as a bridge between this year and the next. Bravo!

## 12 October 2025

The [final chord](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/news/4011951/) of Mayak 2025 is the digest [Nikita](https://t.me/sedmoeiskysstvo/749) and I put together — featuring, as it happens, all the films about parents and children (including the closing series, [*Lighthouse*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/mayak-serial/)).

Big things are best seen from a distance — in this selection the subtle links between the films in the programme are more visible than ever. Recommended reading.

## Two New Series with Danila Kozlovsky: One Call Bar and Igra na vylet

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/dva-seriala-s-daniloy-kozlovskim/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-09-10 (10 September 2025)
Tags: series, Russian cinema, announcements
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/dva-seriala-s-daniloy-kozlovskim/

And more good news: two great shows at once with Danila Kozlovsky, whose roles we have, honestly, been missing for a long time.

First, before the year is out KION (a Russian streaming service) will release the series ***One Call Bar*** («Бар „Один звонок“»), in which the actor has the mystical role of the bartender at the establishment of the title. Among the other characters are those played by Alexander Ilyin, Oksana Akinshina and [Serafima Goshchanskaya, whom I love for her stage roles.](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/vishnevyy-son-teatr/) There’s no date yet, but to brighten our wait the folks at KION have made [a hypnotic ten-hour teaser.](https://youtu.be/3pFl-fFGC38) Nice try, but we’re still waiting for the date.

Second, Wink (another Russian streaming service) has started shooting the series ***Igra na vylet*** («Игра на вылет», “Knockout Game”), in which Danila Kozlovsky, just like in the old days, has a sporting role. This time the actor will transform into a weary tennis coach who dreams of finding a gifted protégé. And he finds one — in the shape of Polina Gukhman’s character. Tennis is a fresh subject, the stakes for the characters are high, and the chances of success are all there.

## F1: The Plastic World Has Won After All

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/f1-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-09-09 (9 September 2025)
Work: “F1” is a 2025 film directed by Joseph Kosinski.
Tags: blockbuster, sport, Hollywood
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/f1-2025/

[*F1*](https://t.me/kino_voice/874) is, of course, masterfully breathtaking at certain moments, but at the same time it reminds you that the plastic world has won after all (a line from a Russian punk anthem).

The film has plenty going for it: Brad Pitt, who hasn’t lost an ounce of conviction as the cool rebel; the camerawork in the racing scenes, which are cut so that you wish you could unlearn blinking; an inspiring story that moves with real drive. And the rules of motor racing are explained as seamlessly as possible, so that we and the characters think in the same terms. It all adds up to a terrific ride that really does live up to the title of the big blockbuster, but there are a couple of “buts”.

At the start the film seems to be doing, to use racing drivers’ slang, a lap to warm up the tyres. We are introduced to the main characters, who don’t exactly invite sympathy (and, being who they are, simply don’t need it), and the coming conflict is sketched out (Brad Pitt’s character versus everyone). For the whole of this warm-up I, as a viewer, am in the passive position of an observer rather than a participant in what is going on, because there is no one for my empathy to latch onto: the characters are set up as script functions, not fully fledged people.

The film’s sterile studio polish has made its character descriptions schematic, as if they skip the stage of emotional make-up and go straight to spelling out for the viewer who is there to do what. Sonny Hayes is a great guy with attitude who will drive everyone up the wall but never betray them. The young driver who needs to pick up some wisdom, not just swagger. The team leader who is in crisis, but Hayes will save everyone. The gifted engineer whose single exchange of glances with Hayes is enough for us to predict a romantic storyline.

Perhaps this technical precision of formulas that work in blockbusters is exactly what secured the film’s success with audiences. But I would have liked to come away with more heartfelt impressions, not rational observations.

---

## A Cool Change: A Pleasant Feel-Good Series

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/krutaya-peremena-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-09-08 (8 September 2025)
Work: “A Cool Change” is a 2023 series directed by Karen Oganesyan.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, comedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/krutaya-peremena-serial/

I’m keeping half an eye on season two of [*A Cool Change*](https://youtu.be/2yESFA1soZs?si=lmDQql7Iim295YF8) («Крутая перемена») — the story of a literature teacher by vocation and by accident, played by Nikita Efremov.

A pleasant feel-good series, especially if an undemanding school story is your kind of thing :) For me the bonus of season two is Ivan Dobronravov’s character — a school headmaster who is a little spineless yet never loses his charm or his air of mystery. Incidentally, the colourful shots of Uzbek patterns and golden-brown flatbreads have your hand reaching of its own accord for travel-planning sites, which, if anything, also counts among the show’s virtues.

## Old School: A Well-Made Mockumentary with a Great Line-Up of Colourful Characters

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/oldskul-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-09-05 (5 September 2025); updated: 2025-10-22
Work: “Old School” is a 2025 series directed by Aleksandr Zhigalkin, Evgeny Shelyakin.
Tags: series, sitcom, comedy, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/oldskul-serial/

## 5 September 2025

After 5 episodes, [*Old School*](https://t.me/kino_voice/665) (*Oldskul*) is in excellent shape — a mockumentary sitcom with a school slant couldn’t have been better.

What’s especially pleasing is that even Maria Pavlovna, that immovable rock, develops as a character. I expected her to spend the whole series (very amusingly for viewers) bending the world to her will (if only because “old school rules”, as the song over the closing credits has it). In fact we get concessions to her granddaughter, a crisis over who she is at her age, and plenty of other purely human things you wouldn’t expect from a conservative maths teacher. Great — long may the series go on smashing stereotypes.

P.S. The caretaker is a genius

## 29 September 2025

The most unexpected revelation in [*Old School*](https://t.me/kino_voice/871)

Maria Pavlovna has surprised us again. It turns out she’s been ignoring the caretaker not because she has no interest in romance, as you might have assumed of a pedantic maths teacher. But because the caretaker simply ~~likes his gooseberries~~ isn’t her type!

And also because the Thursday neighbour, it turns out, really doesn’t come round only “to help about the house”.  And here I suddenly found myself in sync with Taisya Kalinina’s character, for whom accepting this state of affairs took some inner work of its own...

Joking aside, though, here’s a clear example of how the series teaches you to see ~~a dry maths teacher~~ teachers as living people. Isn’t that great!

## 19 October 2025

[*Old School*](https://t.me/kino_voice/922) has reached its end at a brisk pace. The series held its standard steadily all the way through, the one exception being that in the last couple of episodes the storylines for a future season started taking shape rather too briskly. But that’s forgivable, because of course you want to go on watching these characters :)

The result is a well-made mockumentary with a great line-up of colourful characters, consistent humour and the ability to reach all sorts of very different audiences. A phenomenon of sorts — 30 million views, mind you.

P.S.: If the last episode is an advert for what life looks like after a full course of antidepressants, then it’s a success.

## 22 October 2025

So where did the pupils in [*Old School*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1014) go to school?

I worked out the filming location literally during the last episode (though I could have done it sooner — it’s all there on Wikipedia).

In a wide shot from the front steps of the “old-school” school, the spire of one of the pavilions at VDNKh (the huge Soviet-era exhibition park in Moscow) popped into view. A bit of simple fiddling with the map gives us the spot from which the view best matches the shot, and we stumble on a building that looks remarkably like the school in the series. Voilà: the Favorit lyceum was partly shot at Tekhnograd, the innovative educational complex at VDNKh.

That’s the route for a weekend walk sorted.

---

## Moscow Does Not Believe in Tears: An Atmospheric Look at 2003 from 2025

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/moskva-slezam-ne-verit-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-09-04 (4 September 2025); updated: 2025-10-17
Work: “Moscow Does Not Believe in Tears. It’s All Just Beginning” is a 2025 series directed by Olga Dolmatovskaya, Zhora Kryzhovnikov.
Tags: series, musical, remake, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/moskva-slezam-ne-verit-serial/

## 4 September 2025

What strikes you first about episode one of the new [*Moscow Does Not Believe in Tears*](https://t.me/kino_voice/860) (the series sequel to the Oscar-winning 1980 film) is that this is not an exact reconstruction of 2003, the year the three heroines first meet, but rather an atmospheric look at it from our own 2025.

Perhaps that comes with the musical genre, which is full of conventions even without leaps in time, and all the more so with them. Hence the anachronistic details: for example, in 2003 Tina Stojiljković’s and Ivan Yankovsky’s characters dance in the “dry fountain” in Muzeon park, which in fact only opened in 2013.

The main anchors of the Soviet original are still there, in the heroines’ characters and their firm friendship, but otherwise this is a new story. Zhora Kryzhovnikov’s signature style brings the long-awaited jump cuts, the jitteriness and the heroines’ cheerful anger. On first viewing the series feels like something between *The Boy’s Word* and *Kombinatsiya* (“Combination”, the series about the 1980s girl band), the two previous high-profile projects from Wink (the Russian streaming service): in the first, the musical inserts worked at 200%, while in the second they tended to replace dialogue in places (and dialogue is sometimes the more interesting thing to listen to, after all).

Since the heroines’ fates are only sketched in over the course of the episode, what touched me most were the signs of the times: a recognisable pre-Sobyanin marshrutka (a minibus taxi from before Moscow’s current mayor), bus stops plastered with ads, loud eclecticism in the clothes. And the pop-culture artefacts and the prices deserve a special mention:

- *Terminator 3* and *Lara Croft* are showing at the cinema, the Tolkienist movement is in its prime, and the girls dash off to a casting for *Fabrika zvyozd* (“Star Factory”, the Russian pop talent show). It brings a tear to the eye.
- A hamburger at McDonald’s costs 17 roubles. An order of two cheeseburgers, fries and ice creams comes to 160 roubles. To make such prices hurt a little less, you can pretend they are simply in today’s Belarusian roubles.

The one thing that is not yet clear is whether the project will stay on the side of fairy-tale sweetness or cross over to realism (especially in the part with the heroines 20 years on); I’ll keep watching to find out.

## 11 September 2025

I liked the second episode of *Moscow Does Not Believe in Tears* so much that I am ready to forget all the doubts I had [after the first](https://t.me/kino_voice/870).

The sparing use of musical numbers really suits the series. The second episode has just one such scene, but it is brilliant (literally and figuratively): a properly cool music video inside the show. In this number Anastasia Talyzina and Andrey Burkovsky combine comedy, sincerity and a showy display of how they feel about each other, which matters for an inserted number that takes place, as it were, in the heroine’s head. The key difference this time is that the musical scene does not retell part of the plot (as it did with Ksyusha’s miserable job) but adds to the heroine’s emotional backdrop without affecting the sequence of events in the world of the series! Cool, vivid, clear, unobtrusive.

And the definitive acting triumph belongs to Mash Milash: her heroine is, it seems to me, the most distinctive and tangible, and following her is a great pleasure. The second episode is mostly hers in terms of screen time, so the creators are presumably betting heavily on this character. She truly sets the mood, whether she is spinning a yarn for the American or taking the sweetest historical re-enactor, played by Andrey Maksimov, on an emotional rollercoaster: cruel in both cases, but funny. I want to believe that things will work out with the Tolkienist after all, and that Masha, true to the classics, will ask the American where strength lies (the famous line from *Brother 2*).

## 19 September 2025

I keep being reassured that the new [*Moscow Does Not Believe in Tears*](https://t.me/kino_voice/882) gets better with every episode.

The third episode again has just one full-blown musical number, unexpectedly not involving a heroine, plus one half-musical scene with the central characters. Modest and tasteful, as they say, and above all meaningful, with a dramatic foundation under the musical wrapping. I hope things stay sorted in this department right through to the last episode.

As a whole, the events of the episode are in what you might call a state of in progress ❌ The girls have already understood something about their relationships but have not yet had time to come to terms with it, and they keep rolling along the rails laid down in advance. Ksyusha might have got away with the same status too, were it not for her husband, who turned up and brought with him the chilling atmosphere of the phrase “the groom has arrived”. Perhaps the final scene on the balcony rhymes with the moment in the original film when Alentova’s heroine cried herself to sleep in the worst of all possible situations, and after a cut we saw her completely different life years later.

## 27 September 2025

Having watched episodes 4 and 5 of the new [*Moscow Does Not Believe in Tears*](https://t.me/kino_voice/905) back to back, I understood what the 90 million viewers felt who gave the Soviet film its phenomenal box office. This is how the [sources](https://www.culture.ru/materials/257558/istoriya-odnogo-filma-moskva-slezam-ne-verit) describe the frenzy:

> “After the premiere of *Moscow Does Not Believe in Tears*, huge queues formed outside cinemas, with people waiting for the box offices to open. Screenings began early in the morning and ran late into the night, and people came back to see the film several times”

I, too, wanted to rewatch these two episodes the moment they ended, though I have never felt that urge with the Soviet two-part film. The sense of belonging to a time in which the heroines’ lives are transformed like this strikes a very strong chord, of course. You begin to understand Soviet cinemagoers — especially the women — 100%, and to believe in a miracle within your own era.

The musical numbers in the new episodes are better than ever. I personally find Ksyusha’s transformation into a businesswoman easy to believe, like any cinematic convention that still has a right to exist. Even Katerina’s rise to factory director, incidentally, was met with scepticism in its day: she could not have risen like that without any outside help, people said. Again, I quote a [source:](https://moskvichmag.ru/kino/rovno-45-let-nazad-v-etot-den-proshla-vsesoyuznaya-premera-filma-moskva-slezam-ne-verit/)

> “*Moscow* could easily have been pulled from distribution and shelved. The film was attacked by critics and the authorities alike, and ‘vulgar melodrama’ was among the mildest charges. There were objections both to the ‘explicit scenes’ and to the very story of a woman’s success. A poor girl like Katya from the provinces could never have had such a career in the USSR — that was the general verdict”

It is especially pleasing that there is no gulf in quality between the two halves of the series; the only thing I will miss is the young versions of the heroines. But the Tolkienist lawyer played by Andrey Maksimov is still here, and his storyline with Masha will definitely remain the most interesting one for me.

## 3 October 2025

In the second half of the new [*Moscow Does Not Believe in Tears*](https://t.me/kino_voice/919), I am particularly pleased that my favourite male character has aged the most handsomely.

Andrey Maksimov was treated gently, and 20 years have done his character’s looks nothing but good — well, they certainly haven’t made them worse. The same cannot be said of Ivan Yankovsky’s character, who seemed to be about the same age as the Tolkienist student, so this paradox of ageing is beyond me. And, of course, of Andrey Burkovsky’s, who may have been the oldest of them all but has been aged far too harshly (apparently to make it easier for Olya to leave him for Ruzil Minekaev).

The logic of the ageing (for which, on the whole, great respect to the make-up department) remains a mystery, but I am glad my taste did not let me down.

## 17 October 2025

In the finale of [*Moscow Does Not Believe in Tears*](https://t.me/kino_voice/927) I can understand and accept everything except the way things end for Masha and Artyom (who seem to have beaten their alcoholism).

As a fan, it hurt (they are my favourite characters). The reason for the break-up is, to my taste, completely unconvincing, and I simply cannot follow Masha’s logic. To me, theirs is the one situation (out of all the couples!) that looks like “just live and be happy”. With both of them working on themselves, of course, but basically problem-free!

The other heroines’ storylines seem more logical to me: they could have been handled differently, or more interestingly, of course, but the outcome we got raises no questions either. On the whole, the finale clearly echoes the start of the series: the friends, as in the good old days, are each other’s only hope, with the whole world against them. Some things, as they say, never change.

---

## If Cats Disappeared from the World: A Book Where the Author’s Ties to Film Show Through

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/esli-vse-koshki-v-mire-ischeznut-kniga/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-08-31 (31 August 2025)
Work: “If Cats Disappeared from the World” is a 2012 book by Genki Kawamura.
Tags: books
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/esli-vse-koshki-v-mire-ischeznut-kniga/

Having already seen the mind-blowing [*Exit 8*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/vykhod-8-2025/) (highly recommended), I got curious about a book by its director, Genki Kawamura: *If Cats Disappeared from the World*.

The plot: the protagonist learns he is terminally ill and is already getting ready to say goodbye to life, but then gets the chance to strike a deal with the devil and receive a day of life for every thing that vanishes from our world. I read the book in literally a day and I’m very pleased with it. Not least with how you can feel the author’s ties to film right there in the text. For example:

- The “devilish double” the protagonist meets is, judging by the description, dressed in the image and likeness of Tyler Durden from *Fight Club*. He’s in a Hawaiian shirt and sunglasses, while the protagonist sticks to classic office wear. This seems to me the best way to visualise a modern-day devil on the page.

- The woman the protagonist loves lives and works in a cinema. I’m not even hinting at *Inglourious Basterds*; it’s enough that the love interest is tied to film as personally as can be. By the way, the hero’s close friend is a film geek who works in a video rental shop. No hints at Tarantino here either.

- At one point the protagonist wonders whether everything that is happening to him could be put on screen. A true director’s thought.

- The characters’ conversations quote (or mention) films very unobtrusively but fairly often, from *The Matrix* to *Now Is Good* (the latter appears as “the film in which the dying heroine writes down 10 things she wants to get done in time”, but we know which one is meant). The protagonist is pretty well versed in film!

- At one point the devil proposes that all films should vanish (in exchange for a day of the hero’s life). Knowing that the book’s author is a director, I found it as gripping as it gets to follow the character’s decision here.

---

## Sergei Gilev on Russian Cinema Day: “Russian Cinema Is All Right”

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/gilyov-rossiyskoe-kino-v-poryadke/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-08-27 (27 August 2025)
Tags: Russian cinema, interview, industry
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/gilyov-rossiyskoe-kino-v-poryadke/

Timed with a jeweller’s precision for Russian Cinema Day (27 August; happy holiday to everyone involved!), Sergei Gilev came out with words of pure gold [in an interview](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/4011623) for Kinopoisk (Russia’s largest film database, media and streaming service):

> Russian cinema is all right. And it carries on being all right; it’s just that it always has some reason to come down with something. It has always been developing; it’s just that right now that development has been put on pause. A short one, I hope. It will be fine in the end. And the fact that this development is there can be seen from the inside as well.

I never stop admiring not just every appearance Gilev makes on screen, but the example set by his path through life as a whole. From the Kinopoisk newsroom straight into the ranks of the coolest actors around: one of those cases when the stars really did align.

Masha Fedina for Kinopoisk
