## Kinoteatr povtornogo filma: Why We Put On a Favourite Film Again and Again

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kinoteatr-povtornogo-filma-kniga/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-08-26 (26 August 2025)
Work: “Kinoteatr povtornogo filma” is a 2022 book by Boris Lokshin.
Tags: books, rewatch
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/kinoteatr-povtornogo-filma-kniga/

Speaking of favourite (and, accordingly, often rewatched) films.

I’ve been engrossed in the book [*Kinoteatr povtornogo filma*](https://books.yandex.ru/books/OdLZppme?utm_campaign=users_referral&amp;utm_medium=referral&amp;utm_source=direct_link) («Кинотеатр повторного фильма», “The Repeat Film Cinema”): Boris Lokshin’s essays on various films bring together all the phenomena that make us put on a favourite film again and again. For example:

- When we rewatch, we unconsciously notice precisely what we had forgotten since last time, not what we remember well

- Seeing yourself with fresh eyes on a rewatch, thanks to the character you identify with

- A rewatch can feel timely after a director has passed away — then you can see something new in the film about him, too

## Exit 8: An Adaptation That Outgrows the Very Idea of Adaptation

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/vykhod-8-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-08-24 (24 August 2025)
Work: “Exit 8” is a 2025 film directed by Genki Kawamura.
Tags: horror, thriller, adaptation
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/vykhod-8-2025/

I have to confess: I have an unbearably bad sense of direction — learning a new route is always a major ordeal.

Which made [*Exit 8*](https://t.me/provzglyad/4614), already admired at Cannes, all the more interesting to me. I recognised myself on screen — the number of times I’ve wandered around the underground just like that.

It’s an adaptation of the game of the same name, and one that seems to have outgrown the very notion of an adaptation. The hyper-immersion in the unreal atmosphere of the underground, which the protagonist cannot find his way out of, is a real find on the part of director Genki Kawamura.

The character’s wanderings through the labyrinths of his own conscience and memories never turn into a melancholy meditation; instead they create a tension you can feel through the screen. The horror elements, the thriller mood and the gamified structure of events work together so precisely that you’re hit by a quite palpable claustrophobia, half and half with a surge of anxiety. *Exit 8* turns the viewer into an accomplice — as if the protagonist’s fate depended on how observant we are, too. It’s for precisely this kind of gripping experience that the film is worth seeing in a cinema.

In cinemas from 28 August thanks to [@provzglyad](https://t.me/provzglyad). Don’t miss it — a real thriller on the threshold of the autumn daily grind, with its eternal metro rides.

---

## The Author’s Birthday: Thank You to Readers and Film Colleagues

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/den-rozhdeniya-avtora-2025/

I’m also celebrating my birthday today, so let the GIF be in keeping with the most anticipated series.

Over the past year I did things I could never have imagined, overcame fears and doubts, and ended up becoming the best version of myself (in the good [sense](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/substantsiya-2024/)). All so that a year on I could look back at the me of 2024 and see that none of it was, or will be, for nothing. And to get it firmly into my head that dreams do come true if you keep working towards them.

I’m more grateful than I can say to everyone who subscribes to this channel and reads it: it has become something I can’t imagine myself without. Your comments and opinions are priceless. I also want to say a huge, heartfelt thank you to each and every one of my colleagues in film: the Telegram channels, the film media, the streaming services, the production companies, the film festivals and the people whose job is to make the films themselves. Every day, working among you, I marvel at how lucky I once was that a passion for film grew into the chance to be part of such an incredible community.

I’m sending festive rays of love and gratitude; without you none of this would be working out.

## Cherkizon. New Russia’s Hell and Paradise: The 1990s Seen Through a Single Phenomenon

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/cherkizon-ad-i-ray-novoy-rossii-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-08-20 (20 August 2025)
Work: “Cherkizon. New Russia’s Hell and Paradise” is a 2025 series directed by Vadim Vatagin.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, documentary, 1990s
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/cherkizon-ad-i-ray-novoy-rossii-serial/

Yesterday the documentary series [*Cherkizon*](https://okko.tv/serial/cherkizon-ad-i-rajj-novojj-rossii) (the nickname of Moscow’s vast Cherkizovsky market) came out on Okko (the Russian streaming service): one of the most powerful experiences of the documentary programme at Pilot (the Russian series festival in Ivanovo).

We are all fairly used to the 1990s in scripted series, but here the era is shown through one specific phenomenon, and so it looks a little different (besides, the documentary form makes itself felt).

The first episode flies by and leaves you impatient to see what comes next: how one particular empire arose and flourished, and why it vanished. Genre-wise it is a thriller, a comedy and a nostalgic look back at a bygone era all at once, which throws up combinations ranging from ones that stagger you by the mere fact that they can exist to the frankly cringeworthy. And figures we know from show business appear in a very unusual light (and not just Russian ones!)

In short: my plan for the evening, and a recommendation to anyone interested.

## KION Begins Work on Volshebnitsa, with Songs from Mary Poppins, Goodbye

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kion-volshebnitsa-meri-poppins/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-08-19 (19 August 2025)
Work: “Volshebnitsa” is a work.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, announcements, musical
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/kion-volshebnitsa-meri-poppins/

We’re getting a new *Mary Poppins, Goodbye* (*Meri Poppins, do svidaniya*, the 1983 Soviet musical film). Kion (the Russian streaming service) has started work on a series, the musical comedy *Volshebnitsa* («Волшебница», “The Sorceress”).

The cast isn’t known yet. Naturally, the rights to Maxim Dunayevsky’s classic songs have been bought for the show, but it’s a different detail that makes me happy.

The series will be written by Maxim Kudymov — the man who wrote [*Obvious Is Incredible*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/series/5119715/) («Очевидное невероятное»; I love it dearly, though I never got round to writing about it here at the time) and [*Barankins and Power Stones*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/barankiny-i-kamni-sily-serial/) — series, in other words, that are brilliant at combining the fairy-tale with the everyday. So as far as the plot goes, I think it’ll be gripping.

The catch is that another nanny remake is already on its way — [*Nanny Oksana*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/series/8322804/) (*Nyanya Oksana*) — and whether there’ll be demand for quite so much nanny content is an open question.

## Alim Beschokov and Sergey Notarius on Neural Networks in Filmmaking

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/neyroseti-v-kino-beschokov-notarius/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-08-18 (18 August 2025)
Tags: industry, interview, series
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/neyroseti-v-kino-beschokov-notarius/

One of the most interesting moments of our conversation [on set](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/ira-2-sezon-intervyu-olerinskaya/) was Alim Beschokov and Sergey Notarius’s answers about how they feel about neural networks in filmmaking. Are they used there, and if so, how?

Screenwriter [Alim Beschokov](https://t.me/beskinolent) shared his view that AI can currently be used for research and for developing a story, but not for writing an entire script. Reproducing a living person’s turn of phrase, ideas and style is still beyond neural networks.

Director Sergey Notarius, for his part, described 3 real examples of AI being used in film production:

- On the shoot of one series, whose protagonist is forever watching ice hockey, they needed to use clips of match broadcasts a lot — but how do you do that with copyright to think about? A neural network came to the rescue: the editor assembled the scene from stock footage, and the commentator’s lines were generated in ChatGPT. The text was recorded with an actor, and the result was a believable, good-quality broadcast.

- When you’re working with bulky series scripts, a neural network is handy for briefly summarising the events of each episode and building a sort of episode-by-episode timeline — it helps you quickly find who/what/where in each scene without endless scrolling.

- For production designers, AI generates the characters’ family photos and props — with no separate photo shoot. AI is also widely used in creating graphics and visual effects.

I hope that, thanks to technologies like these, our favourite series will get made even faster and more often.

---

## Ingrid Olerinskaya on the Second Season of Ira

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/ira-2-sezon-intervyu-olerinskaya/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-08-16 (16 August 2025); updated: 2025-09-12
Work: “Ira” is a work  Alim Beschokov, Sergey Notarius.
Tags: series, interview
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/ira-2-sezon-intervyu-olerinskaya/

## 16 August 2025

Today I’m sneaking a look at the shoot for season 2 of [*Ira*.](https://youtu.be/94fx-zWjOR0?si=Heo9EnZwxnjGL3WC) It’s one of my [favourite](https://t.me/kino_voice/71) series, so I’m madly grateful to the team at [Norm Production](https://t.me/normproduction) for inviting me on set.

And first up, a tour of Ira’s flat, the very one: here’s the famous living room with the red sofa🪑, and that toilet, and what’s new in season two — baby things :)

I asked Ingrid Olerinskaya herself about the changes to Ira’s character, and also got a couple of comments from the writer and producer Alim Beschokov and the season’s director, Sergey Notarius. Stay tuned, it will all be here.

## 12 September 2025

That’s a wrap on the second season of [*Ira*](https://t.me/kino_voice/71)!

Making the most of my [invitation to the set from Norm Production,](https://t.me/kino_voice/825) I asked Ingrid Olerinskaya about the show’s heroine and the surprises of the season to come.

What can’t you imagine a day on set without?

*Without coffee, without my phone, because there’s a constant stream of work questions and the chat never goes quiet, and without the look on my face. Which quite often matches Ira’s.*

What have you taught Ira, and what has she taught you?

*This is the first role I’ve had where my character gets pregnant, then has the baby, and spends a lot of time around children. I taught Ira all of that, because I have 3 nephews. I’ve been bringing them up since they were little, you could say. Ira, for her part, taught me stamina. I’m a tough little cookie as it is — tempered like iron, let’s say. But here, of course, the sheer amount of work on set forces you to grit your teeth and hold on to the very end.*

Do you think Ira will make a good mother?

*Ira has every chance of becoming a good mother. For all her relationship with the world, which we remember from season 1, season 2 does bring a transformation, and an acceptance of the situation and of her status now. And, of course, the love and the maternal feeling are there one way or another. I think that feeling will grow and win out.*

Which moments on set are the hardest and, on the other hand, which are your favourites?

*The most uncomfortable and maddening thing in an actor’s work is the huge days when I’m the only one talking on screen. On the other hand, that’s a buzz too, because not everyone can do it. I pray this skill never deserts me. But the biggest buzz, of course, is all of Ira’s fantasies. Most of them, let’s say. There’s always a little touch of magic there — the dressing up, the costumes, the make-up. I think it’s really cool — especially when you watch it later in the context of the whole series, it’s very funny. I generally like the bits where I play men of some sort. There was a sultan, a sheikh in season 1. Thomas Edison. And in season 2, I’ll let you in on a secret, there’ll be a fantasy cavalry cornet, my favourite funny character.*

What would you like to say to viewers of the second season of *Ira*?

*When you watch season 2, just pay attention to the script, the dialogue, the humour and, in general, the interesting way it’s built and shot. Non-linear, as if made up of flashbacks and fantasy. I think it’s an interesting device — I believe in our team, and I believe the second season will be even cooler than the first.*

---

## Vishnyovy son at a39: A New Gogol Center Has Arrived

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/vishnevyy-son-teatr/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-08-11 (11 August 2025)
Work: “Vishnyovy son” is a 2025 stage production directed by Oleg Glushkov.
Tags: theatre
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/vishnevyy-son-teatr/

“A new Gogol Center has arrived!” was the thought that came to me in the first minutes of *Vishnyovy son* («Вишнёвый сон», “Cherry Dream”) at a39 (the Moscow theatre).

And really, it turned out to be a superb piece of work in the way it combines Chekhov’s original *The Cherry Orchard* with contemporary stage design. I had been missing this kind of thing ever since the production of *The Misanthrope* at the Gogol Center (the Moscow theatre closed in 2022).

As you watch, you feel that the production is somehow speaking your language without forgetting its source, and that is worth a great deal. Everything, from the design and costumes to the music and how well the actors fit their roles, is simply 100% on target. I do have a weakness for techno in the theatre, I can’t help it, but how perfectly it fits here: the sound of a breaking string that we deserve. And “The Winner Takes It All”, sung towards the end, is, whichever way you look at it, the best musical embodiment of Lopakhin’s tragedy for sheer pith and economy (a tragedy that director Oleg Glushkov at first slyly disguises as a dramedy).

As for the cast, it is very, very convincing. I want to watch again every line of Serafima Goshchanskaya’s Ranevskaya, every monologue of Sergei Kirpichonok’s Petya Trofimov, every coy affectation of Elizabeth Damsker’s Dunyasha and — especially — every scene of Ilya Ozolin’s Lopakhin. I could shower the theatre’s company with compliments forever: every one of them is simply one of a kind, and the sooner they start getting cast more in our films and series, the better (colleagues, take note!)

In the meantime, we’re waiting for Ilya Ozolin’s big dramatic role in Bakuradze’s [*Lermontov*](https://t.me/kino_voice/760): now that he has lived (I can’t bring myself to say “played”) Lopakhin on stage, my expectations have only grown.

---

## Barankins and Power Stones: Brisk Urban Fantasy and a Catalogue of Pop-Culture References

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/barankiny-i-kamni-sily-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-08-07 (7 August 2025)
Work: “Barankins and Power Stones” is a 2025 series directed by Misha Polyakov.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, fantasy, comedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/barankiny-i-kamni-sily-serial/

[*Barankins and Power Stones*](https://youtu.be/sDWYjSvJZpA?si=SE29hVIJ_-hEp0dR) (*Barankiny i kamni sily*) has premiered, and on the evidence of the first two episodes it looks like a brisk urban fantasy. It seems that in Russian series-making today, mixing fantasy with the present day is the best way to go, because, to my mind, the former without the latter no longer really works.

But back to *Barankins*: I like how concisely and briskly the 5–6 main characters are set up (I’ve written that number down and want to stress once again that, when you’re watching, it doesn’t weigh on you at all). In this family of taxi drivers going back generations, everyone is trying to grab their own little slice of carefree prosperity, but the results are funny and not always successful (even with magic stones to hand). It’s fun that the Barankin clan is essentially a reincarnation of the familiar Voronins, Vasnetsovs, Bukins (families from popular Russian sitcoms) and others (hence the typical sitcom surname).

All in all, you could call the show a catalogue of pop-culture references: from the power stones themselves and the time travel to those same families with their unresolved mutual grievances. But the series’ sturdy structure holds all these “clichés” together very neatly, so it leaves nothing but good impressions.

---

## The Surgeon: The Pros and Cons of a Puzzling Finale

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/khirurg-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-08-04 (4 August 2025); updated: 2025-08-30
Work: “The Surgeon” is a 2025 series directed by Ilya Ermolov.
Tags: series, drama, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/khirurg-serial/

## 4 August 2025

And really, [*The Surgeon*](https://youtu.be/Rq1AtLQneY0?si=vvuSDuGoID0MIPmu) (*Khirurg*) is a wonderful story about a rare kind of hero, one you could describe as “*a bad good man*”.

A transplant surgeon who wanted to shut out the terrible reality of how organs are procured has himself ended up a victim of his own indifference. He is an excellent doctor and father, and he means well, but he is a bad husband and a cruel man, and that is his problem.

Sergei Gilev is perfectly contradictory in the role: combining toughness with sincerity, he creates a hero who inspires empathy but not pity. Then again, I’m probably on his side anyway, because the other characters (apart from his daughter) are mostly just bad people.

I hope this story steers its way to a finale where *bad good people* deserve some relative happiness too.

## 8 August 2025

Episode five of *The Surgeon* works as a great follow-through on the long set-up we were given [in the first four episodes](https://t.me/kino_voice/799). The storytelling method changes too: look closely and you won’t come across any more flashbacks.

It’s good to see Yulia, Marina Vorozhishcheva’s character, come to the fore: you don’t often see a promotion from “damsel in distress” to a fully fledged player in the story; now she is a subject, not an object (though not for long, true). That matters especially at a point when the first turn of surgeon Sergei’s storyline seems to be complete: what the hero would do next if it weren’t for Yulia is not very clear. Gilev, by the way, is as superb as ever. That leaves three episodes to sort out all the problems and enjoy the acting (which really is a joy for the eyes and the soul).

## 30 August 2025

The finale of [*The Surgeon*](https://t.me/kino_voice/799) left me puzzled, so I’ll break it down into pluses and minuses:

👆A happy ending for Sergei, his daughter and her suitor. Vera seems to have come out of it content too (this heroine’s soul is, I suppose, a closed book)

👆Storylines unambiguously wrapped up for a whole host of characters (which, with this many of them, is something of a rarity)

👆Genuinely convincing (for the most part) performances

👇Endings that are too schematic; in cases like this I always argue that an extra episode wouldn’t have hurt (for instance, to reveal Batyr’s plan and whether or not Sergei had a hand in it)

👇 So Vera turns out to be a rat twice over? Men had better stay on their guard around her, or they run a high risk of going to prison for their misdeeds. And in general, the female character has been demonised a little.

👇The first half of the series is noticeably stronger than the second: in plot, in dialogue and in pace. It’s a pity there was such a drop-off; the story really did have a great deal of potential.

---

## A Selection for the Okko Blog: 10 Films and Series About Pickup Artists

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/podborka-okko-pro-pikap/
Author: Betsy Isakova

I watched 10 different films and series (there’s even an Asian drama!) about pickup artists (voluntarily!)

All so as to put together the most unconventional [selection](https://blog.okko.tv/selections/podkaty-navsegda-10-filmov-i-serialov-pro-pikap#1) in my portfolio and explore the history of the genre in time for the release of [*Cynics*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/tsiniki-serial/) (*Tsiniki*). In the piece you’ll find out:

- Do they let pickup artists into teaching?

- Which film lets you cringe hardest at Tom Cruise’s character?

- Why is it a bad idea to miscount Casanova’s women?

- And how long ago did they start letting introspective heroines into pickup stories?

Have fun.

## Breathe: It Does Not Much Matter How the Inquiry Ends

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/dyshi-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-07-29 (29 July 2025); updated: 2025-10-03
Work: “Breathe” is a 2025 series directed by Anna Kuznetsova.
Tags: series, drama, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/dyshi-serial/

## 29 July 2025

The [trailer](https://youtu.be/j_KRCRf7tr0?si=g_9r566AZKtvALfh) for Anna Kuznetsova’s series *Breathe*, the winner of Pilot 2025 (the Russian series festival in Ivanovo), came out today.

I [wrote](https://t.me/kino_voice/674) about it back at the festival, including in the very [article](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/4011387/) for Kinopoisk (Russia’s largest film database, media and streaming service) that the trailer quotes, with the words *“heroines you want to watch”*. I’m insanely pleased that it was my impression of this wonderful series that made it into the trailer.

Like the first episode, the trailer sets you up for a very tense pace, with the world seemingly collapsing around every character. Watch it to get a sense of how the series will take your breath away when it arrives, as soon as 15 August.

## 15 August 2025

This summer’s series about doctors are showing just how dangerous and risky the profession is: one for the truly strong in spirit.

On the one hand there is [*The Surgeon*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/khirurg-serial/), with Sergei Gilev’s long-suffering (but wonderful) character; on the other, [*Breathe*](https://youtu.be/j_KRCRf7tr0?si=dhb5Xz-7NQL8ERc7) (*Dyshi*), a series of staggering power that you watch with trembling hands and ragged breath.

The first episode came out today; I [wrote](https://t.me/kino_voice/674) about it from Pilot (the Russian series festival) and I still haven’t got over it, which is a recommendation of sorts in itself. You can feel one way or another about the lead, Lera, but watching her is gripping, because what we have here is a living, troubled human being rather than a stock doctor who fits the classic idea of the profession, and that is both heartening and frightening. Add the frantic pace, the director’s warmth towards her characters, which you can feel through the screen, and the delicate subject matter, and you get something one of a kind.

## 23 August 2025

The second episode of [*Breathe*](https://t.me/kino_voice/818) puts all the viewer’s ideas about the series in their proper place.

First and foremost, of course, they concern Lera. It turns out she finds time to swipe a medical record at just the right moment, to convince a traffic cop of her innocence, and to do a spot of manipulating her children. That is no surprise — we knew she was no ideal heroine — but it helps you shed any idealisation and needless pity **\*️⃣** It’s great when the character in the foreground is one whose likeability you sometimes have to question: it gives you one more chance to reflect on the theme at hand.

And the updated poster strikes me as a good one in this respect: her patients’ lives are in her hands, of course, but first of all, is her own?

## 6 September 2025

With every episode [*Breathe*](https://t.me/kino_voice/841) seems to make it harder for the viewer to choose a character to trust and feel for.

Now that episode 4 has added Lera’s younger children to the plot’s complicated equation as well, it has become clear that the story is not about obstetrics or medical backroom intrigue at all. It turns out that, as with Anna Kuznetsova’s [*Intermission*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kanikuly-2023/) (*Kanikuly*), behind the screen of a private story on what seems at first glance a narrow subject hides a universal, deeply human drama. Which makes it all the more interesting, because in that case the ending really is impossible to predict.

## 3 October 2025

The final episode of [*Breathe*](https://t.me/kino_voice/873) confirms it: in this story it does not much matter exactly how the inquiry ends, whether the child survives, or even who gets the late Motoruev’s car.

What matters far more is the road the characters have travelled over the course of the events we were shown: that is the very truth we have been striving towards for 8 episodes, and it turns out to be nowhere near as dreadful as it might have seemed at first. These are merely the consequences of a chain of choices, which, observed closely, are entirely possible to understand.

In this respect the series has a lot in common with director Anna Kuznetsova’s feature film [*Intermission*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kanikuly-2023/). There, too, the emphasis was not on the event that drives the plot but on the transformation of the people taking part in it. There is (almost) nothing interesting about a youth theatre competition in itself, but in how the adults and teenagers changed over the course of it, there very much is.

A particular pleasure is how absolutely every character, from the youngest to the oldest, gets a clear ending of their own. Together they add up to the finale of the series: ambiguous and never static, like life itself, but with a gap left for air, which everyone who watched will certainly have needed.

---

## Cynics: Explicit Scenes Shot Beautifully and with Care

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/tsiniki-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-07-28 (28 July 2025)
Work: “Cynics” is a 2025 series directed by Irina Bas.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, dramedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/tsiniki-serial/

I’ve watched the first episodes of [*Cynics*](https://t.me/kino_voice/772) (*Tsiniki*), and they do, of course, douse you straight away with a hot-and-cold shower of erotic scenes of varying degrees of explicitness. I confess I wasn’t ready for that, but the element of surprise worked all the better for it.

Besides, it is entirely justified by the artistic world of this story — these are the rules people communicate by here. It’s all shot very beautifully and with care — I think some of the credit goes to the director, Irina Bas, who has looked at everything that goes on in a woman’s way, without cynicism, contrary to the title. With a crime element quickly added to the numerous romantic intrigues, there is no way you’ll get bored with this show. And for Denis Vlasenko fans like me there is a whole storyline with him in it, as well as a scattering of seasoned actors, from Viktoria Isakova and Kirill Käro to Askar Ilyasov and Vyacheslav Chepurchenko.

---

## Inkassatory: Trademark Humour and a Cunningly Constructed Ending

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/inkassatory-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-07-27 (27 July 2025)
Work: “Inkassatory” is a 2025 series directed by Ruslan Danilevich.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, comedy, crime
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/inkassatory-serial/

I’ve finished [*Inkassatory*](https://t.me/kino_voice/758) («Инкассаторы», “The Cash Collectors”), and I’m pleasantly impressed.

By the finale the series has lost neither its trademark humour nor its CCTV gimmick, so on that front it feels very much of a piece. The one thing is that the lyricism and melodrama, which build towards the finale, sit slightly at odds with the straightforward buddy movie and the crime plot. But that still won’t stop you enjoying the cunning construction of the ending.

I have one question: with a poster that green, why did the colour not feature in the series at all? Neither the cash collectors’ uniforms nor their van was that “money” shade, and this detail of the promo is left hanging in the air a little.

---

## The Most Unusual Credits in Russian Series: A Piece for Kinopoisk

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/titry-rossiyskikh-serialov-kinopoisk/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-07-26 (26 July 2025)
Tags: series, Russian cinema, notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/titry-rossiyskikh-serialov-kinopoisk/

With no false modesty, I want to share a cool piece of work: Kinopoisk (Russia’s largest film database, media and streaming service) has published a [big feature](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/news/4011523/) breaking down the most unusual credits in contemporary Russian series — *Outsource*, *Fisher*, *Overheard in Rybinsk* and others.

Liza Kuznetsova and I spent the last couple of weeks rewatching our favourite credits and putting questions to the people who made them and to the streaming services (colleagues, if you’re reading this, thank you very much).

Personally, I’m pleased: I managed to get the absolutely gorgeous credits of [*Morozko*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/morozko-serial/) (“Jack Frost”) into the piece — more people, I believe, should know about them.

And also to rediscover the credits of *Children of Change* — an utterly mesmerising sight with hypnotic music in the background. Incidentally, it was precisely because I was working on the piece in the background that my viewing of *A Trip to the Sun and Back* unconsciously [synced up](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/puteshestvie-na-solntse-i-obratno-serial/) with those credits.

In short, the piece has come off — I’ll be glad if it doesn’t leave you cold either. And let’s share our favourite credits.

## A Trip to the Sun and Back: The Terrifying 1990s You Mistake for a Fairy Tale

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/puteshestvie-na-solntse-i-obratno-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-07-25 (25 July 2025); updated: 2025-08-13
Work: “A Trip to the Sun and Back” is a 2025 series directed by Roman Mikhailov.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, 1990s
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/puteshestvie-na-solntse-i-obratno-serial/

## 25 July 2025

Having watched 4 episodes of [*A Trip to the Sun and Back*](https://youtu.be/hjmw4RrrEZ8?si=clI46UKOtfK36oeq) (*Puteshestvie na solntse i obratno*) in a row, I not only sank into the atmosphere of the genuinely terrifying 1990s (which, tired of them as we are, could not be better here), all the while taking it for a fairy tale, but also made 2 interesting observations:

**1️⃣** Ruslan, the ethereal, fairy-tale-like protagonist played by Oleg Chugunov, really was born under a lucky star. Over the first episodes we watch his little gang of 4 lads seem to melt into thin air in the 1990s. One was killed in prison, the second lost himself to drugs, and what will become of the third is not yet clear. Ruslan, as if at the crossroads of Russian fairy tales, where stones bear inscriptions like “go left and you’ll find death”, takes all the right turnings with great success and comes out of the water dry, out of the inferno alive, and so on. By the standards of the era and its trappings, luck like this is easy to count as a fairy-tale miracle.

**2️⃣** I don’t know why (all right, I do, but I’ll tell you in a separate post), but in atmosphere the series reminds me of the credits of [*Children of Change*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/deti-peremen-serial/). The same hypnotic feeling of watching a vanishing world, with the foot of cruel reality already raised above it, ready to trample the lot. Only, where in the credits it is a montage of what looks like family home-movie footage, in the series it is impulsive attempts to live out a young and vivid life in a stale vacuum unfit for anything living at all. Frightening, and impossibly recognisable.

## 30 July 2025

The fifth episode of [*A Trip to the Sun and Back*](https://t.me/kino_voice/780), as happens with the best episodes of any series, simply demands a checklist of the wonderful things seen in it:

- Ruslan’s trip to St Petersburg, pure Balabanov and in the best traditions of *Brother*: the city where, as usual, all the power lies. Except that he introduced himself as a student rather than a clerk. Except that nobody issued him with Danila Bagrov’s sweater.

- A card-game scene in the spirit of either Guy Ritchie or the upcoming series [*Poker for Us*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/nam-poker-serial/). A wonderful set piece of reality in the middle of a fairy-tale narrative.

- The one-of-a-kind feeling of completely understanding the emotions of Vitya, the young crime boss played by Ivan Ivashov, who delivered an impressive monologue about a broken future and being forced to repeat his parents’ fate on the ruins of his own hopes. For me, he is the real protagonist of the episode.

It seems the show’s magical realism has more and more of the second element in it than the first, and that is unsettling to watch.

## 6 August 2025

The sixth episode of [*A Trip to the Sun and Back*](https://t.me/kino_voice/789) is the penultimate one, and it eases off the pace a little so as to show more vividly what happens when the past inside your head doesn’t get along with the present outside it.

The madness quietly seeping across the screen seems to hint that Ruslan now finds himself at a real crossroads, not a fairy-tale one ➖ Either choose his own time, unsettled and homeless as it is, or stay forever in a bright childhood memory with a bride out of fairy-tale books, like the boy Bananan “in the sheltered world of dreams” (from the film *Assa*), and, as Shpalikov wrote, “where mother is young and father is alive”. Here the father, though physically alive, is not quite alive in spirit — a kind of “former person” from a bygone era. The same, mind you, can be said of the mother, who has lost her bearings in the new world. Come to that, everyone has lost them — the rehearsal of funeral speeches at the New Year table alone says it all.

If earlier the finale seemed to promise a resolution that was bright in spite of everything, now it is frightening more than anything — let’s just hope Ruslan’s choice doesn’t prove ruinous.

## 13 August 2025

[*A Trip to the Sun and Back*](https://t.me/kino_voice/802) is over.

The last episode has, I’d say, soaked up the whole spectrum of emotions the characters lived through over the season. It was frightening, eerie, hopeless, with no way out, bright and sad. The finale keeps you on edge better than any thriller: because the genre is so blurred, it is genuinely impossible to predict what exactly will happen and how irreparable it will be. It is quite a feat to make the resolution gripping without losing the harmony set by the earlier episodes. An ending like this leaves you sincerely grateful to the show’s makers — the characters deserved nothing else.

Of course, because of the plot twist with Laszlo, who came in handy in the criminal schemes, I can’t shake the thought of Balabanov’s Danila. Also a bit of a holy fool, sort of, but he found his place. St Petersburg points the same way.

And the scene in the vestibule of the train is at once horrifying and awe-inspiring. After everything he had been through, Ruslan could have been lost there or been born again. How good that it was the latter.

---

## AMC Theatres Introduces Discounted Tickets on Tuesdays and Wednesdays

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/amc-skidki-na-bilety/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-07-16 (16 July 2025)
Tags: industry, notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/amc-skidki-na-bilety/

Reports say AMC Theatres, the world’s largest cinema chain, is going to sell Tuesday and Wednesday tickets at a discount.

The [news](https://variety.com/2025/film/news/amc-theatres-discount-tickets-tuesdays-wednesdays-1236448263/) appeared on Variety’s website: from now on you’ll be able to go to the cinema midweek at 50% off (and there will be a discount on popcorn and drinks too). This is how AMC is trying to stay afloat, because the cinema business has been hit hard by the pandemic, two Hollywood strikes and the growing popularity of streaming services. And, well, the plan is to use the discounts to boost sales at the concession stand as well :)

Here in Russia, of course, we haven’t had two Hollywood strikes, but a similar trend can be seen all the same: Cinema Star (a Russian cinema chain), for example, discounts its tickets on Tuesdays. I wonder whether this wave of crisis is going to hit our theatrical market too (judging by the talk in the industry, it obviously already is) and whether cinemas will start taking similar measures en masse to bring audiences in.

## Neyrobatya: A Modern Fairy Tale That Balances Kindness, Charm and Humour

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/neyrobatya-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-07-15 (15 July 2025)
Work: “Neyrobatya” is a 2025 film directed by Vitaly Dudka.
Tags: comedy, Russian cinema, family
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/neyrobatya-2025/

There are films of which the fitting thing to say is: “good stuff!”

[*Neyrobatya*](https://t.me/kino_voice/754) («Нейробатя», “Neuro-Dad”) is exactly that film. It’s an absolute treat, going by its balance of kindness, charm and humour. At the premiere, director Vitaly Dudka described it as a “modern fairy tale”, and that’s entirely fair. *Neyrobatya* is strongly reminiscent of my dearly loved [*Legends from the Past*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/legendy-nashikh-predkov-2025/) (*Legendy nashikh predkov*), where the present day mingles with little miracles, and (unexpectedly!) of *The Cyberfarm* (the comedy series). Sergei Chikhachev, by the way, plays a colourful villager here too :) Other references include *The Shawshank Redemption*, *Fargo* and [*Yura the Janitor*](https://t.me/kino_voice/5) (that we respect)

The protagonist, Grisha Besov (Denis Vlasenko), is a crack robotics engineer who dreams of joining a start-up but can’t because of a black mark on his record in the shape of his father, who is in prison. It’s at precisely this moment that this same father turns up in his life, though no longer in the most conscious of states. To sort things out and start a new life, Grisha desperately needs to find his father’s stash of money, the loot from his entire thieving “career”. And since only his father knows where it is, Grisha hooks his consciousness up to gadgets, and that sets off a string of small, lyrical adventures for the two of them.

It’s no exaggeration to say that *Neyrobatya* is the ideal choice for a good time with family and the people close to you. The film is funny in its lines (the dad’s slang is beyond description), in the situations the characters land in, and visually too — the prison mockumentary with *The Office* vibes is sure to amuse you. In cinemas from 17 July; I’m not hinting at anything, but I warmly recommend it.

---

## Open Marriage: So Far, Season Two Skilfully Repeats the Success of the First

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/otkrytyy-brak-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-07-13 (13 July 2025); updated: 2025-08-28
Work: “Open Marriage” is a 2023 series directed by Ivan Kitaev, Anna Kurbatova.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, dramedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/otkrytyy-brak-serial/

## 13 July 2025

The second season of [*Open Marriage*](https://youtu.be/oyCb5VodGxk?si=Z2CVH6Pwb75s0prL) (*Otkryty brak*) is a delight from the off, with a formal gag: a complete replay of the first season’s set-up. Right down to the dialogue and the influence of Artur Beschastny’s character on the main characters’ family :)

In general, skilfully repeating the first season’s success on such a ticklish subject is quite a challenge, and so far the show is up to it. The marital twists and turns of the couple played by Pavel Derevyanko and Yulia Alexandrova are extremely interesting to follow, especially given the actors’ comic personas, which here, in a drama, do a fine job of sharpening the critical moments. And it is interest in the characters themselves, not just in the plot, that comes to the fore, which does a great deal to keep you watching.

## 28 August 2025

Love isn’t love without… what?

I [talked it over](https://theblueprint.ru/culture/specials/okko-open-marriage-interview) with Ravshana Kurkova and Artur Beschastny for The Blueprint (a Russian fashion and culture magazine), to mark the season finale of [*Open Marriage*](https://t.me/kino_voice/744).

The result is a whole ABC that sorts out the many ingredients of the relationships we deserve. It’s always nice to meet people who think the way you do, especially when you’re the one doing the interview. So our conclusion is a shared one too, and it was Artur who put it into words:

> There’s a beautiful idea that a person can’t come to love someone else without first coming to love themselves. And it’s true: first and foremost you need to know how to love yourself, to accept yourself, and only then can you love another person. The ability to love yourself should be put at the head of love: if you are happy, you’ll be able to make someone else happy too. It’s worse when you don’t know how to love yourself or look after yourself, and there’s a person next to you who demands looking after. In the end it comes out insincere and joyless, and all of this builds up excess potential. And in those conditions a feeling of love for someone else cannot arise.

The most mentally healthy of interviews is already waiting for you⬇️

## Sober Village: A Documentary on the Line Between Comedy and Tragedy

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/trezvoe-selo-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-07-09 (9 July 2025); updated: 2025-07-11
Work: “Sober Village” is a 2025 film directed by Yulia Sergina.
Tags: documentary, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/trezvoe-selo-2025/

## 9 July 2025

I love it when a press screening has a well-thought-out concept. Like right now, for example, at the press screening of [*Sober Village*.](https://beatfilmfestival.ru/movies/trezvoe-selo) The film received a special mention at the Beat festival (Beat Film Festival, the Moscow documentary festival), and its genre makes it very interesting: a documentary dramedy about the fight against alcoholism. The competition of the same name, by the way, is held in Bashkiria every year, and it gave the film its idea.

Wink (a Russian streaming service) made it all very conceptual from the moment you walk in: sobriety is left to the guests’ discretion, and the abundance of snacks lets you hold on to it whichever cocktail you choose :) I decided to pick a cocktail to match the film, a sober one, and it is delicious. By the way, they also told us how alcohol-free cocktails are made: it’s in the video for you.

## 11 July 2025

I want to add a few more words about [*Sober Village*](https://t.me/kino_voice/733) (*Trezvoe selo*), because the film has lodged itself in my heart with its cinematic quality and its balancing act on the line between comedy and tragedy. Life really is the best screenwriter.

This is one of those documentaries that capture, in real life, things that seem fantastical until you run into them yourself. The story: the heads of the Bashkir villages of Kopey-Kubovo (the melancholy Rafimir) and Dyurtyuli (the proactive Lyaysan) are taking part in the “Sober Village” competition, along with 52 other villages. The winner, whoever over six months gets community leisure going in their village and brings alcohol consumption down, will receive 5 million roubles towards the annual budget (the usual budget of these villages is 1 million). And every village head badly needs it: one day the sewers break down, the next the local alcoholics start kicking off so that the neighbouring houses complain, and then a bridge goes and breaks altogether and there is no money to fix it. All their hopes rest on this prize.

And here I want to describe the main character in more detail. Rafimir, who runs Kopey-Kubovo, is simply the spitting image of Michael Scott from *The Office*, in the best sense. It’s hard to believe, but the two share, 100%, the same sincere naivety in their drive to make life better for a team of fellow villagers (read: one big family). And it comes out in words, facial expressions and actions so alike that you would think Steve Carell had sometimes drawn his character from life, with Rafimir himself as the model. Take just the scene where the village head, dressed up as Ded Moroz (the Russian Father Frost), goes round his fellow villagers’ houses in person to bring people and their families some festive cheer (think of the entirely analogous scenes in *The Office*).

And it is in this very resemblance, created by life itself, that the film’s chief merit lies. With a set-up that is pure comedy (by the standards of fiction), *Sober Village* touches on the far from funny problems of real people. And it is exactly this combination, I think, that can draw to the film not only documentary buffs but a wider audience too, one that is sure to recognise familiar characters in real people who are easy, and important, to feel for.

---

## Wild Tales: The Wildness Is Off the Charts and Grows with Every Story

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/dikie-istorii-2014/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-07-07 (7 July 2025)
Work: “Wild Tales” is a 2014 film directed by Damián Szifron.
Tags: black comedy, anthology
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/dikie-istorii-2014/

Recently a film-finding [bot](https://t.me/CinemaChoiceBot) tossed me an idea for an evening’s viewing: *Wild Tales*, a nominee for the 2015 Oscar for best foreign-language film, mind you.

The film is made up of short stories, each one like a mini *Final Destination* (though the endings aren’t as samey). After the first story or so, you can tell in what mood the characters’ fates will unfold in the stories that follow. But it’s impossible not to keep watching. The wildness is off the charts and grows with every story, the cringe (in the best possible sense) spills off the screen, so the title is thoroughly earned. One of the stories even brings to mind the series *Beef*, as if it had anticipated that plot about a road-rage feud.

In fact, many of the problems the film touches on could be called “eternal”, at the very least. There’s social injustice, and everyday aggression, and emotional abuse. In 2025 it may seem that none of this is quite so catastrophic any more, but the film uses hyperbole precisely to draw attention to human problems that are not of earth-shattering proportions.

Do watch it to the end: for dessert you get my absolute favourite of all the stories, the wedding one. I howled with laughter at it, because the wildness of what goes on is so unrealistic and yet so convincing that it’s impossible to stay indifferent. It is about a marriage in crisis, after all. If *Bitterly!* (the 2013 Russian wedding comedy) has suddenly come to mind — yes, its vibes are there in the story, but brace yourself for humour far blacker and more misanthropic (hard to imagine, I know, but it is possible), and just enjoy.

---

## Seesaw: The Trailer Is Hurting a Film That Deserves to Be Seen

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kacheli-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-07-06 (6 July 2025)
Work: “Seesaw” is a 2025 film directed by Pavel Timofeev.
Tags: Russian cinema, comedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/kacheli-2025/

Sometimes I notice a film’s trailer doing it harm instead of winning it future viewers.

Take [*Seesaw*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/7006678/) (*Kacheli*), in cinemas right now: the story of four friends who were planning to go to a bar but ended up owing serious money, and now only their wives and girlfriends can save them. What’s more, everything that happens is a screenplay which its author is, in fact, pitching to a capricious producer within the walls of Mosfilm (the Moscow film studio).

As you’ll have gathered, the fourth wall there gave way at once under the weight of post-irony. It’s a film you could call a party and a pitch at the same time: imperfect, but in many ways inventively made. On top of that, the leads are played by lots of cool actors, from Rinal Mukhametov and Sasha Bortich to Olga Lerman and Dasha Kotreleva. And the on-screen madness they act out, though completely divorced from reality, is in many ways charming precisely because of the acting.

So. The trailer shows the prospective viewer of *Seesaw* nothing but the main characters’ wild revelry over nobody knows what. Yes, we find out who is in the leading roles, but what they’re doing is unclear, and so not all that interesting. Which is a shame — the film is actually fun and deserves to be seen.

---

## The Ugly Stepsister: The Cinderella Tale Through the Eyes of the “Villainess”

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/gadkaya-sestra-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-07-04 (4 July 2025)
Work: “The Ugly Stepsister” is a 2025 film directed by Emilie Blichfeldt.
Tags: horror, fairy tales
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/gadkaya-sestra-2025/

I waited until [*The Ugly Stepsister*](https://youtu.be/myAwbsACdu4?si=4Tjw-SbLPsRehe1o) came out online on our platforms, watched it — and regretted not going to see it at the cinema.

*The Ugly Stepsister* turned out to be a stunning blend of *The Substance*, *Marie Antoinette* and the 2021 *Cruella*, fully immersed in the atmosphere of the Brothers Grimm’s fairy tales (which is why the big screen is the best choice). I always enjoy experiments that look at familiar stories from the point of view of a character everyone collectively condemns, and here the choice of the stepsister from the Cinderella tale is a very telling one. We’re used to seeing the stepsisters as nothing more than ugly exploiters of meek Cinderella, without giving a thought to what drives these “villainesses”. But villainy is only one facet of their nature. Once we see the story through their eyes, we start to read both the causes and the consequences of their actions differently. I’m very glad this trend in film is carrying on. And, most importantly, Cinderella is still a victim too — so the new lens hasn’t made the story at all one-sided.

Elvira, the stepsister in question (but is she ugly? the question remains open), sincerely dreams of marrying the prince. In pursuit of happiness (and of the money her mother so badly needs) she makes colossal sacrifices in the name of beauty. To make us understand just how agonising these transformations are, the film very aptly brings in the “theatre of cruelty”. This is a theatrical concept (by now firmly established in cinema) that puts the emphasis on the characters’ physical experience rather than on dialogue. In that sense the film really is frighteningly short on words. We see in detail a bloody 18th-century rhinoplasty, no less painful eyelash extensions and a literally murderous way of losing weight, known historically as the “tapeworm diet”. And yet the heroines (this film’s world is predominantly female) have no intention of talking to one another, with rare exceptions. Perhaps the only person willing to listen and to hear turns out to be the younger sister, who for the whole film seems inconspicuous and insignificant.

In short, you feel sorry for everyone, because we know the ending in advance — and yet it’s impossible to tear yourself away. I’ll certainly be following the future work of Emilie Blichfeldt, the director of *The Ugly Stepsister* (she even put references to *Un Chien Andalou* into the film, which is quite a rarity), and the roles of Lea Myren, who played Elvira, because this is a colossal piece of acting.

---

## Gosudar: The First Episodes Are Livelier Than You Might Have Expected

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/gosudar-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-07-02 (2 July 2025)
Work: “Gosudar” is a 2025 series directed by Sergey Ginzburg.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, historical, drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/gosudar-serial/

Judging by its first episodes, [*Gosudar*](https://youtu.be/ZIevWe4nvrA?si=3zcW8UoIuDfsscKz) («Государь», “The Sovereign”) is livelier than you might have expected. The story of the making of Peter I is very lively, gripping even (which is always the big hope when you sit down to a story of court intrigue). It’s hard to tear yourself away: every episode ends on such a high point that carrying straight on is a natural urge.

The main centre of gravity, of course, is the pair of characters played by Konstantin Plotnikov (his Peter is a properly dashing tsar) and Evgeny Tkachuk (the rogue Alexander Menshikov). We’ve known what a winning double act these two actors make ever since *King & Jester* («Король и Шут»), and here it all works at 100% again. I’m especially glad the show’s makers didn’t linger over Peter’s childhood, sketching it in selectively, and went straight on to the big problems of a big sovereign. The rather one-sided storyline of Tsarevna Sophia points the same way: since this is Peter’s story after all, no complaints (though it would be interesting to see a screen take on her story some day).

So Okko (the Russian streaming service) and Kinopoisk (Russia’s largest film database, media and streaming service) will make interesting neighbours over the coming month: one platform has a historical drama based on real events, and the other has the historical fantasy *Aeterna*, also about a fight for the throne. We’ll be watching!

## The Keys from Dolan’s Mommy: On the Unconscious Influence of What We Watch

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/klyuchi-iz-mamochki-dolana/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-06-28 (28 June 2025)
Work: “Mommy” is a work  Xavier Dolan.
Tags: notes, rewatch, world cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/klyuchi-iz-mamochki-dolana/

On the unconscious influence of what we watch

I saw Xavier Dolan’s *Mommy* many years ago, and the day before yesterday (prompted by a [still that came my way](https://t.me/kino_voice/s/48)) I felt like rewatching at least a bit of it. I put it on from the very beginning and soon stumbled on a surprising discovery about myself.

I give you two bunches of keys. In the clip from the film are the keys of the “mommy” herself, Diane, and in the photo beside it is, well, my own. All my adult life I’ve been hanging as much as I possibly can on my key ring (sincerely believing I do it for practical reasons — so that I can always feel for this huge bundle in my bottomless bag). Now I’m not so sure it’s only about convenience: it turns out there’s an aesthetic to it!

Perhaps you’ve come across this kind of unconscious coincidence between something real and the artistic details of a film? Let’s swap stories.

Conclusions? I’m planning to buy a little keyring pen.

---

## Poker for Us: A Story That Ended Just as Karma Would Have It

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/nam-poker-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-06-20 (20 June 2025); updated: 2025-12-03
Work: “Poker for Us” is a 2025 series directed by Rustam Ilyasov.
Tags: festivals, series, Russian cinema, crime
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/nam-poker-serial/

## 20 June 2025

As fun and as illegal as gambling itself, *Poker for Us* (*Nam poker*) wins you over from the very first shot with stylish camerawork and sharply drawn characters. Respect, by the way, for the pop-up explanations of the gambling terms!

Three friends decide to open a poker club right in their own home, but the illegal business sucks them in. The spirit of illicit fun is catching even through the screen, and before you know it we’re rooting for the hapless owners of the gambling den.

The cast includes Artyom Koshman, Sasha Bortich and Pyotr Skvortsov (I’m always glad to see him). As in *Popados* (“Busted”), what comes of young people stepping onto a slippery path is spelled out from the very first shot. But my favourite mechanism kicks in here: even when you know how it ends, you’re dying to find out how the characters came to this.

## 6 November 2025

The very likeable series [*Poker for Us*](https://t.me/kino_voice/925) has also launched with two episodes.

I took to it back in the summer at Pilot (the Russian series festival), and my review of the first episode was [written](https://t.me/kino_voice/668) right there. The second doesn’t ease off either. In particular, Pyotr Skvortsov’s character, introduced so mysteriously in the first episode, goes on to unfold into madness at full throttle. It’s a long time since I’ve seen the actor in this kind of part — the completely deranged villain — and it suits him very well, so the makers of *Poker for Us* have hit the jackpot here.

The very fabric of this story about two students caught up in an unhealthy scheme involving an illegal casino really pulls you in, because it’s done briskly, in a contemporary way and with less drama than a plot like this might have had. On top of that, the glimpse of the ending we’re given in the series’ opening shots makes you want to know straight away how they came to this.

## 17 November 2025

Gambling-series addicts, all present?

The new episodes of [*Poker for Us*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1057) are nothing short of a meme feast. I’m mad about this show simply for the sheer density of gags that slip through its wall-to-wall bleakness. I’ve put together a little checklist of things it’s better to see once than hear about 100 times:

- a recipe for rat-poison pies, with stylish subtitles
- the funeral of a granny who planted drug stashes, done as flamboyantly performative absurdism
- a humane debt collector played by Ruslan Bratov (the director of the cult short *Merry-Go-Round*, «Лалай-балалай»)
- a lad with a shotgun, in a striped sailor’s vest, with the vibe of Alexei Serebryakov in Balabanov’s *Cargo 200* (attaching it for comparison)

## 3 December 2025

[*Poker for Us*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1089) is over.

I couldn’t be happier with the series, and I’ll be waiting eagerly for news of a second season (by every measure, and given every hook it has cast, a second season is a must here).

Yesterday, as I finished the final episode, I became fully convinced that nothing made in recent years (or nothing I’ve seen) is more believable in the sheer level of game-over disaster unfolding on several fronts at once in the lives of a few particular people. I don’t run an underground casino, of course, but everything the characters go through in that endless cycle of problems, each one spawning the next, is something I can fully understand and relate to. Happily, the story in the series ended just as karma would have it, so there is always hope.

Egor, as played by Timofey Eletsky, is the best of them for my money: a very deep character and, for all that appearances deceive, a touchingly sweet one. He simply nails, one hundred per cent, a good person who wants to do things the right way and because of that sometimes does them the wrong way — and you believe it. Ruslan Bratov (the director of the wonderful [*Express*](https://t.me/kino_voice/52)) is an absolute riot as Javid too — evidently a case of the axiom that “a talented person is talented at everything”. Vitya (Artyom Koshman) has a wonderful character arc with a tremendous transformation, another sheer pleasure to watch — as, for that matter, does Alexandra Bortich’s character. As for the humour, the writers simply scooped the pot — it’s worth rewatching with a notebook just to copy the jokes into your personal collection.

In short, I could go on praising this series for a long time, as you can see — I hope as many people as possible get to appreciate it. I’d hate for it to end after one season without ever revealing the context of that video message from Koshman’s character in the first episode.

---

## Coeval: The 1990s as More Than a Crime Chronicle

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/rovesnik-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-06-19 (19 June 2025)
Work: “Coeval” is a 2024 film directed by Fedor Kudryavtsev.
Tags: Russian cinema, 1990s, drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/rovesnik-2024/

Do make sure you catch [*Coeval*](https://youtu.be/5_0UbyOfzM8?si=x1g73I-hlFGPw5b6) («Ровесник») in cinemas while you can, because it is quite simply a phenomenon of our time, and it is sure to surprise you.

A film that combines mockumentary, screenlife and neural-network technology all at once, it is also good in what it has to say. It is a rare portrayal of the 1990s on film that doesn’t look like nothing but a crime chronicle (though that is in there too) and instead lets you feel the spirit of the time in a completely different way. As he searches for the truth about his father’s past, the protagonist goes through a personal crisis of his own, while we, the audience, get to live through with him the real story of an internet company whose founders’ fates turned out very differently.

A particular joy is seeing how well deepfake has been used to de-age the older generation of characters. Look at Alexander Yatsenko — it’s him straight out of Balabanov’s *It Doesn’t Hurt Me*, what a delight! It’s great that film is making friends with the latest technology and getting more varied and cooler for it.

Speaking of technology, by the way: the filmmakers have given the protagonist his very own [account](https://youtube.com/@rovesnik_film?si=drXFwdD9vjtWA7KO), where various excerpts from his documentary are posted. It’s a great move and a nice chance to rewatch certain moments (which you’ll want to do the minute you leave the cinema).

---

## Something Positive: The Charm Is in the Little Things

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/chto-to-polozhitelnoe-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-06-18 (18 June 2025)
Work: “Something Positive” is a 2025 series directed by Nika Yakovleva.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, comedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/chto-to-polozhitelnoe-serial/

A thoroughly likeable series, [*Something Positive*](https://youtu.be/hvQ4ooUA_lo?si=NNkKE3djGWBPDLUt) («Что-то положительное»), starts on Monday, and on the strength of three episodes it’s safe to say this one is a success.

The show’s charm is in the little things.

- First, it’s a real pleasure to see Taisya Kalinina in comic mode: after her demanding roles in [*The Highway*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/trassa-serial/) and *My Little Nighttime Secret* («Один маленький ночной секрет»), it’s a genuine breath of fresh air. The actors playing the other characters are just as perfectly cast; you can’t take your eyes off them.

- Second, the plot conceit of a fake pregnancy, which the 17-year-old heroine uses to get attention from her parents and the boy of her dreams, doesn’t put you off. Because the lie is declared up front, the theme of teenage pregnancy never slides into the repertoire of the show *Pregnant at 16* («Беременна в 16», a Russian reality show) and stays within the bounds of decency, taste and style.

- Third, the heroine’s misadventures are peppered with animated inserts featuring a white cat that personifies the girl’s conscience. Visually it really freshens everything up, and it also chips away a little at the wall between the audience and the characters: we get a kind of ally on screen, who is also sizing up what’s going on and who, unlike the audience, even gets to influence the heroine’s decisions a little :)

As a bonus, I’ll single out the 20-minute episodes: at that length the series has every chance of becoming a pleasant companion for when you feel like watching a light, funny story without straying too far from your other plans. So far *Something Positive* is giving me powerful vibes of [*Mammoths*](https://t.me/kino_voice/334) («Мамонты»): the same kind of undemanding story about a small family commotion that opens everyone’s eyes to something important.

---

## How to Train Your Dragon: A Thoroughly Successful Adaptation of the Animated Original

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kak-priruchit-drakona-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-06-17 (17 June 2025)
Work: “How to Train Your Dragon” is a 2025 film directed by Dean DeBlois.
Tags: remake, fantasy, family, American cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/kak-priruchit-drakona-2025/

I’ve also caught [*How to Train Your Dragon*](https://youtu.be/22w7z_lT6YM?si=fdLTkX6_hps4U-q2) in its updated live-action version. With its mix of mighty animated dragons and humans, the whole thing looks rather like a prequel to [*House of the Dragon*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/dom-drakona-serial/) — something like “here’s how our ancestors tamed dragons, back before we split into clans and started fighting one another”.

As an adaptation of the animated original it is a thorough success — not least, of course, thanks to the perfect casting of young Hiccup. He is played by Mason Thames — a 17-year-old actor who, I think, we’ll be seeing again more than once — and he nails the character we know from the cartoon one hundred per cent, right down to the outline of his silhouette. The same goes for the Viking chief, played by Gerard Butler at maximum manliness. The comfort and sense of recognition as you watch are, accordingly, at maximum too.

A great pick for imagining that rainy summer days are the bracing climate of the Vikings’ island.

## Lilo & Stitch: The New Version Hasn’t Lost an Ounce of Charm

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/lilo-i-stich-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-06-15 (15 June 2025)
Work: “Lilo & Stitch” is a 2025 film directed by Dean Fleischer Camp.
Tags: remake, family, American cinema, comedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/lilo-i-stich-2025/

I thoroughly enjoyed the new version of [*Lilo & Stitch*](https://youtu.be/m5fMyIImwEY?si=jeI01g4BXo68UnXC), which hasn’t lost an ounce of charm compared with the original.

The animated aliens are as convincing as ever, and the live-action cast is perfectly chosen. I was especially impressed by Billy Magnussen, who plays Pleakley, the funny one-eyed alien who is mad about planet Earth. A superb comic performance. The plot hasn’t changed since 2002, and a good thing too — it’s a classic, after all.

My viewing had one more plus: I saw the film on the big screen, at the Pobeda (“Victory”) cinema in Minsk! Hearing that familiar Stitch accent in the Russian dub is priceless :) The cinema itself, by the way, is gorgeous: it has recently been restored and is very spacious, bright and beautiful. I warmly recommend a visit if you’re ever in Minsk.
