## High Season: Zavtur and Popov’s Chemistry, Broken for the Sake of the Mystery

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/vysokiy-sezon-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-06-12 (12 June 2025)
Work: “High Season” is a 2025 series directed by Stas Ivanov.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, drama, adventure
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/vysokiy-sezon-serial/

There is plenty to catch the eye in [*High Season*](https://youtu.be/XPeC2GdJogs?si=aDrQ1LeKnX-j4IdG): the tropical setting, the terrific chemistry between Zavtur and Popov (I’m always glad to see him after *The Actresses*), the mysterious set-up, with the heroine vanishing in the middle of a perfect holiday with a man who is already all but her fiancé…

But these strengths of the set-up quickly give way to the chaos of the things that happen to the characters. Within the lead couple you end up with a favourite (Misha, the sensible normie played by Popov) and someone you simply cannot understand (the flighty Anya — Zavtur). They were an absolute pleasure to watch together: the dialogue seemed to flow of its own accord rather than from a script, the laughter was genuine and the looks were deep. But it all got broken for the sake of the opening mystery, and now you want to feel sorry for Misha and to judge Anya.

**⤵️** The parallel crime storyline, about a sister’s revenge, is so far unfolding more formulaically. There has been no time to get immersed in the relationship between the two women (unlike with Misha and Anya as a couple), and so the elder sister’s despair is harder to believe in. I’d like to hope the series will pull the second storyline up to the level of the first and become gripping on every front.

---

## The Phoenician Scheme: Wes Anderson’s Signature Style, with Exceptions

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/finikiyskaya-skhema-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-06-08 (8 June 2025)
Work: “The Phoenician Scheme” is a 2025 film directed by Wes Anderson.
Tags: arthouse, comedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/finikiyskaya-skhema-2025/

In Wes Anderson’s [*The Phoenician Scheme*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/5460719/), the signature style we have come to expect from the director comes through more subtly than ever — but with exceptions.

The film’s palette has none of the loudly clashing or, conversely, meticulously matched colours, and the absurdist humour typical of Anderson’s characters comes across as unusually low-key. On the other hand, the work as a whole seems to leave the impression of a summing-up. The key theme of fragile family ties, which flows from one of the director’s films to the next, is present and correct. But we can’t even be quite sure the family is a real one — and blood ties, it turns out, don’t matter all that much. The journey motif, which masks the characters’ inner transformation, now serves not to reset their personalities but to bring about a complete rebirth. And the amount of violence on screen, unusual for Anderson, seems to bring the film closer to reality, which is not exactly known for its colourful aesthetics and symmetry.

I see two patterns in this:

**1️⃣** The protagonist, who does business in defiance of every rule of economics, keeps going through deadly situations and yet stays alive. This is very reminiscent of the path of Wes Anderson himself, who works by his own rules of filmmaking and with every new work goes through the inevitable “death of the author” (Roland Barthes’s concept, according to which the author of a work loses authorial power over its meaning the moment it is published). Perhaps that is exactly why the protagonist of *The Phoenician Scheme* keeps reworking other people’s wording of business papers — just as viewers rework the message authors have put into their films or texts.

**2️⃣** By the end (I don’t think this will be much of a spoiler) the characters arrive, it seems, at an absence of any neat symmetry or colour scheme whatsoever — what we see on screen resembles the reality around us as never before in Wes Anderson. This, it seems, underlines once again the importance of what is inside rather than the outer shell, however beautiful — a very soothing thought.

Though perhaps this is just my reading as a viewer, made possible by the phenomenon of the “death of the author”.

---

## License to Love: A Second Chance Is Something We Must First Give Ourselves

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/muzhu-privet-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-06-04 (4 June 2025)
Work: “License to Love” is a 2025 film directed by Anton Maslov.
Tags: drama, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/muzhu-privet-2025/

The saying that “sometimes life gives you a second chance” is incomplete, and the film [*License to Love*](https://okko.tv/movie/muzhu-privet) (*Muzhu privet*, “Say Hi to Your Husband”) illustrates that very well. A second chance is, first and foremost, something we must give ourselves.

The best Russian film of the 2025 Moscow International Film Festival wraps you, from the very first frame, in warmth and the hope of better things. Katerina, played by Yulia Peresild, seems almost ashamed to be unhappy among the joyful newlyweds at her job in the registry office: life is bubbling all around her, and her day will come too (probably), when her husband comes out of his coma (5 years on from the tragedy). Meanwhile, Katerina’s daughter is planning to rush into marriage with a fiancé who has prospects but whom she doesn’t love, while her son is even trying to court a classmate of strange (not to say non-existent) moral principles. It seems they all need a second chance.

Despite a plot that is as tragic as they come, what happens on screen doesn’t knock you off balance or have you shedding tears straight away. That is probably down to the lightness with which Katerina gets through her troubles: she’ll laughingly answer a telling-off from the cranky old woman next door with a joke, look on her son’s teenage crises with an understanding smile, and give the citizens in the queue at work a friendly wink. Analysing the heroine, I came to the conclusion that this calm comes from certainty: her husband is stuck in a coma and, terrible as that is, she has got used to it. The hardest part for Katerina begins when a real choice appears: what to do with a life that had seemed settled for good.

*License to Love* contains a fleeting but important mention of a Soviet classic, *Moscow Does Not Believe in Tears*. The two films really are akin in their mood and in the way they show a gentle female strength in the fight for one’s own happiness. The acting in *License to Love* is first-rate too: Peresild and Vdovichenkov work beautifully as a pair. All in all, it’s an excellent reason to drop out of reality for a couple of hours and think about the price of happiness and the number of chances one is allowed on the way to it.

---

## Fedor Sheyd’s Bezmyatezhnost: Absurdity, Hopelessness and Angry Optimism

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/bezmyatezhnost-kniga/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-06-03 (3 June 2025)
Work: “Bezmyatezhnost” is a 2025 book by Fedor Sheyd.
Tags: books, black comedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/bezmyatezhnost-kniga/

A bookish aside

If you’re looking for a great summer read with a light style and plots that are anything but ordinary, take a look at Fedor Sheyd’s [*Bezmyatezhnost*](https://books.yandex.ru/books/eun01Io3) («Безмятежность», “Serenity”). It’s the most powerful short-story collection I’ve read lately, and I’m deliberately eking out the stories I have left so that they don’t run out — I like it that much :)

These short pieces have absurdity, and hopelessness, and an angry optimism backed up by the blackest humour (I’m especially fond of the story about working in a text newsroom — the author knows exactly what he’s writing about). In short, the prose is incomparably dense for all its absolute simplicity of form. Naturally, every story is crying out to be adapted for the screen — the descriptions and the dialogue alike are very cinematic. Someone in the film industry is bound to spot that, I hope.

---

## Pilot 2025: Impressions of the Competition Pilots

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/festival-pilot-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-05-31 (31 May 2025); updated: 2025-06-25
Tags: festivals, series, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/festival-pilot-2025/

## 31 May 2025

Festival news!

My beloved series festival, [Pilot](https://t.me/pilot_festival), held in Ivanovo, where I’ll be from 19 to 22 June, has announced its opening series.

It will be *Constantinople* («Константинополь»; formerly titled [*Izgoi*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/series/5895344/), “The Outcasts”), the story of the White émigré Neratov (Alexander Ustyugov), who lost pretty much everything in the Civil War and ended up in Constantinople. No longer as a prominent White Guard colonel, though, but as a rank-and-file refugee and, as we can guess, one with precious few rights. And it is the rights of Russian émigrés that he will be fighting for.

For the second year running, Pilot is opening with a large-scale historical drama. Last year it was the slightly hectic series [*Plevako*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/plevako-serial/), about the famous lawyer of the last pre-revolutionary years, and that’s an interesting coincidence.

Perhaps it is precisely the final years of the Russian Empire and the start of the revolution that are now among the most in-demand historical parallels cinema is making sense of. So I can’t wait to see it!

## 11 June 2025

And [here](https://t.me/pilot_festival/539) is part of the programme of Pilot (the Russian series festival in Ivanovo), which is about to begin!

In this competition I’ll naturally be especially looking forward to the screenings of [*The Surgeon*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/series/5698770/) (*Khirurg*), with Sergei Gilev in the lead, and [*Not at Ease*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/series/7389722/) («Не в своей тарелке»), a sci-fi comedy with Yuri Stoyanov and Denis Prytkov.

## 16 June 2025

And, at last, the main [competition](https://t.me/pilot_festival/541) of the Pilot festival! Time to pick the most anticipated premieres :)

Personally, I’m very curious about:

- *16 let i 9 mesyatsev* («16 лет и 9 месяцев», “16 Years and 9 Months”): a teen story starring Oleg Savostyuk, whom I’m always glad to see

- *Dear Willie* («Дорогой Вилли»): Sergei Makovetsky as Brezhnev, come on!

- *Breathe* (*Dyshi*): directed by Anna Kuznetsova, who made [*Intermission*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kanikuly-2023/) (*Kanikuly*), a very important and much-noticed film from last year

- *Jack Russell* (*Zheka Rassel*): Eldar Kalimulin’s character turns into a Jack Russell terrier. I’m expecting a great comedy :)

- *Old School* (*Oldskul*): this show about an old-school teacher has an atmospheric [teaser](https://youtu.be/imVyvZxeS0I?si=Q74_rd-HxAF3jV6w) that really whets the appetite

- *Popados* («Попадос», “Busted”): Makar Khlebnikov and Timofey Tribuntsev at the centre of a crime story — a promising duo (especially going by the Tribuntsev and Minekaev pairing in [*Overheard in Rybinsk*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/podslushano-v-rybinske-serial/))

I’ll be writing about all of it from the festival.

## 19 June 2025

And over the next 4 days there will be lots of reviews on the channel of what I’ve watched at the Pilot festival (the Russian series festival in Ivanovo).

It’s my second festival, and I’d been really looking forward to the trip: it’s always a celebration of film and a chance to talk to all sorts of people from the industry.

This time 17 “pilots” are in competition: first episodes of series that will later (most of them) come out on our streaming services. Expect reviews (and [here](https://t.me/kino_voice/646) I’ve rounded up descriptions of the premieres I’m most looking forward to)! Last year, for instance, Pilot screened [*She’s So Cool*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/ona-takaya-klassnaya-serial/) and [*Give a Show!*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/dayte-shou-serial/), both of which went on to be big hits.

The festival also has an industry programme and a documentary series competition — I’ll try to write about the most interesting news from there. And at the end the jury hands out awards in various categories: best pilot, naturally, best actor/actress and so on. Last year it was really interesting to [compare](https://t.me/kino_voice/129) my guesses with the jury’s decision, so I’m already looking forward to it.

## 19 June 2025

My colleagues gave it their blessing, so I’ll post a joke I came up with back when the [Pilot jury](https://t.me/pilot_festival/535) was announced

Life is not the same without a Kott! (a play on the Russian saying “life is not the same without a cat”, *kot* being Russian for “cat”)

The joke is that the 2024 jury included the director Vladimir Kott, and this year’s jury has his brother Alexander! A must-have surname at the festival :)

## 19 June 2025

The festival (Pilot, the Russian series festival in Ivanovo) opens with [*Constantinople*](https://t.me/kino_voice/622) — like last year’s opener, a textbook classical historical drama with its own strengths and weaknesses. In the first episode, the adventures of refugees from the Russian Empire in Constantinople are more of a statement of intent, and the plot loses out to the artistry with which this world has been worked out.

We have an officer who has lost his whole family and his faith in military honour, a quick-witted doctor (the most interesting character so far, played by Kirill Käro) and a “businessman” desperate to get back the gold confiscated by Constantinople’s customs officers. It’s hard to tie these storylines together as yet, so that will be a job mostly for the genre’s most devoted fans.

## 20 June 2025

Is it hard to adapt texts for the screen?

Mikhail Kitaev is talking about it in Pilot’s industry section. You can see the arguments for and against on the slide, and on the whole, of course, it’s hard to disagree that these adaptations are a hugely exciting business and, at the same time, a fiendishly difficult one. After all, every reader already has their own picture in their head!

I especially liked how Kinopoisk (Russia’s largest film database, media and streaming service) played on the conflicting reviews of [*Crime and Punishment*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/prestuplenie-i-nakazanie-serial/), the cornerstone of the heated debates of autumn 2024. Half the audience gave it extremely high ratings, and the other half gave it 1 out of 10. It ended up at 5.8 on Kinopoisk. The platform gathered all sorts of reviews and made a brilliant video inviting you to pick a side — a great piece of image-building! Speaking of *Crime and Punishment*, by the way: which side are you on? :)

## 20 June 2025

*Full House* is a story that is interesting first and foremost for being experimental. It mixes a little medical drama, a little of the supernatural, a little procedural and a little of Bulgakov’s *A Young Doctor’s Notebook*. Not everything runs smoothly, but if they keep working on it, as its makers said they would, it could potentially be a good thing.

The story of a principled medical resident in the far north makes for slightly uncomfortable viewing — just enough to convey how the heroine feels in a new place where her colleagues’ trust is at zero and all around her are bureaucracy and hard-drinking surgeons. Pyotr Fyodorov, incidentally, is very good as one of the latter. I’m curious to see how his clearly drawn conflict with the heroine, played by Maria Lisovaya, develops. For a clash of experience and idealism like that, it’s probably worth waiting for the remaining episodes.

## 20 June 2025

Remember the title *Popados* (“Busted”): it’s a brisk crime story with new faces and already seasoned actors. I’d been looking forward to it largely because of the pairing of Makar Khlebnikov and Timofey Tribuntsev — and they really are wonderful here, playing father and son.

The plot structure does a great job of combining flashbacks with the present, where the consequences of the teenagers’ prank have already set in. Flirting with the criminal world lands the characters in big trouble, which brings to mind *Na avtomate* (“On Autopilot”), a series that had substantial things to say on the same themes. At a good pace, the pilot gave every storyline a decent set-up, so you really do want to wait for more.

## 21 June 2025

With all my heart I hope the project *Bukhanka Chyornogo* (“Chyorny’s Loaf”, a pun on the UAZ “loaf” van) finds its platform and gets filmed to the end: it’s a real discovery among the independent projects.

The uproariously funny Lyokha — the protagonist, whom I privately dubbed “the plush gangster” — works as a waiter in his father’s coffee shop, hates hipsters with their almond-milk lattes and threatens them with a pistol when they complain about the food (on closer inspection it’s just a pistol-shaped lighter). A portrait of Sasha Bely (the gangster hero of *Brigada*) hangs on the mirror in his room, and he himself is grotesquely stuck in the 1990s, when his grandfather Grisha Chyorny was running things. In search of former glory he heads to his grandmother’s village in Karelia, where all that is left of his grandfather’s legacy is a UAZ van — that very Chyorny’s Loaf (my applause for the show’s inventive title). An attempt to get his grandfather’s Merc back ends in trouble, and after that all we can do is wait for a whole season :)

My [*Garazhniki*](https://t.me/kino_voice/137) (“Garage People”) of 2025.

## 21 June 2025

Sunny in a southern way and pleasantly naive, the series *Winemakers* neatly sets out a screenwriting device that has become a favourite of late: the working class colliding with arty bohemians.

This time the thing to be split is a winery. A trio of proletarians from Chelyabinsk arrive in Gelendzhik to claim the inheritance of a relative who dropped off the radar 20 years ago (and has now died altogether). The local owners (and the late relative’s business partners), played by Andrey Urgant and Elena Podkaminskaya, are in shock. Podkaminskaya, by the way, plays the winery’s manager — every bit as wonderfully as, many years ago, she played the manager of a French restaurant in *The Kitchen* (the hit sitcom).

The standard comic situations come with added wine snobbery and a mismatch of, shall we say, gastronomic cultures, which is made up for by a romantic match :) I hope the story opens up like a good wine.

## 21 June 2025

It’s great that so many of the shows at this Pilot are specifically about women and their problems.

*Fake* is a superb illustration of how utterly defenceless you are online and, following on from that, how completely exposed you are to people who don’t believe you and pass judgement. A true horror story, in which the monsters hide not under the bed but in the comments.

A starry-eyed biology teacher (Anastasia Krasovskaya, who for the second festival running has landed harrowing scenes of violence) runs into brutal online stalking: it all looks as though she is taking part in erotic chats under her own name. Her identity has literally been stolen. The young woman tries to find the culprit, and that gives the story a headlong pace and the right kind of tension. It’s frightening, and intriguing, to think how this story might end ⬅️

## 22 June 2025

The results of the Pilot 2025 competitions are about to be announced, but my colleagues and I pooled our opinions a little earlier [in a special table by Komendant kinokreposti](https://t.me/textortexel/5837) («Комендант кинокрепости», “The Commandant of the Film Fortress”, a Telegram channel).

I’m very grateful for this chance to compare notes with colleagues and get an objective assessment of what we’ve seen. And, of course, I’ll be watching for matches with the jury’s decisions.

## 22 June 2025

By the way, about the [vote](https://t.me/textortexel/5830) my colleagues and I held on Pilot’s main competition programme: I have a little visualisation and a few interesting facts about us!

It turns out that among us there is a kindest critic (yours truly), a strictest critic ([@ershovfilm](https://t.me/ershovfilm)) and several people whose opinions are very close to one another :)

And opinions differed most over the series [*Full House*](https://t.me/kino_voice/666): its spread of scores is the most noticeable! How cool that we have such different views and opinions, and that we’ve brought them together and put them on record.

## 25 June 2025

And last but not least, in the wake of Pilot!

Kinopoisk (Russia’s largest film database, media and streaming service) and I have gathered all the series from the festival into one [piece](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/4011387/), for which I wrote about 9 of the 18 series. I highly recommend it as a retrospective and as a watchlist for the future :) *(by the way, for a bit of extra entertainment as you read, you can try to guess from the writing style exactly which of the series* I covered *myself)*

I also had a small hand in the [piece](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/news/4011391/) on the industry programme — it gave us not only the much-discussed [portrait](https://t.me/kino_voice/671) of the average Russian woman, but also some interesting news and a few anticipated projects. Short and to the point!

## Fisher. Zatmenie: Greatness in Its Purest Form

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/fisher-zatmenie-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-05-29 (29 May 2025); updated: 2025-12-12
Work: “Fisher. Zatmenie” is a 2025 series directed by Alexander Tsoi.
Tags: series, mystery, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/fisher-zatmenie-serial/

## 29 May 2025

[*Fisher. Zatmenie*](https://youtu.be/_7QB_MyZ1gI?si=t-jsRQLNmEpuN-Up) («Фишер. Затмение», “Fisher. Eclipse”, the second season of the hit crime series) is a delight from the very first episode: Bokov is in fine form, Yatsenko, true to his character, wisecracks like a god, and Starshenbaum’s character fits into this company like one of the family.

The opening shots, with Bokov interrogating Fisher in prison, could have come straight out of the world of [*Outsource*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/autsors-serial/) and stir a pleasant sense of recognition (if that’s deliberate, cool). The exposition runs like clockwork: there’s the tail end of the old case, a full-scale introduction of the new characters (despite the episode’s running time — just 40 minutes!), and a humanising spin on the old characters’ trademark traits.

Bokov, who went around saying “Sho?” (“What?”) in season 1, has, for instance, got himself a little dog — named Sho, naturally. I hope the pooch doesn’t come to any harm while the serial killer is being caught.

## 5 June 2025

A checklist for beating stress, according to episode two of [*Fisher. Zatmenie*](https://t.me/kino_voice/619)

- Learn a foreign language, so you can switch to it at the worst moments and slip into derealisation. If you’re lucky, rhyme it with Russian swearing too, like Bokov.

- Set up a fight club with the delinquent element of a rough neighbourhood. Be reborn, spiritually and physically.

- Put the fear of God into the star of the local radio station and broadcast a coded announcement for the criminals, so that the whole town keeps ringing in, trying to claim a bag of money. Observe.

Whether the methods actually work, we’ll find out in the coming episodes.

## 20 June 2025

Even in the middle of a festival I couldn’t miss the new episode of [*Fisher*](https://t.me/kino_voice/631): the season’s midpoint whets your appetite for the denouement as much as it possibly can.

Besides the superbly worked-out plot (stronger than in the first season, for my money!), the show’s way with language is picking up steam too. This is the most linguistically distinctive series in recent memory. The only one to outdo it, perhaps, is [*El Ruso*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/el-ruso-serial/), where the actors talked like Old Believers :)

But the virtuoso swearing of Yankovsky’s and Starshenbaum’s characters is something you literally want to write down and quote. Say what you like, speech like this adds no end of sincerity and realism to everything that happens, and for this crime story that is vital.

## 26 June 2025

[*Fisher*](https://t.me/kino_voice/659) is not only breaking records on the [Kinopoisk Pro Index](https://t.me/kinopoisk_Industry/5427) but also swerving sharply (and, like Bokov, brazenly) off its plotted course.

Having “slipped”, as Bokov put it (I never stop admiring him) at the very end of the latest episode, the investigation is forced to change direction abruptly? I’d like to hope that the outcome of the investigation won’t boil down to the “the butler did it” formula, and that the culprit won’t be quite as close at hand as it now seems.

This episode also has more of Yatsenko’s character and of Fisher himself. Andrey Maksimov really is an astonishing actor: until I watched the pilot of [*Normalny*](https://t.me/kino_voice/679) (“Normal”), where he plays a man on the autism spectrum, I couldn’t picture him as an even remotely positive character (not a gangster, not a serial killer). And now — what do you think? I can’t see him as a serial killer in *Fisher*: he’s such a sweet, kind lad. But I’m joking, of course — this is my way of praising stunning transformations and a 180-degree change of type.

## 5 July 2025

Meanwhile, the second season of [*Fisher*](https://t.me/kino_voice/706) has decided to be crueller than the first after all, and to take my favourite character away from me.

In episode six everything gets well and truly knotted around one particular character I’ve grown to love over the season, and it doesn’t look as though it will end well. On the other hand, the next two episodes will give me plenty of time to enjoy how well the writers have pulled together a whole heap of storylines that seemed unconnected at first. The cultists, the obnoxious official, the local gangsters — all of it turns out to be interwoven and in play for the approaching denouement.

And by the way, Andrey Maksimov seems to have been lucky enough this season to play every facet of Fisher, and it looks very, very convincing. Above all, the storyline with his interrogations doesn’t feel at all extraneous or alien to what’s going on in Kurortny; on the contrary, it seems to let us look back over the hunt for the new killer and build our own theories from their (the killers’) logic.

## 17 July 2025

To my mind, the finale of [*Fisher. Zatmenie*](https://t.me/kino_voice/619) is greatness in its purest form. All manner of praise for the series itself aside, I’ll be following the future roles of Nikita Khudyakov, who played Vanya Zlobin, with great interest, because in this story he showed himself to be a very powerful actor. Watching him was a real pleasure.

The denouement comes across as swift, rhythmic and free of needless preliminaries, yet with an elegant dash of devilry ➡️ For me that’s the ideal outcome: I don’t like detective stories where the mystery drags on and on, making us watch the investigators’ train of thought for an indecently long time — I, for one, find that sort of thing easy to give up on. Right up to the end I kept wishing that this wouldn’t happen to *Fisher*, and my wishes came true. I had my [guesses](https://t.me/kino_voice/725), but in the event it’s all done more cunningly — literally as unpredictable as fate itself — and that, I think, is the height of craftsmanship. I liked the detail about Zlobin’s transfer “from somewhere up north”: *Fisher* has more in common with *Outsource* than it seems.

I also can’t help admiring the character posters: bamboo, a mourning ribbon, bees — a good set of details both for those who haven’t watched yet and for those who already know everything.

Naturally, my quote book has gained some new entries from Bokov’s vocabulary. The line about there being “no need to repeat it twice” will stay with me for a long time. May this trademark touch live on, if *Fisher* becomes an anthology with an immortal Bokov from season to season.

## 18 July 2025

The more I think about the [denouement](https://t.me/kino_voice/762) of the second *Fisher*, the more extra meanings turn up.

First, I read an [interview](https://seance.ru/articles/fisher-zatmenie) with the screenwriters, Sergei Kalvarsky and Natalya Kapustina. It turns out we have *Assa* to thank for the show’s atmosphere. ~~Anyone who knows me knows this —~~ It’s my absolute favourite film, yet not once while watching did I catch myself making the connection, and now it has reeeally hit me. So that’s what explains this persuasive counterpoint, which makes you suspect something rotten in even the sweetest character.

But when it comes to Zlobin splitting into twins, I have cultural associations aplenty — and that’s my second point. In the few seconds the two of them were on screen together I managed to think of both Cronenberg and Balabanov. The former because of *Dead Ringers*, his film about twins who villainously stood in for each other at work and in life (literally, even with women). And from Balabanov, the screenplay *My Brother Died*, with its self-explanatory title and a truly Balabanovian plot. And, above all, a denouement that very much mirrors *Fisher*’s.

## 2 August 2025

To round off the conversation about *Fisher. Zatmenie*, I’ve gone through [the most common questions](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/4011553/): who went where, who came from where, and who made it out alive?

My favourite idea is the one about Zlobin’s wardrobe; it came to me while I was writing, completely unplanned. Zlobin’s wardrobe consists mainly of polo necks that cover the throat, with a scarf on top for good measure — so that nobody could possibly make anything out there. And at the end, as we know, Zlobin turned up with his throat cut, as part of the cunning twin plan. Evidently not for the first time — and it is the consequences of earlier “plans” that are hidden behind those cosy jumper necks.

## 12 December 2025

Shock content: the “bad” Zlobin from [*Fisher*](https://t.me/kino_voice/762) is not the one we think

A month ago I was on the set of a [podcast](https://vk.com/video-195528184_456244235) by Wink (the Russian streaming service) about the series *Fisher. Zatmenie*, as the podcast’s scriptwriter (thanks to my colleagues for the invitation and the trust). By the time of the shoot a scriptwriter’s main work is already done: all that’s left is to watch the text come to life and soak up the blissful atmosphere, which is exactly what I did. Now, by the way, I understand why the screenwriter Alim Beschokov looked so happy [on the set of *Ira*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/ira-2-sezon-intervyu-olerinskaya/) :)

As you know, I’m the second season’s number-one fan, and of its finale especially. Which made it all the more of a joy to listen to Nikita Khudyakov and the director Alexander Tsoi discuss it (Tsoi, by the way, is far more cheerful in person than the films he works on).

Two things you won’t find out anywhere else:

**1️⃣** Of the two Zlobin twins, it was Vanya who did all the most terrible things — the one who was in plain view, sobbing over the child’s death! We heard this from Nikita during a break and immediately asked him to say it on the record: nobody would have believed it if the actor hadn’t said so himself.

**2️⃣** The recipe is revealed for the mixture the actors — pardon me — throw up on screen. It contains raw eggs, porridge and sugar. Everyday ingredients, but this, as they say, is one not to try at home.

The rest is in the [podcast](https://vk.com/video-195528184_456244235) :) If *Fisher* is your kind of thing, don’t miss it.

---

## Other People’s Money: A Rollicking Crypto Crime Story with Two Maxim Matveevs

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/chuzhie-dengi-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-05-28 (28 May 2025); updated: 2025-06-07
Work: “Other People’s Money” is a 2025 series directed by Igor Tverdokhlebov.
Tags: series, crime, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/chuzhie-dengi-serial/

## 28 May 2025

A little belatedly, I’ve started [*Other People’s Money*](https://youtu.be/4JuxiHkwp64?si=wXLxHfRx4WL8dGcD) (*Chuzhie dengi*), a rollicking crypto crime story with two Maxim Matveevs (hello to *Amura*, *Mickey 17*, *Vasily* and other [films with twins](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/bliznetsy-v-rossiyskikh-proektakh/)).

The first thing that makes a good impression is the camerawork. The camera swoops, zooms in on the characters’ faces and on objects, pushes in and pulls back in time with their showdowns, and even films them from a hidden-camera angle. That kind of visual variety is literally riveting — it’s been a long time since the way a series is shot pulled me in like this. It’s a rarity among today’s shows, and that makes it a winning choice.

Watching Matveev in his two guises is fascinating too — I’m especially glad that the one built to last turned out to be not the cocksure personality but the modest version of the hero, the one capable of changing as a character. For all that the plot is pure fantasy by today’s realities, the very idea of making a show about good old swindlers plying their trade in bitcoin with state-of-the-art technology is really rather appealing. In short, everything points to carrying on watching.

## 7 June 2025

It’s great that [*Other People’s Money*](https://t.me/kino_voice/617) not only kept up its signature camerawork right to the finale but didn’t let us down on the writing either.

Things played out in such a way that the finale is deeply satisfying, morally speaking. Behind all the many cunning schemes with crypto and cashing out, viewers had to pick their favourite ~~Twix bar~~ version of Maxim Matveev — and the writers did the same for the sake of a striking ending. Svin (“Pig”) understandably inspired hatred laced with pity — and, utterly one of a kind as Gosha Kutsenko’s character is, you don’t feel all that sorry for him. Alina (Stasya Miloslavskaya) does raise questions, of course, but she did nothing radically bad (and so didn’t deserve anything radically bad either).

It’s as if a series that feels more like fantasy than reality has ended with fantastic fairness. And that, of course, is a pleasant rarity for a viewer who roots for the characters.

---

## EuroTrip: A Film You Want to Rewatch Right After the Final Frame

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/evrotur-2004/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-05-27 (27 May 2025)
Work: “EuroTrip” is a 2004 film directed by Jeff Schaffer.
Tags: comedy, American cinema, road movie, 2000s
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/evrotur-2004/

Continuing my reviews of [older but very cool titles,](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/yuzzz-serial/) I want to tell you about *EuroTrip* — a film that, even if you haven’t seen it, you definitely know from its meme moments (here’s my favourite, in place of a trailer).

Imagine a cross between *Piter FM* (the 2006 St Petersburg rom-com) and *What We Do in the Shadows* (only without the vampires, and with a firm friendship full of comic situations, plus jokes about Eastern Europe), and you’ll get something roughly as romantic and as funny. *EuroTrip* has the fantastic aura of a summer trip you remember for the rest of your life, and humour that is anything but formulaic, so don’t lump it in with *American Pie* or *Superbad* — this is something else :) And the most interesting thing: it’s the kind of film you want to rewatch right after the final frame, and that doesn’t happen all that often. You find yourself gazing above all at the architecture and the exteriors the characters end up in, even though in reality 95% of *EuroTrip* was shot in Prague, and landmarks like Big Ben were composited into the frame.

And, as always, share in the comments: which classics you missed have you been catching up on lately?

## Radio Day: A Live Take on What We Are Used to Seeing on Film

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/den-radio-teatr/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-05-26 (26 May 2025)
Work: “Radio Day” is a 2001 stage production directed by Sergey Petreykov.
Tags: theatre, comedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/den-radio-teatr/

Another off-topic theatre post. This time it’s about a show I have rewatched some 8 times in its film version.

It’s *Radio Day* («День радио»), a production that Kvartet I (the Moscow comedy troupe) have been performing for 25 years now and that has existed as a [film](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/402979/) since 2008. The show is good precisely as a live take on something we are used to seeing fixed on film. On stage the delivery is livelier and the characters are more rounded; I was especially impressed by Nonna Grishaeva, who doesn’t seem to have changed at all in these 25 years :) By the way, every trademark “*maladtsy!*” (“well done!”; drop a ❤️ if you read that in exactly that voice :)) from Leonid Barats’s character is greeted with applause from the house, and it’s great to see that with your own eyes. But before you go, make sure you don’t know every single joke in the film by heart, or the wow effect is slightly dulled.

Why go to the theatre, you may ask, when there’s both the film and a [televised version of the play?](https://hd.kinopoisk.ru/film/45a12e6a541b9258be4d0bbd8613dae9) There’s one catch: in neither of those versions will you see the magnificent Pavel Maykov singing in his many guises as the frontmen of several bands. Every musical number is an explosion of energy, comedy and showmanship from Maykov and the band Bobry. It was this actor’s presence in the show that clinched it for me: Maykov doesn’t have that many stage roles, and watching him act is always a great pleasure.

## Couple vs. Couple: A Straight-Faced Comedy with Slightly Philosophical Humour

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/para-na-paru-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-05-22 (22 May 2025)
Work: “Couple vs. Couple” is a 2025 film directed by Vladimir Kott.
Tags: comedy, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/para-na-paru-2025/

In cinemas from today: [*Couple vs. Couple*](https://t.me/kino_voice/595) (*Para na paru*), a straight-faced comedy with slightly philosophical humour.

The film turned out to be deeper and more layered than its promotional material suggests, promising as it does the familiar format of a comedy about a cuckolded husband and his little ruse for the sake of love. What we actually get is an uproariously funny story about the tragedy of Kostya, a desperate literature lecturer — this “little man” and “superfluous man” in one (both stock figures of Russian literature) is brilliantly played by Dmitry Chebotarev. To get to see his wife, who is flat-out ignoring him and has already moved in with a rich new suitor (a comic Alexander Robak), Chebotarev’s character hits on one of his students — the daughter of that very suitor — and goes to meet “his girlfriend’s” father at their family estate (given the scale of it, no other word will do).

From there the characters set off on a long journey towards one another and towards themselves, but the main thing is how it’s done! Arguing with this clan of devotees of all things material, whose side his wife has gone over to as well, Kostya tries to prove the value of the spiritual, the importance of art and feeling, and not just of calculation. He quotes poetry endlessly (in Chebotarev’s delivery you could listen for hours), performs small feats and makes big sacrifices. But at first it is like banging his head against a brick wall — against the impenetrable devotion to everything carnal and physical on the part of the rich masters not only of this enormous house but, as it seems at first glance, of life itself.

As Vladimir Kott, the director of *Couple vs. Couple*, said at the premiere, a film always turns out to be about something slightly different from what was originally intended. And I’d like to add that it is precisely for this surprise that the film is worth seeing in a cinema (your mood, like the director’s, is sure to lift).

---

## Red Rocket: The Story of a Textbook “Superfluous Man”

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/krasnaya-raketa-2021/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-05-20 (20 May 2025)
Work: “Red Rocket” is a 2021 film directed by Sean Baker.
Tags: drama, American cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/krasnaya-raketa-2021/

On Saturday I went to a cycling festival and rode the whole of the Garden Ring (Moscow’s inner ring road), and that same evening I watched a film whose main character also gets around mostly by bike. Coincidence? I think not.

[*Red Rocket*](https://youtu.be/P0nnJljdryw?si=aBZGEzWPAeW7ih95) had been on my mind for a long time: I liked [*Anora*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/anora-2024/) so much that I wanted to see something else from Sean Baker’s filmography. My high expectations were fully met: the film turned out to be an impressive, many-layered story of an antihero who has you feeling completely opposite emotions for the full 2 hours. Because the stages of the moral fall of Mikey, the main character, are so clearly marked off, the film becomes a truly unique emotional ride that the viewer, like it or not, lives through.

By and large, this is the story of a textbook “superfluous man” (the classic figure of Russian literature) who is trying with all his might to be a self-made man. And the main thing Sean Baker stresses among the reasons for his failure is the closed nature of a society hemmed in by norms and not prepared to reintegrate a former porn actor. It is precisely the tacit refusal of any socially acceptable work that pushes Mikey onto the slippery slope we watch for the next 2 hours. And once on that slippery slope (yes, yes, the very one Mikey rides down on his bicycle), picking up the prefix “anti-” to go with the title of “hero” could not be easier. The question of whether the winner takes it all, as the song “The Winner Takes It All” has it, hangs in an ominous pause at the end. (And the answer, it seems, can already be partly guessed from the director’s next film, *Anora*, which carries on the same theme of social outcasts.)

By the way, don’t watch it on an empty stomach, and stock up on doughnuts: you are guaranteed to want some :)

## There: The Journey Sometimes Matters More Than the Final Destination

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/tuda-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-05-15 (15 May 2025)
Work: “There” is a 2025 film directed by Ivan Petukhov.
Tags: Russian cinema, road movie, dramedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/tuda-2025/

I had seen all sorts of opinions about the road movie [*There* (*Tuda*),](https://youtu.be/x_oLucseql4?si=D4ko8gtsdB9j59Ml) which is in cinemas from today, so I was a little apprehensive going in, but I needn’t have been. What we’ve got is, you might say, [*Centaur*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/5235968/) («Кентавр»), but with a positive vibe :)

This film about a taxi ride to Ufa and back is deftly constructed at the level of the script. Watching the never-ending dialogue between Irina Starshenbaum’s chatty heroine and the sullen driver played by Pyotr Fyodorov was enjoyable and intriguing, and, most importantly, it is done convincingly enough. It is the dialogue that is the best thing in this film, and the thing the actors have mastered 100% (that goes for the minor characters played by Serebryakov and Dobrovolskaya too, by the way).

Despite a rather weak ending (a meeting with the classmates who hurt the heroine many years ago), the film is a reminder that the journey sometimes matters more than the final destination. The same can be said of the friendship that springs up between the flighty passenger and the driver, and of the experience of watching this film.

## Alexandr Khant to Direct Fury: High Hopes After In Limbo

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/aleksandr-khant-furiya/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-05-14 (14 May 2025)
Work: “Fury” is a work  Alexandr Khant.
Tags: Russian cinema, series, comics, announcements
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/aleksandr-khant-furiya/

Since Monday I’ve been delighted by the news that Alexandr Khant will direct the adaptation of the comic about Fury from Bubble (the Russian comics publisher) and Kinopoisk (Russia’s largest film database, media and streaming service). To explain my delight, let me tell you why my hopes are so high.

I still [consider](https://t.me/kino_voice/542) Khant’s [*In Limbo*](https://youtu.be/_B5tn0EXFAU?si=UmXln91Wi-X3N9xp) («Межсезонье») one of the best films I have ever seen. The story pays enormous attention to its female characters in particular: their emotional lives, the way they see the world, the way they define themselves. Young Sasha, the film’s lead, is drawn with such attention and care in every facet that there can be no doubt about the director’s ability to handle young heroines ready to take on the world.

The comic adaptation also promises to show an alternative Moscow. That shouldn’t be a problem either, as *In Limbo* shows us: just remember how three-dimensional and alive Yekaterinburg was in Khant’s film, how the city spoke to the characters and to the audience. Visual language is the director’s strong suit, and for a comic-book adaptation that is no small thing :)

We’re expecting *Fury* («Фурия») in 2026 (and in the meantime we’re rewatching *In Limbo* and, I hope, catching [*Jackpot*](https://t.me/kino_voice/112) in cinemas).

## Vermiglio: It’s Not About the Village, It’s About the Women Who Live There

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/gornaya-nevesta-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-05-13 (13 May 2025)
Work: “Vermiglio” is a 2024 film directed by Maura Delpero.
Tags: drama, European cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/gornaya-nevesta-2024/

The synopsis of [*Vermiglio*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/6038922/) (released in Russia as *Gornaya nevesta*, “The Mountain Bride”; it recently came out on streaming services) plays up the idea that a soldier who has fled the war changes the life of an Italian mountain village. I don’t think that’s quite right.

As you watch, it becomes clear that it’s not about the village but about the women who live in it. With the patriarchal family, a man at its head, in decline (and that is exactly the kind of family we watch throughout the film), what comes to the fore is the relationships between a mother and her daughters, between friends, between sisters. The soldier, who appears out of nowhere and vanishes again, is a catalyst for character development only where the women are concerned (the male characters all seem to stay just as they were). This piece of dramatic construction, easy to miss at first glance, sets the film apart, to its advantage, from other stories about the home front in the Second World War and gives it an unconventional set of concerns.

Incidentally, the way *Vermiglio* looks is another thing that makes it special. The film was shot by Mikhail Krichman, Andrey Zvyagintsev’s* regular cinematographer and the man behind those trademark cold, detached images — whether they show nature or characters in close-up. It’s nice that, for all the chosen style, the ending of *Vermiglio* is nothing like the unambiguous denouements of *Leviathan* or *Loveless* — which means a fresh cinematic experience is guaranteed.

* Andrey Zvyagintsev (Звягинцев Андрей Петрович) has been designated a “foreign agent” by Russia’s Ministry of Justice (listed on 18 September 2026).

---

## The Postman: A Well-Meant Lie, a Convincing Petrov and a Debatable Ending

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/pochtar-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-05-08 (8 May 2025)
Work: “The Postman” is a 2025 film directed by Andrey Razenkov.
Tags: Russian cinema, war film, drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/pochtar-2025/

Curious about the plot, I watched [*The Postman*](https://kion.ru/video/movie/1225683588) (*Pochtar*) with Alexander Petrov and had a decidedly mixed viewing experience.

Petrov’s character, a village postman at the time of the Great Patriotic War (the Second World War) and a bit of a holy fool, has been delivering letters all his life and knows every villager by sight. But when death notices start arriving from the front, the postman can’t bring himself to hand them to the women, so he decides, for everyone’s good, to write letters on behalf of the dead and deliver them to women who are, in effect, already widows.

I was curious to see how a premise like that would unfold — where would this well-meant lie end up? Unfortunately, the ending (towards which some strange musings on the benefits and harm of the truth turn up as well) is contrived and not very realistic. But for all its debatable moments, what truly lifts the film is, first, Petrov’s performance — he is very convincing in this difficult role — and, second, the absence of the bombast typical of war films of recent years. If you like quiet films that make you think over commonly accepted moral norms, *The Postman* will be just the thing.

---

## Death of a Unicorn: An Epic Absurdist Comedy with a Critique of Modern Life

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/smert-edinoroga-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-05-06 (6 May 2025)
Work: “Death of a Unicorn” is a 2025 film directed by Alex Scharfman.
Tags: horror, comedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/smert-edinoroga-2025/

[*Death of a Unicorn*](https://okko.tv/movie/death-of-a-unicorn) landed on streaming services yesterday — an epic absurdist comedy with a critique of modern life and some horror moments.

Despite a formulaic, sketch-like set-up (a careerist father at odds with his enlightened daughter, even though a shared loss has traumatised them both), the film gets stronger, in both its writing and its ideas, once the unicorn itself appears. Apart from the horror element we already know from A24’s other hits, *Death of a Unicorn* stands out for the atmosphere of irony in which everything takes place. Yes, the issues are the usual ones of late capitalism, social inequality and ecological catastrophe, but they come with a smirk that takes the humour to pitch-blackness and total absurdity. To my taste, moves like these let you avoid taking the film too seriously, and so think over the problems it shows in a calmer mode.

Incidentally, the new release is in many ways reminiscent of [*Mickey 17*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/mikki-17-2025/), in its madcap portrait of the powers that be and in other details. At one point *Death of a Unicorn* even gets as far as choosing its own kind of “expendables” (exactly [the role](https://t.me/kino_voice/388) Pattinson played in *Mickey 17*). So this turns out to be an unexpected recommendation not only for fans of contemporary horror and social issues but also for lovers of Korean cinema with black humour and a dystopian mood.

---

## Summer Will Come: A Frightening Black-and-White Dream with an Unpredictable Ending

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/nastupit-leto-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-05-03 (3 May 2025)
Work: “Summer Will Come” is a 2024 film directed by Kirill Sultanov.
Tags: Russian cinema, drama, arthouse
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/nastupit-leto-2024/

[*Summer Will Come*](https://hd.kinopoisk.ru/film/0d4997e6e35d4e79913a380659905ac8) (*Nastupit leto*) is one of those films that leave you with more questions than answers once you’ve watched them.

To me the film is like one frightening black-and-white dream, unsettling above all because there is no way of predicting how it will end. The effect comes from the fact that none of the characters is fully in control of their own life: they all seem to be drifting on an uncontrollable current of outside forces, with no way of changing course. And this detachment from reality is underlined, among other things, by the black-and-white photography — not something you often see in films today.

Incidentally, despite the powerful crime plot the trailer promises, in practice things are not that twisty. Mark Eydelshteyn’s character certainly commands attention, but comes across more as a carefully worked-out screenwriting construct (childhood trauma, the misanthropic make-up of a psychopath) than as a rounded character. Real empathy, on the other hand, comes from watching the couple played by Mikita Voronov and Tina Stoyilkovich: the way their relationship is rendered on screen has a shot-for-shot quotation from *July Rain* (Marlen Khutsiev’s 1966 film), and sincerity, and a cinematic quality.

All in all, the film leaves a mixed impression, but it definitely grabs you with its unconventional visual language, which stands out from the crowd.

---

## Unprincipled in St-Petersburg: The Spin-Off That Let Kristina Babushkina Truly Shine

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/besprintsipnye-v-pitere-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-05-02 (2 May 2025)
Work: “Unprincipled in St-Petersburg” is a 2025 series directed by Zaur Zaseev.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, comedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/besprintsipnye-v-pitere-serial/

[*Unprincipled in St-Petersburg*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/series/5377368/) (*Besprintsipnye v Pitere*) had the luck to catch the frosty weather over the May holidays, when watching a sunny city, even if only on screen, is already a pleasure.

By the way, the sequel being set here of all places came as no surprise to me: as Alexander Tsypkin [told](https://music.yandex.ru/album/14629532/track/113555328?utm_source=web&amp;utm_medium=copy_link) me on a podcast back in 2023[,](https://music.yandex.ru/album/14629532/track/113555328) the characters would definitely go to St Petersburg one day. What I didn’t expect was to see my favourite pairing, Aglaya Tarasova and Pavel Tabakov, drop out of the cast. Other viewers are bound to miss their favourite characters too, because a lot of them are missing :)

But every cloud has a silver lining: the spin-off lets Valya, played by Kristina Babushkina, come gloriously into her own and show every shade of her character. Igor Vernik is intriguing as a theatre critic who keeps the whole cultural capital (as St Petersburg is called) in fear every bit as well as the mafia. That touch of the fantastical even freshens up the familiar humour of the unprincipled crew. And it’s a pleasure to see Anna Kovalchuk: she slotted into this world perfectly from the very first shot and makes a great addition to the female cast.

## Which Cinema Seats Viewers Choose: A Kinopoisk Study and a Poll

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/mesta-v-kinozale-opros/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-04-30 (30 April 2025)
Tags: notes, industry
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/mesta-v-kinozale-opros/

Are you going to the cinema over the May holidays?

Kinopoisk (Russia’s largest film database, media and streaming service) has just done a [study](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/4011092/) of how popular the various seats are in cinema auditoriums of different sizes. The middle wins everywhere, though how far from the screen depends on the size of the auditorium :) I myself usually end up in large or medium-sized auditoriums, and I pick those very seats — central both relative to the screen and by number of rows :)

**Which brings me to a question for you: which seats do you usually go for?** I suggest picking 2 answers — one for your position relative to the screen and one relative to the number of rows in the auditorium. And if your combination isn’t among the options, go ahead and hit “Other” and come to the comments :)

## Legends from the Past: Costumes as the Film’s Calling Card

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/legendy-nashikh-predkov-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-04-29 (29 April 2025); updated: 2025-07-11
Work: “Legends from the Past” is a 2025 film directed by Ivan Sosnin.
Tags: Russian cinema, fairy tales
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/legendy-nashikh-predkov-2025/

## 29 April 2025

I’m [carrying on](https://t.me/kino_voice/538) telling you about the delights of the film [*Legends from the Past*](https://youtu.be/uI3T9AGLjOc?si=kAcpej7S-i9jobt4) (*Legendy nashikh predkov*), and the first thing I want to point out, without spoilers for now, is the costumes! They, I think, can be counted among the film’s calling cards.

I was genuinely impressed by how much work has gone into the look of the fairy-tale creatures — in particular the shaggy Nyulesmurt of the forest (Anton Kuznetsov) and Shishiga of the water (Natalya Pavlenkova). Given current trends in film, they could have painted in all the tricky details of the costumes with CGI and left it at that. But here — and you can see it in the photos from the set — every hair on Nyulesmurt is real and three-dimensional (look at the first photo, where they are combing his back and putting on a clawed glove at the same time), and every little gill and fin on Shishiga has texture and relief (again, there’s even a close-up photo). So the combined effect of the acting and the characters’ look is absolutely stunning.

It all looks like a cool continuation of the Soviet tradition of fairy-tale costume: compare Georgy Millyar in his roles in *Barbara the Fair with the Silken Hair* and *Morozko* (“Jack Frost”). That Baba Yaga, I think, has stayed with many people for life as the definitive one — and again, no CGI: it all rests on the costume designers’ imagination and the actor’s charisma. So *Legends from the Past*, which has all of this, is worth seeing :)

## 1 May 2025

From today [*Legends from the Past*](https://t.me/kino_voice/559) is finally in cinemas — to my mind the best modern fairy-tale film, which has:

- Alexander Yatsenko as a journalist, a father, a keeper of legends and simply a charming bungler
- Characters from folklore we’re not used to, that of Udmurtia and Khanty-Mansiysk
- The song [“Mesto dlya shaga vperyod” (“Room for a Step Forward”) by the band Kino](https://zvuk.com/track/55138259) on the soundtrack
- Natural locations with a springtime beauty (and the scenes in town, incidentally, are full of writing on the walls of buildings, on fences and on other parts of the landscape — the town seems to be talking to the characters and to us)
- An atmosphere of magic and hope (as in many of Ivan Sosnin’s other films)

I’ve written about the film in a little more detail [in a piece for Kinopoisk](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/news/4011107/), and I declare in all seriousness that it’s the must-have of this weekend’s film viewing.

## 11 July 2025

As the number one fan of [*Legends from the Past*,](https://t.me/kino_voice/569) I wrote about the film for Kinopoisk in its [list](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/4011434/) of the best Russian films of the past six months.

It really does seem to be my favourite of the half of 2025 gone by, because in my personal ranking nothing has overtaken it: not [*The Poet*,](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/prorok-2025/) not [*Mickey 17*,](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/mikki-17-2025/) not even the wonderful [*The Phoenician Scheme*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/finikiyskaya-skhema-2025/).

Watch *Legends* on the [streaming platforms,](https://okko.tv/movie/legendy-nashikh-predkov) if you haven’t yet, and share my feelings.

## From the Life of the ***ed Up: A Set of Sketches on the Absurdity of Social Norms

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/iz-zhizni-nutykh-teatr/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-04-26 (26 April 2025)
Work: “Iz zhizni ***nutykh” is a 2016 stage production directed by Yury Muravitsky.
Tags: theatre
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/iz-zhizni-nutykh-teatr/

Another theatre off-topic. While waiting for Alexandr Khant’s [*Jackpot*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/5266958/?utm_referrer=www.google.com), I decided to go and see a play in which he has one of the lead roles. It’s called [*Iz zhizni \*\*\*nutykh*](https://teatrdoc.ru/performances/1253/?afisha_open_widget=1) (“From the Life of the \*\*\*ed Up”), it’s on at [Teatr.doc](https://t.me/Theatredoc) (the Moscow documentary theatre) and it fully lives up to its name :)

Over a little more than an hour, the audience is shown a set of sketches from different moments in the lives of random people: they might take place in a notional café, office, bedroom or railway station. The way it works is roughly like *6 kadrov* (“6 Frames”, the Russian sketch-comedy show) or scrolling through Reels, only at a slowed-down pace, in an atmosphere of strict minimalism, mild absurdism and an emotional flatness you don’t expect in the theatre (which makes for some serious discomfort).

The thread running through the production is the idea that social norms are absurd. You’re not supposed to show concern for strangers, or talk to people you don’t know, let alone show intolerance towards someone who is annoying you in a public place. In the play, the characters (a.k.a. the \*\*\*ed up) follow exactly the opposite rules: they poke their noses into other people’s business, try to strike up conversations with strangers and even kick street buskers whose off-key playing is unbearable to listen to. How to interpret what you’ve seen is up to each individual, but walking out of this play indifferent is definitely impossible.

---

## Stills from Favourite Films in the Ghibli Style: An AI Experiment

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kadry-v-stile-ghibli/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-04-26 (26 April 2025)
Tags: notes, pop culture
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/kadry-v-stile-ghibli/

I’ve finally got round to restyling stills from my favourite films in the style of Ghibli animation — starting with the classics (Pchyola, of *Brigada*, the cult 2002 Russian gangster series, is the most handsome, as always).

The nice thing is that you can now experiment with AI without leaving Telegram — in the bot [@gpt4telegrambot](https://t.me/gpt4telegrambot). It’s all simple there:
- you tap the [/wow](https://t.me/GPT4Telegrambot?start) command,
- attach a photo of the character
- describe your task (for example, what style to redraw the still in).
Voilà!

By the way, with the [bot](https://t.me/GPT4Telegrambot) you can also make those very figurines of characters in little boxes, your own Telegram stickers and even humanised animals — you’ll be able to see what kind of person your cat or dog would be (I’m leaving what I got with my cat in the comments).
