## Lesson: A Teen Drama That Unwinds Its Plot in Reverse

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/urok-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-04-25 (25 April 2025); updated: 2025-06-13
Work: “Lesson” is a 2025 series directed by Sergey Filatov.
Tags: series, drama, Russian cinema, thriller
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/urok-serial/

## 25 April 2025

I had been waiting for [*Lesson*](https://youtu.be/N8rwCSinSRA?si=ixCXaHvnt_s5QLDq) (*Urok*) for a long time, and it was worth it: the first episode is a success.

Yura Borisov, as a rapper who has lost his career, his money and his girlfriend (literally: she died in a car crash and he survived), is, as ever, meaningfully silent and gazes kindly (especially at kittens). The same cannot be said of Daniil Vorobyov’s character: looking at him, I’m reminded of an entity from Russian literature called the *nedotykomka*. It is the image of the demon lodged inside the protagonist of Fyodor Sologub’s novel *The Petty Demon*. In other words, some small, sly, clinging bit of nastiness, invisible to the eye at first. We’ll see what comes of it in the episodes ahead, but I have no doubt that Daniil Vorobyov’s possessed characters are a winning card.

By all the rules of a pilot episode, the teenagers are getting a storyline of their own too, and I’m glad it is led by Oleg Savostyuk, an actor who, to my taste, has already earned as much trust as Borisov and Vorobyov. It is unusual that after a thoroughly grown-up role in [*Give a Show!*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/dayte-shou-serial/) (*Dayte shou*) he has gone back to a school setting, but it’s a pleasure to see him on screen in any role. By the way, I hope the storyline of Igor the not-quite-tomcat gets developed too; they didn’t put him on the poster for nothing!

On the downside: the country house where the teenagers hang out is giving me Vietnam flashbacks. It is the same location as the fateful party in *Cicadas*. Anyone who knows how that series ended will understand my nervous tic.

## 10 May 2025

I’m still watching [*Lesson*](https://t.me/kino_voice/550), and I can’t help noting that Yura Borisov and Daniil Vorobyov in the leads are a great engine of interest in a series that has turned out to be not quite about their characters’ relationship as brothers.

The story is turning ever more deeply into a teen drama, with bullying, emotional dependency and overprotective parents. And it isn’t that easy to get anyone interested in a set-up that at first glance is so typical and familiar. But then the plot here unwinds in reverse order: in the first episode, before we properly knew anyone, we witnessed a shooting (which in *Cicadas*, for instance, was precisely the final chord), and in the episodes that follow we get to know each teenager better. With the suspense built this way, there is no nagging sense that everything is heading towards something definite; on the contrary, you get the chance to guess for yourself what awaits the characters.

For now I feel sorry to the point of tears for Mila (a girl who gets called Ponchik, “Doughnut”, more often than by her name), because she is completely blind to the manipulations of Artyom, who exploits her feelings for him 100% (an astonishingly vile character from Oleg Savostyuk; a transformation like that sends a chill down your spine). It is frightening even to imagine what will come of their drug escapades together. Adding to the darkness is the sinister transformation of Kostya (Vorobyov) from a harmless, tiresome pedant into a maniacally focused villain. The portrait he spent a couple of episodes unwrapping piece by piece was evidently the last thread of his fragile psychological stability. Now, it seems, as the wrapping paper came off the painting, the character came unhinged along with it.

 By the way, where has the pseudo-tomcat with the kittens gone? We haven’t been shown Igor for quite a while, and we miss him!

## 17 May 2025

A few words on why the series [*Lesson*](https://t.me/kino_voice/584) has such a well-written script.

At first, because of the set-up we are given, we expect it to be Yura Borisov’s character who develops; he is the wildest guy here, after all. But in fact his arrival serves only as a catalyst for the transformation of Daniil Vorobyov’s character, who at first looks more stable than a school bell timetable.

Not a bit of it: judging by half the season, Borisov is by now playing a reliably good guy who, in effect, left his troubles behind before the action even began, off screen. Vorobyov, on the other hand, is precisely the one acquiring them. And the longer his brother is around, the more speed he picks up.

So what makes the script good is precisely this swapping of what we stereotypically expect from the characters for something realistically convincing: at once the plot becomes pleasantly unpredictable.

## 30 May 2025

The new episode of [*Lesson*](https://t.me/kino_voice/596) in 3 points:

Igoressa is back! At last, if only briefly, we got to enjoy a scene with this heroine again.

The way the episode ends is not encouraging: for several central characters the remaining episodes risk turning from a teen drama into a crime drama.

Where we were learning to manipulate people, Daniil Vorobyov’s character was teaching. Clearly Konstantin has broken bad, and from here it will only get worse. It is hard even to imagine how the conflicts that have piled up could be resolved relatively painlessly for all the innocent.

## 13 June 2025

The finale of [*Lesson*](https://t.me/kino_voice/596) did not let me down. It was clear from the very beginning that a tragedy would happen, but it was not obvious whom it would strike. It’s great that this mystery stayed unpredictable to the end, and that when it was revealed, it played out in a very unconventional yet realistic way.

The “superfluous man”, in the person of Anton (Borisov), got the ending that is classic for 19th-century Russian literature (but it was unexpected all the same). And the final monologue from Kostya (Vorobyov) cemented the series once and for all in the genre of psychological thriller.

A particular joy was the scene where Igoressa’s kittens are given away. First, it is as though this were the destiny that meeting Anton bestowed on each of the characters. Second, it is the healthiest way of living through grief that I have seen on screen. Zero hints at a second season, an excellent, complete story that I even feel like rewatching.

---

## VIA “Cornflowers”: A Mockumentary from the World of Music Biopics

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/via-vasilki-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-04-24 (24 April 2025)
Work: “VIA ‘Cornflowers’” is a 2025 series directed by Yuri Sharov.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, music, dramedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/via-vasilki-serial/

I’ve finally got round to the series [*VIA “Cornflowers”*](https://youtu.be/uGWHpMj2GtM?si=BCfub3ioJzxZxAqd) (*VIA “Vasilki”*; VIA is the Soviet “vocal and instrumental ensemble”, i.e. a pop band), and it seems to be a true mockumentary from the world of music biopics: the story of a made-up band, complete with songs written specially for that made-up band and a fairly detailed history of its members’ relationships across no fewer than two time periods.

Overall, *Cornflowers* is like [*Kombinatsiya*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kombinatsiya-serial/) («Комбинация», “Combination”) in a major key (with all its strengths and weaknesses). Here, too, we’re shown the late USSR as a kind of fairy-tale stylisation; here, too, they reconstruct in detail how a legendary band came together and who did a little cheating of whom along the way — only without the tragedy that inevitably arises when the prototypes are real.

There’s also a note of sitcom, accompanying the uncomplicated road movie that the heroine’s daughters are on in the present day. The result is a comedy that is naive in a metamodernist way, with a romantic intrigue, tangled family ties, and friendship and betrayal in the right proportions — all of these things have been tried and tested many times over and offer nothing new, but they work as a sturdy piece of craftsmanship (just take the many songs written specially by Sergey Zhukov (the frontman of the pop group Ruki Vverh!), each of which sounds like a convincing 1970s hit). In short, despite being somewhat formulaic, from an industry point of view the concept is very much of professional interest.

---

## Honey, I Won’t Call You Back: A Collage of Pop-Culture Symbols from Different Religions

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/dorogaya-ya-bolshe-ne-perezvonyu-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-04-22 (22 April 2025)
Work: “Honey, I Won’t Call You Back” is a 2025 film directed by Aleksander Fomin.
Tags: Russian cinema, comedy, analysis
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/dorogaya-ya-bolshe-ne-perezvonyu-2025/

If you do happen to get round to [*Honey, I Won’t Call You Back*](https://okko.tv/movie/dorogaja-ja-bolshe-ne-perezvonju-621795607), be ready for a stunning collage of pop-culture symbols from the different religions that blend together in our post-Soviet mentality. In short, you’ll get a look inside the head of someone who celebrates pagan Maslenitsa (the Shrovetide pancake festival), Orthodox Easter and Soviet May Day with equal enthusiasm. Here’s what awaits you:

**1️⃣** karma points (from Buddhism!) for every one of the souls
**2️⃣** sins tallied according to the religion the main character followed in life (here, Christianity)
**3️⃣** three grannies with knitting needles at the reception desk (the ancient Greek Moirai with their threads of fate)
**4️⃣** purgatory (from the Catholic tradition)

On top of that, Efremov’s character trains for his ordeals in purgatory to the jaunty [*Tantsy po raschetu* («Танцы по расчету», “Dances of Convenience”) by the band Buerak](https://zvuk.com/track/65110653), and then, just as jauntily, quotes the opening credits of the famous *Krutoe pike* («Крутое пике», “Steep Dive”) from *Kalambur* (“Pun”), the cult Russian TV sketch show of the late 1990s (“Broiler 747”, “the ever-cheerful and courageous Commander, \<...> and also the incomparable Miss Murple as Miss Burple” — all of that).

Given the concept — the dying visions of Efremov’s character, an adman who is forever mulling over references — this is a very interesting structure and visual style, which makes the film, for all its flaws, memorable and original.

---

## The Last of Us, Season 2: The Beauty of the Ruins Beats the Dialogue Once Again

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/the-last-of-us-2-sezon-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-04-20 (20 April 2025); updated: 2025-06-01
Work: “The Last of Us” is a 2023 series directed by Craig Mazin, Neil Druckmann.
Tags: series, post-apocalypse, video game adaptation
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/the-last-of-us-2-sezon-serial/

## 20 April 2025

The opening episode of season 2 of [*The Last of Us*](https://youtu.be/_zHPsmXCjB0?si=j7H8MXia3ZHp2wk2) is simply a combination of things that don’t go together.

My first and clearest impression is that, over the 5 years that have passed in the world of the series, Ellie seems to have lost a few brain cells. Seriously, this character bears no comparison with the one in the first season, and it isn’t a matter of growing up: such vivid displays of teenage rebellion at the age of 19 are baffling, to say the least. Naturally, a character transformation like this sets up the necessary level of intrigue, but that doesn’t make it any easier for me as a viewer.

Despite Ellie’s wild energy, the whole episode moves sluggishly, even for exposition. This creates yet another dissonance — one that, paradoxically, really spurs your interest and your desire to keep watching. And that is how, on contrasts, the new chapter of this story begins.

## 27 April 2025

After the expository [first episode](https://t.me/kino_voice/539), *The Last of Us* carried on with a lively zombie invasion and sharp turns in the characters’ storylines, which is what we all came for.

The second episode is striking for the lifelike chaos of everything that happens: before the fateful day, people happen to quarrel, happen to miss each other, and meet only when it is already too late. Then again, the vast majority of encounters in this episode bring grief to at least one of those who meet, and in that I see the season’s dominant principle: “man is a wolf to man”. The rest of the season will evidently be spent trying to deal with the chain of violence Joel unwittingly set in motion, and exactly what the show’s makers will do with the game’s ending is doubly interesting.

In my view, the first two episodes should have been released together, in one go: they form a harmonious opening to the season, with a variety of storylines ⬅️ But we have what we have, and now, I think, it is in the third episode that we should expect the pace to drop. Ellie has a lot to think over, accept and decide for herself before moving on, and in this, incidentally, her situation matches that of the whole town, which has just lived through a horrific attack by the infected. We wait for flashbacks with Pedro Pascal, place our bets on how quickly the characters will shake off their post-traumatic numbness, and keep watching.

## 4 May 2025

Well, the third episode of *The Last of Us* turned out, as I [predicted,](https://t.me/kino_voice/555) to be a sharp drop in pace.

Even the two friends’ journey to Seattle is built less as a dynamic trip than as a meditative ride through locations carried over from the game into the series. The same goes for the scene where Ellie looks around Joel’s now-empty house: I see in it not only a farewell to someone dear to her but also a display of the calm, homely fictional world that, for the characters, remains in the past.

Still, the season is approaching its midpoint — and, with the plot being stretched out like this, it becomes clear why the series has been renewed for a 3rd season :)

## 11 May 2025

The second season of *The Last of Us* has passed the halfway mark and, it seems, something is about to begin other than the positioning of forces, of which we have already [seen our fill.](https://t.me/kino_voice/576)

Seattle has finally been reached, the girls’ secrets from each other are out, and it is clear who the enemies and ill-wishers are. Before the season ends I’d like to get at least a glimpse of the encounter with the adversaries and the long-awaited revenge.

I have a couple of questions for this universe. First Ellie, with the confidence of a seasoned reader of the specialist literature, tells the psychologist everything she wants to hear from a traumatised girl who is on the mend. But a couple of episodes later the very same Ellie can’t for the life of her work out what those rainbow symbols on the walls of the abandoned city are? :)

Such familiarity with the psychological themes fashionable in our own world, unnatural in a post-apocalyptic setting, on the one hand, and complete ignorance of cultural symbols from literally 20 years earlier (in their world) on the other, looks strange, to say the least. Then again, these peculiarities of the on-screen world are, in their own way, an intriguing reason to keep watching.

## 18 May 2025

The fifth episode of [*The Last of Us* 2](https://t.me/kino_voice/586) is frustrating — and I already regret that HBO stretched the game across 2 seasons.

The beauty of the ruins has beaten the dialogue once again, so that even solid suspense becomes less convincing. Obviously, most of the flaws stem from the decision to split the second part of the game into two full seasons: I think this has badly slowed the pace of the storytelling and damaged the character development.

But there is still hope for the last couple of episodes. First, thanks to the cruelty Ellie has shown. In my post about the season’s first episode I [wrote](https://t.me/kino_voice/539) that Ellie seemed to have lost a few brain cells over the intervening 5 years, but now I see that this is more than made up for by her determination and firmness of principle, just as in the good old first season. In the scene of the brutal interrogation of one of Abby’s comrades, I finally found it interesting to watch what was happening, even though the whole scene unfolded in a dark, thoroughly unpicturesque (unlike the rest of the post-apocalyptic world) corner of a basement.

Second, an impressive theme is taking shape: the hopelessness of humans as a species. Faced with a growing danger of total extinction (the infection now also spreads in the form of spores that poison the air, and the infected are evolving rapidly), humanity goes on splintering into small warring factions, finding its reasons purely at the level of principle. Perhaps it would be worth going back to the subject of inventing a cure after all?

Third, a spoiler of a flashback in the closing shots hints that episode 6 may consist entirely of memories. That will give us Pedro Pascal, the plot’s intrigue unwinding and, I hope, gripping dialogue.

## 25 May 2025

In episode 6, *The Last of Us* 2 literally [came alive,](https://t.me/kino_voice/605) and that is encouraging ahead of the final episode.

All episode long I was delighted by the realistic dialogue, the Ellie and Joel double act and the steadily building context (which had been lacking until now). But this is obviously a brief breather ahead of the season finale, which is supposed to leave a powerful question hanging while we wait for the next episodes.

By the way, the episode very rarely shows Ellie and Joel in the same shot — apparently to reflect their estrangement before the fateful quarrel. I fished out a rare exception for this post.

## 1 June 2025

The final episode of [*The Last of Us* 2](https://t.me/kino_voice/612) is very much of a piece with the whole season: ambiguous, contentious and, in places, infuriatingly illogical.

By now we are used to the dialogue sagging noticeably once Joel is gone from the action. But this episode had me yelling at the screen for a different reason. In the scene where Ellie runs into Abby’s comrades and accidentally kills them both, one specific moment bothered me. The pregnant young woman, as she is dying, asks Ellie to make a cut in her belly and take the baby out, spelling out clearly where and how to cut. Ellie’s response is to go into panic mode (🤷‍♀️), not even try to do anything (🤦‍♀️) and, with a shocked look (as if this were unexpected), watch the young woman die. Fine, let’s say that is just the kind of person Ellie is, and nothing can be done about it. But in a world where one of the infected could devour you at any second, your reactions have to be up to scratch. And all this scene shows us is how easily the logic of the world collapses for the sake of “complicating” the inner conflict of the heroine — so conflicted, so misunderstood by everyone, so alone.

The final cliffhanger with the gunshot does, of course, leave things hanging, but after the scene described above it no longer lands with quite the same force. It’s a good thing we’ll have a couple of years to mull it over while we wait for the next season.

---

## Thirty Seconds: Sergei Gilev as a Touching Hospital Clown

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/tridtsat-sekund-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-04-17 (17 April 2025)
Work: “Thirty Seconds” is a 2024 film directed by Ivan Sosnin.
Tags: Russian cinema, short films, drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/tridtsat-sekund-2024/

*We come when someone is going through a hard time and tell them: “Listen, everything is going to be all right! Look, there’s light ahead”*

That line, it seems, is about every film Ivan Sosnin makes, and the short [*Thirty Seconds*](https://youtu.be/SrtT19L_kiA?si=_Zt2dUyt7huhziG4) (*Tridtsat sekund*), which arrived on streaming services today, is the best proof of it.

The hospital clown played by Sergei Gilev, touching and fragile in the extreme, helps one girl’s mother find the strength to look at her daughter with a smile rather than with tears, despite how serious the illness is. In just 20 minutes several lives unfold before us that could have turned out very unhappily — only not in this cinematic universe (and that is the best recommendation there is for giving the film your attention).

## SWWW: A Crime Drama About Turf Wars in Rostov-on-Don

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/yuzzz-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-04-16 (16 April 2025)
Work: “SWWW” is a 2022 series directed by Stas Ivanov.
Tags: series, crime, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/yuzzz-serial/

As part of ~~brushing up on the essentials~~ catching up on important things, I watched the series [*SWWW*](https://youtu.be/kZ1Bk5f28W8?si=SynLIfjFxMlSuGmb) (*YuZZZ*, after the city’s South-West-West-West district), a crime drama about turf wars in the neighbourhoods of Rostov-on-Don.

- The series has stunning locations: the dangerous aura of Rostov-on-Don is shown without embellishment, with the city’s recognisable southern charisma. And it was *SWWW* that brought the look of Rostov (which, as it happens, has a rich [history](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/4006407/)) up to date for the streaming era.

- Kuzma Kotrelev, Maria Matsel and Anton Kuznetsov have created very convincing, fully rounded characters whose fates you find yourself wanting to think over afterwards. Really, these are complex personalities; I couldn’t always understand their decisions, but that only made the show’s plot twist all the more intriguingly.

- For all the seeming transparency of a plot about the price of fast money, there is no sense of morality triumphing at the end. The fate of Rav (Kotrelev) is senseless to the point of hopelessness. And that is probably exactly right: there’s no call to romanticise the lives of drug dealers and assorted gangs, because in reality there will be no lofty finale. In that respect, by the way, the show’s ending recalls the finale of Sangadzhiev’s *Happy End*, if anyone has seen it.

By the way, are you interested in reading not only about new releases but about relatively old things too? Or perhaps you are catching up on something you missed yourselves?

## About This Very Thing: Idealism Versus Reality in the Village

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/pro-eto-samoe-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-04-15 (15 April 2025); updated: 2025-05-07
Work: “About This Very Thing” is a 2025 series directed by Evgeniy Abyzov.
Tags: series, comedy, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/pro-eto-samoe-serial/

## 15 April 2025

I’m a simple person: I see a show with Denis Vlasenko, I press play!

Just yesterday saw the launch of [*About This Very Thing*](https://youtu.be/1uhPwsNq6sE?si=_1eqQkV5FRr_TU_f) (*Pro eto samoe*), a series about a young sexologist (Vlasenko himself) who, after training in St Petersburg, returns to his home village genuinely burning to help people and teach them to see their own bodies in the right way. But his dear fellow villagers first dub him the “willy doctor” and then go so far as to beat him up for his unwanted sex ed. And this is where the main conflict arises, between idealism and reality (senseless and merciless).

Shows from TNT/Premier (the Russian TV channel and its streaming service) have always been good with village life (think of [*Zhuki*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/zhuki-serial/), “The Beetles”), and with the clash between the “regional” and the “metropolitan” too ([*Bodyguards*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/telokhraniteli-serial/) will bear me out here). It has all come off this time as well, even with subject matter that is alien to a mass audience. What’s more, Denis Vlasenko is masterly at playing self-sacrificing young men who suffer for their kindness to the world, so the casting is ideal. And the whole subject is pleasantly freshened by a link, felt somewhere at the back of the mind, to Bulgakov’s *A Young Doctor’s Notebook*. The one difference is that in *About This Very Thing* everything is given a comic spin, but it still stands out favourably among other television shows and has you waiting devotedly for more.

## 7 May 2025

As for the recently concluded series [*About This Very Thing*](https://t.me/kino_voice/534), it surprised me with an ending completely unexpected for its genre.

All season Denis Vlasenko’s character seemed to be fighting prejudice about sex education with success, helping someone here and there, getting his own love life in order — everything was on the up. And even when it all began to come apart towards the end, I didn’t expect the finale to be quite so radical. Anyway, to keep this spoiler-free, I’ll just say that after a last episode like that it’s actually a pleasure to wait for a second season — they’ve got me intrigued! :)

I hope that if there really is a continuation, it will keep the sweet aesthetic the show’s makers came up with. Its chief embodiment is the opening titles: a vivid shot with the show’s name in handwritten script. I admired them every time.

---

## Hypnosis: A Brisk Start, a Powerful Finale and a Middle That Spins Its Wheels

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/gipnozis-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-04-14 (14 April 2025); updated: 2025-05-23
Work: “Hypnosis” is a 2025 series directed by Timofey Zhalnin.
Tags: series, fantasy, Russian cinema, mystery
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/gipnozis-serial/

## 14 April 2025

I thought about it, thought some more, and started [*Hypnosis*](https://youtu.be/pHoWJ67jX5U?si=a8GD2lnx3Fro-1xM) (*Gipnozis*). So far the draw is not even the fantasy side but particular quirks of its alternative reality and its peculiar sense of humour :)

The thing is, the show’s three leads are three friends with superpowers (here they are, left to right): a private detective who can read minds; a lawyer who sees the future; and an Orthodox priest who sees the past. Put them together and you get a real superpower (and that is basically what they do, making use of one another’s abilities like good neighbours).

But how funny it looks in action when the lawyer, needing extra information on some case, asks the priest to swing by the morgue and touch a dead body to learn its past (the ability works only through physical contact). You pick up very strong vibes of *What Men Talk About* (the Kvartet I comedy), only with superpowers added to the plot, and that is no bad thing for an urban fantasy like this: you can’t carry everything on seriousness alone, after all. Indeed, irony and a down-to-earth quality, even in characters with supernatural abilities, sometimes do more to draw the viewer in than a twisty detective plot.

## 23 May 2025

*Hypnosis* has ended, and it made me feel for a hypnotist maniac. But first things first.

The series has a [brisk, catchy start](https://t.me/kino_voice/531) (plus a viral promo that was hard to miss) and a powerful finale, but a middle that noticeably spins its wheels and spoils the impression a little. Its problem is the suspense, which evaporates because the viewer knows the moves on every side.

Still, as soon as the reasons for Piskunov’s crimes became clear, everything fell into place for me. The good guys turned out not to be good enough to feel for, whereas the grief the antagonist lived through does seem a very weighty argument for revenge 20 years on. It even occurred to me that telling the story from his point of view would have been a winning device for the tale of a villain running amok. But even with the hand we were dealt, the flipping of good and evil made the finale truly gripping: what was happening stopped being obvious, and there was a real, not illusory, choice of which side to root for. So to fans of knotty, far-from-obvious detective stories, I warmly recommend it.

By the way, on top of all the merits of the ending, the characters’ soul-searching on screen is appealing. A lawyer, a private detective and a priest sit and discuss: did they have the right to do what they did? It’s great that the ethical reckoning with what we have been shown is not handed over entirely to the viewers but finds a place right inside the work itself: a very metamodernist move. After watching, you feel like recalling the concept of moral relativism and asking yourself once again whether absolute evil and absolute good are possible.

---

## Small Things Like These: A Meditation That Ends in a Clear-Cut Moral Choice

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/melochi-zhizni-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-04-12 (12 April 2025)
Work: “Small Things Like These” is a 2024 film directed by Tim Mielants.
Tags: drama, adaptation, European cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/melochi-zhizni-2024/

[*Small Things Like These*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/5453069/) is a good film to watch at the weekend, without distractions and fully immersed.

For the film’s whole hour and a half we live as though inside the mind of Cillian Murphy’s character, sharing in his traumas, fears and doubts. Despite a certain religious specificity to the story, which you have to get your head around, it’s great that this meditation ends not with a rhetorical question but with a clear answer and a clear-cut moral choice, one that may well help someone on this side of the screen too.

A great chance to drop out of the bustle of the working week and give an hour and a half to thoughts about yourself and the world around you.

## Where’s Our Money?: A Gangster Showdown in the Spirit of Guy Ritchie and Tarantino

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/gde-nashi-dengi-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-04-10 (10 April 2025); updated: 2025-04-11
Work: “Where’s Our Money?” is a 2024 film directed by Vladimir Zinkevich.
Tags: Russian cinema, comedy, crime
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/gde-nashi-dengi-2025/

## 10 April 2025

I’m admiring the stylised character posters for [*Where’s Our Money?*](https://youtu.be/9IQq9yYgefQ?si=X3Yp1WCyAuzm2L_n) (*Gde nashi dengi?*): from today you can catch this beauty in cinemas!

It’s a very lively, fast-moving and just plain great gangster showdown in the spirit of Guy Ritchie and Quentin Tarantino, but with allowances made for our own context. Despite its modest running time, the film is put together very intriguingly in terms of both plot and characters, so your attention will be held throughout by the motley inhabitants of this gangland landscape, each with a special something of their own. The humour is first-rate too: some of it runs on the actors’ charisma, some is purely physical, and some is simply charming absurdity of various kinds. And do concentrate as things head for the finale: the twists there are a thing of beauty :)

In short, I heartily recommend this new release, and I’ll definitely be watching it a second time myself.

## 11 April 2025

By the way, [*Where’s Our Money?*](https://t.me/kino_voice/523) is notable for a couple of other things too.

First, I spotted in it a sweet nod to *Messenger Boy*, a film that serves as a kind of prelude to the gangster era. Like Ivan in *Messenger Boy*, Kuzma Kotrelev’s character, nicknamed Nauka (“Science”), quizzes his friends: do they have a dream? The answers are drowned out by the commotion of the plot, but it’s the question itself that matters, as if to remind us that one should dream “of something great”. Especially in the context of a film preoccupied with easy money.

Second, the way the characters of *Where’s Our Money?* talk is a real linguistic treat. “DelyugA”, with the stress on the “a”, “chikh-pykh” and other euphemisms are great fun to decipher or even to work into your own vocabulary (guilty as charged: I love all these little words myself). And today, to my delight, I also discovered a [glossary](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/4010996/) of this slang from director Vladimir Zinkevich and colleagues at Kinopoisk: the perfect cultural plan for a Friday evening.

---

## Not Like Dad 2: Granddad, a Very Sweet Sequel About a Childhood in the 1990s

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/batya-2-ded-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-04-08 (8 April 2025)
Work: “Not Like Dad 2: Granddad” is a 2025 film directed by Ilya Uchitel.
Tags: Russian cinema, comedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/batya-2-ded-2025/

I’ve finally got round to [*Not Like Dad 2: Granddad*](https://youtu.be/69S2gg5qaTM?si=-Dmp2piQFy9FYJZN) (*Batya 2. Ded*), and it turns out to be a very sweet sequel to the story of a childhood in the 1990s.

The rough-edged humour and the buddy-movie side of things are in the hands of the still-young Andrey Andreev and a radically aged Evgeny Tsyganov. Their double act works even better than the one with Vdovichenkov in the first film: between grandson and grandfather, the strict father-and-son hierarchy seems to give way to a more companionable relationship, with mutual ribbing and tender attachment. Their whole storyline, the holidays in the village, flies by, and you watch it with a warm smile (one that in the first film tended to be crowded out by anxiety over the unstable father figure).

Another particular pleasure was the strand of black-and-white flashbacks to the grandfather’s wartime youth. Some of the camerawork is borrowed from Urusevsky (the cinematographer of *The Cranes Are Flying*) with his “Dutch angles”, while some of the darkest scenes (in particular the labour camp where the grandfather ended up after going through the whole war) are even styled after Wes Anderson’s symmetry — after all, we see them through the eyes of a child who pictures his grandfather’s fate in his own way.

The only thing is that, as in the first film, the present-day scenes slightly spoiled the experience for me personally: the grown-up Max’s relationship with his wife has neither humour nor originality, and only makes you think that the grass used to be greener and love more sincere (though perhaps that is a deliberate effect, meant to heighten the nostalgia) :)

---

## Einstein and Margarita: Serebryakov’s Performance and Disappointed Expectations

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/eynshteyn-i-margarita-teatr/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-04-06 (6 April 2025)
Work: “Einstein and Margarita” is a 2022 stage production directed by Alexander Marin.
Tags: theatre
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/eynshteyn-i-margarita-teatr/

An off-topic theatre post. I went to see [*Einstein and Margarita*](https://teatr-estrada.ru/afisha/einstein_margarita) (*Eynshteyn i Margarita*; the very production about Einstein, his lover and their historical responsibility from which Ksenia Rappoport was recently [dropped](https://t.me/oteatre/9260)) and it has left quite an impression on me, so I decided to break it down into pros and cons:

➕ A stunning performance by Alexei Serebryakov. On stage he grips you instantly: Serebryakov doesn’t just bring this figure to life, he gives Einstein, whom we picture first and foremost from that famous photo with his tongue sticking out, a believable, three-dimensional personality.

➕ A successful transfer to the stage of Alexander Gelman’s play *Almar* (the name the couple, Albert and Margarita, went by, from the first parts of their names). The production manages to keep the source’s laconic style, a brisk pace and the sincerity of what passes between two people on stage.

➖ The replacement of Ksenia Rappoport: when I bought the tickets, she was the one billed in the lead, and that was one of the important factors. Mind you, I have no complaints whatsoever about the performance of Alyona Khmelnitskaya, who stepped in as Margarita: her character is compelling, alive and far from clear-cut. But that doesn’t make my disappointed expectation of seeing one particular performance go away.

## Zhvanetsky: A Concert Film That Plays Like a Comic Sketch

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/zhvanetskiy-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-04-04 (4 April 2025); updated: 2025-05-14
Work: “Zhvanetsky” is a 2024 film directed by Vadim Plokhotnikov.
Tags: Russian cinema, comedy, documentary
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/zhvanetskiy-2024/

## 4 April 2025

Whenever I see projects that experiment with format, I get curious about how they will work.

Right now, for instance, the concert film (unconventional already) *Zhvanetsky* («Жванецкий») is being readied for release. It will be made up of the celebrated comedian’s monologues as read by all sorts of actors: from Nonna Grishaeva and Sergei Makovetsky to Kristina Babushkina and Gleb Kalyuzhny. It’s cool that the actors have been given the chance to work with material as flexible as comic monologues: you rarely get to see actors not as specific characters in the circumstances of a particular plot but in their craft at its purest, free of the constraints of a specific film/play.

And bringing Zhvanetsky’s monologues up to date, now that today’s audiences no longer know them so well, is a good thing too. It will also be a chance to check whether they have aged well.

## 14 May 2025

If you love television plays, cinematic experiments or a blend of the two, you may well enjoy the concert film [*Zhvanetsky*,](https://t.me/kino_voice/516) which arrives in cinemas tomorrow.

It is extremely intriguing to watch, even if you don’t know Zhvanetsky’s work very well. Along the way you will find out, as I did, what is special about the pose comedians with sheets of paper always strike on stage, why Zhvanetsky was never read in print but only ever listened to, and whether he can be called a stand-up comedian.

For all the fascinating footage from backstage, from rehearsals and from the preparations for reading the monologues, the film’s crowning glory is, of course, the actors’ stage performances themselves. Personally, I was spellbound by the monologues as performed by Sergei Makovetsky, Pavel Derevyanko and Vladimir Vdovichenkov. It is a real pleasure to see them not in particular roles but as readers working with a text and showing new sides of themselves. So the concert film as a whole, too, comes across as spirited, light and effortless — like a comic sketch.

---

## Acting: The Chemistry of Lapenko and Nagiyev, and a Crucian Carp Pie

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/aktyorische-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-04-03 (3 April 2025)
Work: “Acting” is a 2025 series directed by Dmitriy Nevzorov.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, comedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/aktyorische-serial/

Judging by the first two episodes, what hooks you in [*Acting*](https://youtu.be/3NpYMT_zCG4?si=RVFCXL_viESbHHIR) (*Aktyorishche*) is, of course, the chemistry between Lapenko and Nagiyev (and between Nagiyev and Ekaterina Stulova, plus Nikita Kasyanenko’s stunningly spot-on turn as the young Nagiyev).

The plot — a film critic decides to make life a misery for the actor who is in fact his favourite — seems to slip into the background a little. And that may even be a good thing: first, it lets the show shake off the parallels that suggest themselves with certain nit-picking film critics; second, instead of the story looming over the actors and boxing them in, it lets the characters ring true in the given circumstances. Happily, for all that, there is no taking away the story’s brisk pace and great humour, or its powerful metamodernist streak — that, of course, is Dmitry Nagiyev’s department.

But what won me over most of all was the show’s own in-house meme about a crucian carp pie, which sprang up almost at once. It’s cool that right after *Outsource* and its squid salad (which has already become a [symbol](https://t.me/KingOfYantar/4537)) another meme-worthy foodstuff has come along.

## Seems Like Love: Walking the Streets of Moscow, Reincarnated in St Petersburg

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/pokhodu-lyubov-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-03-29 (29 March 2025)
Work: “Seems Like Love” is a 2025 film directed by Yana Klimova-Yusupova.
Tags: Russian cinema, rom-com, comparison
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/pokhodu-lyubov-2025/

A checklist of reasons why [*Seems Like Love*](https://t.me/kino_voice/472) (*Pokhodu lyubov*) is a reincarnation of *Walking the Streets of Moscow* (*Ya shagayu po Moskve*, the 1964 Thaw-era classic):

The protagonist, a newcomer to town (in the case of *Seems Like Love*, a heroine), finds in a single day in a new city not only what he came looking for, but friends and love as well.
✅ Along the way the characters are bound to come across a wedding and even join in the celebrations a little.
✅ A run-in with the police is a must — but they are wry and harmless.
✅ The main characters include two guys and one girl. All film long we are choosing, together with her, who should get her heart.
✅ In the course of their walk the characters drop into a record shop — a key place for feelings to spark.
✅ And of course they run into busybody passers-by with caustic remarks, on whom the characters sharpen their wit.

If a modern-day incarnation of the Thaw-era walk-around film, decked out with fashionable music and great young actors, sounds like your thing, but you’re in the mood for a stroll around St Petersburg rather than Moscow, then *Seems Like Love* (in cinemas now) is your plan for the weekend.

---

## The Kidney: Lyubov Aksyonova as an Antiheroine Capable of Kindness

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/pochka-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-03-25 (25 March 2025)
Work: “The Kidney” is a 2022 series directed by Mariya Shulgina.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, dramedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/pochka-serial/

Why didn’t I know about Natakha Kustova when I was 16?!

In time for the finale of the third season of [*The Kidney*](https://youtu.be/bLaOQzTin7s?si=bryEtMmzvajvJ5aZ) (*Pochka*), I decided to catch up on the entire series in a couple of weeks, and came away impressed. You remember my [love of antiheroines,](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/pervyy-nomer-serial/) so I was full of admiration for Lyubov Aksyonova’s work. Through a complex blend of shades of character she has managed to create someone who isn’t bad by nature but carefully keeps up a mask of having no scruples, because otherwise you won’t survive (well, no, you will survive, of course, but in poverty and abstinence).

Special respect to the show’s makers for the fact that a flat, nasty corrupt official who ran head-on into the system because of her illness has, by the end of the third season, become a heroine with depth, one who seeks and loses and, above all, is capable of kindness. Admittedly, to make that kindness convincing, Kustova always has her fists and her snake-like cunning at the ready, but that is something you can only envy and learn from, as you would from a role model. Time to push the boundaries!

---

## A Tour of Mosfilm: The Set Town from The Poet

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/ekskursiya-po-mosfilmu/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-03-24 (24 March 2025)
Tags: notes, Russian cinema, industry
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/ekskursiya-po-mosfilmu/

Yesterday I went on a tour of [Mosfilm](https://www.mosfilm.ru/excursions) (Russia’s largest film studio), and I’m rushing to share.

The most interesting part is a walk through a small town built as a set for scenes of old Moscow or St Petersburg (yes, it’s an all-purpose set). It turns out that scenes from *The Poet* (the 2025 musical biopic of Alexander Pushkin) were shot there — in particular the one where Chipovskaya’s character taught Pushkin to be a star boy. Here’s the best still: to Borisov’s left, a colonnade at head height; to Chipovskaya’s right, cladding in large blocks and, visible in the distance, another colonnade. And here they are again in my photo from the same angle (the apartment block under construction isn’t part of the set, they paint it out afterwards :)).

They say the set can also be spotted in the film *Khitrovka. The Sign of Four* — if you’ve seen it, write in: maybe you recognised the surroundings? :)

And the other photos from the tour are perfect for Telegram stories — true, stories aren’t available to me yet, but that’s all fixable via the link! You know what to do.

## Art in Scale at the Museum of Moscow: What Cinema Has to Do with It

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/vystavka-iskusstvo-v-masshtabe/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-03-22 (22 March 2025)
Tags: Moscow, notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/vystavka-iskusstvo-v-masshtabe/

An off-topic museum post and an idea for the weekend: the exhibition [*Art in Scale*](https://mosmuseum.ru/exhibitions/p/monumental-art/) («Искусство в масштабе») at the Museum of Moscow.

It’s the best way to see the city with fresh eyes: all the Soviet mosaics on façades and inside public institutions (my school, built in 1939, had a huge mosaic wall, for example), the stained glass, the murals and even the painted transformer huts in courtyards — all of that is monumental art. We come across it in the street every day, and this exhibition helps you find the beauty in what’s around you.

What does cinema have to do with it? Here’s the list of what’s what:

Photo **1️⃣**— a fragment of a mosaic from a children’s haematology centre
Photo **2️⃣**— the poster for the series *Patient Zero*. Remind you of anything? :)
Photos **3️⃣** and **4️⃣** — sketches for the façade decoration of the Oktyabr cinema (a landmark Moscow cinema). We don’t notice them as we head straight for the entrance, but they’re right there, and no different from the close-up view in the museum :)
Photos **5️⃣**, **7️⃣** and **8️⃣**— super-cinematic instances of monumental art: bright colours, texture, ornament **➖**
Photo **6️⃣** — the façade of a standard-design cinema: there’s bound to be one like it in everyone’s neighbourhood, you only have to look up and take it in :)
Photo **9️⃣** — this one isn’t from the exhibition but from the courtyard in front of the museum: a cool mosaic glorifying work, Soviet-style, was recently unveiled there. Only the screen beneath it often doesn’t work, which makes for such a cinematic work contrast.

## A Dog Named Palma 2: Sergei Gilev’s Villain Is the Film’s Crowning Glory

## Memoir of a Snail: An Epistolary Novel on Screen

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/memuary-ulitki-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-03-18 (18 March 2025)
Work: “Memoir of a Snail” is a 2024 film directed by Adam Elliot.
Tags: animation, drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/memuary-ulitki-2024/

Meanwhile, I’m just finishing off last year’s nominees: yesterday my choice fell on [*Memoir of a Snail*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/5925061/).

Unlike *Flow* (the winner in its category), this animated film could hardly be called soothing. It is a fairly traumatic story about separated twins, a brother and sister who lost their family early in life and then spent half their lives dreaming of being reunited, with each other at least, sharing their misadventures by letter. Of the two, it is the sister, Grace, who emerges as the main character, but the whole thing could fairly be called an epistolary novel put on screen, which is not something you come across very often. The handcrafted style of the stop-motion animation is rather rare too: although Adam Elliot, the creator of *Memoir*, has already won an Oscar for *Harvie Krumpet*, an animated film in the same technique, to my taste this style adds to the viewer’s discomfort at what they are seeing. Then again, it multiplies your empathy for the characters as well.

Even so, the film pulls you in, because everyone will find something of their own in this diary-like family story. Some will recognise themselves in Grace’s flight from reality (she painstakingly collects anything to do with snails); some, on the contrary, will share the romantic spirit of Gilbert, who burns with the dream of becoming a fire-eater; and some will warm to the worldly wisdom of the third important character, old Pinky, who knows how to savour the moment.

Personally, when the film ended, hers were the words I wrote down:

*Snails never go back the way they came, they always crawl onwards*

---

## An Interview Podcast with Makar Khlebnikov in Pravila Zhizni

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/intervyu-podkast-makar-khlebnikov/
Author: Betsy Isakova

Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/intervyu-podkast-makar-khlebnikov/

A fresh new way of using podcasts has turned up!

I was delighted to find it in an [interview with Makar Khlebnikov](https://www.pravilamag.ru/hero/744775-pravilnaya-lyjnya-podkast-progulka-s-akterom-makarom-hlebnikovym/), which the folks at Pravila Zhizni (“Rules of Life”, the Russian men’s magazine formerly published as Esquire Russia) have paired not just with the standard photo set but with a podcast as well! While you scroll down the long landing page studying the photos of the actor, you can listen to his cosy account of childhood ski outings with his dad and sink completely into the frosty atmosphere. It’s a very creative approach to the formats used for interviews: on top of the photo shoot and written answers we’re used to, the piece gains one more dimension, and one that is sure to draw in part of the audience (as a podcast producer, I sincerely believe that).

I hope it catches on and we get to hear our favourite actors more often.

## Agniya: An Absurdist Fairy-Tale Dramedy with an Ambiguous Ending

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/agniya-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-03-14 (14 March 2025)
Work: “Agniya” is a 2024 film directed by Pavla Stratulat.
Tags: Russian cinema, dramedy, arthouse
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/agniya-2024/

**➖** As of today, [*Agniya*](https://youtu.be/pyen1y1bWos?si=rDt67BRLNBKfBDsJ) is available to stream: an absurdist fairy-tale dramedy with Evgenia Gromova, Sergei Gilev and the gamayun bird (a prophetic bird of Slavic folklore) on the poster (and that bird, as everyone knows, can foretell good fortune and misfortune alike).

The film’s appeal lies in its unpredictable plot: Agniya, a stove-maker by family trade (*pechnik*, not *pechnitsa*: the heroine is against feminine forms of job titles), lives with her little son in a northern town, in a condemned building that, ironically enough, happens to have no heating. Thanks to her acquaintance with the town’s mayor, she gets a chance to improve her living conditions in a highly unconventional way.

I heartily recommend it to anyone drawn to ambiguous endings, as well as to parallels with *Parasite*, *The Killing of a Sacred Deer* and Russian folklore **➖**

## How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies: A Charming Dramedy About Fragile Family Ties

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/babushka-na-million-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-03-11 (11 March 2025)
Work: “How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies” is a 2024 film directed by Pat Boonnitipat.
Tags: drama, Asian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/babushka-na-million-2024/

Now showing in our cinemas is the charming Thai film [*How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies*](https://youtu.be/HrVX_nHNIUA?si=bSsPgrtRjFRcI3tT) (released in Russia as *Babushka na million*, “A Million-Dollar Grandma”), which has already won the hearts of audiences across Asia (there’s a whole flash mob of people showing how they cried after watching it) and even made the Oscar shortlist for best international feature.

The plot of this dramedy about fragile family ties is simple enough: M, a young streamer who hasn’t quite made it, learns that his cousin has inherited her grandfather’s entire house because she looked after him for a long time before he died. Without thinking twice, M pays a call at the home of his grandmother, who, it turns out, has cancer and about a year left to live.

Naturally, once they learn of her terminal diagnosis, the grandmother’s children also get busy in the queue for the inheritance, trying to get ahead of the grandson. And he, at the epicentre of the family feud, turns out to be the only one who is truly close to her (and finds himself filled with the best of feelings, with no ulterior motive at all).

This sweet sentimentality is a great strength of the film, but not its only one.

- First, we follow the characters into Thai homes, to the colourful local altars with tea set out for the gods, to cemeteries where families gather, chat and scatter flower petals over grass-covered mounds. In short, we see life at its most exotic to our eyes and in vivid colour, yet with feelings and worries we know very well: how do you earn your family’s love, how do you forgive them after they’ve let you down, and what is a family anyway?

- Second, the grandmother is played by a 78-year-old (!) first-time actress (!!), Usha Seamkhum — and she does it with inimitable charisma, conviction and a warmth that breaks through the character’s outward grumpiness. Watching her, especially alongside her grandson, is a big and heartfelt experience for a viewer.

- Third, for all the seeming predictability of the plot, the film delights with a surprise ending, three times as touching after everything we’ve watched over 2 hours. And if you’re not afraid of having your heart melted by a wonderful film, this one is definitely for you :)

---

## Mickey 17: Comparing the Book and the Film — Pattinson Outweighs It All

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/mikki-17-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-03-10 (10 March 2025); updated: 2025-04-09
Work: “Mickey 17” is a 2025 film directed by Bong Joon Ho.
Tags: books, science fiction
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/mikki-17-2025/

## 10 March 2025

While [*Mickey 17*](https://youtu.be/tA1s65o_kYM?si=spxE9OVx14Q7_tJh) is playing in Western cinemas, I decided to get acquainted with the source and read the novel in the original (happily, I’d had the foresight to bring it back from holiday 🌴, though I also compared it with the [Russian translation](https://ozon.ru/t/xVOlYEb), which doesn’t lose out in the slightest!).

Edward Ashton’s book is called *Mickey7*, and it comes across as very compact science fiction: just 300 pages about a man who, in the distant future, signed up for an exploration mission as a so-called expendable and is now endlessly reborn after dying in all manner of research. Yet the author doesn’t stop at brisk action built on his hero’s deaths: as early as the first chapter he puts an ethical question to his readers — can the new, resurrected version of Mickey be considered the same person who died the day before? It is thanks to a mix-up that brings two versions of Mickey together that we get to unravel this dilemma, moving along the way between chapters so varied that the feeling is as pleasant as scrolling through a feed of TikToks.

Why has the film ended up with as many as 17 of these Mickeys? I suspect it comes down to the nature of film language: on screen you can show Mickey’s assorted deaths as a thrill ride (remember how much fun everyone had with the [posters](https://t.me/kino_voice/388) alone) rather than make do with the scantier means of text. Besides, the film is directed by Bong Joon Ho, which means all 17 deaths are guaranteed to be brutal in the manner of Korean cinema.

Either way, I’ll definitely finish the novel, and then compare how closely Robert Pattinson (lucky man, getting to play immortals!) matches the hero I pictured from the book :)

## 9 April 2025

Well then, I’ve watched [*Mickey 17*](https://t.me/kino_voice/388) on digital and I’m ready to compare the [book](https://t.me/kino_voice/448) and the text!

On balance I liked the film, even though it strayed from the text, but Robert Pattinson outweighed everything. His performances are meticulously thought through, right down to each character’s posture and shades of voice — to appreciate it, you’re better off watching in the original, without dubbing; you won’t regret it. The dynamic between Mickey 17 and Mickey 18 was gripping too: it is probably the best and most important part of the film, when you are watching from the outside what are literally two parts of one personality, and the personality itself must either get them to make friends or vanish altogether. Just like in life.

The only pity is that the film mangles one of the key moments of Mickey’s entry into the “expendable” profession: the task of committing suicide to prove his faith in the regeneration technology that will be bringing him back. Instead of the actual suicide he steels himself for in the text, the test turns into a crude shot to his head, fired by the woman managing his onboarding. But I can see that in the film this matters for Mickey’s moral portrait, even if the spectacle suffers for it.

On the whole there isn’t that much of the gory thrill ride you expect from a Korean director here, but there is social commentary by the bucketload. And that is the part that struck me as grotesque: clearly, the whole strand about the local demagogue politician is open satire on Trump. Right down to his supporters’ little red caps and the bullet from the crowd that grazes the politician. But this crude, local tie to reality is understandable all the same and, what’s more, graced by Mark Ruffalo’s performance. And the film is definitely worth seeing for its talented performances :)

---

## Chemo Romance: Mixed Feelings About the Finale and an Honest Look at Illness

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/mezhdu-nami-khimiya-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-03-09 (9 March 2025); updated: 2025-04-18
Work: “Chemo Romance” is a 2025 series directed by Karina Chuvikova.
Tags: series, drama, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/mezhdu-nami-khimiya-serial/

## 9 March 2025

As it happened, I started the series [*Chemo Romance*](https://youtu.be/FQjZ9LJUQ_4?si=Sx_q5vAe5rMMuAt8) (*Mezhdu nami khimiya*, “There’s Chemistry Between Us”) while rewatching (and finishing) [*Breaking Bad*](https://youtu.be/HhesaQXLuRY?si=z76qXdtsopEqrPG5). The result was a male and a female take on one and the same premise, side by side.

Tanya, the heroine of *Chemo Romance*, drives a taxi, is bringing up two children on her own (her husband has died), and suddenly finds out she has cancer. Now her main task is ~~to make enough money to last a lifetime~~ to find a husband she can leave the children with, otherwise they’ll be sent to a children’s home.

And while *Breaking Bad* is in many ways a reflection of the male midlife crisis (only instead of realising that death is near, the hero quite literally gets a near death, from cancer), *Chemo Romance* is, as they say, just an ordinary Tuesday for a woman. In the first two episodes Sasha Bortich has played every shade of despair: over her diagnosis, over a friend’s betrayal, over not quite measuring up to men’s lofty requirements, and over having to tell her children the terrible truth. It feels as though the whole world has let her down, but there are the ghostly beginnings of a new storyline with Nikita Efremov’s character, and that is the best reason to look forward to more :)

It’s great that this is the kind of woman-power series that came out for 8 March (International Women’s Day): sincere, ironic, moving to the point of tears, yet driving home an important idea — it’s life you should be thinking about, not death.

## 26 March 2025

I’m still watching [*Chemo Romance*](https://t.me/kino_voice/447), and I’ve noticed two things.

**1️⃣** How differently (and that’s great!) Tanya from *Chemo Romance* and, say, Natasha Kustova from *The Kidney* go after their goals. What Bortich’s heroine has really is soft power: a little naive, vulnerable, held up, you might say, by the audience’s hopes. These days we get to enjoy not just strong female characters but their variety too (and a wave to *Outsource* while I’m here)

**2️⃣** How cool that Nikita Efremov, too, got to play a double role like this (in keeping with the film year’s trends, after *Mickey 17*, *Amura*, *Kalimba*, *Vasily* and other titles with twins played by one actor). All that remains is to work out whether it’s a good thing that, of the two possible plots, in which he could have turned out to be either a ghost or the dead man’s living twin, they chose the second :)

## 3 April 2025

[*Chemo Romance*](https://t.me/kino_voice/494), what on earth are you doing?!

As if the relationship between Alexandra Bortich’s heroine and her children didn’t already have me welling up every episode, now they’ve decided to tug at our heartstrings with music as well. Specifically, with the song [“Ogni goroda”](https://music.yandex.ru/album/36055985) (“City Lights”), performed by Kuzma Kotrelev and the band Eshchyo Nikak. Maximum respect to the guys for the song (and to Kuzma in particular for writing the lyrics), and to the show’s composer, Dasha Charusha, for the find: it’s a stunning scene, and it’s going to be on endless repeat for the next couple of days.

Sorry, but in the contest between Efremov’s and Kotrelev’s characters a favourite has suddenly begun to emerge.

## 18 April 2025

[*Chemo Romance*](https://t.me/kino_voice/494) is over. The finale left me with mixed feelings (and in tears), but one thing at a time :)

It’s great that Tanya’s choice can’t be predicted until the very last moment — precisely because she is a fully rounded character, and it isn’t obvious whether she will choose personal happiness, however brief, or her children’s long-term relative security. The script’s stars aligned so that these incompatible things coincided, but before that there were so many chances to take a wrong turn that the happy ending turned out to be more of a miracle.

The relatively happy finale feels a little blurred — perhaps it’s the possibility of a second season, left open, that makes it so (I had similar feelings about the finale of the first season of [*The Kidney*](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/pochka-serial/), which did indeed get a continuation). Incidentally, if we’re comparing with *The Kidney*, Tanya turned out to be no less of a manipulator than Natasha Kustova, the only difference being that she feels guilty towards the people she has deceived :) But Efremov’s character, it turned out, was “glad to be deceived himself” (as Pushkin put it). In my view, the only big, sincere feeling Tanya had was with Kotrelev’s character, but it turned out not to be meant to be.

For all the debatable points in the melodramatic structure of *Chemo Romance*, it has one indisputable advantage. The series portrays the illness honestly and without exploiting it. The disease is a serious one, but nobody was about to turn up their toes and die on the spot, because there is treatment. It’s a great, realistic view of the situation, and one you don’t find everywhere. In *Acting*, for instance (and this is very disappointing), when the protagonist is found to have multiple sclerosis, everyone just sits on their hands and mourns the fact that in a year he’ll be in a wheelchair, while the doctors shake their heads and concede that the situation is hopeless. In reality there is effective treatment even for diseases like that. If only every series that touches on such serious matters handled the subject as conscientiously as *Chemo Romance* :)

---

## The Brutalist: A Matter of Aesthetics for the World, a Matter of Ethics for László

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/brutalist-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-03-02 (2 March 2025)
Work: “The Brutalist” is a 2024 film directed by Brady Corbet.
Tags: drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/brutalist-2024/

I watched [*The Brutalist*](https://youtu.be/GdRXPAHIEW4?si=fLhACJRsuW6oZAk_) as close to the Oscars as it gets — Brady Corbet’s colossal cinematic canvas about a man against the backdrop of global historical events, and vice versa.

For all its occasional clichés of the “he chased the American dream” genre, the film leaves too much unsaid to fall into that category, and the most terrible scenes (as a rule) stay off screen; time after time, the audience is asked to judge only the consequences. It’s an interesting move, given that brutalist architecture — no less important a character here than, say, László himself — is itself in many ways a consequence of the terrible events of the 20th century. Raw concrete, the basis for rebuilding bombed-out cities from scratch, was a material that was, first, the most practical and, second, the most honest, the one that gave traumatic experience a tangible form. And the fact that Adrien Brody’s character builds his buildings (and his life) in the US of all places, having fled the ruins of post-war Europe, only helps you focus on how starkly he contrasts with the whole world. What is a matter of aesthetics and beauty for the world is a matter of ethics and morality for László. The film reminds us that the horrors of an era have a way of ending, and those who caused or witnessed them of dying, whereas the consequences of what happened will most likely stay before our eyes for a long time yet.

How it’s shot and how it sounds deserve a separate word, by the way. A special film-shooting process used in the 1950s brings our lens closer to the conditions of that time — to perceiving history through the means cinema had at its disposal when that history was still the present. And the soundtrack is itself like one vast architectural harmony — recurring themes that lodge in your head come back throughout the film, but we hear them differently each time, as if finding ourselves in the same place but with different life experience. I think I’ll even be relistening to the film’s score on its own (and rooting for it at the Oscars)

## The Summer Will End: The Most Balabanovian Thing I Have Seen Lately

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/konchitsya-leto-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-02-27 (27 February 2025)
Work: “The Summer Will End” is a 2024 film directed by Maxim Arbugaev, Vladimir Munkuev.
Tags: Russian cinema, drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/konchitsya-leto-2024/

In cinemas from today: [*The Summer Will End*](https://youtu.be/eorh-gGV7S4?si=Shw7hf_DCy4mCG4A) (*Konchitsya leto*), the most Balabanovian thing I’ve seen lately (in the spirit of Alexei Balabanov, the director of *Brother*).

Needless to say, the story of two brothers is eternal, but here it takes a more radical turn than ever. The important thing is that Yura Borisov plays the most unstable, slippery and dubious character of his career — he’s hard to feel for and practically impossible to like. And yet you’d think any gangster played by Borisov would be as comfortable a character as they come; we’ve seen that in *The Bull*, *Peace! Friendship! Chewing Gum!* and *Silver Skates*. It’s great that Borisov can do the opposite too, and that unfamiliar feeling of unease is reason enough to see the film.

Borisov’s character, though, doesn’t change in any noticeable way, unlike Makar Khlebnikov’s. His Tima was due to grow up, only not the way he was counting on (by getting into university in a big city, socialising and building a career) but through endless psychological traumas from the moment his older brother comes back. The title *The Summer Will End* is about him first and foremost. And although he commits what is perhaps the most shocking act in the film, it’s his character who radiates an infectious certainty about what’s right and what isn’t.

A couple more details for the Balabanov tally, by the way: the film is set in Yakutia, a place that mattered to the late-period Balabanov, and it also features Alexander Mosin — a regular in the bit parts of Balabanov’s films, from *Cargo 200* to *Me Too*. For anyone who holds all this dear, it’s a must-see.

---

## Tango: Yulia Snigir as a Woman Frozen by Her Own Need for Control

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/tango-na-oskolkakh-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-02-18 (18 February 2025)
Work: “Tango” is a 2025 series directed by Sergey Sentsov.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, melodrama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/tango-na-oskolkakh-serial/

By the way, in [*Tango*](https://youtu.be/kk_ogX5jl_w?si=E3l8LNOakitZGgF-) (*Tango na oskolkakh*, “Tango on Shards”) itself, judging by the first episodes, the most absorbing thing is the transformation of Yulia Snigir, whom everyone remembers as Bulgakov’s majestic, stately and passionate Margarita. Here she plays a heroine who is uptight, closed off and frozen by her own need to control everything, a woman in a case (after Chekhov’s *The Man in a Case*). And it is extremely interesting to watch her slowly come to life (after 3 episodes it isn’t very noticeable yet, but the thaw has begun) — or rather, to watch how Yulia Snigir pulls it off!

My second big hope for this series is, of course, Rinal Mukhametov as the dance teacher. If I find myself wanting to sign up for tango classes while watching, I won’t be surprised.

## Juror #2: An Improved Version of 12 Angry Men

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/prisyazhnyy-nomer-dva-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-02-16 (16 February 2025)
Work: “Juror #2” is a 2024 film directed by Clint Eastwood.
Tags: drama, American cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/prisyazhnyy-nomer-dva-2024/

I love it when the circumstances in which you watch a film match the course of its plot. So on a recent flight I chose to watch [*Juror #2*](https://youtu.be/EhkkBFhW-MM?si=yMSGW69quTYxQ2Hi), a story about a long and gripping moral journey.

Despite the extremely unhurried pace of the storytelling, it pulled me in with no chance of tearing myself away (which mattered all the more in my viewing circumstances). Watching the one who judges turn into the one who repents is a cinematic experience like no other. Clint Eastwood has, in my view, managed to make an improved version of *12 Angry Men*, precisely by bringing one particular character and his feelings up close.

Nicholas Hoult conveys every waver of conscience flawlessly, in a low-key and not at all demonstrative manner, which is exactly what makes the character sincere. So after watching it you plunge, quite sincerely, into working out a moral dilemma to which everyone will have their own answer.
