## The Poet: What the Film Is Made Of, from Amadeus to Silver Skates

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/prorok-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-02-14 (14 February 2025); updated: 2025-02-24
Work: “The Poet” is a 2025 film directed by Felix Umarov.
Tags: Russian cinema, biopic, musical
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/prorok-2025/

## 14 February 2025

Today is definitely Valentine’s Day, the day of everyone in love… with Russian cinema!

Yes, I mean [*The Poet*](https://youtu.be/_qNBZdfUems?si=yI5MNYMbgLlzzy_k) (*Prorok*) :) I’ll write about the film itself separately; for now I just want to share these gorgeous posters (the actors are a joy!) and my impressions of the screening I went to. Before the showing we stopped for a bite in the same shopping centre as the cinema. Naturally, at the next table two girls were discussing the Pushkin film they hadn’t yet seen: “there’s going to be rap in it too!”, “what, it’s 2 hours long?”

And there was more to come. A whole class of schoolchildren had been at the screening before ours, and on the way to the auditorium I watched the crowd of them. From the sound of it, everyone was thrilled. The only thing was, someone was saying that “the film isn’t really for kids, actually”. Oh well, it happens :)

In short, Pushkin is the new black (pun not intended)! And finding yourself at the centre of that kind of audience excitement is a very rare and precious thing.

## 24 February 2025

Almost 800 million roubles at the box office: high time to set out what, as I see it, [*The Poet*](https://t.me/kino_voice/411) (“The Prophet”, the 2025 musical biopic of Alexander Pushkin) is made of :)

I’ve seen this film compared with all sorts of musicals and even with the film *The Master and Margarita*, but I have my own set of film and theatre associations:

- *Amadeus* is the most gripping and dynamic biopic I have ever seen. In Miloš Forman’s film, Mozart wears a pink punk wig, hangs out at carnivals that feel like modern parties and has an indecently infectious laugh. The textbook example of one of the classics being brought atmospherically to life for millions of modern viewers: they put together a set of conventions associated with the era and details a modern viewer can relate to

- *Marie Antoinette*: the strength of Sofia Coppola’s film lies above all in the clash between image and soundtrack, a kind of audiovisual counterpoint. The young queen of France wolfs down pastries and picks out dresses to post-punk, and gets married (with the full 18th-century ceremonial) to The Cure. Reminiscent of the rap numbers in *The Poet*, which at first glance sit so oddly with the poet’s biography, isn’t it?

- The Gogol Center production of *The Misanthrope*: it made this list because of one particular scene. It’s no spoiler to say that [one of the verbal sparring matches](https://music.yandex.ru/album/35406151/track/136134537) between Pushkin and Nicholas I is staged as a tennis match. And in the 2018 production, one of the scenes with 4 characters was staged in the same way, as a contest at once sporting and intellectual. In both cases the effect is stunning

- *Silver Skates* (yes, I am comparing Borisov’s films with one another, and what are you going to do about it). The living portrait of the city and its inhabitants that opens *The Poet* was shown just as impressively and with just as much depth in *Silver Skates*; it’s great that our filmmakers have learned to do this, and for me personally the association promises a great time from the very first frame.

---

## Outsource: I Haven’t Enjoyed a Series This Much in a Long Time

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/autsors-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-02-13 (13 February 2025); updated: 2025-04-01
Work: “Outsource” is a 2025 series directed by Dushan Gligorov.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, thriller, drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/autsors-serial/

## 13 February 2025

It’s a pleasure to see a story as cool as [*Outsource*](https://youtu.be/TznVzdJyuK8?si=3gxs6xEcgoxdVdfQ) (*Autsors*) arrive practically at the very start of the TV year: a series with Ivan Yankovsky as Kostya, an enterprising prison warder who, in the mid-1990s, decides to sell victims’ relatives the chance to execute the killer with their own hands. This narrative core is surrounded by the hair-raising stories of the hero’s colleagues and other townspeople, which gives the series a densely packed structure! On that note, I like this alternative poster for the series: Kostya is clearly about to stir up some volcano of consequences.

Judging by the first episodes, Yankovsky’s character works as an infernal, otherworldly force that little by little brings out in the locals hidden traits they never even suspected they had — by asking awkward but very simple questions and offering solutions that are not the most moral, but direct. You can enjoy the character largely as an extension and continuation of Yankovsky’s work as Raskolnikov — only a Raskolnikov who feels he has the *right* and gives no thought to repentance.

I hope *Outsource* will set the standard for this year’s other shows too, because so far it’s the strongest thing of 2025.

## 10 March 2025

How brilliantly the details work in [*Outsource*](https://youtu.be/TznVzdJyuK8?si=3gxs6xEcgoxdVdfQ)!

Colleagues [singled out the prosecutor’s housewarming scene](https://t.me/KingOfYantar/4469), but what struck me was the transformation of Natasha’s mother, played by Karina Razumovskaya. The whole time she was handing her daughter destructive advice along the lines of “the main thing is to hang on to a good man”, and behaving not like a mother but like some auntie who is public opinion personified, she never once took off her hat — a symbol of being closed off, insincere, removed from her daughter’s feelings.

But when the irreparable happened in episode 5 (after an abortion she had on her mother’s advice, Natasha ended up in intensive care and will never be able to have children), Natasha’s mother finally took off her protective armour of coldness and constant demands on her daughter. For the first time in the series (it didn’t happen even in the wedding scene!) she appeared before her daughter without the hat and without the airs, even if it came unforgivably late. A small thing, but its effect on the viewer is colossal.

## 13 March 2025

At some point [*Outsource*](https://t.me/kino_voice/449) started turning into *House of the Dragon* in its sheer number of intrigues — my soul demanded an episode-by-episode breakdown.

**1️⃣** I still have my doubts: does Ivan Yankovsky’s character exist at all? He is some kind of disembodied shadow who manages to be here, there and everywhere, persuading anyone he meets with a hypnotist’s efficiency. I wouldn’t be surprised if in the end he vanished, à la Tyler Durden, leaving the jailers with a heap of unsolvable problems. Especially after the line “Who could possibly do anything to me?”…

**2️⃣** The poster with the women turned out to be spot on — judging by episode 6, the ball is passing into their court, and it’s the female half of the characters we should now expect the interesting twists from. Natasha’s mother has put her hat back on, though the only one who has gained in authority is, on the contrary, Natasha herself — which makes her all the more interesting to watch. In fact, all the female characters here are so good that, despite their minimal screen time, I’m ready to praise them separately, over and above my general admiration for the cast.

3️⃣ With each week the episodes fly by faster and faster — given how many plot threads are still tangled, the remaining two episodes have the ultimate resolution in store for us, with answers to every question at once (and surprisingly simple answers at that — as always with Yankovsky’s character). Literally a case of “seven troubles, one answer”, as the Russian saying goes.

## 15 March 2025

[*Outsource*](https://t.me/kino_voice/461) showrunner Anna Kozlova has given [a long interview to Vedomosti](https://www.vedomosti.ru/lifestyle/characters/2025/03/14/1097936-zhizn-vsegda-proigrivaet-ona-vse-nedokruchivaet) (a Russian business daily) — a terribly interesting one, so I’m writing down the main points:

- We viewers have no idea what Kostya (Ivan Yankovsky) was doing before episode one begins. The show’s makers, though, decided that *“Kostya was in Chechnya, so he knows how to kill. And he obviously has PTSD in some form”*. That explains a lot, including the elusive resemblance to Danila Bagrov (the hero of *Brother*, 1997)

- Kostya has a remarkable character, one that at a different moment in history could have played out quite differently. Anna says outright that *“Kostya is ready for anything at all. Had he been born in another time or another country, he could have done something very good for people. But Kostya ended up in the situation he ended up in, and he does what he does”*

- In preparing the series, they studied what the 1990s press wrote about the death penalty as a phenomenon (which, of course, traumatised those who carried it out, too). So the show’s black humour didn’t grow out of nothing but straight out of life: *“In one report a journalist asked an executioner: ‘Tell me, please, what are the most interesting things that have happened to you at work?’ And he calmly told it like a funny story: ‘You know, I swear to you, I had this one guy who dropped dead while we were walking him there’”*.

- Natasha (Mila Ershova) may not be such a victim after all: *“the heroine herself did everything she could to make what happened to her happen. She flirts with an obviously dangerous man, knowing full well who she is dealing with. She is deliberately playing with fire. And when you play with fire, you have no guarantees. You might get lucky and get away, or you might not.”*

- Anna found a great way to sum up her attitude to the eternal excuse for villainy, “for the sake of the family”, which we come across not only in *Outsource* but in culture as a whole (think, for example, of how Walter White in *Breaking Bad* kept harping on that same “for the family” in his day): “*Ask anyone ‘why did you do this and that’, and they will say ‘well, I’ve got a mother, I’ve got children, I’ve got a wife — I’m doing it for them’. In other words, you can commit absolute evil while supposedly having nothing to do with any of it yourself; you are always the victim. Naturally, each of the characters wants power and money but isn’t prepared to sacrifice anything. And here is the result*”*.*

## 21 March 2025

Episode seven of [*Outsource*](https://t.me/kino_voice/461) seems to have shrunk too much (in both running time and incident), and on the whole it looks like a quiet pause in which both sides of the conflict prepare their strategy. Perhaps this haste is needed to bring us inexorably closer to the horrifying denouement (there’s no doubt that is exactly what it will be), but as a viewer I would, of course, like this story to go on for ever.

**1️⃣** The women, just as I thought, have taken matters into their own hands. And, surprisingly, it’s the mothers who turned out to do the most harm — Natasha’s and Roma’s. The first brought home a killer worse than our main characters: the prison governor. As a result, he overheard Natasha’s confidences about the money, which, for some reason (good grief, after all her mother’s abuse and the business with the abortion?!), she had actually brought along as well. And the second was so impressed by Volkov’s warnings about “the old prostitute” that she squirrelled her son’s money away for good, who knows where (my guess is that, in the simplicity of her heart, she may well have handed it to that same Kostya Volkov “for safekeeping”).

**2️⃣** Kostya Volkov’s daughter does seem to have a soul after all. If Ivan Yankovsky’s character gets wind that his daughter is now lying to him too (and he has already worked it all out from the suitcase and the dirty boots), I wonder what fate awaits her.

**3️⃣** Speaking of Volkov. There was so little of him in this episode that I’m more and more convinced he was never there at all. Still, one thing in favour of his existence is the prison governor’s order to deal with Volkov. I think that will be the main attraction of the final episode — who ends up dealing with whom.

**4️⃣** The prosecutor’s wife delivered a very interesting character transformation in this episode. I always had a particular soft spot for her, and now, for the brilliant self-organisation of the prison staff’s wives, I respect her even more. It’s just a pity that this looks set to lead to roughly nothing.

## 27 March 2025

*Outsource* is over. I haven’t enjoyed a series this much in a long time (not since *Give a Show!*); to put it briefly, it’s really something (I’m as pleased as Mila Ershova in this still). And to put it at greater length, here are a few thoughts:

- I kept hoping that Volkov didn’t exist, but the show’s makers went one better and made him immortal! I can’t remember when I was last as happy for any screen character as I was when Volkov turned out to be alive. (All right, it’s all simpler than that: either the convict doctor gave the wrong recipe for the cocktail, which is why he was laughing so hard at the end of the episode, or the prison doctor got it wrong, or the potion simply worked on the gravely ill, and Yankovsky’s healthy character survived it).

- By the way, I’m also glad that Volkov didn’t carry out the final shooting with his own hands — that would have gone against his character. And now it’s clear, too, what happened at Volkov’s previous job and why he was transferred from it — evidently his former colleagues also failed his simple little test of what they were made of.

- Hooray, they showed us, if only for a few seconds, our friends’ business collapsing because the death penalty was abolished. On the one hand, as the memes say, it’s a joy — the death penalty is gone, along with the people who turned it into a way of making money. On the other — what else, if we hypothetically continued the series, could prison warders sell to the powers that be once the death penalty has been abolished? Demand creates supply, as we know, so inventors like Volkov will probably never die out either.

- The women, as usual, are on fire. In this episode, specifically the characters of Mila Ershova (her character’s strut with the Raffaellos has already become a meme) and Darya Kotreleva (a spectacular escape from everyone gave her character perhaps the happiest ending of all). It’s very good that all the female characters, supporting ones though they were, got some clear full stop in the finale or a trajectory for the future — after all, supporting heroines don’t always get that kind of attention.

- It’s good that the story has partly come full circle — now Kostya Volkov will head off to a new job at another penal colony and stir things up there. That’s even better than a standard ending — now a second season of this story is definitely not needed (unless it’s as an anthology).

And what do you think of the finale?

## 28 March 2025

To close the subject of *Outsource*, I took part in a big [Kinopoisk discussion](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/4010914/) (Kinopoisk is Russia’s largest film database, media and streaming service) of the series finale.

My colleagues’ opposing opinions show just how topical a screen event *Outsource* really turned out to be. I hope the truth is hiding somewhere in our argument.

## 1 April 2025

All right, I hadn’t quite finished talking about [*Outsource*](https://t.me/kino_voice/500) after all.

There is an interesting detail in the scene where Mila Ershova saunters grandly, Raffaellos in hand, all the way to the Dolphin bar. When her character walks into the bar, the usual baroque music breaks off and Mumiy Troll (the cult Russian rock band) take over with the song [“Dolphins”](https://music.yandex.ru/album/217021/track/2192798?), specifically its lines about breaking one day and about poison.

What we hear is, essentially, an outright spoiler: very soon Natasha Rybkina will break; to get her husband back, she will poison Volkov (unsuccessfully), and she will be poisoned herself by that same poison of seeming impunity.

The best moment in the show’s entire soundtrack, if you ask me.

---

## Home: Yulia Peresild in the Lead Role, and Practically the Only One

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/on-i-ona-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-02-12 (12 February 2025)
Work: “Home” is a 2024 film directed by Evgeny Korchagin.
Tags: Russian cinema, science fiction, thriller
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/on-i-ona-2025/

In cinemas from tomorrow: [*Home*](https://youtu.be/lQVg1ro2eyk?si=Y4lKk62IULGr9HNV) (*ON i ona*, “ON and Her”), with Yulia Peresild in the lead role, and practically the only one. The thing is, the second main character is a disembodied artificial intelligence built into the house that the heroine, Ksenia, has rented for a holiday somewhere by the sea. Ksenia herself has everything to do with AI: she developed a whole smart voice assistant for decision-making, but her ungrateful employers, sadly, didn’t appreciate it and packed Ksenia (now out of favour) off on this very holiday. But the happy, harmonious break in a super-smart house turned into something between a horror film, a psychological thriller and a sci-fi drama.

It’s hard to describe this film without spoilers, so I’ll break it down into pluses and minuses:

👆 The film has an extremely well-chosen subject. In a world where AI can generate the looks and voices of people who don’t exist, and where for many people ChatGPT or something like it serves as an authoritative adviser, it is always useful to reflect on the flip side of technology’s blessings and on the importance of the human being.

👆 The metaphorical, chamber-piece way it makes its point: thanks to the extreme artifice of what happens, the inner conflict of Peresild’s heroine comes to the fore and remains genuinely central throughout the story.

👆 Yulia Peresild’s performance. Being on screen alone 90% of the time, with no acting partner, and staying convincing is a great skill, and one that the plots of contemporary cinema don’t offer many chances to use.

👆 The ending, which has remained a mystery to me in the good sense of the word. I don’t usually like resolutions that leave me baffled as to why the hero decided what they did. But here, watching the heroine’s (rather misanthropic) decision, I felt a pleasant curiosity.

👇 The extreme artifice of everything that happens is the very plus that turns into the main minus. I suspect that to the vast majority of viewers the technically perfect world the heroine lives in, crammed with the very latest gadgets, may seem like a parallel universe that stirs no sympathy whatsoever.

---

## Yura Borisov’s Success in Anora: The Novelty of His Persona for Western Viewers

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/sekret-uspekha-yury-borisova/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-02-04 (4 February 2025)
Tags: notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/sekret-uspekha-yury-borisova/

By the way, I’ve lately been seeing a lot of [musings](https://t.me/cult_insight/2690) on Telegram channels about Yura Borisov’s success.

After a post by colleagues from the Telegram channel [Kulturny insayt](https://t.me/cult_insight) (“Cultural Insight”), I got to thinking about it myself. I think the general enchantment with his role in *Anora* comes down to how new Yura’s screen persona is to Western audiences. We all got to know his trademark, sincere way of playing simple guys with complicated lives many years ago (and we’ve been walking around enchanted ever since!). On top of that, Borisov has an excellent list of roles — every appearance he makes on screen becomes, without exaggeration, an event. Whereas for people unfamiliar with the actor’s work, 15 minutes of screen time in *Anora* is enough to leave an unforgettable impression :) Among Western actors, it seems to me, you really won’t find a similar type.

And what do you think is the secret of Yura Borisov’s success?

## Overheard in Rybinsk: Black Humour and Irony Against Nordic Noir

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/podslushano-v-rybinske-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-01-31 (31 January 2025); updated: 2025-03-13
Work: “Overheard in Rybinsk” is a 2025 series directed by Pyotr Todorovsky.
Tags: series, mystery, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/podslushano-v-rybinske-serial/

## 31 January 2025

Like my [colleagues,](https://t.me/kinoprotebya/22306) I’m in awe of the opening titles of [*Overheard in Rybinsk*](https://youtu.be/bt_AtHO7nhY?si=om2VYAzOm323s8Ho), a new “ironic detective story”, as its makers themselves define it, starring Timofey Tribuntsev and Ruzil Minekaev.

But here, I’d venture, there is more than a nod to *Brother 2* and to the visual art of Viktor Tsoi (the frontman of the band Kino)! The little red man, the hero of this short animation, runs into several other characters: there are several storylines hidden in the titles. Could these be hints at events to come in the series?

“Quiet” spoilers like these turn up in series quite often: from *House of the Dragon* (I broke down its titles [here)](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/dom-drakona-serial/) to *Squid Game*, where the games to come are sketched on the walls around the contestants. I hope the titles of *Overheard in Rybinsk* will likewise let us overhear a little of the plot to come.

## 13 March 2025

The real charm of [*Overheard in Rybinsk*](https://t.me/kino_voice/403) (*Podslushano v Rybinske*) is its black humour and irony, which keep a twisty and fairly dark series, one with a touch of the mystical even, from turning into a po-faced Nordic noir and let it remain a more layered piece of work. One in which, what’s more, the main characters break out of detective-story clichés and surprise you with unconventional traits.

That is exactly why the shocking finale (I kept expecting Shirmik to stun us yet, and it happened) is doubly impressive. It turns out that all this time we were watching the fates of Shirmik and the TV presenter unfold in parallel, in circumstances that seemed to leave no choice. And while the latter most likely had no alternatives left — though he wasn’t much of a person anyway — Shirmik turned out to be a hostage to his own principles. A superb transformation by Ruzil Minekaev, I have to say!

Incidentally, the series has one understated element that cuts to the depths of the soul: the soundtrack by Roman Litvinov (Mujuice), to whose music we have already watched the stories of the characters of [*Peace! Friendship! Chewing Gum!*](https://music.yandex.ru/album/25336347) and [*Dropper*.](https://music.yandex.ru/album/23531291) He alone knows how to fuse, in sound, naivety and a bright hope for the best with the inevitable chthonic murk that breaks into our lives from every side (from our own souls too). It worked 100% and reflected the substance of the series exactly: please get Mujuice to score series more often.

---

## The Enchanted Tinderbox: A Breath of Fresh Air Amid the Flood of Fairy-Tale Films

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/ognivo-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-01-27 (27 January 2025)
Work: “The Enchanted Tinderbox” is a 2024 film directed by Alexander Voitinsky.
Tags: Russian cinema, fairy tales
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/ognivo-2024/

January weekends are given to us so that we can catch up on everything we didn’t get to over the holidays, and yesterday my choice fell on [*The Enchanted Tinderbox*](https://youtu.be/TtUQSMUcVws?si=N_SikwDt3BFLJYFO) (*Ognivo*).

This film feels as fresh as can be against the rest of the flood of fairy-tale films. First, an important caveat: all that is left of Andersen’s original text is the tinderbox itself, as a magical object in the hero’s hands — there are no dogs with enormous eyes, no witch, no real soldier. What there is instead is a usurper, a coup d’état, conspirators, a road-trip buddy movie, time travel and a chancer who pretends to be a soldier to get out of prison (in short, things rather closer to home than the pure magic of the original text).

Second, the lead is the wonderful, vivid, charismatic Roman Evdokimov. While watching, I realised that this is exactly the kind of fairy-tale hero we have been missing: a kind character who keeps screwing up and gives in to temptation and to his own self-serving interests; there is no telling what to expect from him, which makes him all the more interesting to watch right to the very end. Roman himself talks about this in an [interview with my colleagues at Kinopoisk](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/4010173/); I recommend it as a great companion to the film!

Third, there is no love story here at all! Usually, after all, our hero performs heroic deeds only on the way to the princess he wants to marry. In *The Enchanted Tinderbox*, kindness comes from humanity and compassion, not romantic interest. I have nothing against heroes being motivated by feelings, but how nice it is to see a plot develop differently :)

These factors add up to a resourceful plot in which every twist is bracingly unpredictable, and they give us a unique type of fairy-tale hero who goes not with the logic of the “good guy” (like, say, Emelya or the Troubadour from the recent adaptations) but against it — like a jokey version of “that power which eternally wills evil and eternally works good” (Mephistopheles’s words in *Faust*). For that, *The Enchanted Tinderbox* is, so far, my favourite contemporary fairy-tale adaptation.

---

## Arseny Kasperovich on the Series Ghostbusters: An Interview for The Blueprint

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kasperovich-okhotniki-za-prizrakom/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-01-25 (25 January 2025)
Work: “Ghostbusters” is a work  Dmitry Tyurin.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, interview, supernatural
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/kasperovich-okhotniki-za-prizrakom/

To go with the recently launched series [*Ghostbusters*](https://youtu.be/PgsHvYJ9l9Y?si=pk5zabb9E7VNx3L8) («Охотники за призраком»), I [talked](https://theblueprint.ru/culture/specials/okko-ghost-hunters) to Arseny Kasperovich, who plays a mysterious mute ghost-catcher nicknamed Lysy (“Baldy”) in it. When you’re immersed in material this supernatural, it’s hard to stay a sceptic — and that’s what we discussed:

> I think the mystical is always present in our lives, in every movement and every step. What you call it is a matter of your own perception and faith. \<…> And I think the time spent with our series is precisely a chance to feel the mystical world through the screen. Perhaps to believe that it is somewhere close by and, as it were, to come up for air from everyday life. Sometimes coming up for air from everyday life is an important thing to do, and getting to know our characters will give you the chance to do it.

For my part, I’ll add that the series also lets you come up for air from the cinematic everyday: here actors who traditionally play good guys (Denis Prytkov, Eldar Kalimulin, Alexander Robak) play properly bad ones, driven, naturally, by evil spirits. I’ll watch to the end at the very least for this interesting experience — where else will you see actors like these as villains? :)

## Robert Eggers’s Nosferatu: The Best-Crafted, Most Successful Remake I’ve Seen

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/nosferatu-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-01-24 (24 January 2025)
Work: “Nosferatu” is a 2024 film directed by Robert Eggers.
Tags: horror, remake
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/nosferatu-2024/

Robert Eggers’s [*Nosferatu*](https://youtu.be/9H7bQkAfHyo?si=C2rcOjhc4mKoikCM) seems to be the best-crafted and most successful remake I’ve seen. I enjoyed every minute of the film, and here is why:

- The remake is exactly twice as long as the original, but in return it shows in more detail the chains of cause and effect, the characters’ motivations and other half-tones that are barely perceptible in the original film — and my viewing experience was the better for it. Sometimes spelling out certain facts in dialogue is not spoon-feeding the obvious but widening the context

 - Eggers’s film popularises the story of Nosferatu, which until now mostly interested a narrow circle of initiates. Now the reminder that light conquers darkness is back in plain view for everyone.

- Nicholas Hoult is the ideal Hutter. I’ve heard it said that he is a blank in this film, but that is exactly what makes him ideal: his character is the real victim of this whole Nosferatu business, stripped of the right to decide his own fate in roughly the first scene, so being a “blank” is just what the logic of the character requires.

- Lily-Rose Depp is an extremely strong actress when it comes to physical performance. It is the bodily side of her acting that has given this whole supernatural story a kind of tether to physical reality, where the evil force is anything but a ghost.

- Nosferatu’s new look (and distinctive way of speaking) is an excellent touch. The Nosferatu of 1922 inspired nothing but fear. In his new guise the vampire stirs up a whole range of mixed emotions and reminds us that nothing human is alien to evil. But let’s not forget that this doesn’t stop it being evil.

---

## Squid Game: Types Instead of Names, and a Decent but Imperfect Finale

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/igra-v-kalmara-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-01-18 (18 January 2025); updated: 2025-06-29
Work: “Squid Game” is a 2021 series directed by Hwang Dong-hyuk.
Tags: series, thriller, Korean cinema, analysis
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/igra-v-kalmara-serial/

## 18 January 2025

The first season of *Squid Game* was in many ways a fairground attraction: both at the level of plot, where deadly games among the poor entertained the elite, and at the level of how viewers took it in — the show’s vivid meme-symbols stuck in the memory for a long time (whereas its twisty finale, in my case at least, was all but forgotten).

The second season is short on amusements of that kind, which is why it plays differently. We are eased into the action very unhurriedly, yet without being reminded of some important details forgotten over the past few years. There’s no vital need for that, but personally I’d have liked not just to assume in general terms that Seong Gi-hun means to stop the games, but to recall in proper detail (seeing as the games themselves have been pushed back all the way to episode three) how things ended back there.

And, most importantly, the second season has lost the lightness of a reality show while piling on the moral analysis of what is going on. Now we aren’t simply watching from the sidelines as the hero lands in a tight spot: we share his point of view from the start — after all, we too have already “played these games”, when we watched the first season. Hence an even greater temptation to map the events of the series onto our own reality, and even less room for escapism while watching. And the finale, cut short essentially to divide the seasons formally, is more disconcerting than intriguing. In short, it’s all rather idiosyncratic and an acquired taste — and just how many have acquired it, the numbers for the third season will show as early as this year (a season that will no longer have the head start of such gigantic expectations).

## 29 June 2025

Ask yourself: how many characters from any season of [*Squid Game*](https://t.me/kino_voice/381) do you remember by name? Well, Seong Gi-hun. Well, the Front Man. If you remember anyone else, you must be a member of the show’s fan club.

Most likely you aren’t, and yet everything is clear without the names and you keep on watching. What we have here is an interesting industry case.

The thing is, the casting of the roles in *Squid Game* is special. We don’t get to know everyone in detail; we have neither the time nor the chance to memorise this crowd by name, or even by number (which is in itself a very winning device for an international show — but again, who, apart from 456, do we know by heart?) The secret is this: each of the actors is a very distinct type turned up to the max, recognisable from episode to episode even without a name.

It is exactly this reliance on types that is one of the reasons the show has been talked about for 4 years. We remember the characters as “that vile junkie rapper”, “the kind old lady”, “the weakling mummy’s boy” or “the greedy old man”, and that’s enough for us to understand one another and to remember the events of the previous season far better. The credit for this effect goes to the actors’ types and the work done to bring them out. It’s great that genuine innovations can be found in such a mass-market product.

## 29 June 2025

And on the whole, the third season of [*Squid Game*](https://t.me/kino_voice/710) is a decent, if not perfect, conclusion to the main part of the franchise (not counting the future American *Squid Game*, of course).

The finale’s pitting of 8 grown men against a baby girl looks like a neat device, hinting to the viewer at who, in the makers’ view, the future belongs to. What bothers me about this whole nobly built construction is that neither the organisers of the games (grown men just the same) nor the games’ main consumers, the so-called “VIPs”, have gone anywhere. And the two girls (222’s daughter and Seong Gi-hun’s daughter), having come into that kind of money, may sooner or later become “VIPs” themselves. In short, what we got was a sort of sham catharsis.

But that doesn’t bother me nearly as much as the secondary storyline about the collective search for the island. I don’t think I’ve felt like this since reading *The Master and Margarita* at school, when, from one chapter of Woland’s Moscow antics to the next, you suffer your way through the text about Yeshua. Only in Bulgakov all of it is justified, meaningful and equally valuable (and once you outgrow a schoolchild’s view of things just a little, you see that). Whereas here we got this storyline, completely unproductive as far as any effect on the ending goes. It was made almost purely so that one game, which fits perfectly well into a season, could be turned into two seasons — by means of a side plot. I honestly didn’t appreciate the plot being split in two like this, and I hope that in future seasons (they are inevitable) the makers will manage to concentrate on exploring human nature in extreme circumstances.

---

## Catching the Big Fish: David Lynch’s Voice on Life, Creativity and Cinema

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/poymat-bolshuyu-rybu-kniga/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-01-17 (17 January 2025)
Work: “Catching the Big Fish” is a 2006 book by David Lynch.
Tags: books
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/poymat-bolshuyu-rybu-kniga/

Back in the day I was really taken with David Lynch’s book [*Catching the Big Fish*](https://books.yandex.ru/books/zGZCj0gp) — we were just then making an [episode](https://music.yandex.ru/album/24773100/track/119517390) of the podcast *Listay vpravo* («Листай вправо», “Swipe Right”) on the subject.

This text is a real chance to hear the director’s voice first-hand, along with his views on life, on creativity and on cinema in particular. In short, exactly what is needed right now:

> Cinema is a special language. You can say anything in it, express big, abstract ideas. That is exactly what draws me to it.
> I am not always deft with words. Some people are allowed to be poets and to express their thoughts beautifully. But cinema is a different language altogether. You can speak in it too, because you have time, you have a sequence of images. There is dialogue, there is music. There are sound effects. You have a whole toolkit at your disposal. You can put a thought and a feeling across in a way that is entirely its own. It is real magic.

I’m off to reread it.

## Zhora Kryzhovnikov Breaks Down Office Romance: The Key Points from the Video

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kryzhovnikov-razbor-sluzhebnyy-roman/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-01-14 (14 January 2025)
Work: “Office Romance” is a work  Eldar Ryazanov.
Tags: Soviet cinema, analysis, comedy, film history
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/kryzhovnikov-razbor-sluzhebnyy-roman/

If you, too, have seen that Zhora Kryzhovnikov has put out a [director’s breakdown](https://youtu.be/Xiq1GpJ4T9U?si=Cwpq3w3kVhf8bVG_) of *Office Romance* (*Sluzhebny roman*) but haven’t got round to watching it yet, this post is for you.

I watched the whole breakdown and noted down the most interesting points *(and added, in brackets, scraps of my own thoughts, whether called for or not**)*

- Kryzhovnikov, like Ryazanov himself, considers *Office Romance* a more cohesive piece of directing than *The Irony of Fate*, despite the latter’s greater popularity

- The “giant” on whose shoulders both *The Irony of Fate* and *Office Romance* stand is Billy Wilder’s *The Apartment*. It is an American comedy about the pre-New Year commotion in one particular apartment, that of a humble insurance company clerk *(reminds you of something, doesn’t it?)*

- *Office Romance* has a unique plot conflict which, contrary to the usual rules, doesn’t involve a single likeable character: all we have is a *mymra* (“old frump”, as the heroine is nicknamed) and a worn-out senior statistician *(I, by the way, never thought of either of them as an unlikeable character; neither is a particularly* *off-putting person)*

- Unlike the original play, Ryazanov’s version adds the Ryzhova and Samokhvalov storyline to the story of Novoseltsev and Kalugina *(an unconvincing one in Kryzhovnikov’s view, which I’d tend to disagree with)*. A romance for Verochka the secretary might have been added too, but owing to circumstances all that is left of it is the phone conversations :) *(ah, what a pity)*

- Ryazanov is a director of comedies of character, where the characters evolve and show the audience new sides of themselves, and where the engine of the plot always lies in the hero’s unhappiness. Gaidai, by contrast, is a director of comedies of situation, where the characters are set up as types who land in particular situations that push the plot along

- Mark Zakharov taught his students, Kryzhovnikov among them, that the first 7 minutes of a film are an advance the audience gives you. After that, something actually has to be happening

- Until the 56th minute of the film, Lyudmila Prokofyevna is not a protagonist at all, only a mask. But in the scene where she cries for the first time, we start to connect with her emotionally and to see her as a character in her own right

## Zhuki: An Unexpectedly Lively Return in Season Four

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/zhuki-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-01-13 (13 January 2025)
Work: “Zhuki” is a 2019 series directed by Konstantin Smirnov, Konstantin Kolesov, Maksim Peshkov.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, comedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/zhuki-serial/

Season 4 of *Zhuki* («Жуки», “The Beetles”), the one called [*Novye Zhuki*](https://youtu.be/MKy3oyw_org?si=fequCjRoH4VC6XAw) (“The New Beetles”), is in great shape!

After what was, to my mind, a rather weak finale to season 3 (not much happening, and running time taken up by dancing and feasting to folk dance tunes), the series about IT guys in a Russian village has come back with an unexpectedly lively continuation. Now our dating-app developers are helping the locals win their village back from the governor, who has decided to tear everything down and build an IT cluster there (what? yes!)

What I like about the new season is the show’s original tone and humour, intact despite the long break, the feeling of “returning” to a world I’d grown fond of, and the refreshed intrigue. In short, I needn’t have put off watching it for fear of disappointment.

## Aeterna: A Series You Cannot Watch with Your Back to the Screen

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/eterna-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-01-09 (9 January 2025); updated: 2025-07-20
Work: “Aeterna” is a 2025 series directed by Sergey Trofimov.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, fantasy, adaptation
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/eterna-serial/

## 9 January 2025

First day back at work, so I’ll share something work-related :)

In December my first [piece](https://theblueprint.ru/l/L6Kh20s) came out in The Blueprint (the Russian fashion and culture magazine): a special project about the upcoming series from Kinopoisk (Russia’s largest film database, media and streaming service), [*Aeterna*](https://youtu.be/OGSXYcM5M3Q?si=FkPebPaxjkfZxFfY) («Этерна»). For it I talked to Lyosha Lukin, Vanya Trushin, Anton Rogachev and Ilya Vinogorsky about fandoms and fan works. Along the way the guys made heartfelt declarations of love for *Game of Thrones* and *Star Wars*, for *Aeterna*’s future fans and for merch as a phenomenon. On that last one we are a 100% match — honestly, Vanya Trushin simply spoke for all of us:

> I have an *Aeterna* hoodie that we were given last New Year, and I think it was the most wearable thing I owned all year, whether it was hot or cold. I just wanted to put it on and go. \<…>
**If there were always merch, I’d wear nothing else — I wouldn’t even buy clothes.**

The piece comes with stunningly beautiful photos — may we all spend the year that has just begun at least as luxuriously.

## 3 July 2025

If you have already heard of *Aeterna*, I have something interesting for you ahead of its premiere on 5 July.

I got to see the first episodes and, I must say, the series is visually very varied: the costumes, the locations the characters find themselves in, the objects that turn up in their world. At Kinopoisk’s request I talked to people who worked on the *Aeterna* shoot about how all this splendour was created, and it turned into a fairly hefty [piece!](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/4011269/)

You’ll find out⬇️

- which actors have steel armour and which have plastic
- which characters look like chess pieces
- which scenes were shot in Uzbekistan (and, more to the point, how!)

Recommended for anyone who likes a peek behind the scenes of filmmaking, and for everyone looking forward to [*Aeterna*](https://youtu.be/VXb81_Xs9bo?si=9JB8XDIqWenHvgqX) (it will also help you find your way around the characters’ fanciful names, and there are a great many of them).

## 5 July 2025

[*Aeterna*](https://youtu.be/VXb81_Xs9bo?si=9JB8XDIqWenHvgqX) launched today, and I want to say that opening this series with two episodes at once is exactly the right call. They give you the full picture of what is going on and let you connect emotionally with the characters (and there are a lot of them!).

There are series you can watch with your back to the screen, but *Aeterna* is the opposite kind. It needs 100% of your attention: first, so that you can appreciate all the [artistic variety,](https://t.me/kino_voice/719) and second, so that you don’t miss anything in the plot. The kaleidoscope of characters, their fates and their cunning schemes is so dense that after two episodes the balance of power is only just coming into focus. And on top of all that come the peculiarities of fantasy. But all this work on the viewer’s part is rewarded with a terrific cast (my favourite, for one, is Yuri Chursin’s sinister character) and a plot that visibly moves — you won’t get the chance to be bored. The series might even suit a binge-watch (but I can no longer test that myself, so if you give it a go, do share your impressions).

## 20 July 2025

With the final episodes of *Aeterna* approaching, here is something useful: every week Kinopoisk publishes a [recap](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/news/4011439/) of the latest episode, as told by your admin.

The plot is twisty enough as it is, but I get extra entertainment from the autocorrect in the notes on my laptop. Here is how this champion of correct spelling sees the characters’ names and the place names of the show’s universe:

Talig — Tallinn
Roque Alva — Rok Alla (“rock” + Alla)
Okdell — Otdel (“department”)
Agaris — Avariya (“accident”)

Perhaps somewhere in a parallel universe there is a series in which the heroes are heading to *Tallinn* for a *rock* concert by *Alla* Pugacheva (the Russian pop diva), but have an *accident* on the way and get stuck in a police *department* — but that is another story altogether…

## One Day in Istanbul: A Sweet Film with Modest Ambitions

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/odin-den-v-stambule-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-01-05 (5 January 2025)
Work: “One Day in Istanbul” is a 2024 film directed by Avet Oganesyan.
Tags: Russian cinema, comedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/odin-den-v-stambule-2024/

Over this New Year break I didn’t rewatch any of the classic Kvartet I (the Moscow comedy troupe), but I did get round to their new film [*One Day in Istanbul*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/5379163/) (*Odin den v Stambule*). A writer, a producer, an official and a doctor go to visit their mutual billionaire friend in Turkey (no, this isn’t the start of a joke). It turns out that the friend has died, so the reunion of friends on the yacht that has been booked is now going to be a not altogether ordinary one.
The film is sweet but not very ambitious, so I’ll break it down into pluses and minuses:

👆The traditional Kvartet I humour: dark, absurd and simple alike. The actors are still on top form, and the jokes in their trademark style give you a pleasant sense of recognition

👆A separate mention for the funny (and not very kind) jokes about Alexander Tsypkin

👆The intimate scale of the action and the richness of the visuals. In our winter greyness it’s always nice to spend time with a film full of shots of sun, sea and resort bliss.

👆An unexpected ending that freshens up your impression of the film

👇New characters, male and (in deference to the new ethics) female, bolted on to the main foursome and not quite belonging there. It’s not really clear who they are or what their presence adds to the story and the humour

👇 A disconnect from a reality in which everything can be googled in a second. For example, one of the comic situations hinges on a female character not knowing what her favourite writer looks like (though she adores him so much that she carries a paper copy of his book around with her — so why not google what your favourite writer looks like?)

## Zigzag of Success: Ryazanov’s Small, Terribly Well-Made New Year Film

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/zigzag-udachi-1968/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-01-04 (4 January 2025)
Work: “Zigzag of Success” is a 1968 film directed by Eldar Ryazanov.
Tags: Soviet cinema, comedy, New Year
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/zigzag-udachi-1968/

By the way, on the subject of advertising as a marker of its era. In the original *The Diamond Arm*, released in April 1969, Gaidai discreetly slipped in a promo for another 1968 comedy, less well known today as a Soviet New Year tradition but no less wonderful. I’ve screenshotted the advertising poster that briefly comes into view when the smugglers’ car pulls away from the pier in the 23rd minute :)

[*Zigzag of Success*](https://youtu.be/rjeWVIBUbuE?si=wFq9nsKcptyLawNq) (*Zigzag udachi*) is a small and terribly well-made New Year film by Eldar Ryazanov, which really did come out just before New Year, in 1968. A young photographer (Evgeny Leonov in the stock role of a little man with vices of his own) dreams of having his own camera and, trusting to luck, takes money from the contributions pooled by the staff of his photo studio and buys a lottery ticket. What follows is an impossibly comic struggle between the personal and the collective in one particular workplace: imagine a mix of *The Garage* (Ryazanov’s satire), the series *The Office* and the pre-New Year bustle in which everyone is trying to become happy, and you get roughly this film.

I watched it purely because of the poster inside *The Diamond Arm* and enjoyed it enormously! Every type on the photo studio’s staff is as convincing as can be, the characters’ problems are thoroughly familiar (one wants to get married, another to get a flat), and the humour really is inventive: the kind we have come to expect from the best of Soviet cinema. In short, if you fancy watching something charmingly New Year-ish and Soviet, but not one of the overplayed hits, give *Zigzag of Success* a look: Gaidai won’t steer you wrong.

---

## The Non-Diamond Arm and New Year Shows as a Time Capsule

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/novogodnie-parodiynye-shou-kapsula-vremeni/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-01-03 (3 January 2025)
Tags: pop culture, New Year, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/novogodnie-parodiynye-shou-kapsula-vremeni/

I’m starting the new year with something less than obvious!

You can slate *The Non-Diamond Arm* («Небриллиантовая рука», a New Year parody of the Soviet comedy *The Diamond Arm*) and *Ivan Vasilyevich Changes Everything* («Иван Васильевич меняет всё», after the Soviet comedy *Ivan Vasilievich: Back to the Future*) all you like for the advertising, the odd cameos and the general whiff of cringe, but these products do have one undeniable advantage.

Parody New Year shows like these are a terribly fascinating object of study. Like a time capsule, they gather up (with, it has to be said, a certain ingenuity on their makers’ part) a colossal swathe of the past year’s censor-friendly Russian pop culture. Memes, jokes, trends — everything that was on people’s lips and minds, on the internets and offline, from outright cringe to things that are actually quite funny. And that same excess of advertising only completes the picture: this is the year we lived through, these are the products they were selling in it, this is the marketing that drove us up the wall.

*The Non-Diamond Arm* also has the wonderful Alexey Vorobyov and Vladimir Epifantsev — if you do happen to decide to watch it, check them out, because they’re the best thing in the film.

---

## The #yanetakusya Relay: Unpopular Opinions About Film

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/estafeta-yanetakusya-nepopulyarnye-mneniya/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-12-30 (30 December 2024)
Tags: notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/estafeta-yanetakusya-nepopulyarnye-mneniya/

The \#yanetakusya relay (roughly “#I’m not like the others”) has reached me too: I’m taking the baton from [KinoKotik](https://t.me/kinokotik) and gathering all my unpopular opinions about film in one pile :)

- I can’t stand what *La La Land* actually has to say: I don’t understand the main characters or their decisions, and the ending strikes me as the result of plain emotional immaturity. The visuals and the music are stunning, of course!

- I don’t get what the big deal is with *Dune*: I think it’s the most boring film I’ve ever seen in my life

- I see no point in publicly trashing works I didn’t like or that didn’t live up to my expectations. I’d rather write about something good, and the content I didn’t like will find its own judges or fans without my help.

I modestly pass the baton to [the Kinorevizor channel](https://t.me/kinorevizorr).

## The “Top 10 Best Films of 2024” Video: A Heartfelt Round-Up of the Year Now Ending

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/rolik-top-10-filmov-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-12-28 (28 December 2024)
Tags: list, notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/rolik-top-10-filmov-2024/

And here it is, my new [surprise format](https://youtu.be/fNaCb4Xtn80), which I recently announced [here](https://t.me/kino_voice/341).

With New Year coming, I felt like making a cosy, heartfelt, unhurried round-up of what has stayed with me from the year now ending! The result is this free-form top list — with voice-over commentary, of course: it is “kinovoice”, after all!

This is my first video in this format, and I’ll be very grateful for views, ratings and comments on YouTube: for example, which films of 2024 do you think are the best?

By the way, if you have a couple of minutes to spare, you can help my video become a little more visible on YouTube! Just type its title, «Топ 10 лучших фильмов 2024» (“Top 10 Best Films of 2024”), into the YouTube search bar and find the video by its thumbnail; let’s try to give YouTube’s recommendations a nudge. A plus for your karma and all my gratitude.

Happy holidays in advance, and enjoy the video.

## V banyu!: A Sports Drama Set in a Men’s Bathhouse

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/v-banyu-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-12-22 (22 December 2024)
Work: “V banyu!” is a 2024 film directed by Danil Ivanov.
Tags: Russian cinema, dramedy, sport, New Year
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/v-banyu-2024/

I’ve brought you an underrated and properly New Year film with a telling title: [*V banyu!*](https://youtu.be/rNKCvbLgay4?si=vEBf0h1yihVocKIg) («В баню!», “Off to the Bathhouse!”, also a Russian way of saying “Get lost!”).

It’s a dramedy about a hero who, at the start of the story, can safely be called a doormat. For years Vanya Plotnikov is used, and then screwed over altogether (both just like that and out of his money), by his lying business partner, after which his wife, her patience finally exhausted, throws him out of the house. Our hero, by contrast, is better at patiently putting up with things than at anything else in life, so he zones out for hours on end, sunk in his own thoughts, sitting in the steam room of a public bathhouse. This unusual phenomenon catches the eye of the local floor polisher, who makes Ivan compete in bathhouse sport (drop a 👀 if you didn’t know such a thing existed either).

What makes *V banyu!* good is its mix of genres: the success story and the sports drama play out here within the walls of a men’s bathhouse, which instantly deflates the bombast (so tiresome in its fellow films like *Going Vertical* or *Legend No. 17*). So the hero does overcome himself, and there is plenty of sporting tension, only none of it is po-faced: you can feel the happy ending coming, which makes it much easier to connect with him (he’s played, by the way, by Mikhail Troynik, who is great in comic roles). And the bathhouse associations with *The Irony of Fate, or Enjoy Your Bath!* (the Soviet New Year classic), the cold landscapes and the good-natured humour put this film among the likeable choices for holiday viewing.

---

## Almost 30 New Books of 2024: A Selection by Kinopoisk and Yandex Books

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/knizhnye-novinki-2024-kinopoisk/

The season of round-ups of every kind goes on, and this time it’s about books!

And my main reason for advising you to run through this list is not that I wrote a few words myself about Mrshavko Shtapich’s [already much-praised](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/ustoychivoe-razvitie-shtapich/) [*Ustoychivoe razvitie*](https://books.yandex.ru/books/mArXedHL) («Устойчивое развитие», “Sustainable Development”), but so that you can top up your own reading list.

## Poplar Fluff: Lapenko’s Great Character and an Overly Choppy Plot

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/topolinyy-pukh-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-12-12 (12 December 2024)
Work: “Poplar Fluff” is a 2024 film directed by Artyom Lempert, Kirill Klepalov.
Tags: Russian cinema, comedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/topolinyy-pukh-2024/

The winter season had me craving the summery [*Poplar Fluff*](https://youtu.be/Ewz3gof6deI?si=d7Hc6UbKFta-Ypsc). As in any confusing situation, I’m breaking it down into pros and cons:

👆Lapenko’s great portrayal of a person in a borderline state
  **👆** An interesting look at events from different characters’ points of view
  **👆** Original humour: about existential things, sort of, yet it doesn’t get you down
  **👆** A fun side plot about the relationship between a grandfather and his grandson

 👇Very sketchy plot conflicts (and, at times, characters). On the one hand, this raggedness in the story can be put down to the comedy genre; on the other, to cause and effect simply not having been worked out properly
 **👇** Too little screen time for the central character (Lapenko), who links all the chapters
 **👇** The division into chapters makes the plot too choppy: it all sort of falls apart, though the idea was a good one
 **👇** In places — cringe

## Dream Scenario: A True Transformation from Nicolas Cage

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/geroy-nashikh-snov-2023/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-12-10 (10 December 2024)
Work: “Dream Scenario” is a 2023 film directed by Kristoffer Borgli.
Tags: tragicomedy, science fiction, American cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/geroy-nashikh-snov-2023/

I finally got round to [*Dream Scenario*](https://youtu.be/gqjY6rBU2ho?si=xvnq6_iJmb-OFJsy), and I’m glad Nicolas Cage didn’t turn up in my dreams afterwards.

Although this tragicomedy about a man who suddenly starts appearing in the dreams of a great many strangers is focused first and foremost on the unhealthy trend for “cancel culture”, I’m more impressed by Nicolas Cage’s performance. He managed to play — convincingly, without caricature, without tipping into parody — a grey, utterly nondescript drip of a professor with inflated ambitions and a diminished grip on reality. That, it seems to me, is almost harder than the showy roles of charismatic heroes or villains. Cage didn’t mug, and didn’t even just imagine himself in the given circumstances, as he might have; he truly transformed.

As for the rest, it’s extremely stylised and built around a single central fantastical premise (yes, almost like *The Substance*). Who knows, perhaps this is one of the emerging trends in indie film.

## The Wild Robot: A Wealth of Themes Nested Inside Like Matryoshka Dolls

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/dikiy-robot-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-12-07 (7 December 2024)
Work: “The Wild Robot” is a 2024 film directed by Chris Sanders.
Tags: animation, family, American cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/dikiy-robot-2024/

I couldn’t miss one of the most notable animated releases of late: [*The Wild Robot*](https://youtu.be/67vbA5ZJdKQ?si=aVYx49yj7XoIqsDr).

This animated film about Roz, a helper robot who ends up on an island without a single human being, is interesting above all for the wealth of themes tucked inside it, like dolls in a matryoshka:

- The modern need for constant self-improvement — quite literally, in that our heroine rewrites her own programming to communicate with the animals

- How unpredictable and unique every experience of motherhood is — in an animated film about a robot (!)

- The traditional foray into stranger-in-a-strange-world territory, in the best traditions of *Avatar* — but! With a more mindful ending that comes down on the side of the safety of the world the hero wants to protect. It’s interesting to see how this has evolved over 20 years

- The imperfection of all living things. Even the kindest helper character in this “fairy tale” is self-serving, sly and deceitful. A good, sober look at reality

But really, the film (from the makers of *How to Train Your Dragon* and *Lilo & Stitch*!) is worth watching simply for the beauty and vividness of its animation, its lush colours and the cosiness of a woodland fairy tale — here’s a selection of my favourite stills.

## First Issue: Telegram Channels Are the New Glossies

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/pervyy-nomer-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-12-05 (5 December 2024); updated: 2025-01-06
Work: “First Issue” is a 2024 series directed by Klim Kozinsky.
Tags: series, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/pervyy-nomer-serial/

## 5 December 2024

A checklist for watching the series [*First Issue*](https://youtu.be/ufgnauYcWiQ?si=BWPAGlTg2Q4gR_ZS) (*Pervy nomer*):

- Make sure it’s been long enough since you watched the series *The Thaw*, because here Evgeny Tsyganov has landed exactly the same role (only instead of the cameraman Khrustalyov he’s the writer Inozemtsev), and you may get bored

- Make sure it’s been long enough since you watched the series *Unprincipled*, because the chronotope of Moscow-for-the-rich is the very same here, and you may get bored

- Make sure you have no experience of working in today’s Russian media, otherwise you may not buy the details of newsroom life on screen, where half the staff walk out overnight on principle (presumably so as to pay their living expenses with those same principles)

- Make sure you aren’t watching the series *Give a Show!* at the same time, because you’ll inevitably want to compare the two stories about what goes on behind the scenes in the media

- And yet! Leave yourself time to watch the credits (they’re gorgeous here) and pay attention to the supporting cast: there are wonderful characters from Denis Vlasenko, Lukerya Ilyashenko, Pavel Derevyanko and Egor Koreshkov

## 6 January 2025

I’ve finished the series [*First Issue*](https://youtu.be/ufgnauYcWiQ?si=xGj0P38j9EWSlEaa) and am struck by the irony of what happened to it. The plot is supposedly about glossy magazines: you’ve got a magazine that needs to be ~~resurrected~~ relaunched, and editors and publishers, and media, God forgive me, holdings, and full-strength newsroom backstabbing…

But what it actually ended up being about is that the new glossies are Telegram channels, influencers and their blogs and bloglets of every calibre. Everything in the series that was alive, active and generating intrigue happened on the internets: the magazine’s fate was shaped by what got leaked, which interviews were done, which posts were written and which stories went up. And the magazine itself seemed to be merely a decoration on the table at which everyone had sat down to discuss completely different things.

If that effect was intended, it’s cool!

P.S.: Of all the characters in this series, the one I love is Lukerya Ilyashenko’s. What dark, hypnotic, wicked charisma she has, and how good she is at playing traitors, schemers and witches. She first enchanted me in the series *Happy End*, and did so again in *First Issue*. I looked forward to her appearing on screen more than to anything else.

---

## The Substance: A Film That Weighs Surprisingly Heavily on the Psyche

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/substantsiya-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-12-03 (3 December 2024)
Work: “The Substance” is a 2024 film directed by Coralie Fargeat.
Tags: horror, science fiction, drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/substantsiya-2024/

With the year almost over, I finally got round to [*The Substance*](https://youtu.be/CZIdRUCO-_0?si=uzhUgptWTQZJ0LNP). It’s a film that weighs surprisingly heavily on the psyche — you feel uneasy even if you went in thinking, “I basically know the plot and I realise there’s a lot of body horror in it, so I’ll try not to get emotionally involved.” No such luck.

The devil of *The Substance* is, as they say, in the details. Because Demi Moore’s and Margaret Qualley’s characters are all too thoroughly realised (to the point of conveying even tactile sensations), the film becomes extremely believable. And yet the plot is extremely figurative and metaphorical: by the end we realise that this whole half-fantastical story about a serum and a better version of yourself is no more than an extravagant, eye-catching way of getting across the basic idea that you need to love yourself in every form you take, because you are the only you you’ve got.

---

## The Thaw: Not Everyone Was a Protagonist, but Everyone Lived Their Own “Thaw”

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/ottepel-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-11-29 (29 November 2024); updated: 2024-12-14
Work: “The Thaw” is a 2013 series directed by Valery Todorovsky.
Tags: series, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/ottepel-serial/

## 29 November 2024

Series really did have to change when they moved from television to streaming :)

I’ve been watching *The Thaw* (*Ottepel*), a classic among our series, full of dreamy nostalgia, by Valery Todorovsky (by the way, drop a 👀 if you’d like a more detailed opinion of the series).

And then I come across a shot of a whole newspaper column devoted to one of the main characters. Naturally I hit pause — I want to read it all! But no such luck: it soon turns out that the text is a single paragraph, copied and pasted as many times as it took to fill the space.

Of course, the series was shown on television back then, and it never crossed anyone’s mind that somebody would pause it and start studying the whole text. And yet it seems that in today’s series of a similar calibre you no longer come across small, harmless bloopers like this (they’ll all be big and painful ones now; yes, just give us a freeze-frame to pore over).

## 14 December 2024

Valery Todorovsky’s *The Thaw*, about the filmmakers of the 1960s, had long been sitting on my watchlist, but the final kick came after I watched [*Namedni* 1961](https://youtu.be/BB7A6w7f1uY?si=1xpb-a1pS1gxwamQ) (Leonid Parfenov’s documentary chronicle of Soviet life) :) I wanted to stay immersed in the era a little longer. And [here](https://t.me/kino_voice/313) the 👀 reactions came pouring in, which means I owe you a full review of the series!

To convey just how well, how vividly and in what detail, on every level, this story immerses you in a world of its own, I’ll give one example that I liked (and, more importantly, a spoiler-free one). When watching/rewatching, keep an eye on the nameless passer-by who witnesses the naked performance staged by the girl whom Evgeny Tsyganov’s character has hurt, at the very beginning of the first episode. A whole era will go by in the series after that moment, but you will remember this passer-by: Egor Koreshkov’s character looks at the seated girl with such astonishment, with such a spectator’s curiosity. He is a true wordless witness to the era: we never even learn his name. But he will get a second appearance, in the very last scene, and it will be deliberately underlined so that we notice.

Alongside the characters we have been following, this lad will live a life of his own, one that stays off screen, and he too will say goodbye to the Thaw in his own way (I won’t retell the final scene). He is you and me, the viewers, who walked into the story because it began so vividly and walked out of it a little different, yet having absorbed everything we watched from the sidelines. And to feel, through the screen, an era handled with such depth, an era in which not everyone was a protagonist but everyone lived their own “thaw”, is a very valuable emotional experience.

---

## Streets of Broken Lights on the Sezonnoe Obostrenie Podcast: Behind the Scenes

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/sezonnoe-obostrenie-ulitsy-razbitykh-fonarey/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-11-28 (28 November 2024)
Work: “Streets of Broken Lights” is a work  Aleksandr Rogozhkin, Vladimir Bortko, Dmitriy Svetozarov.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/sezonnoe-obostrenie-ulitsy-razbitykh-fonarey/

I spent almost the whole of November like in these memes: with my head a mush of Larins, Dukalises, cutlets (with mash, without fail), crimes and “saddle up!”.

All because, as producer, I was putting together [the first video episode of the podcast *Sezonnoe obostrenie*](https://youtu.be/qcHqnw5Lf0I) («Сезонное обострение», “Seasonal Flare-Up”)! We watched dozens of hours of episodes, picked our crushes, recalled the memes and recorded almost 2 hours dissecting this sixteen-season TV giant.

And, as always when I share something from work, a few interesting facts from behind the scenes:

- The table draped in a cloth of the podcast’s brand green is pure chance. Right before the shoot, the studio staff offered to let us try out their new service: picking a tablecloth to our own taste for the (boringly wooden) table. I’ve no idea how many shades they had bought in, but our perfect pine-emerald one turned up. There’s the magic of a shoot for you!

- The host, Lera Davydova-Kalashnik, was wearing gorgeous Valentino shoes that never made it into shot! The biggest mistake of this production…

- As props I printed out 20 colour photos of various characters from the series, from Larin and Dukalis to the cameos by Druzhko and Lera Kudryavtseva (Russian TV hosts). You can study the full variety of them on the table in the video. Amazingly, the office printer not only didn’t eat the image quality but actually seemed to improve it (using up, I suspect, most of the ink — sorry, colleagues!)

- For this episode, [Artyom Remizov](https://t.me/remizorro/31360) specially ordered a new T-shirt with a print of his own and wore it for the first time to the recording. Hear the full story [in the episode](https://youtu.be/qcHqnw5Lf0I)!
