## Children of Change: Russia’s Three Paths — Raves, Vodka and IT — Adjusted for 1995

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/deti-peremen-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-11-21 (21 November 2024); updated: 2026-01-30
Work: “Children of Change” is a 2024 series directed by Sergey Taramaev, Lyubov Lvova.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, 1990s
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/deti-peremen-serial/

## 21 November 2024

“Russia”, as the [song](https://music.yandex.ru/album/17719679) went, “has three paths: raves, vodka and IT”. That (adjusted for 1995) is exactly what [*Children of Change*](https://youtu.be/7RAPJDHKWik?si=xbQKsxySIgZ68O-Y) (*Deti peremen*), the series that launched today with two episodes, is about.

What’s fresh in the set-up: an unusual family of a mum and three sons by different fathers (our “three paths” — a cool way in). What’s familiar: the ubiquitous 1990s. Perhaps a series this high-profile should have been released at more of a distance from *Daring* (*Likhie*), which also has pretensions to being a family saga set in hard times, but let’s watch the competition play out!

I don’t think the series will get lost in the crowd, because from the start we have:

- Charismatic, one-of-a-kind representatives of opposite worlds. Viktoria Isakova as Flora, a mother of three lads with a passion for life no matter what. And Timofey Tribuntsev as Zhigalin, an unhinged, infernal gang boss who does evil on an unearthly scale

- Contrasting types among the young: a philosophising gangster (Slava Kopeikin, tormented by Hamlet’s questions), an anarchic artist (Makar Khlebnikov, my favourite of the sons so far — he draws film posters, by the way) and the youngest son, who hasn’t really shown what he’s made of yet (which, in a context like this, may be just as well — he’ll stay in one piece), played by Khetag Khinchagov

- The supporting cast: the wonderful Alexander Yatsenko, Artyom Bystrov and Lev Zulkarnaev (who, they say, will recite poems of his own somewhere in the series!)

- An interesting dramatic engine: the mother has no idea what her eldest son does. She will, of course, be forced to find out that he’s a gangster, but what happens after that is the real intrigue. That’s what we’ll keep watching for.

## 30 January 2026

[*Children of Change 2*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1038) has come charging straight out of the gate

The first episode clearly assumes a certain number of events that stayed off screen — which also leaves room for flashbacks that, I hope, we’ll see over the course of the season. They would make a harmonious link between the “before” and “after” of all the characters who need some context to be understood — literally from Flora (Viktoria Isakova in heroin chic) to Genrikh (the endlessly many-faced Sergei Gilev).

What is striking, though, is how the new season instantly divides its characters into those who managed to rebuild themselves and survive in hard times, and those who stayed themselves and so didn’t make it into the future. Perhaps this will become the season’s key theme: give up a piece of yourself and live on, or stay true to yourself but perish.

---

## Chef: Principled Kai, Who Has an Ember for a Heart

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/shef-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-11-19 (19 November 2024); updated: 2024-11-26
Work: “Chef” is a 2024 series directed by Mikhail Raskhodnikov, Evgeny Puzyrevsky.
Tags: series, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/shef-serial/

## 19 November 2024

Well, I really did watch 6 episodes of [*Chef*](https://t.me/kino_voice/297) (*Shef*) back to back (yes, the crafty [@fridaytv](https://t.me/fridaytv), the Pyatnitsa channel, held back the 7th and 8th all the way until Sunday — well, they did promise to bring us to the boil!) And it truly was good.

Our initial expectations have been borne out, thanks to the story of the principled Kai (who, his name notwithstanding, has not a shard of ice for a heart, as in *The Snow Queen*, but an ember). Offhand, you can’t name any other present-day heroes capable of uttering the words *“I’m not going anywhere, because this is my home, and anyway, why on earth should I?”* (episode 2). Denis Prytkov has delivered his second stunning role of the year (the other was [*She’s So Cool*](https://t.me/kino_voice/182)) — and it’s an absolute treat.

As the story went on, the focus spread out to other characters — or rather, to the women who work in the penal colony’s kitchen. There is nothing complicated about this part: the mechanics of a team bedding in with a new boss (our Kai) are a traditional component of any film about the road to a dream, about overcoming everything on the way to a goal and to success. But the main strength of this part lies in its sense of proportion and its transparency. The inmates don’t reform in 5 minutes, bowled over by the greatness of the chef who has landed on their heads out of nowhere; they keep showing attitude until the respect of each one has been won. And despite the modest running time, the way Kai arrives at mutual respect with each of the women is shown, put into words and dramatically justified (rather than — may the series *Kombinatsiya* forgive me — played out as a wordless scene set to jaunty music in place of a convincing speech by the hero in the background). The music, by the way, in the moments where it is present and needed, is not bad at all — they play the band Dayte Tank (!), and that I respect.

Towards the finale Pyatnitsa pulls an ace from its sleeve and turns episode 7 into the thing it does best. Yes, yes — a reality show. Well, with material like this it would be a sin not to wrap it in its favourite packaging. And that is good too. We have got to know Kai and his new team from the prison kitchen well enough. Now we can pull back and look at it all in the third person. As for the angle from which this series will serve us its final, dessert episode — we’ll find out on Sunday.

## 26 November 2024

I thought for a long time about what to make of the finale of the series [*Chef*](https://t.me/kino_voice/301). Then I realised it reminds me of this photograph — beautiful and yet chaotic, but worth looking at all the same.

On the one hand, in the finale, as in the series as a whole, every cog meshes, the drama works and passions run high. This is exactly the kind of content I don’t speed up, because the pace is wonderful as it is :) Prytkov is superb, the other characters have fully opened up and come alive by the finale, and all the scenes of the restaurant opening are done with filigree precision.

On the other hand, for all my love of the series, I started to notice how constructed it is: the little seams needed to keep the action moving, the coincidences in the characters’ fates that try to pass for cinematic conventions. It seems to have come out too contrived — both the twist with the health certificate forgotten in his own pocket and, even more so, the one with Kai being sent to prison for a year. As screenwriting it’s fine, but isn’t Kai rather too smart a hero for that?

While I was mulling it over, I read my Kinopoisk colleagues’ [interview](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/4010300/) with Denis Prytkov (that’s where the photo is from, too). I found no downsides: it is hands down the best companion piece to the series, and as proof, here’s a quote (about food and about love, of course):

 *— Do you have a signature dish?*
>
**— French-style meat! That’s exactly how I won my wife’s heart. One day, before Covid, I made her invite me over. I spent the last of my money on groceries and went round to hers to cook. Sadly, I didn’t stay the night, but the dish, as history has shown, was a success.**

---

## Give a Show!: The Best Series of 2024

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/dayte-shou-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-11-18 (18 November 2024); updated: 2024-12-25
Work: “Give a Show!” is a 2024 series directed by Dmitry Litvinenko.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/dayte-shou-serial/

## 18 November 2024

I started falling for the series *Give a Show!* (*Dayte shou*) back at Pilot (the Russian series festival), and [wrote about it](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/festival-pilot-2024-izbrannoe/) at the time. But I was afraid that, as tends to happen, the brisk start would give way to a sagging plot, a slackening pace and all the other ways a show stops convincing you.

I can hardly believe it: 4 episodes in, *Give a Show!* isn’t just keeping up its quality but raising it with every episode. At the end of each one you think, “right, that’s it, it can’t get any better, this must be the peak, time to brace for the fall…” Then you put on the next one and once again revel in the powerful writing, the sharp plot twists and the performances.

What I like most of all is the mix of themes: you get the bleakness of starting a career in the Russian media, a love story (Savostyuk and Krasovskaya, bravo — it’s been a long time since I believed in an on-screen couple this much), corruption, the seamy side of show business and anything else you care to name. I’m describing it as though we were looking at a new “encyclopedia of Russian life” (as Belinsky called *Eugene Onegin*), but why not? All the more so since the talk-show format this whole whirl revolves around really can be seen as an encyclopedia of life in the country over the last 20 years, if not more.

## 25 December 2024

The finale of the series [*Give a Show!*](https://t.me/kino_voice/300) landed perfectly in December, just when it’s time to pick the year’s best — and for me this really did turn out to be the best series of 2024!

It’s been a long time since I watched a serious drama this absorbed and this tense, because in these heavy genres some false note usually jumps out at me and spoils the whole thing. Here everything worked — from the first episode, which I saw back at Pilot, to the last, which gave every one of the characters exactly what karma owed them. As I always do with shows I love, I’ve recorded my full impressions as a voice message, and here I’ll leave a couple of points worth carrying over from this series into next year:

- Oleg Savostyuk is sheer acting power and one of the best characters I saw in 2024. Honestly, if it weren’t for Lev Zulkarnaev and his character in *She’s So Cool*, this would have been an uncontested triumph

- Russian series have started venturing (and very successfully) behind the scenes of the media. We got *Give a Show!*, and *First Issue* followed. If this is a new language for talking about the reality around us (besides fairy tales and the 1990s), it will be interesting to follow

- Black humour is our be-all and end-all, and it looks as though Russian shows are only going to have more of it

---

## The Apprentice: The Eternal Story of “You Shall Not Make for Yourself an Idol”

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/uchenik-voskhozhdenie-trampa-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-11-12 (12 November 2024)
Work: “The Apprentice” is a 2024 film directed by Ali Abbasi.
Tags: biopic, drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/uchenik-voskhozhdenie-trampa-2024/

[*The Apprentice*](https://youtu.be/o023dg0Zbgw?si=MAOpVNqTpRSKONyv) is so formal that its main characters remain objects that arouse neither sympathy nor empathy, only the desire to watch from the outside (but for no more than two hours). And that is what makes the film good: on either side of a neutral stance it is easy to slip into liking or disliking the characters, and where serving politicians are concerned that risks ruining the whole film. Don’t get me wrong, though: the performances here are each better than the last — Sebastian Stan’s Trump creates a literally documentary effect, and Jeremy Strong’s Roy Cohn is so natural that he eclipses everyone else involved.

But the neutral storytelling and the documentary-style performances don’t stir the emotional response you might count on before watching: some outrage, at least, that people like these get their hands on money, or, on the contrary, inspiration, the motivation to go and “attack and deny” as well, as the characters recommend. Taken as a whole, the film resembles Ouroboros, the mythical serpent devouring itself from the tail end. The circular structure of the plot, combined with the way the main characters mirror each other, leads us round one turn of a spiral that will probably never be broken. So to watch a film like this is to get a slightly better feel for the eternal story of “you shall not make for yourself an idol” (except, perhaps, of yourself).

---

## Twins Played by One Actor: Amura, Gudbay and Vasily

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/bliznetsy-v-rossiyskikh-proektakh/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-11-11 (11 November 2024)
Tags: Russian cinema, series, list
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/bliznetsy-v-rossiyskikh-proektakh/

**Seeing double…**

… from the number of films and series about twins swapping places! It feels as if everyone here suddenly remembered the film *What a Mess!* («Ширли-мырли») (or, well, *Ivan Vasilievich: Back to the Future*) and decided to riff on the theme of twins played by one and the same actor. So I got thinking and, off the top of my head, jotted down 3 new titles built around this device:

[*Amura*](https://youtu.be/2cRO3MvDCQU?si=5rTcK7W2t-KSXDFl) («Амура») — a crime action story about twin sisters trying to reunite somewhere between Vladivostok and Japan. The leads are played by Alena Mikhailova (who got some practice at this sort of thing in *Kalimba* («Калимба»))

[*Gudbay*](https://youtu.be/UvP1VTh3XpI?si=3yvLPGBdU1Xp8AjO) («Гудбай», “Goodbye”) — a fantastical spoof series about Biden’s visit to Moscow. This time it’s Dmitry Dyuzhev on twin duty.

[*Vasily*](https://youtu.be/LXZAnFKEHH8?si=-Oxfmg4m7HwsnE8B) («Василий») — an upcoming comedy about twin brothers: a Russian schoolteacher of basic life safety (OBZh) and a man in debt to a Mexican cartel. Both are played by Alexander Petrov.

Does anyone know what’s behind this pile-up of twins? :) If you’ve spotted anything else like it, share it in the comments! (I haven’t forgotten *Mickey 17*, but it’s not one of ours)

## A Book for November: Ustoychivoe razvitie by Mrshavko Shtapich

For the birthday of Kinopoisk (Russia’s largest film database, media and streaming service) on 7 November (a belated happy birthday to us!) we’ve put together a fresh [shelf of great books from the editorial team.](https://t.me/booksyandex/3725)

My recommendation is the new Mrshavko Shtapich, [*Ustoychivoe razvitie*](https://books.yandex.ru/books/mArXedHL) («Устойчивое развитие», “Sustainable Development”). In any case, *Ustoychivoe razvitie* is ideal reading for November, that stretch of the year when everything around is already cold, gloomy and bleak, and the feast of life is still a long way off. But that state has a charm of its own too.

## Intermission: On the Courage to Taste Life’s Whole Spectrum of Emotions

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kanikuly-2023/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-11-07 (7 November 2024)
Work: “Intermission” is a 2023 film directed by Anna Kuznetsova.
Tags: Russian cinema, drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/kanikuly-2023/

> - I want to gobble up that mask over there.

> - The sad one or the happy one?
> - Both.

In Russian cinemas from today: [*Intermission*](https://youtu.be/GZ9ORVnK8jg?si=G-BDIysXndwCb6rc) (*Kanikuly*, “Holidays”), the winner of Mayak 2023 (the film festival in Gelendzhik). A film that has soaked up *One Hundred Days After Childhood* and *We’ll Live Till Monday* (two Soviet coming-of-age classics), yet speaks to its audience in a language of its own, and that language is the reason to see it. Take the quote I put at the top: like the film as a whole, it is about the courage to taste the whole spectrum of emotions life has to offer and to accept every experience you are capable of living through.

The plot: Tanya, the young head of a drama club, is taking her charges, aged 3 to 16, to a children’s theatre competition in Sochi. Travelling with them to keep the creative types in check, Tanya first among them, is the deputy head, Maria Genrikhovna. And although the set-up leaves you fully convinced that Tanya and Maria will be the ones at odds, the story turns out to be deeper and more layered. And where, for the 5 days of the trip, Tanya fills the role of the comfortable, decent adult for the children and teenagers, for Tanya herself that adult turns out to be Maria. Maria, though, has no such adult of her own, and that is just one facet of the tragedy of an ending in which, on the face of it, nothing fatal has happened.

What I most want to single out is the overall mood of the film, which is naive in a down-to-earth way and recklessly funny. Sleepless nights on the road, teachers’ humour, lodgings as uncomfortable as they come yet cosy, an emotional overdose from a hot-and-cold shower of feelings: this is, as the joke on social media now goes, “just a regular Tuesday” on any group trip, be it a school club, an olympiad team or any other kind of club. The nostalgia hit me at full force. So *Intermission* really is a little holiday: you can sink into it and walk out of the film, as they say, 120 minutes older.

---

## Yura Borisov in Crystal Swan: How the Actor Stole the Film from Me

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/yura-borisov-khrustal/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-11-05 (5 November 2024)
Tags: Russian cinema, notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/yura-borisov-khrustal/

[Here](https://t.me/alperina/20648) [@alperina](https://t.me/alperina) (in anticipation, I hope, of an Oscar for Yura Borisov) has launched a flash mob: tell everyone where and when you first saw this actor and what you thought of him. And I adore telling this story, so I’m delighted to join in!

Autumn 2018. At random, quite by chance, I go to see Darya Zhuk’s film [*Crystal Swan*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/1045133/) (*Khrustal*), about a DJ from Minsk who, in the 90s, dreams of leaving for America. The film is vivid, original and atmospheric, with the kind of plot that makes you want to hold your breath and not blink while you watch.

And then a minor, almost insignificant character appears on screen: maybe the heroine’s colleague, maybe her boyfriend, or even 2 in 1. Very soon he vanishes from the screen, but by then it is impossible to forget that crazed look of his and the inimitable way he moves, like a man forever swaying to a beat only he can hear. He stole the film from me. And that, as I found out after studying the film’s page on Kinopoisk (Russia’s largest film database, media and streaming service), was Yura Borisov!

From that moment I remembered the name and the face and started watching out for where else this incredible actor would turn up (“he’s got to be in something else, he’s madness on legs!” I thought). Now, of course, he is everywhere, but back then the release of *The Bull* (*Byk*; incidentally, remarkably similar in mood to *Crystal Swan*) was a celebration: at last someone had cast the actor in something else.

---

## Crime & Punishment: Ivan Yankovsky Is the Perfect Raskolnikov

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/prestuplenie-i-nakazanie-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-11-02 (2 November 2024); updated: 2024-12-02
Work: “Crime & Punishment” is a 2024 series directed by Vladimir Mirzoev.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, adaptation
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/prestuplenie-i-nakazanie-serial/

## 2 November 2024

Splitting [the series based on *Crime and Punishment*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/series/5377359/) into two parts is an excellent idea.

Not just because it’s fashionable in the TV world right now (think of *Baby Reindeer*, divided in two by its meaning, or *I Know Who Killed You*, with its two literal blocks of episodes). But also because of the way the meaning of the story is structured. Today you and I saw the exposition — the crime (crimes, plural, even), while the punishment, as happens in life, is not only delayed but also more gruelling than the crime itself (in our case, 6 episodes against 4).

A very simple but effective formal device all but guarantees that we’ll be waiting for the second part of the series. Together with Raskolnikov and his Devil from the Dostoevsky metaverse, we commit the crime almost playfully; it practically falls into our hands. The punishment, though, will come later — when every thought has been thought through, every hypothesis put forward and all patience exhausted (all the more so given the premiere’s postponements).

Just one question: how do I now stop seeing this structure in every series I happen to be watching alongside it?

## 2 December 2024

*\*tag yourself on Monday\**.

Ivan Yankovsky, it seems, is the perfect Raskolnikov. Misanthropic and merciful, unstable and rational, majestic and gone to seed all at once. His take on the character works especially well for the ending that [*Crime & Punishment*](https://youtu.be/RchRWY4waQI?si=xzvvRm0keRfB1SiJ) gets in Vladimir Mirzoev’s reading as director (no spoilers, but the way the denouement is handled is intriguing).

After watching all 10 episodes of the new *Crime & Punishment*, it becomes obvious that the on-screen madness and devilry surrounding the crime itself are absolutely necessary and fitting. And, just as fittingly, they fade away towards the end of the story (or rather jump from Raskolnikov to Luzhin, Svidrigailov and other characters — incidentally, every one of the supporting performances is absolutely outstanding).

And this is where a great moment of skilfully subverted expectations comes in, leading to an impressive denouement. The series pretends that everything is heading where we expect — Raskolnikov and Sonechka going off to penal servitude, that kind of thing. But not a bit of it. And it’s for the sake of this final surprise, when there would seem to be nothing left for sudden twists, that the series is definitely worth watching to the very end.

---

## The Highway: The Poster, the “Spiral of Silence” and an Ending You Judge for Yourself

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/trassa-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-10-31 (31 October 2024)
Work: “The Highway” is a 2024 series directed by Dushan Gligorov.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, thriller
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/trassa-serial/

Halloween is a date chosen with a jeweller’s precision for the finale of *The Highway* (*Trassa*) :)

Over 10 episodes the story has proved to be a succession of utterly unfathomable horrors that befell a handful of characters. So as a horror for the pumpkin feast it will do perfectly :)

But I want to dwell separately on the current poster, which makes everything the show contains clear at a single glance. Here we have the heroine in a strangling noose made of the highway — the one around which all the insanity happens.

On the one hand, obviously, circumstances are strangling the heroine; she is literally risking her life trying to save her daughter. On the other — allow me to turn to media theory (there it is, the dear old thing, coming in handy in adult life). It has a concept called the “spiral of silence”: a situation in society and the media in which a person is less likely to voice their opinion on an issue if they feel they are in the minority and face retribution or isolation for holding it. The silence spirals on through the years, and you get the situation in the series: sick freaks tormenting defenceless people for decades on end. The poster is astonishingly on target, bravo!

Whether the heroine managed to break the “spiral of silence” and the chain of violence in the finale is for each viewer to decide. In my view she didn’t, but what happened was just, and such a brutal outcome actually pleased and surprised me :)) If you’ve watched it, what do you think of the finale?

---

## An Exhibition About Boris Ryzhy Instead of the Unreleased Film About the Poet

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/vystavka-boris-ryzhiy/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-10-28 (28 October 2024)
Tags: documentary, notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/vystavka-boris-ryzhiy/

You can’t see the film about Boris Ryzhy (the Yekaterinburg poet of the 1990s), but you can go to the exhibition!

Which is what I did. I came away with mixed impressions, from the pleasant feeling of recognising the little material things so often mentioned in Ryzhy’s poems to a certain boredom, because the curator’s tour of the exhibition is put together in a fairly loose and at times even long-winded style.

But the exhibition does have one special touch: a documentary about the poet playing on a non-stop loop. It was shot in Yekaterinburg, and in it Ryzhy’s life is recounted by his sister, his father and many other people who knew Boris personally. All in all, it is atmospheric, touching and informative.

A pleasant way to spend some time for anyone who is interested in the poet (or simply wants to fill the hole in their heart left by the film that never reached cinemas).

## Daring: A Crime Saga with Every Chance of Standing Alongside Brigada

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/likhie-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-10-24 (24 October 2024); updated: 2025-09-18
Work: “Daring” is a 2024 series directed by Yuri Bykov.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, crime
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/likhie-serial/

## 24 October 2024

The series [*Daring*](https://youtu.be/ZZsPnO0dr4A?si=HgfimuYLnzc-InsK) (*Likhie*, “The Dashing Ones”, a nod to the “dashing 90s”) has every chance of standing alongside *Brigada* (the cult 2002 gangster series) as a saga of equally epochal sweep about crime and the people who get drawn into it (not) of their own free will.

As always with Yuri Bykov, *Daring* spells out its characters’ starting motivation very clearly. Artyom Bystrov’s character, Pavel, a simple taiga gamekeeper who makes his living from honey, finds that in 1991 there is nothing to live on, even as a former fellow villager is buying an entire flat in Khabarovsk. A craving not even for the high life but simply for a life that isn’t humiliating takes hold of him, and from there he is ready to take the word of that fellow villager, who promises him the same kind of “well-paid job”. Naturally, there is nothing good behind a job like that.

The story is really well put together, made up of two stories unfolding in parallel, in the present day and in the 90s. On the one hand, we don’t even have to wait 16 episodes to find out where our protagonist’s son (his chief accomplice from the very first episodes) has ended up 30 years on. On the other, the glimpses of the present let us do more than silently watch, yet again, the deeds of days long gone in the 90s: we get to see that era’s delayed consequences, which by now seem invisible. A series I’ll be watching closely to the end.

## 18 September 2025

The contrast between father and son Likhovtsev in the second episode of the follow-up to [*Daring*](https://t.me/kino_voice/893) is built as convincingly as it could possibly be.

Since the start of the season, only the very worst has been coming out in Zhenka, even when he means well (the “help” with his younger brother’s screw-up, for instance). The character turns out to be somehow rotten, insincere, two-faced — even by the standards of the company he keeps. Maybe the psyche of a child steeped in bloody business from an early age couldn’t take it, or maybe he simply soaked up the worst of the atmosphere of his time, but the result is plain to see. I’m in awe of Egor Kenzhametov in this role. By a curious coincidence, he also played the younger brother of Yura Borisov’s character in the film *The Bull* — in that role Egor had, on the contrary, to stay clear of any hardness of character, whereas here he makes up for it in full.

Next to him, strangely enough, it is the father, Pavel Likhovtsev, who seems the brighter figure. It’s astonishing how, with so much blood on his hands, the character has managed to hold on to (or, at any rate, has been able to recall) a sincere, pure love for his wife and a value system of sorts. Artyom Bystrov’s performance in the role was superb from the very start, but now it takes on a new kind of importance.

---

## The Alien: Simple Science Fiction That Could Really Have Happened

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/prishelets-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-10-24 (24 October 2024); updated: 2024-12-24
Work: “The Alien” is a 2024 film directed by Ivan Sosnin.
Tags: Russian cinema, science fiction
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/prishelets-2024/

## 24 October 2024

Yesterday I was at the premiere of Ivan Sosnin’s [*The Alien*](https://youtu.be/REDTP-7B_jU?si=e16bmSzMvAlBXeQa) (*Prishelets*). As always with this director, the film fills you with faith in better things and charges you up with kindness, while sunshine and bright colours break through the impassable Russian snows on screen.

Lyosha, a young guy (everyone in the village thinks he’s odd, but that isn’t true at all), can’t wait for aliens to arrive: he draws crop circles, tunes the radio equipment in his house, picks up signals and, basically, lives for his idea. In the end he does meet an alien woman, and that, of course, opens his eyes to life.

The science fiction here is simple, without the glut of special effects we are all so sick of. This is exactly how an alien might turn up in an ordinary village, among the snowy Russian landscapes we know so well. Deliberately steering clear of special effects like this makes the science fiction endearing and close to home, and gives you the feeling of a story that could really have happened.

The protagonist, as played by Maxim Stoyanov, could not have been any other way. It’s a wonderful performance, combining vulnerability and defencelessness with righteous anger at a world that holds nothing good in store for people like Lyosha. Stoyanov’s natural presence works for the character too: on the outside he looks like a mighty giant, but inside, as we see, is a very fragile world, which the actor manages to convey. After *The Alien* I saw this actor with new eyes — one of the many things I have to thank the film for.

And another thing: in Ivan Sosnin’s films even the villains get a shot at something better and, without meaning to, set off down the path of good. The film’s ending is proof of that.

In cinemas from today — I warmly recommend going with the people closest to you and sharing the bright, happy feelings a worthwhile film brings.

## 24 December 2024

In the [end-of-year film round-up](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/4010434/) I put together with my Kinopoisk colleagues, I was, as has become the custom, in charge of kindness and wrote about [*The Alien*](https://t.me/kino_voice/269). What is striking about Ivan Sosnin’s new film is not so much the idea of people’s refusal to accept their neighbour (the usual set-up for this author’s stories) as the language chosen to convey that problem:

> In the hands of Ivan Sosnin, the kindest director in Russia, the cruel axiom “man is a wolf to man” turns, to a Mujuice track, into a gentle but unmistakable reminder: “man is an alien to man”.

Whereas in 2022’s *Dalyokie blizkie* (“Distant Close Ones”) contact could be made on Earth, by driving a few thousand kilometres in a little van and having a heart-to-heart, by 2024 an entire sci-fi with an ambiguous ending is being set in motion. And that is the very reason no round-up of 2024 is possible without *The Alien* — a snowbound, intimate story that in fact concerns every one of us.

---

## Yug and Ira: The Voice-Over as a Lifestyle Podcast About the Hero’s Life

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/yug-i-ira-zakadrovyy-golos/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-10-21 (21 October 2024)
Tags: series, Russian cinema, analysis
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/yug-i-ira-zakadrovyy-golos/

**How do you make the story of a 14-year-old lad or a single 30-year-old woman interesting?**

(Or, to be precise, the stories of the series *Yug* and *Ira*)

> For those who haven’t seen them:
>
> *Yug* (“South”), 2024: Ivan Sosnin’s dramedy about a 14-year-old boy who sets off across the whole of Russia to look for his father
>
> *Ira*, 2023: the story of a 30-year-old woman (Ingrid Olerinskaya) whose love life hasn’t worked out.

Use a voice-over! Alim Beschokov, who wrote both shows, evidently takes pleasure in using this device :)

Generally speaking, a voice-over is used in film either as the subjective voice of a character who tells the audience something himself, or as the objective voice of a third-person narrator who takes no part in the action and comments from the outside.

In *Yug* and *Ira* the voice-over always belongs to the protagonist — which means it shows hidden sides of their inner world. Literally a non-stop lifestyle podcast about the hero’s life :)

The trick is that a voice-over usually voices the details left off screen — the things we don’t see. But in these series the voice-over often duplicates scenes shown on screen and doubles the effect. In *Yug*, for example, there is a scene where the hero goes to buy a new SIM card: we see it on screen. And in voice-over Yug tells us how he went to buy it, and why. Visually we see the situation in the third person, while the experience of living through it reaches us by ear, in the first. So the chances of growing close to Ira or Yug are much higher thanks to this device.

---

## A History of Russian Film Festivals: From the 1935 Soviet Film Festival to Kinotavr

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/istoriya-rossiyskikh-kinofestivaley/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-10-15 (15 October 2024); updated: 2024-10-30
Tags: festivals, film history
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/istoriya-rossiyskikh-kinofestivaley/

## 15 October 2024

All last week I was following Mayak, the Russian film festival in Gelendzhik, and along the way I got curious about the history of the festival movement in Russia. So please welcome a small (but the first on this channel) **special project about Russian film festivals!** As it happens, I have already [written](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/rekonstruktsiya-kinoteatra-udarnik/) about the cinema where it all began :)

Over the next two weeks, in a series of five posts, I will tell you about the life and death of Russian film festivals from the early 20th century to the present day, lay them out across the calendar year and even try to match them with Western counterparts by the profile of their programmes.

The first part is coming today!

## 15 October 2024

**1️⃣** **Part ⅕. The second-oldest**

Where did film festivals come from in the first place?
It all began with European film clubs in the 1920s; then came curated screenings with programmes that ran for several days; and then, with the arrival of sound in 1927, things sped up many times over. So in 1932 the world’s first film festival took place: Venice. It emerged as part of the Venice Biennale, an international art exhibition held since 1893 (as old as cinema itself!). There was no competition yet; that arrived with the second festival in 1934, when the top prize was not yet the Golden Lion but the Mussolini Cup (yes, cinema was the most important of the arts for all kinds of regimes).

And this is where we get to the second-oldest film festival — the Russian one! Or, to be precise, the Soviet Film Festival in Moscow. 1935, the Udarnik cinema, an international competition, *Chapaev* as the opening film. On the jury: Sergei Eisenstein, Vsevolod Pudovkin, Alexander Dovzhenko. What made it happen: political hostility to the regime then ruling Italy, and the 15th anniversary of the Soviet film industry, celebrated everywhere in January of that year.

Sadly, neither of the first two festivals flourished for long. Venice went underground for the whole of the Second World War and regained its flagship status only in 1946. And the Soviet Film Festival in Moscow was never held in its original form again. Its successor was, and still is, the Moscow International Film Festival (MIFF). From 1959 it was held every two years, and in 1999 it became annual (who was behind that, by the way, I will explain in one of the next posts). Until 2022 it was Russia’s only A-category film festival (that is, accredited by the International Federation of Film Producers Associations alongside Cannes, Venice, Berlin and a dozen or so other major festivals around the world).

In short, with film festivals everything seems to happen not thanks to circumstances but in spite of them. But when has that ever bothered us? :)

In the next part: who made MIFF annual, what is odd about its programme, which festival split off from the Moscow International, and much more.

## 23 October 2024

**2️⃣** **A History of Russian Film Festivals.** **Part ⅖. Changes**

So, [in the previous part](https://t.me/kino_voice/247) we reached the moment when MIFF became a regular Soviet film festival held every two years. It was an astonishing time: Federico Fellini, Sophia Loren and Francis Ford Coppola came to the USSR just as they did to Venice and Cannes, and in 1987 the jury president was Robert De Niro. In short, MIFF grew by every measure to truly Hollywood proportions.

And by 1988 MIFF had grown so much that its documentary programme split off, taking shape as a separate (and also international!) festival, at that point purely for documentaries: Poslanie k cheloveku (“Message to Man”). At the suggestion of the documentary filmmaker Mikhail Litvyakov, the event moved to Leningrad and was first held there in 1989, and its symbol (in the first photo) was named the “Kentavryonok”, the little centaur (yes, this image hovered over the Russian festival movement even before Kinotavr appeared!). Message to Man is still going strong, and now takes in experimental film, fiction and animation as well. Kinopoisk has a wonderful [article](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/4006929/) with a more detailed history of the festival and unique photographs (I was especially struck by the shot of Leni Riefenstahl receiving an award in 2001)

Meanwhile MIFF began to falter: the collapse of a country, crisis and social upheaval do nobody any good. In 1998 it could not be held at all because of financial problems. In 1999 Nikita Mikhalkov took up the post of MIFF president (something tells me no such post existed before), and the festival has been held annually ever since. A reminder of the context: in 1999 Mikhalkov is a man in triumph, with *Burnt by the Sun* (the Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film and the Grand Prix of the 47th Cannes Film Festival) and the internationally shot *The Barber of Siberia* already behind him. So the magical disappearance of the financial problems should come as no surprise, all the more so since various researchers describe the Mikhalkov of that period as a rather effective manager ([I relied](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/istoriya-rossiyskogo-blokbastera-kniga/), in particular, on the book [*Istoriya rossiyskogo blokbastera*](https://books.yandex.ru/books/JZRDAukA), “A History of the Russian Blockbuster”).

In short, MIFF survived hard times for the second time in its history, but other major Russian festivals had already appeared on the horizon: Kinotavr and Okno v Evropu (“Window to Europe”). Where they came from and how they differed — in the next part!

## 30 October 2024

**3️⃣ A History of Russian Film Festivals. Part ⅗. How Kinotavr Got Its Name**

So, MIFF survived, and Kinotavr and Window to Europe appeared. Let us take a closer look at them.

Kinotavr did not appear overnight. Its prototype, the Festival of Unsold Films, [took place](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/3374283/) in Podolsk in 1989 on the initiative of Mark Rudinstein, a businessman (if you can call him that; the man has an interesting biography). The thing is, at the height of perestroika the volume of auteur cinema shot up, but cinemas would not buy it, because the new market economy wanted crowd-pleasers, not art films. The result was a mass of films with no chance of reaching cinema screens and audiences. That is where Rudinstein stepped in, giving these films and their makers a chance. The filmmakers’ delight inspired him so much that he decided to stage a bigger festival by the sea — in Sochi, naturally. But unwanted auteur films alone would not do for an event on that scale.

The festival held by the sea in 1991 ended up with a programme in two parts: one for audiences (“Cinema for Everyone”) and one for critics (“Cinema for the Chosen”). [They say](https://kinoart.ru/texts/mezhdu-banditami-i-skrepami-kak-rodilsya-kinotavr-etalonnyy-rossiyskiy-kinofestival) that this led someone to joke that it was turning into “some kind of centaur” (*kentavr*). And the film critic Alyona Bokshitskaya corrected them: “Kinotavr!” — giving the festival its name. That is how it would exist for the next 30 years, becoming the symbol of an entire era in film. Incidentally, the post of “festival president” (and we remember who holds it at MIFF) first appeared at Kinotavr, where it was held by Oleg Ivanovich Yankovsky. It sounds honorary, but it served a thoroughly practical purpose: for state sponsorship you needed someone whom officials would be glad to receive in their offices and would not send away empty-handed. For Kinotavr’s first ten years the arrangement with Yankovsky worked, but then something stalled, and the question of selling the festival arose.

In its early days Kinotavr had an international programme (as, in fact, did all the festivals mentioned above). And in 1993 Window to Europe was launched in Vyborg: the oldest national film festival in Russia focused specifically on Russian cinema. A festival with a surprisingly calm history, it outlived Kinotavr and is still running today.

In the next part: the rebirth and death of Kinotavr, and lots of film festivals with one-word names

---

## How to Stay Focused: Podcast Volume Slightly Above Normal

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kontsentratsiya-na-rabote/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-10-14 (14 October 2024)
Tags: notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/kontsentratsiya-na-rabote/

**A Monday post: on staying focused on work tasks**

Recently I found myself wondering: why do I listen to podcasts for work louder than music or other content in everyday life? (I do love the hosts’ voices, of course, but not that much.)

Because I work with podcasts every day, I can sometimes lose focus after recording sessions and listening through other episodes :) My solution is to set the volume a little higher than for the ordinary music I listen to. It’s still within the normal range, I’m not taking on any risk of going deaf, but practically every distraction drops out of my sensory field: from sounds, obviously, to visual or tactile ones. With the volume turned up, I literally cannot get distracted by anything else.

This seems to be one particular application of the general rule of concentration: remove distractions and clear unnecessary things off your desk! Only here it comes in a podcast version, for gathering sound edits.

What are your life hacks for staying focused? Bring your experience to the comments and we’ll swap notes.

## Anora: A Tragic Farce That Works, Remarkable for Its Directness and Simplicity

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/anora-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-10-10 (10 October 2024)
Work: “Anora” is a 2024 film directed by Sean Baker.
Tags: drama, tragicomedy, American cinema, festival films
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/anora-2024/

[*Anora*](https://youtu.be/BUtvdzMxw3U?si=GB6RXypwgWxXcMEx) is, of course, a film remarkable for its directness and simplicity.

Having seen it, I now completely understand the raptures of my colleagues at Mayak (the Russian film festival in Gelendzhik) and at festivals around the world. The film is a tragic farce that works (even if it walks the very edge of restraint and taste): you watch it with genuine tears running down your face, and yet every now and then you catch yourself smirking. And that means a guaranteed emotional response and a conversation about something serious in a place where none seemed to be on the cards. All this even though everyone reacts to the film in an entirely individual way, anywhere from boredom to bright hope. As for me, from somewhere around the midpoint I was frozen with dread for the heroine, so much so that not even the solid gangster humour could help. But it was worth it.

A review with spoilers will follow later; the film is in cinemas from 17 October, and I warmly recommend it.

## Amura: The First Three Episodes Are Brisk, to the Point and Inventive

Airing alongside it, meanwhile, is [*Amura*](https://youtu.be/2cRO3MvDCQU?si=f-ToctKsKE2rJQQR) («Амура») — one more series about the Russian colliding with the foreign-slash-alien (not really, in fact: it’s the same old line-up of universal human problems in the ring).

## El Ruso: Simple Truths in a Complicated Argentine Setting

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/el-ruso-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-10-08 (8 October 2024)
Work: “El Ruso” is a 2024 series directed by Sergey Mokritskiy.
Tags: series, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/el-ruso-serial/

[*El Ruso*](https://youtu.be/fSM0IunUOGI) is now out in full — a series about simple truths in a complicated Argentine setting.

As I [wrote](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/festival-pilot-2024-izbrannoe/) after Pilot (the Russian series festival), I was curious to watch the Balabanov-style concept of the “city as an evil force” at work, so I put on the third episode without a second thought. And then the fourth, the fifth, the sixth… And every time the story broke off at a point where it was impossible not to keep watching. Not one dull filler episode. Not one abandoned storyline. Every little knot tied along the way was neatly undone, one after another, by the finale — and, to its credit, not in a soulless montage that cuts from character to character in turn, but in action just as distinctive and stirring as the series as a whole.

The idea that love and treating one another like human beings matter, in spite of everything, can be put across in different ways. But in the case of *El Ruso*, amid Old Believer calico and the criminal neon of night-time streets, it came out not as a preachy moral we have all had our fill of, but as a deftly drawn line, underlined three times over by the finale. And thanks to that structure (which the sets and the performances both serve without getting in each other’s way, as do certain cinematic conventions), the series pulls even those who can usually stop themselves at any second into a proper binge.

This seems to be one of those cases where a series packs in everything, for every taste, and drops nothing along the way. A rarity and a pleasant discovery.

---

## The Most Anticipated Films of Late 2024: Nosferatu, Jackpot, Moana 2

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/ozhidaemye-filmy-kontsa-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-10-04 (4 October 2024)
Tags: list, announcements
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/ozhidaemye-filmy-kontsa-2024/

I’m delighted to take the baton from dear [@Age_of_Cinemaa](https://t.me/Age_of_Cinemaa) (thank you!) and tell you about my top three most anticipated films of what’s left of 2024:

[*Nosferatu*](https://youtu.be/2TN9DnF2Yhw?si=0INkfJZ1iOfNi39F)
As a rule I’m not very keen on horror and all its neighbouring genres, but this is an exception! Nicholas Hoult looks great surrounded by all manner of unholy creatures, as anyone who remembers *Warm Bodies* knows — that film about a zombie with a human heart is exactly where I first noticed him. What I expect from the *Nosferatu* remake is the old-school spirit of German Expressionism (luckily, Eggers’s directing style is in many ways its heir) and a realisation of what problems society has today and whether they differ much from the anxieties of German audiences in 1922.

*Jackpot* (no poster, but with a telling still)
As a devoted fan of *How Viktor “The Garlic” Took Alexey “The Stud” to the Nursing Home* and especially of *In Limbo* by Alexandr Khant, I’m looking forward to this film perhaps most of all. All the more so because its source novel, Kirill Ryabov’s *777*, [left my head spinning](https://t.me/kino_voice/112) as a supremely cinematic text that is simply begging to be put on screen. And what I expect from the film — as always with Khant — is a story about a person in a borderline state inside our merry chthonic murk.

[*Moana 2*](https://youtu.be/kvDuoTAbDko?si=8CfF95GQr__6vK4Y)
In the winter of 2023 I watched the first film with delight — I confess I was won over by the villainous crab, voiced in the Russian dub by Ilya Lagutenko of Mumiy Troll (the Russian rock band). I’m looking forward to the sequel so that I can once again enjoy the sweet humour (which is also just dark enough — remember how many times the rooster and the piglet nearly got eaten in the first film), the bright tropical colours and the feeling of a sea wind in my face :)

I’m passing the baton to [@kinorevizorr](https://t.me/kinorevizorr), [@kinobloknotik](https://t.me/kinobloknotik) and [@kinokotik](https://t.me/kinokotik).

## Pharma: A Series That Won My Heart with Its First Episodes

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/farma-serial/

The series [*Pharma*](https://youtu.be/iXRyvIA0mQ8?si=ZQXS6sJB2-6Ts6Py) simply won my heart with its first two episodes. By the start of the third that feeling had faltered a little, but it soon came back as I watched :)

The plot’s great virtue is how much it can hold: you get the family of Eydelshteyn’s terminally ill character, who raps, and gangster cliques of every calibre, and nods to *Brother* (*Brat*, 1997) and to Balabanov in general, and a woman official stewing in her own personal cauldron of hell, and already 4 (at the very least) love interests among the characters. The main thing is for the show’s brisk rhythm not to flag, for the humour not to tip over into cringe, and for a couple of the storylines not to get lost by the finale.

And I do wonder how many more times Mark Eydelshteyn will land the part of a guy with a soft spot for strippers (in [*Anora*](https://youtu.be/BUtvdzMxw3U?si=KpuFlLc-SlfABGwO), which is about to reach our cinemas, his character has a romance with a girl in the same line of work).

## Wolfs: When the Wolves Are Fed and the Sheep Are Safe

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/odinokie-volki-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-09-29 (29 September 2024)
Work: “Wolfs” is a 2024 film directed by Jon Watts.
Tags: comedy, crime
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/odinokie-volki-2024/

The film **Wolfs** (released in Russia as *Odinokie volki*, “Lone Wolves”) is a case of, as the Russian saying goes, “the wolves are fed and the sheep are safe” — both in its plot and in terms of its artistic merits.

This unpretentious comedy about a clash between two underworld fixers, in the shape of George Clooney and Brad Pitt, strikes an ironic tone from its very first shots. These cleaners, of a sort, to the criminal world are at first squeezed into the format of a chamber TV play set in a luxury suite, which makes their disagreements look pettier still. And then (in place of Chekhov’s gun on the wall) the duo is gatecrashed by the corpse of a clueless zoomer come back to life (played, no less superbly, by Austin Abrams).

And everything about their little night-time adventure is grotesque, hyperbole and exaggeration. The fixing industry proves far too small a world, with one nurse, one HR person and one Albanian gang between the two of them; the gap between the generations is drawn far too boldly, with our zoomer trying to process his feelings while the fixers hurry him along for information relevant to the job. That is why the humour works for any audience, and the all-too-rosy happy ending (our stern wolves let the lad go unharmed) is spoiled, if at all, only by a rushed final scene that pointedly leaves something unsaid. But, much as I dislike open endings, I’m still happy with the film.

In short, a great thing for an evening, whatever people say about it! If you like this kind of film, I have 2 more recommendations. First, Ilya Naishuller’s film [*Nobody*](https://youtu.be/bZOHmDYCo2I?si=U7jLBklli8ErVW3b), with Bob Odenkirk and no less criminal fun. Second, a Russian counterpart: the series [*Hello Again!*](https://youtu.be/c1E9atEi7mw?si=iDRjBvpeX20bi2J4) (the first 2 seasons). Merzlikin as the fixer, Vlasenko as the zoomer, pleasant humour and slices of Russian reality thrown in for free :)

---

## A Real Pain: An Unassuming but Insanely Talented Film

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/nastoyaschaya-bol-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-09-25 (25 September 2024); updated: 2025-01-10
Work: “A Real Pain” is a 2024 film directed by Jesse Eisenberg.
Tags: drama, tragicomedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/nastoyaschaya-bol-2024/

## 25 September 2024

A promising trailer for the new film [*A Real Pain*](https://youtu.be/b2et8Vpu7Ls?si=goC-lIRZG4KsYfY_): two brothers set off for Poland for their grandmother’s funeral and learn a lot about themselves and each other along the way.

It was written and directed by Jesse Eisenberg, with Emma Stone producing, and I follow everything these actors do with great interest! All the more so since the film has already won the award for best screenplay at Sundance, so we’re waiting for the premiere in November.

## 10 January 2025

I don’t know how your first day back at work went, but I, whatever that may mean, rounded mine off by watching Jesse Eisenberg’s *A Real Pain* with Kieran Culkin.

Just kidding: in fact I’d been waiting for the film [ever since the trailer](https://t.me/kino_voice/216). I’m always interested in what Eisenberg is doing, and after the Golden Globes I got a move on with watching it — I had to find out what it was that got Culkin past our own Yura Borisov :)

The upshot: I’m impressed. I can’t remember the last time I saw anything as well-knit, harmonious and densely packed as *A Real Pain*. Despite its modest hour-and-a-half running time, the film finds room for reflections on how subtle and complicated family ties are, for attempts to understand the phenomenon of collective grief/guilt, and for the search for a cultural identity that the characters were thrown out of before they were even born. That sounds fairly tragic, but the film is also rich in a life-affirming irony that lets it look at these serious themes without unnecessary drama.

Culkin and Eisenberg are a treasure all of their own. From the first minute you believe they are brothers, yet radical opposites. And the contrast the film sets up is not formulaic but credible, deep and realistic. You believe that people like this can exist, can be brothers and can turn up somewhere among us. Culkin’s award is thoroughly deserved, and I’m glad he got it. The only question is that his role is really more of a lead than a supporting one, but that’s a different problem.

And the costumes subtly underline how the brothers evolve over the course of their journey. In the first half of the film Eisenberg’s character favours a muted blue, and Culkin’s a rich burgundy. Next, the difference in their characters is spelled out for us: on Eisenberg everything is in an orderly check of the same shade (the character has a steady job, is married and is raising a child), while Culkin gets blurry, chaotic blotches of random shape (and, to avoid spoilers, the life he leads is pretty chaotic too). And in the film’s final minutes the two seem to have accepted each other, grown close again and traded a little of their best qualities — so Eisenberg is in the rich burgundy, and Culkin, by now, in the muted blue. It doesn’t leap out at you, which makes it all the more pleasing to spot — like the film as a whole: unassuming, but insanely talented.

---

## The Reader: Watch the Film and Read the Novel as a Set

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/chtets-2008/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-09-24 (24 September 2024)
Work: “The Reader” is a 2008 film directed by Stephen Daldry.
Tags: adaptation, drama, books, comparison
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/chtets-2008/

My reading chakra suddenly opened up, so recently I watched the film [*The Reader*](https://youtu.be/JA1J2WmFGUw?si=RnM7Qgw-vmnhfPE2) and read the book of the same name in a single day (it’s very short, a quick and easy read).

As ever, comparing one with the other would be out of place, but putting the two media together to get a fuller picture is definitely worth doing. The film lacks the chain of cause and effect laid out in the text, and the novel lacks the captivating charm that Kate Winslet and David Kross create on screen. So watching and reading them as a set is just the thing. The still and the quote from the novel’s afterword both say as much.

## Final Trailer for Gladiator II: A Sequel 24 Years After the First Film

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/finalnyy-treyler-gladiator-2/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-09-23 (23 September 2024)
Work: “Gladiator II” is a work  Ridley Scott.
Tags: announcements, historical, blockbuster
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/finalnyy-treyler-gladiator-2/

The second and final [trailer for *Gladiator II*](https://youtu.be/Ts0N8swyWFI?si=pLjFir7fbpfglfrV) is out, so for the next 2 minutes you are officially allowed to think about the Roman Empire!

The scale of it all is, of course, impressive in every sense, given that the production stood idle for 4 months mid-shoot because of the actors’ strikes, and that the director, who has come back for a second film 24 years after the first came out, turns 87 this year. The film opens internationally as early as November.

---

## Love is Evil: An Intimate Dramedy with No Moralising but a Cheap Soundtrack

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/lyubov-zla-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-09-22 (22 September 2024)
Work: “Love is Evil” is a 2024 film directed by Gayk Asatryan, Denis Gulyar.
Tags: Russian cinema, dramedy, rom-com
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/lyubov-zla-2024/

On Saturday evening I found myself craving what they call a guilty pleasure. I watched [*Love is Evil*](https://youtu.be/Qfw-URjc06k?si=4DPxvw-k16aaKLG8) (*Lyubov zla*), with Nikita Kologrivy and Katerina Kovalchuk. Let me break it down into pros and cons:

👆An intimate atmosphere and a compact plot about a young woman who has lost her fiancé but found a friendly burglar in her flat instead.
👆Good humour (a few jokes aside) and the pleasant effect of a dramedy that doesn’t moralise.
👆Interesting work from the principal cast: Kologrivy and Kovalchuk really do look great together, as do Sychev and Ardova as the heroine’s parents. And, by the way, the hero develops noticeably over the course of the story.

👇The soundtrack. Not only does it not suit the mood of the story, it sounds cheap as well. By all appearances, they skimped on it.
👇Fairly weak work from the supporting cast. The scenes with the heroine’s girlfriends caused me great suffering.
👇Nikita Kologrivy’s character jokes that he doesn’t bite. Jokes that play on actors’ biographies are fun, but not when they concern violence against other people that actually happened.

## Kombinatsiya: A Band’s Story Told from Behind the Scenes

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kombinatsiya-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-09-14 (14 September 2024); updated: 2024-10-26
Work: “Kombinatsiya” is a 2024 series directed by Nikita Vlasov.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, music
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/kombinatsiya-serial/

## 14 September 2024

In [*Kombinatsiya*](https://youtu.be/F4R5Et6LW9w?si=yU3aIVrIbDV7kMa7) (“Combination”), the series about the producer of a cult girl band of the late Soviet years, a lot didn’t work, as my colleagues write. But what surprised me most was a fault in one particular mechanism.

They try to sell us the friendship between Tanya and Alyona, the band’s singers, through exactly the same mechanism that *The Boy’s Word* used with Maratik and Palto (“Coat”), right down to the physical resemblance. Dark-haired Tanya is, like Maratik, a street tough and a tearaway who turns out, unexpectedly, to come from a comfortable and, by late-Soviet standards, thoroughly petit-bourgeois family, while fair-haired Alyona is simply Andrey-Palto as he is when the story begins: for all things good (and musical) and against all things bad. And so they meet, fast-forward their way from hate to love and find a noble friend in each other, which we are meant to gather from a run of scenes in which they trade barbs and knowledge (of life or of books, it doesn’t matter) and show the odd flash of female solidarity. It’s the very idyll of Palto and Maratik, who practised their push-ups, their English and their singing of “Sedaya noch” (“Grey Night”, the Laskovy May hit) and chased it all down with borscht.

And as a device for showing a budding friendship it’s a really good one: it brings out the standout traits of both heroes (or both heroines) and helps the viewer warm to them and get attached. The two young women’s performances as a duo are first-rate as well, especially Elizaveta Bazykina’s — she is a sheer pleasure to watch, honestly! But for me, a wholesale repeat of the mechanics used on another series’ characters instantly severs my emotional connection to what’s happening on screen and kills the suspense. And in their place comes the uncanny valley effect (and sadness that things should have fallen out this way).

## 20 September 2024

By the third episode of *Kombinatsiya* (a very touching one that also fires you up to go and achieve things), I finally understood why I do like the show after all.

As a viewer with a background in producing, I’m grateful that at last we are being shown not the story of the singers, who were hired to be the faces and sing lyrics written for them to music written for them. Instead we’re told the story of the producer who runs the whole thing and, just a little, of the composer who drives it all creatively. These are the people without whose work the band really wouldn’t have existed, the concerts wouldn’t have been put on and Moscow wouldn’t have been conquered. In reality, of course, they were and remain off camera, but how nice it is, if only in a fictional reimagining, to look at a band’s story from that very behind-the-scenes side, where Shishinin has to cut a deal with everyone and Okorokov has to write the music.

Of course, bands come in all kinds, and sometimes the singers are a band’s authors and masterminds, but *Kombinatsiya* is a different case, and the story’s priorities are, quite rightly, different too. And where we have, say, the wonderful series *King & Jester*, about frontmen who doubled as the band’s founders, there ought to be a good series about a band with a different background as well. Thank you, *Kombinatsiya*, for that!

## 26 September 2024

The new, fourth episode of *Kombinatsiya* has nowhere near enough of my favourite character — the composer Vitaly Okorokov, played by Vladimir Kanukhin. To my mind he is the subtlest and deepest character of them all, and his every appearance on screen is well judged and well placed.

On that note, I recommend my Kinopoisk colleagues’ [interview](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/4009440/) with the actor — it’s the most pleasant and calming interview I’ve ever read, bar none!

## 26 October 2024

The finale of *Kombinatsiya* certainly makes the series noticeably more of a mixed bag than it had been all along anyway. Behind the grand story of the band’s rebirth after Apina’s departure, the stories of the individual members (except, perhaps, Tatyana Ivanova’s) get lost even further — and Shishinin’s most of all, with its sad end.

The last episode, sadly, fell victim to the curse of so many final episodes of Russian shows: it turned into a quick montage of resolutions, one for each storyline. Down the list: Apina’s solo career — launched; Ivanova’s crisis — over; Shishinin’s bender — finished; the new line-up — recruited; the murder — committed. On the plus side, there’s a minimum of the music-video scenes that used to stand in for dialogue, and plot development, and a good deal else. But this was exactly where there wasn’t enough time to talk things through, and that, of course, is a noticeable imbalance.

**\*️⃣** But in the end the series did its job all the same: it gave me a little of what I call “angry energy”, when you want to follow the hero and barge through any obstacle; some aesthetics, because it really does look beautiful; and additions to my playlist, and for that I’m grateful.

---

If you’ve always wondered where podcasts come from, I highly recommend giving it a read :)
