## Yuryev’s Island: The Magic of Cinema in Action

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/ostrov-yureva-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-08-25 (25 August 2024)
Work: “Ostrov Yuryeva” is a 2024 film directed by Aleksandr Barshak.
Tags: Russian cinema, festivals, road movie
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/ostrov-yureva-2024/

The magic of cinema in action

I’m talking about [*Yuryev’s Island*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/5451180/) (*Ostrov Yuryeva*): I managed to catch it at its premiere screening at the Budem Zhit (“We Shall Live”) film festival, and it was, honestly, an unusually pleasant experience. The plot: a Muscovite with no initiative to speak of, having just celebrated his 32nd birthday, suddenly becomes fixated on the idea that in a past life he was the sailor Yuryev, who very nearly discovered a new island but died without ever recording the discovery. The hero sets off for Vladivostok by train (yes, it’s a road movie), meets a *gopnik* (a street tough) there, and from then on the two pals are inseparable on the road to their discovery.

Despite having no budget whatsoever (before the screening the filmmakers told us they had spent 5 years shooting it practically for food), the film is very interesting. What comes to the fore is solid craftsmanship, and that is where the sense of magic comes from. Everything is simply done the way it should be, and it works: the actors are convincing, the script, for all its utmost realism, is resourceful and generous with unexpected turns, and the direction never leans on the viewer.

Take the way it reflects the best traditions of Soviet cinema of the Stagnation era: a hero locked in his inner world and running away from his problems, an inability to make up one’s mind about anything, reproachful but loving women (I sensed this while watching, rushed off to rewatch my Kinopoisk colleagues’ [video essay](https://youtu.be/1aDB1TksfUU?si=VzWODF2mUNkMlRVX) about the era, and had it confirmed).

Or the Gospel motifs: at one point in the film the hero preaches a sermon to fishermen from a boat, becoming an out-and-out Christ figure.

And then — this matters especially to me — part of the action takes place in Vladivostok, where our filmmakers (for reasons unknown to me) seldom venture, though they should. I’ve long wanted to visit the city, and that is exactly where I plan to spend my holiday!

As for you, if you spot it in cinemas or at one-off screenings somewhere, do go.

---

## Morozko: The Opening Credits as the Quintessence of the Story

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/morozko-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-08-14 (14 August 2024)
Work: “Morozko” is a 2024 series directed by Yulia Lysova.
Tags: series, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/morozko-serial/

Back to credits again, by the way. I want to tell you about what I think is the best Russian series of the first half of 2024: [*Morozko*.](https://youtu.be/OXVxBLnxk50?si=3l6Kr99P34ORrUh3)

I’ll begin with the series’ opening credits themselves, because they are, to my mind, the quintessence of the story. Hypnotic in every way, from their rhythm and frenzied collage style to the sound of the music behind them, they seem to herald each of the series’ distinctive features. *Morozko* is:

- A plot based on the true story of the series’ creator, Yulia Lysova — the credits use real photographs, letters and drawings. Yulia, by the way, [wrote](https://t.me/jlisova/1202) about how it all came together on her channel, where there’s a great deal of interesting stuff about the series in general!

- Incredible (seriously, you won’t be bored) plot twists. Everything hurtles, races and now and then glints with neon, like the elements in the credits.

- A sense of authenticity. You can feel that behind every element of the story there is a personal experience, a trauma or a memory, which Aglaya Tarasova and Nikita Efremov convey brilliantly.

- Form and content in harmony: in the first episode, for example, the heroine says that photographs are all she has left of her family, and straight away we see a selection of them in the cool format of the credits

In short, these credits have everything just as in life: something flashed past before you had time to appreciate it, and you regret that, while something else stuck in your memory for good, though at the time it didn’t seem special. About 30 per cent of my love for *Morozko* is down to them :)

---

## The Episode-by-Episode Podcast on Games 80: From Launch to Finale

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/poseriynyy-podkast-igry/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-08-04 (4 August 2024); updated: 2024-09-17
Work: “Games 80” is a work  Evgeniy Stychkin.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/poseriynyy-podkast-igry/

## 4 August 2024

I don’t write about work here all that often (not as often as I’d like). But today is a special case: under my supervision as producer, an episode-by-episode podcast has launched for the series [*Games 80*,](https://music.yandex.ru/album/32566883) about the organising of the 1980 Olympics. And here is a short list of reasons to listen to it, with some inside details mixed in:

- Launching a podcast on the very same day as the series is an Olympic Games to organise in its own right :) On big studio projects it’s not unusual for episodes to be re-edited, for the decision on how many episodes come out at launch to change, for technical lags and other such treats. And so that nobody would guess any of it, we re-edited the first episode 3 times :)

- Got it on already? Listen closely to the opening jingle: unlike in our other podcasts, the music in the episode-by-episode ones is always closely tied to the subject under discussion. You can hear this same tune in one of the first scenes of the first episode of *Games 80*.

- The disclaimer that the hosts watch the episodes no further ahead than the viewers do is the plain truth. What’s more, at the time of recording nobody on the team knew how the characters’ stories would end. So there is 0% play-acting in the podcast about *Games 80*! Only sincere film criticism

## 17 September 2024

The episode-by-episode podcast [*Games 80*](https://music.yandex.ru/album/32566883), which I produced, has come to an end (I confess I love it even a little more than the series itself :)). I spent 3 months working on it (in my head, even longer), and here are my favourite moments:

- In the final episode the hosts come out with a simply brilliant idea: that Igor is a kind of Forrest Gump of the 1980 Olympics era. And it’s true! He saw Brezhnev, and Vysotsky (the Soviet bard and actor) too, he even ended up in Afghanistan — he got to feel all the good and bad symbols of the era for himself, so to speak.

- Alexandra Remizova told a great story about her cameo as Alla Granina (read: Pugacheva, the Soviet pop diva). It turns out she could have had a different role, a bigger and more visible one, but then the show would have been left without its showrunner’s oversight, which is unacceptable.

- Until about episode 7 I thought I was seeing the actress Maria Karpova for the first time and ought to remember her. It turns out she transforms so brilliantly from one show to the next that, having watched the series [*I Know Who Killed You*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/series/5331465/), where Maria has a prominent role as an investigator, I didn’t recognise her in *Games 80*! By the way, Grigory Vernik didn’t recognise Maria straight away on set either, and he tells the story hilariously in [episode 4](https://music.yandex.ru/album/32566883/track/130352481) :)

- From the inside we knew how the plot of the series would end, but not exactly how it would be presented visually. I was terribly glad when I saw the funny wedding photo of Igor and Irina — it really livened up the finale and made the standard happy ending a little more unexpected.

---

## She’s So Cool: Fun, Wild, Absurd, Fresh

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/ona-takaya-klassnaya-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-07-30 (30 July 2024); updated: 2024-08-19
Work: “She’s So Cool” is a 2024 series directed by Alexander Domogarov Jr..
Tags: series, Russian cinema, comedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/ona-takaya-klassnaya-serial/

## 30 July 2024

But the main thing that brightened up my Monday evening was a [live stream](https://vk.com/kionru?w=wall-203493283_54660) with a screening of the first episode of ***She’s So Cool*** (*Ona takaya klassnaya*), where Lev Zulkarnaev, Denis Prytkov and the screenwriter Kirill Dyshlovoy were on hand to comment.

The moment I saw the post about the stream I dropped episode 7 of *House of the Dragon* (honestly!), and I don’t regret it: the atmosphere was unique — do take a look at my screenshot collage. I learned some wonderful details:

- The *slovo patsana* (“a lad’s word of honour”) that Denis’s character gives was thought up before the phrase became iconic thanks to the series of the same name (*The Boy’s Word*, the 2023 Russian hit series). Life itself brought that line to life!

- The screenwriter was on set for every single shift, and in film that is a great rarity. Perhaps that’s one of the reasons the pilot (like, I hope, the series as a whole) came out so alive

- The script was born of a chance observation in a café: a boy having a lesson with his tutor kept getting quite charmingly distracted by a host of more interesting things around him, and announcing it loudly to the whole café

- Lev’s character (according to the actor) is a lot like Myshkin from Dostoevsky’s novel *The Idiot*. +1 reason to definitely watch the series

In short, if you’re getting ready to watch (I am), be sure to watch the stream with the guys, you’ll get a huge kick out of it — luckily, it has been [saved](https://vk.com/kionru?w=wall-203493283_54660) in full by our colleagues at Kion, a Russian streaming service (thank you to them for that!)

## 19 August 2024

The series *She’s So Cool* is over, but it has left a great many cool moments in my heart! I’ve put together my favourite stills:

**\*️⃣** Katya (whose old man is a nutcase with a shotgun) and Batya (“the Old Man”, who is actually Egor) in a fort made of bedsheets, discussing a future that never came to be. My one regret about the series is that Katya never did become part of this story — she and Batya would have made a lovely couple. I hope the guys meet Katya on the way back, and that this time she makes a different decision. By the way, Maria Gerasimenko, the actress who played Katya, is simply out of this world: whenever she appears on screen she outshines everyone, no question

**\*️⃣** The trashing of the porn studio amid its fairy-tale sets and the final demolition of the (fourth) wall. A wonderful note to end the series on: fun, wild, absurd, fresh — what more could you want?

**\*️⃣** The funny porn producer, angry at everything and everyone but trying very hard to stay unflappable. He’s an antihero and a caricature, of course, but he did stir a drop of professional, producer-to-producer solidarity in me.

**\*️⃣** The guys reciting in chorus, “What am I going to do I’ve got no money at all put that away what are you doing my mum’s in the next room oh god yes”. Now that is some kind of performance poetry!

**\*️⃣** Denis Prytkov’s character with a Chinese café in the background. That’s the second cool series with him in it to end in a Chinese café! (yes, I mean *Dropper*, «Капельник»). I think I know what I’ll be expecting from the finale of the next story he’s in :)

---

## The Restoration of the Udarnik Cinema: Why It Matters

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/rekonstruktsiya-kinoteatra-udarnik/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-07-28 (28 July 2024); updated: 2025-03-30
Tags: film history, Moscow, notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/rekonstruktsiya-kinoteatra-udarnik/

## 28 July 2024

How lovely to see that the Udarnik cinema (a historic Moscow cinema) is genuinely being renovated as a cinema (judging by the signs on the hoarding), and not as a shopping centre housed in a Soviet building! I can’t wait — it stood derelict for so many years.

Why does it matter? I’ve put together a couple of facts:

- The Udarnik was the first cinema built specifically for showing sound films

- It was at the Udarnik that the first Moscow International Film Festival (back then still simply the Soviet Film Festival in Moscow) was held

- Its unique domed roof slid apart to reveal the sky, but only once: on the cinema’s first day of operation in 1931 (then the mechanism jammed, and the roof never opened again). I’d like to believe that after the restoration it will be opened many more times.

## 30 March 2025

I’m still [following](https://t.me/kino_voice/150) the restoration of the Udarnik, and still rejoicing.

Some interesting infographics have appeared, and even renders showing what everything will look like. The revamped Udarnik will have lots of screens, a bookshop, a café and, as far as I understand, the famous domed roof in working (at last!) order.

The renovation will go on until the end of 2027, so in 2028 we’ll surely be able to pick up a couple of tickets for a screening there and wander round a building that’s practically a hundred years old (construction of the [Udarnik](https://t.me/kino_voice/150) first began in 1928).

---

## Clean: The Story Finds Its Spine in Episode Three

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/chistye-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-07-26 (26 July 2024)
Work: “Clean” is a 2024 series directed by Nikolay Khomeriki.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, drama, historical
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/chistye-serial/

I’m still watching *Clean* («Чистые») — as you [remember](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/festival-pilot-2024-izbrannoe/), I’m waiting to find out what the finale is going to shock me with. And, evidently as a reward for my research stamina, a press box themed around the series has landed on my doorstep from Wink (a Russian streaming service)! I’ll unbox it in a video circle (a round Telegram video message); drop a 👀 if you’d like a look inside.

It was a questionable move to show us Mark Eydelshteyn, Rinal Mukhametov and Viktoria Isakova in the first episodes and then, very quickly, get rid of them entirely (or almost entirely). But the sacrifice was not in vain: from episode three the story gains something of a spine, some intrigue and the right kind of tension, and it becomes a real pleasure to follow.

It is odd, though, that a series with such ambitions (and well-founded ones, as is clear by episodes 4–5) opened with a slideshow of fine actors that was gorgeous to look at, not especially substantial, and nothing more. As if nobody quite believed that anyone would watch without a pretty line-up in the shop window (and the scandalous “erotic thriller” promo)?

Oh, we will — the plot has well and truly taken off; you just have to stick with it long enough to get there.

## House of the Dragon: Seasons Two and Three, Episode by Episode

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/dom-drakona-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-07-16 (16 July 2024); updated: 2026-08-10
Work: “House of the Dragon” is a 2022 series directed by Clare Kilner, Geeta Vasant Patel.
Tags: series, HBO, fantasy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/dom-drakona-serial/

## 16 July 2024

As gripping and tense (in a good way) as the fourth episode of *House of the Dragon* was, the fifth came out every bit as incoherent and empty, wrecking all the narrative momentum the season had been building until then.

The only thing I enjoyed watching was Daemon slowly losing his mind while one-eyed Aemond takes over his spot as “the wild one who’s fun to follow”. Except that in episode five even he was boring to follow. To say nothing of Alicent’s attempts to get through to that sulker Cole, or to the council in its all-male entirety (Rhaenyra has the same problem, but at least she has Mysaria now).

## 24 July 2024

A couple of words about episode 6 of *House of the Dragon*.

The stale rhythm of the last episode has been livened up a little, but still not enough for a situation called “the season ends in 2 episodes”. Sad as it is to admit, the storyline of Daemon’s chats with his own conscience has become, for me, that very spot in the series where you feel the urge to speed up playback or skip ahead. I expect this synchronised suffering of hero and audience to be rewarded with a triply impressive payoff (and in the meantime I’m consoling myself with memes).

Alicent, as was to be expected, has reaped exactly what she sowed. But her dismissal was far less epic than the business with Larys Strong: he and Aemond delivered the best exchange of the whole episode, if not the season. I thoroughly enjoyed watching this high-speed about-face in mid-air, at which Aemond proved even slicker than Larys himself, and that takes some doing. All that’s left is to look forward to the revenge of the humiliated and insulted Larys.

Rhaenyra’s entire role this season, meanwhile, seems to be mirrored in the scene of a knight’s (failed) attempt to tame a dragon. Rhaenyra stands off to one side and watches, mostly in silence. But the slap she deals a bore of a courtier and the “gifts” sent to King’s Landing bring back the days of the Rhaenyra who could mouth off to noble ladies and break up Daemon’s stand-off with Otto Hightower by flying in on a dragon. I hope that’s the heroine we’ll be watching for the rest of the season.

P.S. Before I had even watched episode 6, I learned from a post by colleagues that it would contain a certain scene Russian streaming services would have to cut. Deep down I was hoping it would finally be Daemon with Daemon in Daemon’s hallucinations :) But I spent the whole episode eyeing every pair of characters with suspicion. Lady Jeyne Arryn and Rhaena? Okay, I’m ready. Daemon and Viserys? Go on then, they’re hallucinations, we’ve seen all sorts in there already. But the show’s makers outdid my imagination: I didn’t see it coming, respect.

## 30 July 2024

Episode seven of *House of the Dragon* is, at last, lively, eventful and spectacular (we are heading for the season finale, after all).

The episode’s chief virtue, of course, is its wealth of meme-ready moments. From the stream of Targaryens of varying degrees of purity arriving at the Blacks’ castle (the shot got a decent round of [jokes](https://t.me/FBChu/40714) in the wake of [Durov’s post](https://t.me/durov/339) about his sperm donation) to Daemon suddenly seeing a goat in the castle corridors (obviously both as his own reflection and as a reminder of Blackwood, the scapegoat he executed relatively undeservedly). And life, of course, teaches Aemond nothing, so he has once again run up against the fact that Vhagar cannot be controlled. I hope his careless driving won’t kill any more of Rhaenyra’s children.

A feature that is staking a claim to regular status this season, which I can only welcome: “The Most Epic Mid-Jump About-Face”. This time we’re admiring young Lord Tully, who didn’t just outplay Daemon but literally destroyed him morally, because the self-proclaimed king consort could never have imagined such a thing.

And the sulker of episode seven (no, Criston Cole took no part in the action), Alicent, simply walked off into the woods, so I’m already bracing myself for hallucinations like Daemon’s in the castle. Still, this shift in the balance between the two heroines towards the end of the season looks very harmonious: Rhaenyra began this season feeble (and has gained in resolve, not without Mysaria’s help); Alicent will (very probably) end it every bit as broken.

By the way, what was that moment with Mysaria in the last episode for, if in this one everything carries on as though nothing had happened? Of course, I don’t worry about their relationship any more than I do about my own, but I’d like to see it continued :)

## 31 July 2024

That said, it would be criminal to pass over how gorgeously Alicent’s flight into the woods is shot: simply an advert for a new Dior fragrance, nothing less.

## 6 August 2024

**The finale of season two of *House of the Dragon*!**

Experience had taught me to go in with fairly lowered expectations. Perhaps that was for the best, because the episode left me with a very pleasant impression: it is still pieces being moved into position, but with painstakingly worked-out surprises, intrigues and set-ups for new storylines. Something of a breath of fresh air after such a stuffy-ish season.

What freshened this episode up, of course, was every scene in Essos. Watching the Lannister and Admiral Lohar fight in a puddle of mud, I had a very pleasant feeling of being back in the *Game of Thrones* universe (it sounds very strange, I know, but that is where my associations went). We were shown two worlds crossing paths, fresh faces and customs, and the comic surprise of the admiral being a woman (and one with quite the tastes, too), and she was the one who caught our Lannister (who had come to hash things out with serious men) off guard.

Remember how I hoped that our long-suffering vigil over Daemon’s hallucinations would pay off with something super epic? Well, it did! More than unexpectedly, Daemon was granted a brief recap of 8 seasons of *Game of Thrones*, attained enlightenment and grasped his place in the universe. The insert was so sudden, so unlike the rest of the series even in its visual style, that at first I couldn’t believe my eyes. Nevertheless, *HotD* has taken a big step towards Winter, war and the other horrors that the descendants of these characters will face.

The suffering caused by Daemon’s storyline is over, and the suffering caused by Rhaena’s storyline has begun :) Her handful of scenes in this episode bored me more than Daemon’s entire storyline did all season. But such, it seems, is the road to a dragon (or a mountain wyrm, if some breakdowns are to be believed): I can only hope that Rhaenyra’s children stay in one piece and that the dragon finally ends up in the right hands (and that we never see this running around the hills again).

Finally, the regular feature for the episode’s outstanding dialogue goes to Rhaenyra and Alicent, who has come to her senses after her mini-retreat. Rhaenyra, with the authority of someone who has already tried to negotiate and has compromised her own moral principles more than once, as good as declares: “you’re no sister of mine any more”. Both as a viewer and in terms of the drama, I get it; too high a price has already been paid for Alicent’s intransigence: Rhaenys killed, Jace mortally offended, the lives of the false Targaryen bastards sacrificed (and riff-raff like Ulf let into the castle). It reminded me of [one of the episodes](https://music.yandex.ru/album/6820951/track/107996163) of our episode-by-episode marathon *V predydushchikh seriyakh* (“Previously On”) on the first season of *HotD*. The hosts there reckoned that Rhaenyra and Alicent would surely have come to terms. Now we have been shown that, sadly, they twice failed to. And failing to come to terms is an outcome too, and a resolution for a season.

## 11 August 2024

What’s the secret of the *House of the Dragon* opening titles? *(a post with sound)*

These [titles](https://youtu.be/9Dk3OOgXlzo?si=bqS6cSBqkbh5NBOa) are a bonus in their own right to the plot of season 2. In them the whole history of House Targaryen is embroidered, as it were, on a tapestry (which is also a nod to the fact that Helaena, with her gift of foresight, is often shown to us at her needlework, and her embroideries surely foretell something too).

By the way, compare the titles of the first episode with those of the last and you’ll see which plot details have been added (from the execution of the ratcatchers to the funeral procession with the beheaded infant). And here is what’s going on in the screenshots with the Targaryens’ history, in the order of my screenshots:

- The Doom of Valyria: a natural cataclysm that wiped out a great many dragons and every dragon-owning family except the Targaryens. Hence their chosen status and unique power over dragons by the time *HotD* begins. In the embroidery you can make out the silhouettes of a volcanic eruption and of falling dragons.

- Aegon the Conqueror crushes the Lannisters and the Gardeners (yes, he crushed the latter so thoroughly that we never even heard their name in either series): look closely at the shields of the fallen warriors and you can see the Lion and the Hand, elements of the coats of arms of the subjugated houses.

- The death of Maegor the Cruel: nobody knows for certain whether the Iron Throne killed this Targaryen or he chose to take his own life, but as a picture of what power does to a person it is telling

- The fourth image is familiar to us from the first season: the very council at which Viserys, not Rhaenys, was chosen as heir to the throne (and how calm and nice everything could have been)

## 3 July 2026

Two episodes in, the new season of [*House of the Dragon*](https://t.me/kino_voice/170) looks packed.

And although its opening scenes give no such impression at all, it quickly makes amends. That familiar feeling of “hang on just a little longer, it’s about to kick off”, which we had more than our fill of over the first two seasons, quickly gives way to “whoa, this as well?”. Ideally, of course, the rhythm of the action would be evened out somehow, but maybe it really is a strategy.

Don’t get me wrong, but at the start of the season the secondary characters’ storylines were a bit of a nuisance. Even for the second season they looked like fairly recent arrivals, and at the start of the third they leave you mildly baffled: is this really what we’ve all gathered for? Then again, let me try once more to rationalise this on the showrunners’ behalf: if it’s a plan to lull us into a false sense of security before a run of sharp twists, it worked a treat (apart from the fact that for the first half of the opening episode I was almost physically fighting the urge to stop watching).

## 11 July 2026

As for the original [*House of the Dragon*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1620), so far it is a pleasure, albeit with some very unoriginal ideas.

To put the phrase “heavy is the cap of Monomakh” (the Russian equivalent of “heavy is the head that wears the crown”) on screen, the series has slowed its pace considerably, all but locking the episode’s action within the four walls of the royal castle. It turns out that the long-awaited “after” of Rhaenyra taking the throne instantly turns into “all that talk, and for this?”.

I was amused by the neatly condensed chain of searches for the state treasury, or at least for the nobleman in charge of it. Anyone who has had the good fortune to work somewhere even remotely corporate knows the situation: the project is old, more than one team has come and gone on it, and then comes the moment when the successors discover to their horror that there is no documentation and no staff who hold the information either.

Same with Rhaenyra: she got no onboarding and no welcome pack, nothing but worries and rats.

## 23 July 2026

A few notes as I watch [*House of the Dragon*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1635)

- Sulkers don’t change. Especially if they’re knights. Especially if it’s Criston Cole. As a result, the storylines that form around him are predictable (because of the stupidity of what goes on), and their outcome comes as a surprise only to the characters whose lot it is to witness it all, not to the viewer.

- Psychological rebirths do Targaryens good. Especially one-eyed ones. Especially when there’s a witch with a powerful moral compass close by. One of the most interesting storylines right now is unfolding around Aemond Targaryen. He is also at the centre of a heap of conspiracy theories (right up to the idea that he could have become the leader of the White Walkers who appeared to Daemon in a vision at the end of the second season). None of these theories is very convincing, but they are telling as a symptom of the audience’s interest in the character.

- Had the history of the Targaryens gone a little differently, perhaps their totem animal would have been cats rather than dragons. Either way, thank you, episode five, for that sweet detail.

- New characters who arrive with a rich context and a properly scripted personality from the off are great. Ormund Hightower is the prime proof of that (unlike certain characters whose only reason for taking up screen time is an inferiority complex about not having a dragon). On the whole, by the middle of the third season you start to feel something forgotten since *Game of Thrones*, the sense of a three-dimensional, densely populated world, and that is a pleasure.

## 10 August 2026

And actually, the season 3 finale of [*House of the Dragon*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1652) is greatness.

If we’re dealing in comparisons with *Game of Thrones*, it is at least on the same level, if not better. We were shown everything:

- a magnificent battle scene (with the horrors of war in detail)
- attempts at wise diplomacy (which, as in life, nobody appreciated)
- the despair of a queen as the only real hostage of power
- comedy on the edge of madness (does the cry “I’m alive, imbecile” ring any bells?)

The way this episode spans genres is truly admirable. The writers have laid on a whole array of emotional rides, brilliant performances from at least 3 actors (in my subjective opinion, the ones who shone here were the actors playing Rhaenyra, Gwayne and Aegon) and an extremely brisk pace (those who watched the season know that far from every episode can be praised for that). In short, watching the season for this episode alone is more than worth it; as a resolution before a two-year break it is wonderful in every sense.

---

## Inside Out 2: The Device Remains, but No New Meaning Has Grown Around It

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/golovolomka-2-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-07-09 (9 July 2024)
Work: “Inside Out 2” is a 2024 film directed by Kelsey Mann.
Tags: animation
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/golovolomka-2-2024/

I’ve watched the second *Inside Out*. An unpopular opinion is coming (not a rarity for me, though usually it leans the positive way), but first, some praise.

It’s cool that they not only kept the trick of having all these emotions coexist but added new ones too. Anxiety, of course, is ferociously like the real thing — the revulsion she stirred up was quite palpable. The jokes are genuinely funny and original. And it’s nice that the seriousness of the problems the film touches on has grown up along with Riley: we’re shown a panic attack here, no less.

But it is still predictable and boring. It is extremely hard (for me personally) to empathise with a dazzlingly white, healthy, well-socialised teenage girl from a two-parent, stable, comfortably-off family living in a developed country. She goes through adolescence without any outside shocks that would make watching her emotions and moral ideals in particular especially valuable (they are still valuable and important, as any emotions are, but they have no cinematic spark). She gets no more and no less traumatic experience than any standard teenager. Actually no, less — in the finale she makes the team of the best hockey players (and what goes on in the heads of the girls who didn’t make it??)

And what goes on in the heads of orphans? And what goes on in the heads of teenagers with chronic illnesses? And how do Joy and Anxiety share the console when a teenager’s relatives die? And how is Anger kept in check in those for whom dyeing a strand of hair red isn’t enough to be accepted?

Possible answers to questions like these are what I’d have liked to be turning over after watching an expensive, long-awaited sequel to a story built on a very original formal device. But the device remains, and no new meaning has grown around it.

---

## Uncle Alex: Nods to Soviet Classics and a Stunning Cast

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/dyadya-lyosha-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-07-04 (4 July 2024); updated: 2024-12-16
Work: “Uncle Alex” is a 2024 series directed by Dmitriy Nevzorov.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, dramedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/dyadya-lyosha-serial/

## 4 July 2024

Here’s a recommendation for these sweltering days — with the same sunny and, in a good way, predictable mood as any summer month.

For our mid-year [round-up](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/4009624/) I wrote a few words about the series [*Uncle Alex*](https://youtu.be/sMC-Iw0I-Eg?si=CxA1jYbJ-p6blShE) (*Dyadya Lyosha*):

> Imagine Yuri Detochkin from *Beware of the Car!* (the 1966 Soviet comedy) turning up as the hero of Zhora Kryzhovnikov’s short film
[*The Curse*,](https://youtu.be/4XqwA8WxEn8?si=gUdOMuHnKPNh9tEq)
>  where auditions for the role of Robin Hood are under way. That is exactly the feeling you get watching *Uncle Alex*. Charming and light (cheaply melodramatic in places, but that really is forgivable), the series was made to remind us of the true meaning of the word “dramedy”. Here Tribuntsev is an orphanage janitor who steals from the rich of the town of Rybinsk to make life better for the orphans.
>
> *Uncle Alex* stands out for two things: its nods to Soviet classics, done with taste and humour (from *Beware of the Car!* to *Office Romance*), and a stunning cast in which young and old alike (in terms of acting experience, that is) nail their roles 100%. And Timofey Tribuntsev is the real driving force of this story. It’s no surprise (though always a joy) to see how good he is at playing little men with a touch of devilry of their own.

The only condition for watching this series is to look kindly on what you see (otherwise all the magic will dissolve in a haze of minor flaws and genre conventions).

## 16 December 2024

My colleagues at Kinopoisk (Russia’s largest film database, media and streaming service), other writers and I have [put together a list of the best Russian series of 2024](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/4010426/)! My favourite, *Give a Show!*, didn’t make it in, but I’ll write about it separately :)

And in the round-up, [for the second time this year](https://t.me/kino_voice/139) (such, apparently, is my lot), I praised *Uncle Alex*, an unassuming story about an orphanage janitor, thief and benefactor in the person of Timofey Tribuntsev. Since the series has made both of the year’s round-ups, that’s a mark of quality of sorts!

## Pilot 2024: The Picks I Will Definitely Be Watching

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/festival-pilot-2024-izbrannoe/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-06-27 (27 June 2024)
Tags: series, festivals, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/festival-pilot-2024-izbrannoe/

I haven’t finished talking about Pilot (the Russian series festival in Ivanovo), and for it to let go of me, I need to finish :) Here are my picks — the ones I’ll definitely be watching.

***The Big Lie Theory***

A lovely story about the harm and the good that lying does — over the pilot episode there was definitely an equal measure of each. If *She’s So Cool* hadn’t been in competition, this series would have had all my sympathies. The characters here have to lie to make money, lie to save a relationship (or build a new one) — in short, lie so that, paradoxically enough, their conscience doesn’t torment them. All of it is, naturally, extremely funny and inventively done, so I sincerely recommend it — this, to my mind, is the best script at Pilot.

[*Give a Show!*](https://youtu.be/3sRut1jp4Ww?si=ZRl8LRYJAnL1o2NF)

As I wrote for our piece on Kinopoisk, “a fairground attraction of unprecedented vileness”. Not because the series is bad, but because Miloš Biković is all too convincing as a king of the pop stage who has lost his moral compass (and drags everyone he meets down to the bottom with him). But I’ll be following this series for the stories of Pasha Goncharov (Oleg Savostyuk from *Three Minutes of Silence* is terrific in the part) and Vera (Anastasia Krasovskaya). They were side by side on screen for just a couple of seconds, and in a flashback at that, but I already badly want to watch the two of them as a couple.

As for Pasha’s storyline, my empathy and sense of recognition there are off the scale. Everything it shows about his internship on a big talk show, working 25/8 for 0 roubles, is the plain truth about the life of journalists starting out. So it’s out of a personal stake in this story that I’m guaranteed to watch the series.

***[Clean](https://youtu.be/ozXtd9w4wg8?si=wIiRqmT09H_P4Gcn)***

Billed as an erotic thriller, the series ended up catching my interest for something else entirely. I have a modest hunch that it will be like *The Boy’s Word*, only with heroines in place of heroes. We are introduced to several young women on the brink, in the most troubled circumstances imaginable, and from there they have options for how to live with it (or die). And by the finale we’ll definitely be sitting there open-mouthed, much as we were when we watched what became of Palto, Adidas and Maratik in the finale of the aforementioned *Boy’s Word*. And that is how I’ll be watching *Clean*: as something that might unexpectedly floor me.

***[El Ruso](https://youtu.be/TUicVx3jLSw?si=oZ0lgoaXQbF7-vKg)*** (this is not a trailer but a rather interesting commentary on the series by its makers; I recommend it)

I’m not yet entirely sure whether I’ll watch the series in earnest, but since I’m in doubt, it needs writing about. I’m drawn by an idea straight out of Balabanov (the director of *Brother*) — “the city as an evil force” — which is here, and by its declaration that human dialogue matters against all odds. And from its very first shots the series mesmerised me with the printed cottons of the Old Believers’ costumes and with a tension akin to what you feel watching a horror film: everything seems fine, colourful and bright, yet there’s a chill in the air. So it’s enticing.

---

## Plevako: An Overload of Sensation and Meaning in the First Episode

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/plevako-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-06-21 (21 June 2024)
Work: “Plevako” is a 2024 series directed by Anna Matison.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, historical, mystery
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/plevako-serial/

I’ve watched *Plevako* — a historical detective story of sorts, with Sergey Bezrukov as an outstanding lawyer with an elevated level of justice in his system.

It seems this really was an opening-night series, because it’s unclear how to rate it. On the one hand, there is a very detailed and beautiful recreation of the period, biopic ambitions, a great team of actors. On the other, it is cut exactly like a trailer, and five minutes in you start thinking, “So when does the film start?” — and, worst of all, there is a disproportionate pile-up of different issues.

In a single episode Plevako manages to bury his mother, discuss the problems of women’s rights in the 19th century with his sister, fall in love with another man’s wife (even though his own wife is shown fairly often and in a flattering light) and, naturally, win a court case in style. Clearly this is a mix of serialised and episodic storytelling, but in the first episode the set-ups for motifs that will stretch across the whole series create such a crush that the result is an overload of both sensation and meaning.

And then the pilot leaves it completely unclear what audience this is for: the story is as classic as they come, made for background viewing, but you can’t watch it with your back to the screen — there are too many small details; the theme of feminism is there, but a sophisticated audience won’t find anything new in it; there are gestures towards mystery and suspense, but not enough to glue fans of those genres to their screens. It will be interesting to keep an eye on it once the whole series is out.

---

## Baby Reindeer and I Know Who Killed You: The Same Device, but with a Difference

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/ya-znayu-kto-tebya-ubil-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-05-08 (8 May 2024); updated: 2024-05-22
Work: “I Know Who Killed You” is a 2024 series.
Tags: series, analysis, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/ya-znayu-kto-tebya-ubil-serial/

## 8 May 2024

if you haven’t watched *Baby Reindeer* yet, here’s a great option for the long weekend!

I devoured the whole series in one go myself, in 4 hours, and, you know, it wasn’t hard: *Baby Reindeer* may show social anxieties that we seem to have already had our fill of in the public sphere, but it does it so *differently* that there are simply no words

fed up with typical stories about abuse and its victims? watch *Baby Reindeer*
worn out by samey attempts at a psychological thriller? watch *Baby Reindeer*
can’t manage to feel for the characters of social-issue series because they’re unconvincing? once again, watch *Baby Reindeer*

[and instead of a voice message, this time please watch the Short](https://youtube.com/shorts/YQFDZhMeuEg?si=vMnQfbsD_hosAKCQ) that I (exercising my rights as the producer of these very Shorts :)) recorded for our channel at Kinopoisk (Russia’s largest film database, media and streaming service).

## 22 May 2024

**A new trend in series**

In my last post I talked about **Baby Reindeer**, one of the most powerful viewing experiences of the year, not least because of the way the storytelling changes halfway through the series. It turns out that the point is not the woman stalking the protagonist at all, but an episode of abuse he went through before that, so *Baby Reindeer* does a complete genre U-turn and goes from a dramedy that is awkward in places to a thriller about the human psyche at various stages of suppression (it gets a special episode for this, twice as long as the others).

“Phew, that’s a heavy series,” I thought, and went straight on to watch **I Know Who Killed You** (*Ya znayu, kto tebya ubil*)

And what do you think? That’s right: bang in the middle, the series turns round and goes from an action-packed spectacle of chases, shoot-outs, scandals and intrigues to a classic drama about a little orphan girl piecing together, bit by bit, the life she never got to have with a family lost for ever.

The device is the same, but there is, of course, a difference:

In *Baby Reindeer* the mid-series break masterfully deepens the themes, adds a whole heap of new aspects to our understanding of the characters and heightens the intrigue

In *I Know Who Killed You*, to my mind, the change of genre worked against it: it dragged a change of protagonist along with it (and there was I, having come to watch Yatsenko for all 8 episodes), and it moved the tragedy from the plane of Hamlet’s “to be or not to be” down to the scale of Reels about living through psychological trauma as a teenager, which to an adult (one who hasn’t yet taken on the role of a teenager’s parent) seems not all that interesting

## 22 May 2024

That said! *I Know Who Killed You* has a heap of undeniable pluses

1) Alexander Yatsenko’s inimitable, simply outstanding and whatever-else-you-like performance: he is just magnificent in this series — touching and cruel, cowardly and resolute, funny and indifferent, empathetic and manipulative, with the viewer too — he simply left us no chance of not admiring him

2) A reference to *Cargo 200* that is as unexpected as it is welcome: Agniya Kuznetsova moves into Yatsenko’s house as a live-in nanny, announces on the doorstep that nobody is to try anything with her because *her fiancé is serving in the paratroopers*, and then spends 6 episodes watching *a bloke with unprocessed trauma keep a kidnapped little girl in a locked flat*. She was only a step away from turning fully into the blind old woman with her signature line “we’ve got flies”…
That said, I’m terribly glad that in the universe of this series the fiancé of Kuznetsova’s character apparently came back alive and well, because in the second half of the series she is already a happy mother of many children.

3) The vibe of the series of my childhood, in particular *And Still, I Love…*: a proper soap opera with betrayals, lies and broken lives and, above all, a change of heroine in the middle of the series
Don’t judge me too harshly, that was a thing too, and I liked it more than *Daddy’s Daughters* and *Ranetki* put together

---

## Tantsuy, Seledka!: Why It Is Our Aftersun

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/tantsuy-seledka-solntse-moe/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-04-26 (26 April 2024)
Work: “Rock It, Stone Fish!” is a work  Alexandra Lupashko.
Tags: Russian cinema, comparison, notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/tantsuy-seledka-solntse-moe/

**Why [*Tantsuy, Seledka!*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/5134592/) (“Dance, Seledka!”) is our [*Aftersun*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/4948281/)** (released in Russia as *Solntse moyo*)

(no, not only because the heroine spends the whole film rummaging through her father’s cassette tapes :))

here’s a checklist of similarities:

- a daughter’s last journey with her father: it doesn’t matter that in the case of *Seledka* this is literally a final journey, to the morgue, while in *Aftersun* it is a trip to a holiday resort. What matters is that these are the last hours in her father’s company

- the soundtrack: no, really, never mind that “Under Pressure” has turned into Malikov’s “Do zavtra” (“Till Tomorrow”) in our version; the sense of irreparable loss (but with hope for the future) is the same

- the carpet: in *Aftersun* that sad carpet, bought on holiday in Turkey, comes down to the heroine as her inheritance, while in *Seledka* the corpse of Pavel Maykov’s character gets wrapped in a traditional Soviet carpet, all but taken down off the wall

- the tapes, and my traditional passion for finding references to *Assa* in everything: we all remember that *Aftersun* is built on rewatching tapes, whereas in *Tantsuy, Seledka!* the heroine is given a cassette that her father recorded specially for her, and he even says a few words of introduction at the start of the tape. If the day has turned out really lousy, he says, you have to dance. We don’t hear what comes next on the cassette (that’s just how the plot goes), but for some reason I’m sure it would have had the song “Chudesnaya strana” (“Wonderful Country”) on it, the one Drubich’s character sat sadly through in someone else’s coat at the end of *Assa*. Otherwise, what else is there to listen to when things get really grim and you have to dance

---

## An Award for the Krupnym Planom Podcast: What Else Happened at the Ceremony

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/nagrada-podkast-krupnym-planom/

Published: 2024-04-15 (15 April 2024); updated: 2024-04-16

picked up the best podcast statuette for *Krupnym planom* («Крупным планом», “In Close-Up”) and on behalf of our whole team! Almost like an Oscar, only it’s Gagarin

- the local “could have come but didn’t” segment, in the form of “this category was supposed to be announced by Nikita Kologrivy, but he didn’t show up. Kirkorov (the pop superstar) couldn’t find the door either, unfortunately”

a great experience.

## Blockbuster History in the New Russia: Non-Fiction About Film That Reads Like a Thriller

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/istoriya-rossiyskogo-blokbastera-kniga/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-04-14 (14 April 2024); updated: 2024-07-20
Work: “Blockbuster History in the New Russia: Movies, Memory, and Patriotism” is a 2012 book by Stephen M. Norris.
Tags: books, Russian cinema, film history
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/istoriya-rossiyskogo-blokbastera-kniga/

## 14 April 2024

if you feel like reading some non-fiction about Russian cinema and working out how on earth we ended up like this, but want it to feel like a thriller, a horror film and a historical epic all at once, open the book *Blockbuster History in the New Russia* («История российского блокбастера» in Russian) right now (for example, [on Bookmate)](https://bookmate.ru/books/JZRDAukA)

don’t fall for the title — it is a very crafty one, posing as a run-of-the-mill, niche and possibly tedious study by an American Slavist while actually concealing a rich, lively text with answers to almost every question about Russia and Russians (it is not for nothing that ever since Lenin we have had “cinema is the most important of the arts”; a century on, Norris’s book proves it)

I haven’t read much of it yet, but I already have the distinct feeling that this is the most important thing to have come out in Russian about Russian cinema in recent times — besides, an outsider’s view of a cultural phenomenon always has its advantages over analysis from within

*barely tore myself away from the book to write this post, so, as you can imagine, I’m off to read on*

## 20 July 2024

Remember that [book](https://t.me/kino_voice/107) I recommended? I’ve finished it and [recommended](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/4009627/) it all over again :) The most interesting things I took away:

I finally understood what Nikita Mikhalkov is all about (in a good sense, as far as that is possible)

In the USSR art mattered more than life — that is, it was a way of escaping an unpleasant reality. Under modern capitalism life (that is, the material side) has turned out to matter more than art. Hence we have what we have

We owe the rise of Russian cinema in general (and of the blockbuster in particular) to Alexei Balabanov and his *Brother* duology (I knew it, I knew it, I knew it)

## Listay Vpravo Podcast: Season Four Has Started

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/listay-vpravo-chetvertyy-sezon/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-03-15 (15 March 2024)
Tags: books, notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/listay-vpravo-chetvertyy-sezon/

And the podcast *Listay vpravo* («Листай вправо», “Swipe Right”), which I’ve been producing for over a year now, kicked off its 4th season yesterday!

Behind us are 31 episodes, 62 (actually more) books, several versions of the cover (few people remember, but it didn’t always have that great big red hand on it), thousands of subscribers on streaming platforms and plenty more figures and details, which are what my work on the project is made of. And ahead there is even more of everything (well, all right, we’ll try not to change the cover again).

Somehow, without planning it, we landed the first [episode, on eating behaviour](https://music.yandex.ru/album/24773100/track/123749543), right on Maslenitsa (the Russian pancake week that sees off winter). And a good thing too: we have our professional holiday, all around there’s a pagan holiday, and the conversation is about love for the world around us and for ourselves, as in most of our episodes. It seems that love is exactly what makes *Listay vpravo* worth listening to (and making).

## Elena Voytovich on the Screenplay of Inye: How Fantasy Works

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/elena-voytovich-o-stsenarii-inykh/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-01-30 (30 January 2024)
Work: “Inye” is a work  Vladimir Raksha.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, fantasy, interview
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/elena-voytovich-o-stsenarii-inykh/

**The most interesting cases often turn up where you have a cool head and a rational approach :)**

Here, for example, we talked to the wonderful Elena Voytovich, the screenwriter of *Inye* («Иные», “The Others”), the new series from Kinopoisk (Russia’s largest film database, media and streaming service), about creating a fantasy plot, a fantasy world, fantasy characters and fantasy circumstances (and everything else with “fantasy” stuck on the front).

*The thing here is that I’m no ardent* *fan of the fantasy genre, but that made it all the easier to peer into how the genre is built with a researcher’s curiosity and work out how it functions at all, where it comes from and where it leads; I recommend it to anyone who wants a look inside the machinery of TV series*.

So if you happen to have always wanted to understand how a 21st-century screenwriter can picture the events of the 1930s with precision, or create characters who not only belong to their own time but also make sense to today’s viewers, [listen to the episode](https://music.yandex.ru/album/14629532/track/121630330)! You’ll find out where in Moscow fantasy gets written best (and, I think, other genres too) and whether a writer can have favourites among the characters :)

## Bodyguards: A Simple, Fun Series, Just Like Crisps

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/telokhraniteli-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-01-24 (24 January 2024); updated: 2025-02-28
Work: “Bodyguards” is a 2023 series directed by Konstantin Smirnov, Vladimir Bitokov.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, comedy, sitcom
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/telokhraniteli-serial/

## 24 January 2024

And first up in this column is the series [*Bodyguards*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/series/5059049/?utm_referrer=www.kinopoisk.ru): simple and fun, but sometimes a bit of a guilty pleasure, just like... crisps!

Yes, yes, those very crisps, preferably onion or cheese flavour, that you don’t always allow yourself and that not everyone approves of, but that you sometimes crave so badly of an evening, sitting on the sofa…

Crisps are constant in their shape and, as a rule, their ingredients, and that’s what makes them wonderful: we always know what to expect from them :) In the same way, each episode of *Bodyguards* ostensibly tells the story of three (simple-as-crisps) guys — the stories come out with different shades of meaning, but they reliably bring pleasure and jolt you out of the monotony of routine life

All you have to do is allow yourself an episode of *Bodyguards* of an evening, never mind that it’s a standard sitcom, that it isn’t the most nourishing thing for a viewer’s development (just like crisps for the stomach, let’s be honest) and that its humour is sometimes a long way from decent — and suddenly your mood lifts and you even feel like watching some serious cinema with Oscar nominations

Then again, which edible thing serious cinema should be compared to is a question for future posts in this column!
*In the meantime, please tell me your favourite crisp flavour in the comments*.

## 28 February 2025

A pleasant way to spend a Friday evening: watching the second season of my beloved [*Bodyguards*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/series/5059049/).

Compared with the first season, the follow-up not only doesn’t sag, it even pushes the whole concept a touch closer to the absolute. The adventures of Yurok, Tucha (“Storm Cloud”) and Yashcher (“Lizard”) are now even dafter, their lawyer boss is an even bigger snob, to the point of absurdity, and Sergei Makovetsky’s character is still a wily old grandad on a level no one else can reach. I was laughing heartily by the second minute.

It’s a particular pleasure to watch the supporting characters (who here are mostly the women) come into their own. Yurok is now in a relationship with the lawyer’s daughter, that same lawyer’s young wife has become a force in her own right and even a catalyst for some of the storylines, and the team has gained a new character, a secretary. In short, the series has improved on every count.

---

## Express: The Fleeting Accidents That Fill the Film with Life

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/ekspress-2022/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-01-22 (22 January 2024)
Work: “Express” is a 2022 film directed by Ruslan Bratov.
Tags: Russian cinema, comedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/ekspress-2022/

In the voice message I talk a little about the gripping opening shots of films/series — and here’s an unusual case where the film’s poster is its first and most gripping shot, and one with interesting camerawork to boot: so the device is doubled, it turns out :)

By the way, another thing I liked about *Express* («Экспресс») is the abundance of fleeting accidents, of people and even hedgehogs that flit across the screen, of situations that come out of nowhere and seem to have nothing to do with the plot. For one thing, this really fills the film with life; for another, it reminds me of the films of Sergei Solovyov, which I love: there too, every now and then, some odd book with a biography of Paul I will burst into the frame, or an improvisation about Gagarin, or anything else unexpected but arresting, the kind of thing that leaves you with a genuine impression of the film for a long time.

## 2023 Work Round-Up: Year of Birth, Cicadas and Listay vpravo

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/rabochie-itogi-2023/

Published: 2024-01-14 (14 January 2024)
Tags: notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/rabochie-itogi-2023/

the start of a new year seems like the best time to look back at everything done towards the end of the last one and gather it in one place — and that’s how this post is going to be laid out

- yet again I talked about my beloved *Year of Birth* (*God rozhdeniya*) in the episode of *Krupnym planom* (“Close-Up”, the film podcast) about the hidden masterpieces of 2023 — this time without spoilers, so if you haven’t seen it yet and are in two minds, [listen from the timecode](https://youtu.be/Jh7Uc5rlRRQ?si=5cc1813RkvIvungo&amp;t=2620) (the rest of the episode is very interesting too, by the way)

- I also wrote about *Year of Birth* in our editors’ picks — if you happen to prefer reading, [it’s all for you :)](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/4008861/)

- the podcast [*Cicadas*](https://music.yandex.ru/album/27907695) (*Tsikady*) has wrapped up — my work as a producer! in 8 episodes we went through, episode by episode, a briskly paced and visually beautiful series about the tragic consequences of parental irresponsibility — and all of it in interviews with the makers and with expert psychologists: my favourite episodes are the ones [with Sonya Arzhanykh and Grisha Vernik,](https://music.yandex.ru/album/27907695/track/119714003) and with [cinematographer Gleb Filatov](https://music.yandex.ru/album/27907695/track/119091107) — they’re interesting to listen to even if you haven’t watched the series, that’s how upbeat they are and how much love of film they charge you with (and the photo above, by the way, is from the special screening of the final episode and the discussion with the team that I moderated — a suitably symbolic end to the project)

- and right on the eve of New Year the 3rd season of the book podcast [*Listay vpravo*](https://music.yandex.ru/album/24773100) («Листай вправо», “Swipe Right”) came to an end — over 2023 we went through 30 pairs of books, that is, 60 of them (and with the passing mentions of other texts, there’s no counting them)! there are now episodes for every taste, but my own taste by the end of the year was, of course, on the side of [the episode on *The Boy’s Word* (*Slovo patsana*, the book behind the 2023 Russian hit series) and *Multiki* (“Cartoons”, Mikhail Elizarov’s novel)](https://music.yandex.ru/album/24773100/track/120384753) — a great companion to watching the series and a widening of its context through artistic interpretation, the very pair of books I decided to read in full myself :)

## The Irony of Fate: Myagkov’s Character Now Has an Excuse

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/ironiya-sudby-1976/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-01-10 (10 January 2024)
Work: “The Irony of Fate, or Enjoy Your Bath!” is a 1976 film directed by Eldar Ryazanov.
Tags: Soviet cinema, analysis, New Year, comedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/ironiya-sudby-1976/

since there’s no getting through the New Year holidays without *The Irony of Fate* (*Ironiya sudby*; sooner or later it pops up somewhere, even if it wasn’t in your plans), you might as well do some research on the film!

that’s how I ended up at Lev Karakhan’s 1978 article in *Iskusstvo kino* (“The Art of Cinema”, the Russian film journal), and found something interesting:

> We meet Zhenya Lukashin on the day before New Year. He is one of the inhabitants of a modern city of many millions, a panorama of which passes before us at the start of the film. He is “one of” for another reason too: in his standard-issue flat, in his New Year tree set up in the corner of the room, and indeed in his fiancée, we readily recognise the likeness of dozens, hundreds, thousands of identical flats, trees and fiancées. As soon becomes clear, however, “one of” is exactly what Lukashin has not yet become. He is only striving
> to be, trying to fit into the general order of city life. But he cannot. Something inside Lukashin resists his own aspirations and will not let him merge with that rigidly organised stream of people, divided into neat rivulets, which the filmmakers show on screen and in which everyone hurtles along what seems to be their own route but is in essence a standard, well-worn one.
>
> \<…>
>
> Myagkov’s Lukashin is incapable of adapting to the settled standards of modern urban life, yet he sees no other way out for himself either, nor does he look for one. And so he marks time, shifting from foot to foot in indecision, stuck in a position that is strange for this neatly ruled, “standard-issue” world: that of a man who is neither one thing nor the other. It is this very strangeness that gives Myagkov’s performance, and the film as a whole, its distinctive genre character, making the story of the hapless Lukashin now naively touching, now charmingly funny.
>
> \<…>
>
> Coming round after his accidental flight, no longer in Moscow but in Leningrad, in Nadya’s flat, Zhenya suddenly discovers that he can express himself openly, with nothing to constrain him any more. Although everything here would seem to be as before (the same standard-issue flat, the same tree, even the fiancée is in a sense the same: Nadya and her intended, Ippolit, are marrying less for love than out of necessity, because the time has come), there is also something in this situation that is, for Lukashin, fundamentally new. The situation is non-standard, and the relationship between Nadya and Zhenya, unexpectedly left alone with each other, takes shape outside anything prescribed or predetermined that weighs on a person, purely according to unwritten rules and laws that no one invented: as their hearts dictate. And this is where the barriers dividing two modern city dwellers come down, and come down literally overnight! Real love comes to them.

I left out of the quotation the points where I don’t quite agree with the author, but what he says about the distinctive kind of hero Myagkov plays is, I think, spot on: a year after *The Irony of Fate*, in *Office Romance* (*Sluzhebny roman*), Myagkov plays Novoseltsev, who is at first so afraid of his boss that he stammers and later falls headlong in love with that same boss, the only difference being that he didn’t have to end up in another city to find love in those very same atypical circumstances, outside the routine template. a curious type of hero it turned out to be!

so there: in my eyes Myagkov’s character from *The Irony of Fate* now has an excuse, and, while we’re at it, an interesting alternative version in an office setting.

---

## Radio Day: Not a New Year Film, but One for the New Year Spirit

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/den-radio-2008/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2023-12-31 (31 December 2023)
Work: “Radio Day” is a 2008 film directed by Dmitry Dyachenko.
Tags: Russian cinema, comedy, rewatch
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/den-radio-2008/

A quick pre-New Year recommendation for anyone who has lost (or perhaps never found) their New Year spirit.

I certainly hadn’t found mine, but on Friday I put [*Radio Day*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/402979/) («День радио») on in the background, a film I’ve seen close to a hundred times by now, and… it was the best decision! It isn’t a New Year film, of course, but the story of a fictional radio station and its irony about the daily grind of so-called “creatives” of every stripe work perfectly: for seeing yourself from the outside, for laughing at the absurd situations that crop up in any job, and simply for switching into a positive frame of mind (because, as the film’s Kak by Radio (“Sort-of Radio”) reminds us, there’s no such thing as a hopeless situation)

As a bonus, you get musical interludes with performances by all sorts of bands (just like on *Goluboy ogonyok*, the New Year TV variety show), including my beloved Mumiy Troll (the Russian rock band) — I’m attaching a still of them!

Happy ~~Radio Day~~ New Year in advance! :)

## The Giant Ants of Novosibirsk: A Graphic Novel That Puts You Off Your Guard

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/gigantskie-muravi-novosibirska-kniga/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2023-12-16 (16 December 2023)
Work: “The Giant Ants of Novosibirsk” is a 2023 book by Vitaly Terletsky, Evgenia Chashchina.
Tags: books, comics
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/gigantskie-muravi-novosibirska-kniga/

not only do I talk, I sometimes write too (and not only about films, but about books as well!)

for instance, my colleagues from Kinopoisk and Bookmate and I have summed up [the year in books](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/4008810/), and I cast my vote almost without a second thought for a graphic novel I had only just read (at the time the list was being put together), Vitaly Terletsky and Evgenia Chashchina’s *Gigantskie muravyi Novosibirska* (“The Giant Ants of Novosibirsk”):

> Stas, a jobless 22-year-old, tells his friends in minute detail about his childhood memories: the giant ants of Novosibirsk. The only trouble is that Stas comes from Kirov and has never been to Novosibirsk. Around this clash between memory and fact, the adventures of the Decembrist Muravyov-Apostol, love, sculptures of giant dinosaurs and the search for one’s own self flicker past in elegant chaos. And the protagonist, for his part, brings to mind Solovyov’s Bananan from *Assa*, dropped into the world of the film *Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind*.
>
> Cinematic and escapist, yet nowhere near as lightweight as it seems at first glance, Terletsky and Chashchina’s graphic novel puts you off your guard with its rainbow watercolours. And for a finale it offers a hard choice (but one that has gained in relevance over the last couple of years) between soul-saving but false memories and looking a hopeless reality in the face. And for the hero, it seems, the choice is obvious.

before settling on my recommendation for good, I also thought about Alexei Ivanov’s *Broneparokhody* (“Armoured Steamers”) — I sincerely recommend that book (which is also on our list!) every bit as much as *The Giant Ants*; it is without question among my top reading experiences of the year :)

but *Broneparokhody* lost out to *The Ants* on one subjective criterion of mine, code-named “my jaw dropped and I had to pick it up off the floor”.

every film and book (and piece of music, and \[insert as appropriate\]) that I’m prepared to remember as one of the best (of the year or of my life) has to give me roughly that feeling, otherwise the way to the podium is closed :) and my tastes are peculiar, so sometimes completely unpredictable things fit that subjective criterion — but that’s another story...

and in general I’ve been reading Terletsky for a long time, and I heartily recommend not only the new novel but also things that have stood the test of time (and of rereading), such as *Russkie obedinyayutsya s krokodilami i napadayut na Evropu* (“The Russians Join Forces with the Crocodiles and Attack Europe”) and *Padenie Yeltsina s mosta* (“Yeltsin Falls off a Bridge”) — here, it seems, the titles themselves are the best recommendation

---

## A Podcast About Cicadas: The Episode with Cinematographer Gleb Filatov

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/podkast-tsikady-gleb-filatov/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2023-11-18 (18 November 2023)
Work: “Cicadas” is a work  Evgeniy Stychkin.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, interview
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/podkast-tsikady-gleb-filatov/

For almost a month now we’ve been working on a podcast about a cool series from Kinopoisk (Russia’s largest film database, media and streaming service) called *Cicadas* («Цикады») :) I didn’t grasp its complex structure straight away, but once I did, I fell for it irrevocably!
And now, making the podcast with various people from the shoot, I notice that every one of them speaks so warmly about working on set, about their colleagues and about the story as a whole that this observation alone earns the series a huge advance of trust for all the episodes to come.

My favourite has been the episode with Gleb Filatov, the cinematographer of *Cicadas*. First, he is simply an incredibly sunny and positive person who, even while talking about the working process of the shoot, shared such a store of love for his craft and for life in general that I’ve already decided to come back to this episode in sad moments and listen again to part of the interview with Gleb :) Second, his feature debut was the film *The Bull*, and when I found that out, I first remembered how I had waited for that film, gone to see it at the cinema and come away hugely (and pleasantly) impressed — that was when I started following everything Yura Borisov does in film. And then, having remembered all that, I decided to rewatch *The Bull*! A 100% good decision, and this time I also took a close, appreciative look at the camera techniques similar to the ones Gleb talked about in the context of *Cicadas*.

In short, I recommend that everyone [listen to this interview,](https://music.yandex.ru/album/27907695/track/119091107?utm_medium=copy_link) even if you aren’t watching the series itself — just hearing what magical accidents happened during the shoot is inspiring and lifts your spirits :)

## Year of Birth: A Solovyov-Style Farce and an Ending Open to Many Readings

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/god-rozhdeniya-2023/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2023-11-14 (14 November 2023); updated: 2023-11-14
Work: “Year of Birth” is a 2023 film directed by Mikhail Mestetskiy.
Tags: Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/god-rozhdeniya-2023/

## 14 November 2023

yes, I’ve finally seen *Year of Birth* (*God rozhdeniya*)! I adore this kind of film: the kind where, during the second half, you simply switch off and pick your dropped jaw up off the floor, because you can’t even begin to guess how it will all end. Filipp is an absolute Bananan (the hero of Sergei Solovyov’s *Assa*) with his room of magical escapist artefacts, and the plot itself is fairly Solovyovian too, combining tawdry everyday life with an unimaginable farce from a parallel universe (by the way, the moment I saw Solovyov’s influence here, I instantly remembered the head of the boy Bananan in *2-Assa-2*, cut off from its owner and sewn onto a market trader selling sunflower seeds, so now there’s no unseeing the connection)

special props for the song “Allo, Marina”: joking aside, it’s literally our version of “I’m Just Ken”! getting people to go crazy over a song by ~~Ryan Gosling~~ Yura Borisov before they’ve even seen the film is a great move :) I, for one, fell for it — only Yandex Music knows how many times I’ve replayed it already (and I will again)

and overall, I simply very much recommend going to see the film: it’s almost universal, and everyone will be able to find something of their own in it, thanks to an accessible plot about the difficulties of unconditional love (why else would Eldar Kalimulin be the spitting image of Joseph Gordon-Levitt in *500 Days of Summer* here?) and an ending open to many readings: I counted 3 of them… but those are spoilers! So I’ll go through my readings of the ending in the voice message below

## 14 November 2023

A bonus post! (almost like [*Bonus-trek*](https://music.yandex.ru/album/14629532), “Bonus Track”, heh-heh)

do you know why the song “Allo, Marina” opens with the line “*I live without feeling my trousers under me*”? I’ve found an explanation :)

no, it’s not just an allusion to Mandelstam (whose poem begins “We live without feeling the country under us”).

when he tells Filipp the truth about Soplya, his father (formerly Kostolom, “Bonebreaker”) adds that he gave Soplya his own trousers so that he would have something to be buried in. And it is Kostolom who turns out to be the character who, after Soplya’s death, lives “without feeling his trousers under him”: he grows disillusioned with life and betrays his dream, his ideals and any creative ambitions. that would explain both this character’s bitterness towards his son and his disillusionment with life

I haven’t picked apart the rest of the lyrics, but if you have theories, leave them in the comments :)

---

## The Channel’s First Post: Cinema in Voice Messages and Texts

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/pervyy-post-kanala/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2023-05-18 (18 May 2023)
Tags: notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/pervyy-post-kanala/

Hi everyone! My name is Betsy, and I love conversations about film.

I did just that for a long time as a podcast producer at Kinopoisk (Russia’s largest film database, media and streaming service), and by now I can’t imagine myself without audio formats :) And this channel is an attempt to combine business with pleasure: analysis of the films I like, and a conversational format

Here I’ll talk about the most impressive films and series in voice messages (like podcasts, only very small ones), and as for everything else, I’ll write posts and add pictures, memes and round video messages! And, of course, share what’s going on in my life as a producer (and beyond). Let’s go!

---
